5\. CONCLUSION

Artificial neural network (ANN) techniques can enhance predicting capability of the model when mathematical or statistical methods are difficult to formulate and fails to predict with desired accuracy. In the present work, estimation of sorption efficiency using mathematical and analytical tools is involved because the physical phenomenon for removal of chromium (VI) by living cells of Bacillus cereus is complex one. The network is found to be working satisfactorily as seven neurons are selected in the hidden layer when mean square error starts decreasing. Learning and momentum parameters are set at 0.20 during the training phase. The network is trained till minimum root mean square error is observed. A root mean square error of 0.68 is observed at epoch number 23, 835, 76. The network is found to be working satisfactorily as absolute relative percentage error of 0.567 during training phase. Comparison between the model results and experimental data gives a high degree of correlation R² = 0.984 indicating that the model is able to predict the sorption efficiency with reasonable accuracy.

# Chapter 11

*   E. A. Olajubu  
    Obafemi Awolowo University, Nigeria
*   Gbemisola Ajayi  
    Obafemi Awolowo University, Nigeria
*   Isaiah Oke  
    Obafemi Awolowo University, Nigeria

    Obafemi Awolowo University, Nigeria

ABSTRACT

Rapid industrialization has contributed immensely to the discharge of heavy metals into receiving water bodies untreated. The quantity of heavy metals prediction in industrial wastewater is very essential before treatment so that the quantity is precisely removed. This article formulates, simulate and evaluate a predictive model that mimics electrochemical treatment of lead and cadmium ions present in paint industrial wastewater using artificial neural network. The predictive model was formulated using Fuzzy Logic toolbox in MATLAB and the simulation was done in the environment. The prediction of the model was evaluated by comparing the predicted quantity of lead ions and cadmium ions with the result of the experimental work in the laboratory. The article concludes that the developed prediction model demonstrated very high prediction accuracy in predicting the percentage of lead and cadmium ions present in paints wastewater.

INTRODUCTION

The accumulation of heavy metals in human environment is responsible for many of the global health challenges of today. This is because heavy metals are non-biodegradable and carcinogenic. The rapid increase in industrialization has brought about an enormous amount of wastewater which contain very high quantity of heavy metals as pollutants (Somsak et al., 2016; Wolfova et al., 2013). Heavy metals are highly toxic with density of about five times that of water and also can penetrate the human body through various ways such as ingestion, absorption, and dermal contact. The presence of these metals in the environment also affects other living organisms, for example the production and quality of crops, the quality of the atmosphere, aquatic animals’ health and the life of humans. Examples of heavy metals include but not limited to Lead, Zinc, Iron, Mercury, Cadmium and Arsenic metals. Among these metals, Lead and Cadmium are the most toxic, and they are readily available in the environment (Sardar et al., 2013; Singanan, 2011). Lead is a microelement that is naturally present in trace amount in all biological materials such as soil, water, plants and animals. It is one of the oldest metals known to man which is capable of causing an extensive environmental contamination and health problems in the world (Naja & Volesky, 2009). Lead when exposed to human body can cause damages to the vital organs of the body such as, kidney, brain, liver, bones, reproductive system, nervous system and gastrointestinal system (El-Wakil et al., 2014). The important sources of lead poisoning in the environment include Lead based paint, Lead pipes, Lead crystal, mining, refining, soldering, ceramics, lead acid batteries, jewelry making, volcanic activity, geochemical weathering, electronic waste, gasoline, and building materials (Tiwari et al., 2013). The source of Lead ions into the waterbody in Nigeria is from the proliferation of paint companies even in the rural areas (Onugbu et al., 2013; Mahre et al., 2007). Cadmium is a soft silvery white, slightly malleable and easily fusible metallic element that is found naturally in the earth crust. Cadmium is highly toxic at extremely low and high levels in man and animals. This is because of its ability to accumulate quickly. Cadmium is released from various sources such as electroplating, soldering, paints, weathering of rocks, waste incineration, batteries, television sets, ceramics, yellow pigments, photographic, insecticides, alloys of copper, fuel combustion, and agricultural products (Kabir et al., 2014). The effects of Cadmium poisoning in the environment can also lead to very serious damage health hazards. Like Lead, it could also lead to the kidney, renal failure, high blood pressure, bone demineralization and lung cancer because of its carcinogenic properties (Ismail et al., 2009; Järup, 2003).

The recent growth in industrial activities especially in the Paints industry in Nigeria is a possible treat to the health of Nigerians. This is because majority of the Paint industries in Nigeria are sited within residential areas with little or no regulation on how their effluences are discharged into the nearby streams or waterways. When these wastes find their way into the human system, through contaminated water, terminal illness such as cancer, kidney or liver diseases often ensue. It should be noted that there is some correlation between the increase in terminal diseases and the new industrial activities in Nigeria due to the release of their effluence, which are either partially or not treated at all (Olaoye & Oladeji, 2015; Egwuonwu et al., 2012; Onuegbu et al., 2013). These terminal diseases and associated illnesses impart natively on social-economic development of a nation. The affected individuals who are in their productive age have their man-hour withdrawn from national productivity and the cost of management of these diseases is detrimental to national development. So, the health of individuals in a nation contribute significantly to the development of the nation (Mathias et al., 2013). Health is wealth for individuals and the nation collectively (Odrakiewicz, 2012; Consolata, 2017). The concept of national development of a nation underscores an effective health delivery system which is strongly rooted in diseases prevention. Diseases prevention is an effective means of ensuring a healthy and productive society. To handle the aforementioned challenges, this study proposes an artificial neural network model that will be useful to predict the quantity of the heavy metal that are present in any wastewater before their removal. The proposed model mimicked the existing electrochemical process to predict the quantity of lead and cadmium ions that are present in industrial wastewater. This model will also be useful to aid the determination of the quantity of lead and cadmium ions present in the wastewater before the treatment of the effluence. This is with the aim of removing entirely pollutants from the wastewater which will ultimately minimizes societal health hazards. The proposed model will assist manufacturing companies to determine the quantity of heavy metals present in effluence, before experimental works are done in the laboratory to remove the metals. Also, it serves as a guiding tool for the Department or governmental agencies involved in assessing the degree of treatment of effluence from manufacturing companies before such water is discharged to water ways for human consuption. The next section presents existing work in this area. Section three then discusses our artificial neutral network model, while section four explains our data collection and management. The simulation result is presented in section six, while section seven concludes the paper.

RELATED WORKS

A number of works have been reported in the literature on the modeling of heavy metals from aqueous solution; however, the literature on modeling of the efficacy of electrochemical treatment process for predicting lead and cadmium ions in industrial wastewater is rare. Artificial Neural Network (ANN) has been adopted by various researchers in different areas of science and technology as an effective modeling tool to solve problems on pattern recognition and function approximation. Likewise, the ANN has been useful for identification, classification, control systems, and various wastewater treatment applications. It has also shown a lot of usefulness for controlling wastewater treatment plant, predicting the concentration of effluent parameters, effluent quality prediction, and n the evaluation of wastewater treatment plant performance (Rani and Govardhan, 2013). Yasin et al. (2014) developed an ANN model in hybrid with genetic algorithmic approach to optimize the removal of lead ions from aqueous solution using intercalated tartrate. A multilayer ANN back propagation with levenberg marquardt algorithm was used for training the network. The input parameters for the model included adsorbent dosage, time, pH, and initial lead ion concentration, while the output parameter was the removal of lead ions. The network with 5 neurons in the hidden layer was the best model with a coefficient of determination value of 0.99986. The optimized percentage efficiency of the removal of lead ions was at 98.7% with a pH solution of 4.5, adsorbent dosage of 0.054g, time of 11.8h, and lead ion concentration value of 10.0mg/l. Amouei et al. (2013) worked on the removal of cadmium ions from aqueous solutions of sunflower powder. The model was developed using bio-sorption kinetics and neural network with hidden neurons including bias. Contact time, and cadmium initial concentration was used as input variables and adsorbed pollutant was the output variable. The overall result showed that the best efficiency of cadmium removal by sunflower residues was obtained at a pH of 6, dose adsorbent of 1mg/l, and an initial concentration of cadmium of 60mg/l. The ANN was able to predict accurately the concentration of removal of cadmium ions. Arora and Srivastava (2010) proposed a model to predict the efficiency of the removal of cadmium (II) ions from aqueous solution using saraca indica leaf powder. A recurrent back propagation algorithm with levenberg marquardt algorithm was applied for training the network. The input parameters for the model included biomass dosage, cadmium (II) ions concentration, volume of the test solution, pH, while the output parameter is the efficiency removal of cadmium (II) ions. The optimum removal efficiency of cadmium (II) ions was achieved at 92.60% with an initial cadmium (II) ion concentration of 25mg/l, contact time of 40 minutes, volume of 200ml, and a pH of 6.5.

For Kardam et al. (2010), two-layer ANN model was adopted to predict the efficient removal of cadmium (II) ions from aqueous solution using shelled Moringa Oleifera Seed powder. Five input variables (biomass dosage, Cd (II) concentration, volume, pH, and time) were considered in this work. The optimum removal efficiency of cadmium (II) ions was achieved at 85.10%, with an initial cadmium (II) ion concentration of 25mg/l, contact time of 40 minutes, volume at 200ml, and a pH of 6.5. In Yetilmezsoy and Damirel (2008) a three-layered ANN model was developed to predict lead (II) ions removal from aqueous solution by antep pistachio shells. This work employed five input variables; adsorbent dosage, initial lead (II) ions concentration, initial pH, temperature, and contact time to predict the removal of lead (II) ions. The Levenberg Marquardat algorithm with a tangent sigmoid transfer function using 11 neurons in the hidden layer and a linear transfer function in the output layer was employed. The model result gave a correlation coefficient value of 0.936. In recent years, the application of ANN has been considered as an alternative approach in the determination of complex relationships between variables, because of its reliable, robust, and salient characteristics in capturing non-linear relationships between complex variables (Thambavani et al., 2014). ANN are massively interconnected networks in parallel of simple elements with hierarchical organizations which try to interact with the objects of the real world in the same way that biological nervous system does (Eduardo, 2002). The development of ANN computational techniques emerged from the desire to develop an artificial system that could perform multiple, complex and intelligent tasks similar to those performed by the human brain (Rene & Saidutta, 2008). The ANN can be adopted for two main categories of problems; data classification and variable prediction. In data classification problems, the ANN makes use of a specified algorithm to analyze data or patterns for similarities and then separates the data into a pre-defined class. In variable prediction problems, when given sufficient input variable information, the ANN will learn from the variables, so as to accurately predict the value of an output variable (Vyas et al., 2011). ANN consists of a simple interconnected processing element called neurons, which assists in modeling any non-linear process, through a set of unidirectional weighted connections (Nourani et al., 2013). The basic architecture of the ANN is composed of three layers; input layer, hidden layer and output layer (Madhloom, 2015)

The proposed model in this paper focuses on the application of ANN to predict the quantity of these ions in industrial wastewater. Unlike, several proposed models; the efficiency of the model is anchored on the electrochemical process it mimicked and this is embedded in the ANN model for prediction. This enhanced the prediction of ANN up to about 0.9999 as shown in our result.

MODEL DESIGN

The predictive model for lead and cadmium ions’ removal was formulated using ANN with the feed forward back propagation algorithm. The model components are the normal ANN three sub-layers, which are Input layer, Hidden layer and Output layer as shown in Figure 1.

Input layer: The input layer consists of five variables that serve as input to the system. These variables are Time (hr), Current (Am), Temperature (^o C), Dissolved Solid (Mg/L), and Lead/Cadmium initial concentration (Mg/L). Each of the inputs are assigned weights. The summation of the weighted inputs is passed through a transfer function and forwarded to the hidden layer. Weights are adaptive coefficients that determine the intensity of the input signal as registered by artificial neuron. The activation function, which is also as known as the transfer function(s) are squashing functions that limit the permissible amplitude range of the output signal to some finite value of \[0, 1\] or \[-1, 1\]. The most widely used activation functions include the threshold, piecewise-linear, tangent sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent activation function (Hajek, 2005). In this work, a tangent sigmoid transfer function was used between the input layer and the hidden layer as shown in Equation (1)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch011.m01](i/ch011.m01.svg) (1)

where v in equation (1) is the activation function inputs in the system.

Hidden Layer: The hidden layer is the collection of neurons which acts as intermediate layer between the input layer and the output layer. The output from the input layer was passed into the hidden layer in a forward direction. The presence of neurons in the hidden layer had an excellent effect on the global characteristics of the network and the training time following the practice in (Abdomaleki, 2013).

The number of neurons in the hidden layer was selected using trial and error approach and the most favorable number of neurons that was selected for the lead model was 16 while 11 neurons was selected for cadmium model. The neurons in the hidden were meant to layer perform two operations: one, the summation of the weighted inputs and the bias, which is passed through a transfer function. Two, the output produced from the hidden layer now becomes the input to the output layer. Biases are additional weights that are added to the network to make it learn the intended patterns better. In this work, a linear transfer function was used between the hidden layer and the output layer as shown in Equation (2)

y=f(x) (2)

where x is the input to the activation function.

Output Layer: The output layer consists of one variable which is the percentage (%) of Lead/Cadmium ions that is to be removed (%). The output of the network was compared with the output of the experimental data, and the error was propagated back into the network by adjusting the weights until the error in the network became minimal. The output layer presents the final output to the external environment.

DATA COLLECTION

Data on electrochemical treatment of paint wastewater were obtained from existing literature (Oke, 2006). The data consist of five input variables and one output variable for lead and cadmium. The data from existing literature were limited, in order to develop the predictive model, additional data were generated using interpolation method. The validity of the interpolated data for Lead and Cadmium was carried out using the analysis of variance with respect to the input and output variables. The result of the analysis showed that F values was less than F critical values, and the probability values, were greater than 0.05 at 95% confidence level. This indicates that there was no significant difference between the mean and standard deviation of the actual data and the generated data.

A total of 257 data sets were analyzed and used to predict the percentage of Lead and Cadmium pollutants to be removed from the paint wastewater. A portion of the data set that was used for developing the model is as presented in Table 1 for Lead and Cadmium respectively. The data sets were divided randomly into three divisions; training, validation and testing respectively. 60% of the data were used for training, 20% were used for validation, and 20% were used for testing. The training data were used to compute the network parameters and update the network weights, while the validation data were used to ensure that the network is generalizing and stop training before over fitting occurs. For the testing, data were used to evaluate the effectiveness of the network parameter.

DATA VALIDATION

The performance of the ANN model that is developed in this study was evaluated using the three different performance metrics: Total error (Err²), Mean absolute error (MAE), and Coefficient of determination (R²) to access the accuracy and reliability of the model.

Total Error: The sum of the square of errors between the calculated values and the observed values were obtained for the models as their total error. It was used to find the measurement of error between a set of estimates and the actual value. The lower the total error the higher the accuracy, validity, and good fitness of the method used (Turp et al., 2011). The total error was computed using equation (3):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch011.m02](i/ch011.m02.svg) (3)

Mean Absolute Error: This is the mean of the sum of the absolute value of the difference between the calculated values and the actual values obtained by the model. This showed the distribution of the prediction errors as well as the percentage of variability that can be explained by the model. It can be computed using equation (4):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch011.m03](i/ch011.m03.svg) (4)

Coefficient of Determination: This was interpreted as the proportion of expected data variation that can be explained by the obtained data. Higher values of the coefficient of determination indicate higher accuracy, validity and good fitness of the method (Oke, 2007). This was computed using equation (3):

Tools Used for Simulation

A feed forward ANN using back propagation algorithm was employed to develop the predictive model. The global architecture of an ANN model depends on the input parameters, number of neurons, selection of the best training algorithm and activation functions (Pandharipande and Deshmukh, 2013). The back-propagation algorithm is a supervised learning process that was used to influence the gradient descent algorithm to determine and adjust the weights between interconnected neurons in such a way that the error between the predicted output and the target output was minimal following the practice in Gardner and Dorling (1998).

Levenberg –Marquardt training algorithm was selected for training the network. It is one of the fastest methods for training moderate-sized feed forward neural network. It uses the second order derivatives of the mean squared error between the desired output and the actual output. It performs better than other methods and also converges faster (Ahangar et al., 2013). There are different transfer functions that can be used in the network, but the most widely used transfer function between the input layer and the hidden layer is the sigmoid transfer function; this transfer function was used to bring in the concept of non-linearity into the network. Thus, a linear transfer function was used between the hidden layer and the output layer, so as to generate a continuous valued target (Rene & Saidutta, 2008).

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The result of the performance metrics gave a total error value of 0.00034 and 0.00083 for lead and cadmium respectively and a mean absolute error value of 0.00243 and 0.00273 for Lead and Cadmium respectively. This showed that the prediction accuracy was very high, since the lower the error, the higher the prediction accuracy and validity of the model. A coefficient of determination value of 0.99999 and 0.99999 for Lead and Cadmium was obtained, which was high; and the higher the value, the higher the prediction accuracy and validity of the model. The data presented in Table 1 presents the relationship between experimental values and predicted values of Lead ions and Cadmium ions.

The foregoing result is consistent with the result of the experimental work of Oke (2006 & 2007). While the final output of the percentage of Lead ions removed from the laboratory research effort of Oke (2006 &2007) is 99.0700% that of the proposed model predicted the final output of the percentage of Lead ions to be removed to be 99.0685%. The result of the experimental work of Oke (2006 & 2007) revealed the final output of the percentage of cadmium ions removed to be 98.4800%, while the proposed model predicted the final output of the percentage of cadmium ions to be removed is 98.4822%. This shows the reliability of the proposed model in predicting the efficiency of Lead and Cadmium ions removal.

CONCLUSION

In this study, a three-layer feed forward ANN was employed to efficiently predict the quantity of Lead and Cadmium ions present in paint wastewater before the removal of the substance. The predicting model mimicked electrochemical treatment process. The model design consists of input layer, hidden layer and output layer; with 16 neurons in the hidden layer for the Lead model and 11 neurons in the hidden layer for the Cadmium model. To achieve the foregoing, the Levenberg-marquardt back propagation algorithm with tangent sigmoid (tansig) transfer function was introduced between the input layer and hidden layer, and the linear transfer function (purelin) between the hidden layer, and the output layer was then used for training the network. The findings from the present study revealed that the prediction of the proposed model in removing Lead and Cadmium pollutants present in paint wastewater gave a high prediction accuracy. Hence, the proposed model can be successfully employed to predict the quantity of heavy metal pollutants in industrial wastewater before the effluence is discharged to the waterways for human consumption.

# Chapter 12

*   Dipu Sarkar  
    National Institute of Technology, Nagaland, India
*   Joyanta Kumar Roy  
    MCKV Institute of Engineering, West Bengal, India

ABSTRACT

Issues related to power system voltage levels have become increasingly important issue during last two and half decades. In power networks, low voltage situations may result in the loss of stability, voltage collapse and eventually to cascading power outages. Large number of incidents of voltage collapse has been reported in different countries across the globe. A simple indicator that has the potential in real time, i.e. L indicator has been used to find voltage profile at different switching condition and simulated using ANN in network reconfiguration for the improvement of voltage stability. A method for improving voltage stability in a power network comprising of multiple lines and switches has been suggested in this chapter based on system reconfiguration approach. ANN based fast and efficient methodology has been developed to obtain the optimum switching combination to achieve best voltage stability. The proposed scheme has been tested on an IEEE 14-bus system.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Intelligent algorithms are algorithms with an element of artificial intelligence. They can decide their next course of action based on the current state of the system. The ability to take self-guided decisions is called heuristic, which comes from experience. Some algorithms follow human defined heuristics and some follow nature’s heuristics. Those following human defined heuristics are called Artificially Intelligent Algorithms, and those following nature‘s, are called Nature Inspired Algorithms. Hill-Climbing (HC), Depth First Search (DFS), Minimal Spanning Tree (MST), etc. are some of the artificially intelligent algorithms, while Genetic Algorithms (GA), Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) etc. are some naturally intelligent algorithms. The advantage of such algorithms is that they make use of human or natural intelligence to reach a solution in a short time preventing the investigator from taking exhaustive approaches.

The breakthrough of artificial intelligence in the electric power system which started in the mid-eighties has resulted in the development of numerous expert systems and knowledge-based system tools for solving various power system problems (Huneault, Rosu, Manoliu, & Galiana, 1994). Lot of works in the field of power system protection, distribution planning, design and management have been reported which utilized artificial intelligence. Over the last decade, a number of papers have been reported in the field of distributed automation using Hardware based systems and as well as various soft computational techniques (Warwick, Ekwue, Arthur & Aggarwal, 1997). The present discussion proposes the applications of ANN for optimal operation of a power system at highest voltage stability and minimum active and reactive power losses.

2\. OVERVIEW OF VOLTAGE STABILITY ISSUES IN GENERAL

Issues related to power system voltage levels have become increasingly important during last two and half decades. In power networks, low voltage situations may result in the loss of stability, voltage collapse and eventually to cascading power outages. Large number of incidents of voltage collapse has been reported in different countries across the globe (Taylor, 1994) & (Aboytes & Arroys, 1987).

It is a well-established fact that there is a strong relationship between real power transmission (MW) and rotor angle (δ), and reactive power transmission (MVAR) and the voltage (Chakrabarti & Mukhopadhyay, 1989) & (Aboytes & Arroys, 1987). In other words, the availability of MW is dictated by machine angle, which in turn is decided by the input to the prime mover. On the other hand, voltage magnitude is related to MVAR availability at that point of time. Voltage instability can be ascribed to lack of VAR support necessary to maintain the voltage profile within specified levels (Davidson, 1975) at certain load condition.

Voltage stability is concerned with maintaining ‘acceptable voltage levels’ all system buses under normal conditions as well as when the system is being subjected to a disturbance. The main causes of voltage instability are lack of reactive power resources, heavy loading and severe contingencies. During instability, voltage magnitude of some of the system buses decrease gradually and then rapidly to reach the collapse point (Aboytes & Arroys, 1987). The excess load on the transmission lines, large distance of the generating sources, and lack in local reactive compensation (Chakrabarti & Mukhopadhyay, 1989) are the also caused the voltage instability.

Some of the researchers have been developed a number of voltage stability indicators in the last two decades. Due to this fact, accurate preventive control actions can be taken easily with the help of voltage stability index. Voltage stability assessment can be done with the help of different indicators (L-index indicator, V-Q sensitivity indicator, Voltage Collapse Proximity Indicator (Warwick, Ekwue, Arthur, & Aggarwal, 1997), which involves numerous load flow solutions under both normal and abnormal operating conditions like outage of transmission lines, outage of some generating source etc.

Maintaining voltage stability and voltage levels at all important nodes in a large and heavily loaded power network are critical and challenging tasks for power engineers. A number of different approaches have been traditionally used for improvement of voltage stability. The improvement of voltage stability is achieved by incorporating additional hardware installation. These include i) shunt capacitor ii) tap-changing transformers iii) FACTS devices etc. at proper position at the transmission line and load side of a power network. Voltage Stability enhancement can be done using Network Reconfiguration Technique. The following sections give a brief idea of Network Reconfigure Technique.

3\. NETWORK RECONFIGURATION AND VOLTAGE STABILITY IMPROVEMENT

System reconfiguration means restructuring the power lines which connect various buses in a power system. Restructuring of specific lines leads to alternative system configurations. System reconfiguration can be accomplished by placing line interconnection switches into network. Opening and closing a switch connects or disconnects a line to the existing network. If there be N switches in a network, there will be 2N possible switching combinations. Reconfiguring of power network can also provide voltage level improvement and voltage stability improvement. Improving voltage stability by network reconfiguration involves study of switching options which enhances voltage stability under a given load and generation condition. The challenge in the proposed method however lies with the task to find the optimum switching pattern that would maximize the overall voltage stability of the system.

Manual Reconfiguration at an every operational period is a difficult task as the decision has to be based on operating load, optimized power loss, consideration of load ability and voltage stability. It is however imperative that for a large networks, manual reconfiguration is not feasible. The present work encompasses applications of Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to accomplish the task.

4\. CONCEPT OF MANUAL NETWORK RECONFIGURATION TECHNIQUE THROUGH A MODIFIED IEEE 8- BUS SYSTEM

In a power system, reconfiguration process is used to reroute the power by changing the status of sectionalizing switches and altering the topological structure under both normal and abnormal conditions. The reconfiguration of a power system is performed to achieve objectives, such as power loss minimization, voltage stability improvement in some event.

In the present section, a 8 bus system is considered. The standard system has been modified by adding two lines. In the network 15 numbers of lines are present. For network reconfigurations, sectionalizing switches are placed at each of the line in series. Opening and closing switch connect and disconnect a line from the existing network. In the present network there are 16 switches. The total possible configuration will be 2^(16). Each possible configuration is not feasible at practical point of view, while some configuration may have better performance in some event such as fault, over loading condition etc.

In the next section, the effect of reconfiguration for a standard system has been simulated. The performances of some arbitrary feasible configuration have been studied guided by two important parameters voltage stability and over all active and reactive power losses of the system.

5\. EFFECT OF RECONFIGURATION ON VOLTAGE STABILITY, ACTIVE AND REACTIVE POWER LOSS OF THE OVERALL SYSTEM

The primary objectives of power suppliers are continuous, economical and quality power supply to customer. In other words, quick restoration of supply is desirable after the occurrence of fault maintaining voltage stability and voltage levels at all important nodes in a large and heavily loaded Power network. A number of different approaches have been reported in papers for improvement of voltage stability.

In the proposed reconfiguration technique, there may be large number of feasible alternative combinations of lines and switch in a model network for fixed loading condition. Attempt has been made to find out the best possible combination of switches & lines which results in highest voltage stability occurring with least amount of active and reactive power loss of the overall system. The present work reveals that careful and optimum selection of power network lines and inter connection switches can provide the best voltage stability solution for a given loading condition.

In this section illustration of one case study has been presented by IEEE-modified 8 bus system. The IEEE –modified 8 bus system overall voltage stability index has been calculated for each of the load bus for different configuration. Over all aggregate gives the performance of voltage stability index of the overall system.

6\. A TYPICAL CASE STUDY

6.1 Voltage Stability Indicator (L indicator)

The objective of the present topic is to make familiar with a simple indicator that has the potential to be implemented in real-time. The L indicator (Kessel, & Glavitsch, 1986) has been used to find voltage profile at different switching condition.

6.3 Computational Aspects

A fast and efficient method of calculating L index value of each bus and also the L index average value for the whole system for various switching patterns has been developed and implemented. Here, for each of the configuration, Newton Raphson Method (Kessel, & Glavitsch, 1986) Load Flow has been run with corresponding admittance matrix.

The basic algorithm can be described as follows:

*   1\. Run the load flow analysis program to obtain the values of bus voltages and complex powers.
*   2.
    
    Estimate:
    
    L[j]\=|1+ V[0j] /V[j]|=S[j] /V[j]2Y[jj],
    

where V[0j] is generator bus voltage V[j] bus voltage at jth bus S[j] is jth bus power.

*   3\. Estimate L[avg] value for the system for each switching pattern.
*   4\. Analyze the results and find out which switching combination gives the lowest value of L[avg]., i.e. the best voltage stability.

The main advantages of this algorithm are the small amount of computation time needed, and its limited requirement of information about the system.

6.4 Discussion of the Results and Inferences

The case study has been conducted on a modified IEEE 8 bus system (Figure 2). The standard IEEE 8 bus system has been modified with the addition of 2 power lines with line connection/disconnection switches. Also connection / disconnection switches have been placed in series with the existing lines. The system data are given in Table 1 and Table 2. It was assumed that loads are constant during each switching operation. The system under study is illustrated in figure 3. By closing or opening a switch, the line can be added or removed from the system respectively. ‘0’indicates switch is open, ‘1’ indicates switch is closed. In normal condition or base configuration of the given system S[3]\=0, S[4]\=0, S[8]\=0, S[15]\=0 and all the other switches are closed. Total 201 possible switching combinations have been studied and each combination has been designated by a unique configuration number. For example the configuration code 00 indicates normal condition. The proposed system under study has been analyzed to evaluate voltage stability index for each bus of the system as well as overall stability from average L index of the given network. Few sample cases of lines and switching combinations, their corresponding system configuration code and computed L index values have been presented in the Table 3.The computed average L-index value for normal system configuration (00) is 0.3037 in Table 3. That many alternative system configurations result lower value of L[avg] as compared to normal configuration and hence can improve overall voltage stability. The best possible switching option for the given loading condition is obtained for the configuration code ‘111’ corresponding to switch status ofS[1], S[2] and S[14] open and all remaining switches closed. However, there are few switching patterns and corresponding system configurations which decrease the value of L[avg], and should therefore be avoided by all means. Variation of L[avg] value with the change in system configuration is illustrated in Figure 3.

7\. APPLICATION OF ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORK (ANN) IN NETWORK RECONFIGURATION FOR IMPROVEMENT OF VOLTAGE STABILITY

It has been described in the previous section that voltage stability of a system can substantially improve by reconfiguration of the network topology. It has also been stated that in a large power network comprising of multiple lines, objective of network reconfiguration is to obtain the optimal combination of these lines which result improvement in voltage stability. Usually this is being achieved by opening/closing of sectionalizing switches placed in series with a power lines. Thus the primary task is to derive the switching state of these power lines (On/Off) which will improve system voltage stability in a given operating condition. However, in a practical large system switching combinations can be so large that it is almost impossible for an operator to determine which of this huge number of switches combination is optimal one. However, this optimal selection can be efficiently done using artificial neural network (ANN).

In this section an ANN based fast and efficient methodology has been proposed to select the optimal switching combinations to achieve the highest voltage stability in a large multi bus system. The proposed method has been successfully implemented and verified on IEEE 14 bus system and results indicate that ANN based optimal selection of switching states can improve voltage stability.

8\. APPLICATION OF ANN IN VOLTAGE STABILITY ENHANCEMENT USING NETWORK RECONFIGURATION

Neural networks are often perceived as powerful function approximation. They have excellent ability to approximate continuous functions based upon a few available sample values, i.e. ANN can evaluate and approximate a smooth curve, even if the data supplied to the network is discrete. Hence while approximating any mathematical functions, neural networks do not require the entire information, but requires only a few discrete data points lying on the function’s graph and sampled at appropriate intervals over the whole range of the function. The network reconfiguration problem has extremely nonlinear relationship between the input status of dynamic switches and corresponding voltage stability indicator of the overall system. A neural network based function approximation can be used to model this complex non-linear relationship. A multi-layer Perception model with error back propagation algorithm has been chosen for estimation and prediction of voltage stability for different system configuration. The block diagram of the proposed ANN based system voltage stability estimation technique has been shown in Figure 4.

| Figure 4. ANN block with switch status as input and Voltage-Stability Indicator as output |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch012.f04](i/ch012.f04.png) |
| --- |

In the present case study on the IEEE 14-bus system, each of the power line is assumed to be connected through series sectionalizing switches. During the course of reconfiguration the following two important criteria must be maintained:

*   1\. No buses can be left out of service.
*   2\. During each operation, active power flow through a line should be within maximum power transfer capability of the line.

There are 20 lines in the test system and hence total number of possible network configuration would be 2^(20). The best voltage stability condition will result from a unique switching configuration out of these 2^(20) combinations. However it would be impractical to study each of this huge number of probable combinations as repetitive Load Flow solution would take unacceptably long time. Thus for online operation repetitive Load Flow solution is not a practical solution to the problem. In the proposed method optimum switching state for a given operating condition is obtained by using ANN technique. Only three hundred sets of Load Flow Solution data are collected offline by Newton Raphson Load Flow analysis of the IEEE 14 bus system for different switching configurations. These data are used as training set for the ANN. A 20 bit binary code is generated for each network configuration, which serves as the input vector to the ANN. Corresponding voltage stability indicator is used as the Target output, which has to be predicted by the ANN. This process begins with the input vector code ‘000000000000000’ corresponding to first probable configuration and ends with the code ‘11111111111111111111’ corresponding to last probable configuration. The three hundred training samples are selected judiciously for a broad based representation of the probable system configurations. Few samples of training patterns are presented in Table 4. The trained ANN is finally exploited to predict voltage stability indicator values for unknown system configurations. From the predicted voltage stability indicator values the minimum value of voltage stability indicator is marked which corresponds to best voltage stability of the overall system. The corresponding switching status code will represent the optimum system configuration for the given operating condition. A flow chart showing the proposed method has been shown in Figure 5.

| Figure 5. Flow chart showing ANN based determination of optimal switching configuration |

| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch012.f05](i/ch012.f05.png) |
| --- |

9\. TOPOLOGY OF THE ANN

Input layer, hidden layer, and an output layer.

9.1 The Input Layer

In the present problem, input to the ANN is the various possible switching states. Since, there are 20 lines, each having a sectionalizing switch, there would be 20 switches altogether. Thus the input layer comprises of 20 neurons.

9.2 The Hidden Layer

Computational power of the ANN is a result of the addition of hidden layers. But there are no general guidelines to determine the number of hidden layers and neurons. Many applications have proved that ANN’s with one single-hidden layer possess sufficient capability of capturing complicated relations between input and output variables. Our studies demonstrated that 1 hidden layer with 40 hidden neurons are quite sufficient for estimation of voltage stability index for the purpose of enhancement of voltage stability. The weighted input value is limited between two limits using an activation function f (x), where ‘x’ is the summation of weighted inputs. In general tan sigmoidal function of the type: (e^x + e^(\-x))/ (e^x - e^(\-x)) or log sigmoidal functions of the type: 1/ (1-e^(\-x)) are used as activation functions. In the present work a tan sigmoidal activation functions have been used for all neurons in the hidden layer. Sigmoidal activation functions are most suitable for any nonlinear mapping of the input-output combinations, as they have noise immunity for low inputs, normal outputs for range inputs, and saturation for large inputs, ensuring stability of the systems.

9.3 The Output Layer

Determination of the output layer is quite straight forward. The number of output layer neurons is one because, only voltage stability index has been determined as output of ANN. The linear activation function is used for the output layer neurons.

10\. CASE STUDY RESULTS AND INFERENCE

As mentioned, a case study has been conducted on the standard IEEE 14 bus system as shown in Figure 6. The relevant data for the system are presented in Table 4 and Table 5. The lines are connected between the buses through sectionalizing switches. The loads on the buses are assumed to be constant during the process of restructuring. Under normal condition of the system, all the sectionalizing switches are assumed to be in closed position (switch status ‘1’). Opening of a switch will now disconnect a Power line from the system and this will lead to a new network configuration. As said earlier, three hundred such alternative system configurations have been studied in the present work and voltage stability indicator has been computed for each different network configuration. The training data have been collected from the Load Flow simulations of the IEEE-14 bus system. A few samples of voltage stability indicator data corresponding to different switch combinations and corresponding system configuration have been presented in the Table 6 to train the ANN model.

The ANN comprise of 20 input neurons to match the dimension of the input data (switching status of the 20 sectionalizing switch), 10 hidden layer and a single output layer to predict the overall voltage stability of the system. The target output (computed voltage stability indicator) vs. the ANN output (predicted voltage stability indicator) graph for training data sample is presented in Figures 7 and 8. The graph illustrates excellent learning of the training data samples. After the training is complete, the generalization ability of the network and its prediction accuracy was tested and 11 samples of unknown switching combination and corresponding voltage stability indicator, as shown in Table 7. The prediction accuracy is found to be very good.

Finally, after training of the ANN by 300 known sets of configuration has been completed and prediction efficiency of the trained ANN has been verified with unseen data, the ANN is exploited to predict VSI (Voltage Stability indicator-L index) for all the probable 2^(20) system configurations. The least value of VSI (best voltage stability) has been searched for and the corresponding system configuration is marked as the optimum configuration which will lead to best possible voltage stability under the given operating condition. The switching status and system configuration for best voltage stability as predicted by the ANN has been presented in Table 7.

11\. OTHER APPLICATIONS OF NETWORK RECONFIGURATION

Apart from voltage stability solution, Network Reconfiguration technique can be utilized for loss reduction, congestion management, Power Quality and Reliability Improvement and distributed generation system. In the following section some of the techniques have been described to meet the above mention objective using Network Reconfiguration which was reported by the previous researchers:

11.1 Loss Reduction

This is one of the objective for which more attention has been paid in the domain of Network Reconfiguration (TzongSua, Changb, Morrison, Gao, & Kundur, 2005). Many soft Computational and optimization techniques such as ANN, GA, Ant Colony, and Particle Swarm have been applied. In optimization approaches (Ant Colony, Particle Swarm) to obtain the configuration for minimal system power loss, considering the operating constraints as bus voltage violation and line under a certain load pattern is taken into care. In case of ANN (HoyongKim, YunseokKo, & Jung, 1993) and GA (Vulasala, Sirigiri, & Thiruveedula, 2009) approaches some of the pre requisite system data are required for training and initial population respectively.

11.2 Congestion Management

Line load ability limit can be changed by Network Reconfiguration Method (Granelli, Montagna, Zanellini, Bresestib, Vailati, & Innorta, 2006).

11.3 Real-Time Reconfiguration of Distribution Network with Distributed Generation

This is a new methodology (Hossein, Shariatkhah, Haghifam, JavadSalehi, & Moser, 2012) where distributed generation is incorporated to the grid by automatic reconfiguration. The distributed generation wind turbines, solar photovoltaic panels and small hydropower are incorporated to the grid by means of reconfiguration process. Each distributed generating unit is connected to the grid through series switch which is remotely controlled by SCADA. The real-time reconfiguration process can be done by heuristic algorithm to obtain the best possible settings at significant improvement on network performance, reducing losses and increasing reliability.

11.4 Voltage Sag and Reliability Enhancement

Voltage Sag is one of the important issues of Power Quality in Power System. The bus which is far away from the fault point will have low severity due to the effect of Voltage sag propagation. It effect on the system component and reliability. Frequent Line faults are the main reason of voltage sags. During such kind of disturbances, system restoration and reliability improvement (Shareef, Ibrahim, Salman, Mohamed, & Ling Ai, 2014) and voltage sag minimization can be done by Network Reconfiguration.

12\. PARALLEL NEURAL NETWORK TECHNIQUE IN ELECTRICAL ENGINEERING: NEURAL ENSEMBLES OR COMMITTEE MACHINES

Decisions can be taken based on switching outcomes from independently different neural networks working in parallel. This arrangement is called Neural Ensemble or Committee Machine, where each neural network unit is an expert independently trained (Haykin, 1999). They can be unique ones following different learning approaches and transfer functions.

Each neural network unit is fed with the same data pattern parallel, and switching combination output is awaited. Output of each such unit is then combined to produce the ultimate output of the Ensemble or Committee. This approach ensures more accomplished predictions (Figure 9).

13\. CONCLUSION

A method for improving voltage stability in a power network comprising of multiple lines and switches has been suggested in this chapter based on system reconfiguration approach. ANN based fast and efficient methodology has been developed to obtain the optimum switching combination to achieve best voltage stability.

The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. It is observed that Voltage stability has been varying in wide range for different topological structure of test network which can be made by manually or with the help of ANN. In the present study a method for improving voltage stability in a power network comprising of multiple lines and switches has been suggested based on system reconfiguration approach. ANN based fast and efficient methodology has been developed to obtain the optimum switching combination to achieve best voltage stability. The proposed scheme has been tested on an IEEE 14-bus system comprising of 20 power lines connected through interconnecting and sectionalizing switches, making the total number of possible network configuration to be 220. The ANN is trained with just 300 samples of Load Flow solution data corresponding to 300 judiciously chosen system configurations. After training, the ANN successfully predicts the optimum system configuration and the corresponding switching states, which would lead to best voltage stability. This scheme is easy to implement in any power distribution network using modern SCADA and PLC based automation. The network performance in regards voltage and other electrical parameters can be optimized or visualized for manual or intelligent process through development of SCADA package for power system conditioning and monitoring using the developed ANN based approach as a future scope of work.

ABSTRACT

This article describes how modeling is an integral part of design and development of any system that provides the theoretical characterization of the system and helps in understanding the relations between various parameters of the system, before the system is developed. The capability of an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) to model the complex relations between a set of inputs and outputs is exploited to model the motional resistance and resonance frequency for a contour mode disk resonator. The solution was to develop a multilayer feed forward neural network. The data set required to train the ANN is obtained by developing an electrical equivalent model and through the MEMS simulation software Coventorware. The network is trained using a Levenberg Marquardt algorithm. The number of hidden layers and the number of neurons in each hidden layer is optimized using a genetic algorithm. The ANN model developed an efficient model of the motional resistance and resonance frequency of the disk resonator. The ANN output is compared with the output of an electrical equivalent model and a reported fabricated structure.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Modern wireless communication transceivers operate in various frequency range. Many of the modern-day transceivers operate in GHz range. Resonators are integral part of these transceivers. High level of integration and reconfigurability are the two important requirements of the resonators used in today's wireless transceivers. The various types of resonators used in RF wireless communication are coaxial resonator, dielectric resonator, crystal resonator, ceramic resonator, Surface Acoustic Wave (SAW) resonator and YIG resonator. Out of these the most widely used resonators are quartz crystal resonator and SAW resonators because of their very high-quality factor and very good thermal stability. All though these resonators provide extremely high-quality factor, they are bulky off chip components which are usually integrated at board level making miniaturization a difficult task. One of the important requirement of modern day miniaturized wireless transceivers is on chip integration of all the components. This has made the MEMS resonators a more feasible option for RF wireless communication (Jokic, Frantlovic, Djuric & Dukic, 2015). MEMS resonators have started replacing crystal resonators because of their on-chip integration capability and quality factor comparable with crystal resonators.

A MEMS resonator comprises of some mechanical structure, an input transducer to convert incoming electrical signal into mechanical vibrations and an output transducer to convert the mechanical vibration into electrical signal. To set the structure into motion a DC bias voltage is applied to the structure and AC input voltage is applied to the input electrode. This creates a time varying electrostatic force because of which the structure vibrates. When the frequency of the applied input voltage is equal to the natural frequency of the structure, the structure vibrates with maximum amplitude. In mechanical structures such as cantilever beam, clamped-clamped beam and free-free beam the dominant stress is bending stress and the structures vibrate orthogonally to the bending stress. For these kind of resonators as the dimensions of the structure is scaled to obtain higher resonance frequency, the quality factor decreases. Hence beam type of resonators are not suitable for high frequency and high-quality factor applications. Mechanical structures such as disk and square plate resonators have large stiffness and vibrate in plane because of the formation of longitudinal waves (Sutagundar, Sheeparamatti & Jangamshetti, 2014). Disk resonator is preferred over beam type resonator in high frequency and high-quality factor applications because of its large stiffness (Basu & Bhattacharyya, 2011).

The electromechanical nature of the MEMS resonators makes the design and development of MEMS resonators a challenging task. Modeling is an integral part of design and development of any system that provides the theoretical characterization of the system and helps in understanding the relation between various parameters of the system, before the system is developed. The modeling of resonator requires the understanding of relation between various mechanical and electrical parameter. Conventionally, Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD) and Finite Element Techniques are the two most widely used modeling techniques. These are numerical techniques which are computationally expensive and are time consuming. ANN, having the capability of extracting the complex relation between various input and output parameters, can be used for modelling of MEMS resonators. The ANNs require a huge amount of training data particularly when the input output relation is non-linear. Obtaining the training data for modeling of disk resonator through simulation or experiments is time consuming and difficult task. Knowledge based artificial neural networks are hybrid networks that use the domain knowledge along with measurement/simulation data to model a system. The empirical equations or an electrical equivalent circuit of the system to be modelled can be used to generate the training data. Because of the theoretical domain knowledge, these ANNs require less amount of training data (Towell & Shavlik, 1994).

This paper presents knowledge based ANN modelling of motional resistance and resonance frequency for MEMS radial mode disk resonator. A multilayer feed forward neural network is developed. The ANN uses radius of the disk, thickness, gap and bias voltage as input. Resonant frequency and motional resistance are the output of the network. Two different approaches are used to decide the number of hidden layers and the number of neurons in the hidden layer. In the first approach, a trial and error method is used where several networks are created with different number of hidden layers and number of neurons and the performance of the network is analyzed. The network with best performance is selected. In the second approach, Genetic algorithm is used to decide the number of hidden layer and the number of neurons in each hidden layer. The ANN requires huge amount of data for training. An electrical equivalent model is developed using MATLAB and data set is generated by varying the various input parameters for the equivalent model. Along with this data set, additional dataset is generated using MEMS simulation software Coventorware. The data from the simulation software and electrical equivalent model is used to train the ANN.

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides literature review in the field of MEMS resonator modeling and simulation. Section 3 describes the proposed system followed by electrical equivalent modelling. Section 4 describes the ANN modeling of the disk resonator followed by results and discussion in section 5. Finally, section 6 provides a brief summary of the work.

2\. LITERATURE SURVEY

With the advancement in technology there is a constant increase in frequency range of wireless communication. The reason is high frequency implies immunity to noise and efficiency in propagation. Rapid advancement in the wireless technologies have created the need for highly reliable and accurate oscillatory circuits. The need of hour is circuits which are reliable, multifunctional and small in size. MEMS components and devices are becoming integral part of such circuits because of their low insertion loss and high-quality factor. MEMS resonator is one such component that has started replacing the conventional resonators such as quartz and SAW because on its inherent advantages such as on-chip integration capability, high quality factor and excellent frequency stability (Basu & Bhattacharyya, 2011).

The mechanical structure of resonators can be broadly categorized into two types: beam type and disk/plate type. The resonance frequency of the mechanical structure depends on the properties of the material used and the structure dimensions. Smaller the structure higher is the resonance frequency. The most important performance parameter of MEMS resonator is frequency-quality factor product. For beam resonators, as the structure dimensions are reduced, the quality factor also decreases rapidly. However, in case of disk resonators higher resonance frequencies can be attained without significant reduction in the dimensions of the structure. In addition, the quality factor will also be high (Chorsi, Chorsi & Gedney, 2016).

As the requirement for single chip solutions is increasing, it has become inevitable to place many analog and RF components on the single chip. The major challenge here is modelling, simulation and optimization of the design. Particularly for RF components where the relation between various parameters is complex, accurate modeling becomes critical (Zhang, Gupta & Devabhaktuni, 2003). The design, development and optimization of MEMS resonator is still largely based on experimentation and hence requires more time and resources. Because of the electromechanical nature of MEMS resonators, the design and development requires understanding of multi-physics effects such as electrostatic actuation, air damping, mechanical motion, capacitive sensing etc. Modelling and simulation serve as an important phase in the development of MEMS resonator that provides the theoretical characterization of the device before it is actually fabricated. Modelling and simulation provide a faster design cycle and helps the designer to visualize the device behaviour before it is actually fabricated. This provides a scope for optimization of the device. Modelling and simulation of MEMS resonator is a challenging task because of its multi-physics nature. Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD) and Finite Element Techniques are the two most widely used modelling techniques in MEMS resonator modeling (Idris Ahmed Ali, 2012). The conventional modelling techniques such as numerical modelling, analytical modelling and empirical modelling have certain limitations. Numerical techniques are computationally expensive whereas for new devices obtaining analytical model is a challenging task. On the other hand, empirical models have limited accuracy and range.

ANNs imitate the way in which human brain learns from observation and generalize from the information gathered. The ANNs have processing units known as neurons. Each neuron has an activation function. The neurons are arranged in the form of layers and the neurons in one layer are connected with the neurons in the other layers through links known as synapse. Each link has an associated parameter known as weight. The neural network model is trained using a input-output data set so that the model learns the relationship between various parameters (Qi-Jun Zhang, Kuldip C Gupta & Vijay K Devabhaktuni, 2003)

The Neural networks models are becoming popular as modeling tools for RF components because of their ability to learn and generalize. There are several ANN structures such as Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Radial Basis Function(RBF), wavelet networks, recurrent networks etc. The choice of ANN structure depends on the nature of the problem. MLP is the most widely used neural network structure (Zhang, Gupta & Devabhaktuni, 2003). ANN require huge amount of training data. If the input output relation is non-linear, then a huge data set is needed to train the ANN. The training data can be obtained either by simulation or by measurement. For modeling of MEMS resonator obtaining entire dataset for training through simulation/measurement is difficult. This is because the simulation needs to be done for different dimensions of the mechanical structure and different values of input parameters such as bias voltage. The currently available simulation tools cannot provide the system behaviour for various dimensions and different values of input parameter simultaneously. The device has to be modelled for different dimensions and input values which is time consuming. Obtaining the data from measurements is impossible as it is not possible to fabricate the structure with different dimensions. Hence, a feasible approach is to use the prior knowledge of the structure such as empirical equations or electrical equivalent model to generate the required data for training the neural network. the prior knowledge about the system being modeled enhances the learning and generalizing capability of neural network. (Wang & Zhang, 1997).

ANNs have the ability to learn from example and generalize. The number of neurons in the input layer depends on the number of inputs to the network. The number of neurons in the output layer depends on the number of outputs from the network. The number of hidden layers and the number of neurons in the hidden layer are to be selected so as to minimize the difference between the output of the network and the desired output for a particular input. This is conventionally done by using trial and error method, where several architectures with different combinations of the number of hidden layers and number of neurons in each hidden layer are tested for performance and the best performing network is selected. The other way of deciding the number of hidden layers and number of neurons in the hidden layer is by using optimization algorithms such as simulated annealing, genetic algorithmm etc. (Idrissi, Ramchoun, Ghanou & Ettaouil, 2016).

The relation between the physical dimensions and the various electrical parameters of the resonator can be obtained by developing an electrical equivalent model. MEMS resonator comprise of mechanical structure as resonating element. When such resonators are used in completely electrical environment, it is essential to represent the mechanical structure using an electrical equivalent model. This helps in the further analysis of the electrical system. The components of the electrical equivalent model can be obtained from the mechanical lumped element values. There are two widely used analogies for mapping mechanical lumped element values to equivalent electrical component: force-voltage analogy and force-current analogy. The electrical equivalent networks provide the relation between the various mechanical parameters and electrical parameters of the resonator. In general, the MEMS resonator can be represented using a RLC circuit. The circuit elements are the functions of resonator physical properties and bias voltage \[T. Veijola,2007\].

3\. PROPOSED WORK

In the present work an ANN is developed for an electro statically actuated disk resonator. The mechanical structure comprises of a circular disk suspended above the substrate, supported by a single anchor at the centre. Two electrodes surround the disk by a narrow gap. One act as input electrode and other as output electrode. Figure 1 shows a disk resonator.

| Figure 1. Disk Resonator |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch013.f01](i/ch013.f01.png) |
| --- |

A DC bias voltage is applied to the disk, and an AC input signal is applied to the input electrode. This results in a time varying electrostatic force between the disk and the electrodes. The disk vibrates radially when the frequency of the input AC signal is equal to the resonance frequency of the structure. This results in a time varying capacitance between the disk and the output electrode which in turn generates a time varying current at the output electrode \[Joydeep Basu and Tarun Kanti Bhattacharyya, 2011\]. The various steps in the development of ANN model of disk resonator is shown in Figure 2.

| Figure 2. Modeling of disk resonatorv |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch013.f02](i/ch013.f02.png) |
| --- |

The resonance frequency f of the disk resonator depends on the material used and the radius of the disk and is given by equation (1).

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch013.m01](i/ch013.m01.svg) (1)

where E and ρ represents the Young's modulus and density of the material used respectively. R is the radius of the disk. K is the parameter which depends on the Poisson's ratio of the material and α is the mode dependent parameter.

The motional resistance is an important performance parameter of resonator that plays an important role in RF communication. Typically for RF circuits, an impedance matching as low as 50Ω is desirable. Lower motional resistance implies lower power consumption and higher output power (Jokic, Frantlovic, Djuric & Dukic, 2015). The motional resistance of MEMS resonator depends upon the dimensions of the mechanical structure, the bias voltage and the transduction mechanism. The motional resistance can be decreased by reducing the gap between the disk and the electrode and by increasing the bias voltage (Babazadeh & Keshmiri, 2009). To understand the dependency of disk resonator on the physical dimensions of the disk, gap between the disk and electrode and the bias voltage an electrical equivalent model is built.

Disk resonators exhibit large stiffness and higher quality factor compared to beam resonators. The response of the resonator is dependent on the bias voltage and the atmosphere conditions in which the resonator is operated. 4\. MODELING AND SIMULATION USING COVENTORWARE

The 3D model of the disk resonator is developed in CoventorWare. The CoventorWare is a MEMS design and simulation software which is used for modeling and simulating variety of MEMS devices. There are basically five steps involved in the modelling and simulation of any MEMS structure as follows: Selection of materials, defining the fabrication steps in the process editor, creating a 2D layout using layout editor followed by creation of 3D structure, meshing and finally analysis.

The first step is to enter the properties of the materials associated with the fabrication process in the Material Property Database(MPD). Only the materials that are available in MPD can be used in further steps. Once the properties of materials is entered in the MPD, the next is description of sequence of steps involved in the fabrication process in process editor. The process editor provides the information needed to construct the 3D model of the disk from the 2D masks provided in the layout editor. The layers are created in a deposit and etch sequence that theoretically models the fabrication process. The sequence is created by selecting prototype steps from a Process Library, displayed by default on the right-hand side of the Process Editor window. Each step has parameters that must be specified. It also contains user defined prototype, called Modelling Actions, which has three basic layer deposition type i.e. Sacrificial, Conformal and Stack. The process file for modeling a disk resonator is shown in Figure 5. The first step is defining a substrate of particular thickness. This is followed by deposition of an oxide layer and passivation layer. A layer of Si[3]N[4] is used as passivation. This is followed by a series of deposit and etch steps that leads to a disk structure with surrounding electrodes.

5\. ANN MODELLING

Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) are biologically inspired mathematical models that can model the complex relation between various input and output parameters. ANNs learn the relation between the input and output parameters using the set of data provided. ANNs comprise of processing units called as neurons. The neurons are arranged in the form of layers. The transfer function of the neurons is commonly known as activation function. The most commonly used activation functions are log sigmoid (Logsig), tan sigmoid (Tansig) and pure linear (Purelin). The selection of a particular activation function is problem dependent. The neurons in each layer are connected to neurons in other layer through interconnections known as synapses and each synapse has an associated parameter known as weight. Each neural network has a input layer, an output layer and one or more hidden layers. The number of neurons in the input layer depends on the number of inputs to the network. The number of layers in the output layer depends on the number of outputs from the network. The number of hidden layers and the number of neurons in each hidden layer is problem dependent (Zhang, Gupta & Devabhaktuni, 2003; Lee, Park, Niu, Bachman, Gupta & Filipovic, 2004; Tino, Benuskova & Sperduti, 2015).

5.1. ANN Modelling of Disk Resonator

A multi-layer feed forward network is developed for modelling the resonance frequency and the motional resistance of the disk resonator. Multilayer feed forward network is a supervised training where the network is provided with the desired output, using which the network adjusts the weight coefficients (Svozil, Kvasnicka & Pospichal, 1997). The radius and thickness of the disk, the gap between the disk and electrode and the bias voltage are taken as input for the model. The output from the model are resonance frequency and motional resistance. Figure 9 represents the ANN developed for modelling the disk resonator.

| Figure 9. ANN Structure with inputs and outputs |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch013.f09](i/ch013.f09.png) |
| --- |

The ANN is trained using Levenberg Marquardt (LM) algorithm. The learning rate is denoted as μ. The weight matrix w denotes the weights of all the interconnects between the neurons. The learning rate μ and the weight matrix w is initialized. The sum of squared errors between the desired output and actual output of the neural network is used as performance index by the LM algorithm. The objective is to minimize the sum of squared errors. The sum of squared error is represented as (9)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch013.m08](i/ch013.m08.svg) (9)

where s is the total number of samples presented to the network, n is the total number of outputs (number of neurons in the output layer), t[kl] is the target output and a[kl] is the actual output of the network. Then Jacobian matrix J(w) is computed. The weight update vector Δw is calculated using the equation (10)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch013.m09](i/ch013.m09.svg) (10)

where I is the identity matrix. The error is recomputed using updated weight vector. If the recomputed error is not less than the previously computed error then the learning rate μ is incremented by 10 and using this updated μ new Δw is computed. The algorithm is said to be converged when the error goes below some preset value (Sutagundar, Sheeparamatti & Jangamshetti, 2016).

The data generated from the MEMS simulation software Coventorware and the electrical equivalent model is used for training the ANN. The range of input and output parameters used for training is given in the Table 1.

Table 1. Range of input and output parameters used for the training

| Input Parameters  || Radius || 10-40µm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Thickness || 1-2µm |
| Gap || 50nm-1µm |
| Bias voltage || 6-35V |
| Output Parameters || Resonance Frequency || 71.3 - 276.19MHz |
| Motional Resistance || 15.88kΩ - 93600MΩ |

The ANN has four neurons in the input layer and two neurons in the output layer corresponding to four inputs and two outputs. The hidden layer comprises of LOGSIG neurons. Since the LOGSIG activation function is used in the hidden layer, the data set is normalized before being used for the training. The number of hidden layers and the number of neurons in the hidden layer is selected on the basis of Mean Square Error (MSE) using two methods. In the first method where trial and error approach is used, the ANN is trained by varying the number of hidden layers and number of neurons in each hidden layer and observing the MSE. One hidden layer is considered. The number of neurons in the hidden layer is varied and MSE is computed. It was observed that a minimum MSE of 8.26x10^(\-12) to 7.23x10 ^(\-11) was obtained for a networks with 35 to 40 neurons in the hidden layer, after which the error kept on increasing. Hence the number of neurons in the hidden layer is selected as 35.

In the second method, Genetic Algorithm (GA) is used to find the number of hidden layers and number of neurons in each layer. GA is an evolutionary algorithm based on the principal of “Survival of fittest”. The two basic functions of genetic algorithm are selection of the individuals with best features from the population and passing the features to next generation i.e. evolution. In the proposed work, GA is used to find the number of hidden layers and number of neurons in the hidden layer that provides minimum MSE.

Genetic algorithm works on a set of solutions known as population. Initially the population comprises of 50 different networks or individual known as chromosomes. Each chromosome represents two parameters: number of hidden layers and number of neurons in each layer. Each of the network is trained using the data set and its performance is analyzed using the MSE. The network with minimum MSE is the best performer. Genetic algorithm uses this MSE in the fitness function and ranks the network according to their performance. The networks are sorted according to their ranks. From the sorted set of networks top 2 are selected to create next generation whereas the bottom 2 are discarded. The selected 2 networks are used to breed the new off springs which are going to replace the discarded networks, so that the population remains constant. The new off-springs inhibit certain features of the parent networks. The process is repeated for fixed number of iterations. The Algorithm for evolution of the network is as follows:

*   Step 1: Initialize 50 random networks which forms the initial population.
*   Step 2: Evaluate each network and assign a fitness value.
*   Step 3: Sort the networks according to their fitness value.
*   Step 4: Top 2 networks are selected as parents to breed the next generation of networks.
*   Step 5: Bottom 2 networks are discarded.
*   Step 6: The two selected parents are used to create two new off springs.
*   Step 7: The generated off springs are applied with mutation operator.
*   Step 8: The generated off springs replace the discarded networks.
*   Step 9: Go to step 2

After 100 iterations, the individual with the highest fitness was selected. It was observed that the network that was selected had one hidden layer and 37 neurons in the hidden layer.

The two methods of selecting the number of hidden layer and number of neurons in the hidden layer is compared. In trial and error method trying out every possible combination is difficult and also there is no guarantee that the final solution is optimal. There may be better solutions which were not tried at all. The second method which uses genetic algorithm for evolution tries to give the best possible solution by inheriting the features of fittest individuals(solutions) and thus provides an optimal solution. Also, the second method provides faster result compared to the trial and error method.

6\. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Table 2 lists the output of ANN for different combinations of the input parameters. The table also compares the ANN output with the output of electrical equivalent model. Also for some input combinations the ANN output is compared with the measured output provided in fabricated structure (Wang, Ren & Nguyen, 2004).
