CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

In this paper, we proposed to extend the convolutional neural networks based deep learning technique by incorporating a bootstrapping algorithm. Moreover, to achieve faster computation speeds and better handling of unstructured key-value pairs of the TRECVID video data, we harnessed the power of Apache Spark. Our Spark system is implemented on a dedicated Spark cluster developed solely for the computational needs of our research group. In the bootstrapping stage, pseudo balanced training batches are rendered and inserted into the CNN for classification. The experimental results establish the effectiveness of the proposed framework for accurately classifying highly imbalanced multimedia data. Different from many existing methods in deep learning that take the required raw media data in the input layer, our deep learning framework works efficiently on the low-level features, which largely reduces the required training time in deep learning. Furthermore, a computational boost is achieved with the power of distributed computing using Apache Spark and better information retrieval results are generated by the features from the pre-trained CNN models.

Though we propose a powerful imbalanced big data processing system using Spark in this paper, running deep learning algorithms on GPU is much more efficient than on CPU. Therefore, it is better to extend the system for accelerating deep learning on Spark applications using GPUs. Since GPUs provide both high-computation capabilities and high-memory bandwidth, they can be used to accelerate both computation-intensive and memory-intensive Spark jobs. In the future, we plan to enhance our system and run deep learning applications on distributed GPUs with Spark.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Multimedia Data Engineering and Management (IJMDEM), 8(1); edited by Shu-Ching Chen and Chengcui Zhang, pages 1-20, copyright year 2017 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).

*   R Vinayakumar

ABSTRACT

This article describes how sequential data modeling is a relevant task in Cybersecurity. Sequences are attributed temporal characteristics either explicitly or implicitly. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a subset of artificial neural networks (ANNs) which have appeared as a powerful, principle approach to learn dynamic temporal behaviors in an arbitrary length of large-scale sequence data. Furthermore, stacked recurrent neural networks (S-RNNs) have the potential to learn complex temporal behaviors quickly, including sparse representations. To leverage this, the authors model network traffic as a time series, particularly transmission control protocol / internet protocol (TCP/IP) packets in a predefined time range with a supervised learning method, using millions of known good and bad network connections. To find out the best architecture, the authors complete a comprehensive review of various RNN architectures with its network parameters and network structures. Ideally, as a test bed, they use the existing benchmark Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency / Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (DARPA) / (KDD) Cup ‘99’ intrusion detection (ID) contest data set to show the efficacy of these various RNN architectures. All the experiments of deep learning architectures are run up to 1000 epochs with a learning rate in the range \[0.01-0.5\] on a GPU-enabled TensorFlow and experiments of traditional machine learning algorithms are done using Scikit-learn. Experiments of families of RNN architecture achieved a low false positive rate in comparison to the traditional machine learning classifiers. The primary reason is that RNN architectures are able to store information for long-term dependencies over time-lags and to adjust with successive connection sequence information. In addition, the effectiveness of RNN architectures are shown for the UNSW-NB15 data set.

INTRODUCTION

Over the years, information and communication technologies (ICT) systems have been bringing fruitful benefits to the human activities. Most of the businesses, government, academic and other organizations activities largely rely on ICT systems. On the other side, cyber-attacks to the ICT systems continuously evolving due to the fact that computer systems have constantly evolving from a handful of monolithic computing systems to distributed computing systems. In addition, recent days even a novice user can capable to attack many malicious activities easily with the freely available existing advanced attack toolkits in internet. The various cyber-attacks and its techniques occurred from 2001 to 2013 is briefly outlined by (Vaidya, T. 2015). These issues demand the necessity of flexible and interpretable integrated network security solutions to the ICT systems.

There are various approaches exist to attack malicious activities, namely (1) static approaches: firewalls, encryption and decryption techniques of cryptography, software updates and many others and (2) dynamic approaches: anomaly and intrusion detection (ID). In that, ID system has become a prominent method by achieving a great success in identifying various kinds of complex and diverse malicious foreseen threats. ID has been actively studied area since from 1980’s, a seminal work by (Anderson, J. P. 1980) on the computer security threat monitoring and surveillance. Mainly, ID is categorized into 2 types based on the network behavior and network type. One is network-based ID system (N-IDS): most commonly used in both academia and industries, it analyzes all the network traffic by looking inside the packet level information to find the suspicious activity, the second one is host-based ID system (H-IDS): focuses on the information of each particular system or host, heavily depends for data on the sources of log files such as sensors, system logs, software logs, and many more. Mostly, organizations use combination of both of them to get benefited largely in real-time IDS deployment. The experiments used in this work are devoted to N-IDS using openly available data sets, KDDCup ‘99’ and UNSW-NB15.

Primarily, analysis and classification of network traffic data is done using misuse detection, anomaly detection and state full protocol analysis. Misuse detection detects known specific attacks patterns accurately based on the predefined static signatures and filters. This method typically relies on human inputs to create and update the signatures and filters continuously whenever a new attack happens. In contrast to misuse detection, anomaly detection follows heuristic approach that enables them to find the unknown or novel attack patterns. However, this may result in a high false positive rate in most cases. To reduce this, most organization uses the combination of both the static and heuristic approaches, usually termed as hybrid approach. A third most power full method is state full protocol analysis that follows the similar approach as anomaly detection to identify the deviations of protocol state by using vendor’s predetermined specific standards and specifications; usually these are generally accepted benign network traffic. This has become potential method and widely being discussed due to the capability to act on the network layer, application layer and transport layer. However, most commercial N-IDSs that are built to date and exist in market have predominantly based on the basic statistical measures or threshold computing approaches that uses traffic parameters such as packet length, inter-arrival time, and flow size and so on to model the network traffic in a categorical time slot. However, this still limit the performance in detection of complex pattern due to its built on simple statistical measures that are computed from packet header and packet contents. Due to the advancement in mathematics has given a birth to the new field called self-learning systems (SLS). SLS’s are one of the potential methods that overcome the aforementioned limitations by leveraging the machine learning (ML) mechanisms. ML mechanisms are particularly supervised learning algorithms that learn the network traffic events of normal and malicious behaviors to identify the complex unknown patterns of attacks automatically. In addition, they have the capability to detect the previously unknown patterns of attacks. Moreover, ML methods are the current promising approach to ID that can detect and classify the complex network traffic events more accurately with low false positive rate including reasonable computational cost. Additionally, these methods can not only be able to analyze and detect most possible threats in real time but also takes the necessary countermeasures in a timely manner.

Developments of machine learning (ML) solutions to ID have received paramount of interest. Researchers have continually devised the various ML based solutions to ID in the last years. But the applicability of the same in real time ID is still in the beginning stages of development (Paxson, 1999). This is primarily due to, most of the methods having failed to achieve low false positive rate with less computational cost and some other methods outputs large number of misclassifications of network connection events (Lee, Fan, Miller, Stolfo & Zadok, 2002). The background reason to that, most methods have largely focused on learning attack patterns locally with tiny and simple input features of normal attack patterns. However, advance the research in ML, results in a more robust method typically named as deep learning (DL). Notably, DL is a set of ML algorithms that have the ability to detect the attack patterns globally by learning the complex hierarchical feature representations and hidden sequential relationships from a large-scale sequence data of TCP/IP packet information. These characteristics are the major factors towards the remarkable performance of DL algorithms in various long standing artificial intelligence (AI) tasks in the field of natural language processing, image processing, speech recognition and many others (LeCun, Bengio & Hinton, 2015).

Recurrent neural network (RNN) is a type of deep learning architecture generally applied for time-series data modeling. The RNN and its variant networks have showed remarkable performance in long standing AI tasks such as machine translation, language modeling and speech recognition (LeCun, Bengio & Hinton, 2015). Despite the popularity of RNN in sequence data modeling, applying the same in cyber security task is in early stage of development in contrast to other aforementioned areas. This paper focuses on RNN techniques and applies them to N-IDS. Specifically, this paper analyzes the effectiveness of the various RNN architectures for N-IDS. The RNN and its variant networks is complex and understanding the inner mechanics of particular RNN model remained as a black box. Thus, an adversary may not be able to reverse engineer the deep learning based detectors easily. In order to defeat the deep learning based detector, an adversary may require the same set of training samples.

In the rest of the paper, we firstly review the related work carried out on neural network and deep learning solutions for ID. And the necessary notion of deep learning methods particularly RNN and its variants in a mathematical way is described. Next, the necessary details of data sets, KDDCup ‘99’, and UNSW-NB15 and hyper parameter tuning approaches related to network parameters and network structures are discussed. At last, we present the detailed evaluation of experiments and followed by conclusion and future work directions are presented.

RELATED WORK

In initial days, deep learning algorithms were partly used due to possibly hard to train. These were typically called as neural networks in earlier days. The most commonly used neural network methods for ID are deep belief network, restricted Boltzmann machine, deep Boltzmann machine, deep neural network and auto encoder.

The taxonomies and other published works of shallow and deep learning algorithms in the context of ID are comprehensively discussed by (Hodo, Bellekens, Hamilton, Tachtatzis & Atkinson, 2017). In (Gao, Gao, Gao & Wang, 2014, November) represented the deep belief network as deep neural network (DNN) to apply on KDDCup ‘99’ data set. They used combination of RBM to pre-train in unsupervised way and backpropogation to apply fine-tuning. In (Moradi & Zulkernine, 2004, November) represented the efficacy of multi-layer perceptron (MLP) for ID with early stopping criterion in generalizing the capability of network with more than one layers. In (Mukkamala, Sung & Abraham, 2005) showed the combination of classical ML classifier, SVM and neural network. In (Xue, Sun & Zhang, 2004) presented the modified Jordon recurrent network to extract rule set of intrusion patterns and with various experiments proved the performance improvement. In (Yang, Deng, Li & Hao, 2017) used support vector machine- restricted Boltzmann machine (SVM-RBM) combination in which RBM extract features and gradient descent in Apache Spark facilitates to train the SVM in a distributed manner. The hybrid classifiers are also used for other tasks other than the intrusion detection Chatterjee, Dzitac, Sen et al. (2017), Chatterjee, Dey, Shi et al. (2017), Banerjee, Rana, Parui et al. (2017), Chakraborty, Chatterjee, Dey et al. (2017), Chatterjee, Nag, Sen et al. (2017).

Fortunately, the recent advancement in optimization techniques, parallel and distributed computing has enabled deep learning algorithms to train for large scale learning in an efficient way. In (Niyaz, Sun, Javaid & Alam, 2015) proposed a deep learning approach that consists of two stages for classification. In first phase using the sparse auto encoder the good feature representation is learnt from unlabeled data and later applied NB-Tree, Random Tree, or J48 for classification. In (Kim & Kim, 2015) modeled the network traffic data as a sequence using RNN with Hessian-Free optimization method. Recently, they used LSTM to train the ID data set (Sak, Senior & Beaufays, 2014). In recent studies, (Wang, 2015) has explored the deep learning approaches, particularly deep neural networks for traffic identification without the feature relevance analysis.

With the aim to identify attacks and take necessary countermeasures in a timely manner (Al-Subaie & Zulkernine, 2006) used the importance of sequential relationships between events that represent the normal and abnormal behaviors property of connection. They reviewed Hidden Markov model (HMM) based IDS to learn temporal patterns of TCP/IP connection sequences and consequently, improved the efficacy of attack detection rate. In addition, they showed sequential learning technique, namely HMM performance is better than the structural pattern recognition technique, MLP. In (Al-Subaie & Zulkernine, 2007), (Chowdhury, 2008) discussed the comparative analysis between neural network and RNN towards IDS. They summarize RNN performed well due to the ability to memorize the previous sequence information and to combine with the current sequence input. (Staudemeyer & Omlin, 2014; Staudemeyer & Omlin, 2013; Staudemeyer, 2015) had conducted series of study for ID using KDDCup ’99’ dataset. Firstly, paper published by studying the important features with the data mining and network security experts (Staudemeyer & Omlin, 2014). It presented the class distributions with visualization. Second one evaluated the performance of LSTM-RNN towards classification of attacks or normal class (Staudemeyer & Omlin, 2013). Subsequently, the detailed version of previous method published in (Staudemeyer, 2015).

BACKGROUND

The purpose of this section is to discuss the concepts of deep learning paradigms, particularly various recurrent neural network (RNN) architectures concisely and promising techniques behind to train these various RNN networks.

RECURRENT NEURAL NETWORK (RNN)

Recurrent neural network (RNN) is an extension to traditional neural network found in 1990’s for time-series data modeling (Elman, J. L. 1990). It is same as feed-forward network (FFN) with an additional internal feedback loop that results in a cyclic graph. These loops are the short-term memory to store and retrieve past information over time scales and thereby execute the temporal task. In contrast to FFN, RNN shares its parameters across time-steps to avoid not being generalized on playing with the unseen sequence of arbitrary length. The computational flow of RNN can be mathematically formulated, ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m01](i/ch018.m01.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m02](i/ch018.m02.svg)

where ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m03](i/ch018.m03.svg), ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m04](i/ch018.m04.svg) and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m05](i/ch018.m05.svg) x[t], o[t] are the input, output vectors respectively, w[zh], w[hh] and w[ho] are weight matrices, f is the hidden layer nonlinear activation function, particularly sigmoid function (σ) applied on element wise. H is a short-term memory to the RNN’s network. This H can be further fed to other stacked recurrent layer or final layer in which a layer has nonlinear activation function, namely softmax function (sf).

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m06](i/ch018.m06.svg)

The cyclic connection in RNN makes difficult to understand the dynamics of RNN entirely. So RNN intricate network structure is cleverly transformed to FFN structure by unfolding or unrolling over time-steps, as shown in Figure 1. The newly transformed simple FFN can be analytically analyzed easily and they are flexible to the back propagation. Generally, the input sequence of length l is transformed to FFNs in which the FFN consist of l hidden layers. Unfolded RNN at time t is defined as a function ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m07](i/ch018.m07.svg) where S[T] represents the unfolded graph of time-steps t.

| Figure 1. Schema of RNN and unfolded RNN in time (t = 1, t = 2) |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.f01](i/ch018.f01.png) |
| --- |

The loss function in RNN is a sum of all input-output pairs in a sequence over all the time-steps.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m08](i/ch018.m08.svg)

Figure 1 shows that RNN cyclic connections can be represented as deep neural network, where each layer represents the per time-step information. Further, unfolded RNN looks similar to deep neural network except that RNN shares weight parameters ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m09](i/ch018.m09.svg) across time-steps. However, the network performed the same recurrent task with various inputs over time-steps. In addition to learning the temporal patterns with cyclic connections, unfolding allows the RNN model to learn the association of static features between the input and output sequences. In backward pass, the aforementioned concept, back propagation is used to compute the gradients for weight parameters across time-step ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m10](i/ch018.m10.svg). According to Figure 1, the computation of gradient at t\=2 involves to back propagate 1 step and add them to find the recurrent weights. This technique is called as back propagation through time (BPTT) (Werbos, 1990). RNN with BPTT is not efficient in modeling large scale sequence data due to the vanishing and exploding gradient problem (Bengio, Simard & Frasconi, 1994). This occurs normally when we back propagate the error back in many time-steps in the deep unrolled RNN’s network models.

LONG SHORT-TERM MEMORY (LSTM)

Principally, LSTM is a second order neural network architecture that acts as the supplement to the traditional RNN (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997). LSTM has introduced memory block instead of conventional simple RNN unit, which handle vanishing and exploding gradient problem by forcing the constant error flow. A memory block is a complex processing unit that is composed of one or more memory cell and a pair of multiplicative gates as input and output gate. A memory cell has an in-built recurrent connection with a value 1 called as constant error carousel (CEC). The value will be active across the time-step and triggered when a memory block has not received any value from outside signals. The entire operations of a memory block are controlled by a set of adaptive multiplicative gates. An input gate performs allow or discard operation for an input flow of a cell activation to a memory cell and an output gate performs allow or discard operation for an output state of a memory cell to the other nodes. Towards the research on LSTM, forget gate (Gers, Schmidhuber & Cummins, 1999) and peephole connections (Gers, Schraudolph & Schmidhuber, 2002) are added to the existing LSTM network. The forget gate is used instead of CEC mainly the internal values of a memory cell could increase without any constraints. The peephole connections from a memory cell to all of its gates learn the precise timing of the outputs and including the internal state of a memory cell.

In general, we give TCP/IP packet information sequences of arbitrary length ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m11](i/ch018.m11.svg) to LSTM architecture as input and that estimates an output sequence ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m12](i/ch018.m12.svg) with continuous write, read and reset operations by 3 multiplicative units (input (in), output (ot) and forget gate (fr)) on a memory cell (cl) in an iterate manner from t\=1 to T in the recurrent hidden layer of LSTM architecture. The computation of recurrent hidden layer function at time-step T can be generally defined as follows,

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m13](i/ch018.m13.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m14](i/ch018.m14.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m15](i/ch018.m15.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m16](i/ch018.m16.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch018.m18](i/ch018.m18.svg)

As the LSTM memory block is a complex processing unit with many units. This might be one of the reasons to further enhancement with the introduction of many variants of LSTM. Among them, Gated recurrent unit (GRU) (Cho, Van Merriënboer, Gulcehre, Bahdanau, Bougares, Schwenk & Bengio, 2014) is the most prominent algorithm.

NETWORK BASED INTRUSION DETECTION SYSTEM (N-IDS) DATASETS

Due to privacy issues in networks, the choice of adequate data set publicly available to build reliable IDS for ML is very less. A few among many IDS datasets are DARPA / KDDCup ‘99’^, refined version of KDDCup ‘99’: NSL-KDD (Tavallaee, Bagheri, Lu & Ghorbani, 2009) and most recent UNSW-NB15 (Moustafa & Slay, 2015; Moustafa & Slay, 2016). KDDCup ‘99’ has been one of the most widely used intrusion dataset for the evaluation of effectiveness of ML classifier to N-IDS. In this paper, the comprehensive analysis of custom-built dataset of KDDCup ‘99’ is carried out and in addition the experiments are shown to UNSW-NB15. These are the publicly available, most valuable asset to the IDS research community. However, as far as from the large study on published papers except UNSW-NB15, all of them had their own harsh criticisms. But yet, these are most commonly used and publicly available labeled connection records for IDS research. In the following, we discuss the details of these IDS data sets including the techniques behind TCP/IP packets collection and the mechanism employed by them to label each TCP/IP connection.

The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) was conducted an experiment with 1000’s of UNIX machines and 100’s of users at a time in Lincoln Labs continuously for nine weeks that composed of 7 weeks training and 2 weeks testing to obtain the raw TCP dump data in an air force LAN environment. Using Windows NT and UNIX workstations, most of the attacks were instigated from external location of air force LAN opposed to Solaris, UNIX, Linux, Windows NT and SunOS machines. Totally, the data set had 300 attacks that were strained from 32 distinct attacks and 7 distinct attack scenarios. For evaluation, the data set is distributed in KDDCup ‘98’ and KDDCup ‘99’ competition. Both of these competition results were discussed explicitly and published in (Lippmann, Haines, Fried, Korba & Das, 2000; Lippmann, Fried, Graf et al., 2000). Approximately the data composed of 5 million train connection records enclosed of distinct 24 attack types with 100 bytes each and 2 million test connection records enclosed of an additional 14 distinct attacks with the existing 24 distinct attacks in train connection records. So, test data has distinct probability distribution in comparison to train data set. Hence the classification learning typically can be considered as pragmatic. Each connection record represents information about TCP/IP packets with a specific time window and data flows from both direction of sender and receiver internet protocol (IP) address with respect to specific protocol type. These connection records contained 41 features and 5 classes; normal and 4 types of attack (‘DOS’, ‘Probe’, R2L, and U2R) category. Among 41 features, 34 are continuous and 7 are discrete valued and the whole 41 features were categorized into basic features in the range \[1-9\], content features in the range \[10-22\], traffic features were quantified with time window of two seconds in the range \[23-31\] and host based features in the range \[32-41\]. KDDCup ‘99’ competition has made data available in 2 forms (1) full sets including train and test (2) 10% stratified subset class of full sets. Full sets consist of large amount of connection records in that most of them are belongs to ‘DOS’ category. To alleviate this, they were created 10% subset version of full sets with a close attentiveness in adding ‘DOS’ connection vectors within a specific time window particularly used only 5 minutes interval. The detail statistics of KDDCup ‘99’ is listed in Table 1. It shows that both the normal and DOS have more number of records in comparison to the other attacks in 10% KDDCup ‘99’. As a result, the detection rate related to normal, DOS and probe connection will be higher in comparison to the other attacks, U2R and R2L by the IDS model. The full data set contains more number of connection records in comparison to the attacks. In order to prevent it, we ideally formed a new training data set by adding 400 connection records to R2L and 100 connection records to U2R (Kim, Kim, Thu & Kim, 2016). Moreover, we randomly removed 250 connection records from both the normal and DOS connection records.

Recently, cyber security research team at the Australian Centre for Cyber Security (ACCS) has investigated the issues that are exist in the KDDCup ’99’ and NSL-KDD and introduced a new data called as UNSW-NB15 (Moustafa & Slay, 2016; Moustafa & Slay, 2015, November). This is generated in a hybrid of normal and attack behaviors of live network traffic using IXIA PerfectStorm tool. The data is available in two forms; (1) full connection records, consist of 2 million connection records (2) A partition of full connection records that are composed of 82332 test connection records and 175341 train connection records enclosed with 10 attacks. In this paper, the experiments are done on the partition of full connection records.

EXPERIMENTS

In this section, we discuss the effectiveness of the various RNN architectures in terms of attacks detection rate on publically available ID dataset, KDDCup ‘99’. All experiments are trained using backpropogation through time (BPTT) with ADAM optimizer on Google’s open source data flow engine, TensorFlow (Abadi, Barham, Chen et al., 2016). TensorFlow allows programmers to deploy computations on heterogeneous platforms such as one or more CPU, GPU, or mobile devices. To accelerate the gradient descent computations, all experiments are run on GPU enabled TensorFlow in single Nvidia GK110BGL Tesla k40. A memory cell in LSTM network has used hyperbolic tangent which in range \[-1, 1\] as their input. Gating and other units have used sigmoid as their non-linear activation function which in range \[1, 0\]. All experiments related to traditional machine learning classifiers are implemented using Scikit-learn (Pedregosa, Varoquaux, Gramfort et al. 2011).

HYPER PARAMETER SELECTION IN LSTM NETWORKS

As recurrent neural network approaches such as RNN, LSTM and GRU are parameterized functions, thus the optimal parameters have direct impact on the attack detection rate (Goodfellow, Bengio & Courville, 2016). To find out the optimal values for parameters such as learning rate, number of units / memory blocks and network structure such as number of hidden recurrent layer, various configurations of experiments done.

Initially, we used the moderately sized LSTM network which contains an input layer, hidden recurrent layer and an output layer. The input layer contains 41 neurons and a hidden recurrent layer contains 4 memory blocks containing one cell each and an output layer includes 5 neurons. The connection between neurons in input to hidden and hidden to output is fully-connected. The values in training and testing data set are normalized. Two trails of experiments are run for network parameter; memory blocks in range \[4-64\]. All experiments are run for 400 epochs with batch size 32, ADAM as an optimizer, categorical cross entropy as loss function. LSTM with 32 memory blocks has shown good performance in comparison to the others. When the number of memory block increases from 32 to 64 and 128 in LSTM network, the detection rate of all traffic types has followed similar detection rate of 32 memory blocks. Moreover, LSTM network with more number of memory blocks has attained good performance within a few numbers of epochs. To attain acceptable detection rate of all traffic types, the experiments with 32 memory blocks in LSTM networks are run till 1000 epochs. The epoch wise accuracy of each class is shown in Figure 2. For the rest of the experiments, we decided to use 32 memory blocks.

To find a suitable learning rate during training, two trails of experiments done for learning rate in the range \[0.01-0.5\]. The experiments with lower learning rate have showed superior performance in categorizing the connection records to their classes. Moreover, lower learning rate has required more number of epochs to achieve acceptable detection performance for low frequency attacks. We decided to use 0.1 learning rate for the rest of the experiments by considering the training time, cost and detection rate of all traffic types. The detection rate of each class across learning rate \[0.01-0.5\] is shown in Figure 3. It shows that the detection rate of ‘R2L’ and ‘U2R’ attacks is very less in comparison to the other attacks. When the same experiments are run till 1000 epochs, LSTM has increased detection rate for ‘R2L’ and ‘U2R’. This infers that 400 epochs are not sufficient to learn the patterns of low frequency attacks. However, other attacks have attained acceptable detection rate with learning rate 0.1 till 400 epochs.

*   • RNN/LSTM/GRU 4 layer with 32 units/memory blocks

Three trails of experiments are run for each of the network topologies till 500 epochs. Each experiment of RNN and its variants has showed acceptable detection rate for the classes such as ‘Normal’, ‘DoS’ and ‘Probe’. Moreover, the experiments with simple LSTM and its variants performance for ‘Normal’, ‘DoS’ and ‘Probe’ is good in comparison to the other attacks such as ‘R2L’ and ‘U2R’. This infers that the low frequency attacks require more number of parameters with each of LSTM network topology. The simple RNN and its variants networks have learnt the patterns of high frequency attacks within 350 epochs. Though, at last the complex networks have attained highest accuracy too. Most notably, the complex network topologies have taken a higher number of epochs, possibly more than 500 to attain the considerable detection rate of high frequency attacks. For low frequency attacks, the complex RNN and its variants networks performed well in comparison to the simple RNN and its variants networks. Moreover, simple RNN and its variants have required more number of epochs during training to learn the patterns of low frequency attacks such as ‘R2L’ and ‘U2R’. Each network topologies have followed different epochs for learning the patterns of each attack. Moreover, the simple RNN and its variants networks have started to overfitting after 450 epochs for high frequency attacks. It specifically means that the network has started to memorize the train data samples and results in decreasing the generalization performance for that specific attack. By considering the detection performance for both high frequency attacks and low frequency attacks, we decided to use 4 layers for each of the recurrent layers. In most of the cases LSTM network performed well in comparison to the RNN networks. However, the performance of GRU networks is comparable to the LSTM networks. The detailed accuracy of each network topologies across epochs is shown in Figure 4. All 3 networks have seen sudden increase in accuracy after 100 epochs. After that, they attained fluctuations in their accuracy. At last, after 800 epochs, all 3 networks have seen an increase in their accuracy.

PROPOSED LSTM NETWORK ARCHITECTURE

The proposed architecture for identifying attacks and categorizing into their category is shown in Figure 5. This contains an input layer, hidden recurrent layer and output layer. The input layer contains 41 neurons, hidden recurrent layer contains 32 memory blocks with one memory cell and output layer contains 5 neurons. The connection between the units of input and hidden recurrent layer and hidden recurrent layer to output layer are fully connected. RNN and GRU has also follows same architecture as Figure 5. But, RNN includes units instead of memory blocks, GRU includes modified memory cell in recurrent hidden layer. The proposed architectures of RNN, LSTM and GRU networks are used for the following experiment configurations.

*   1\. Distinguishing normal and attack connection records using all features
*   2\. Distinguishing normal and attack connection records and categorizing attack to their family using all features.
*   3\. Distinguishing normal and attack connection records using minimal feature sets
*   4\. Distinguishing normal and attack connection records and categorizing attack to their family using minimal feature sets

EVALUATION RESULTS

Four trails of experiments are run for RNN, LSTM and GRU networks. The detailed results of best performed networks in classifying the connection records as either normal or attack is reported in Table 4. LSTM performance is good in comparison to the RNN and GRU. However, the performance of GRU is comparable to LSTM. Moreover, to understand the detection rate of each traffic types accurately, the performance of classical machine learning as well as RNN and its variants are shown in Figure 6. LSTM has achieved highest AUC of 0.999. Additionally, the performance of RNN, LSTM and GRU networks is evaluated for UNSW-NB15. The detection rate of all traffic types of deep learning methods for UNSW-NB15 is less in comparison to the KDDCup ‘99’ due to the fact that the UNSW-NB 15 includes more classes of attacks with different unique patterns. In order to achieve the best performance, we need to follow hyper parameter tuning.

We run eight trails of experiments for each RNN networks in identifying an attack and categorizing to their categories. All trails of experiments are run for 1000 epochs. The detailed performance of best performed trails is reported in Table 2 and Table 3 for KDDCup ’99’ and UNSW-NB15 respectively. To know the performance of other classical machine learning algorithms, the experiments are run for KDDCup ‘99’. The experiments with RNN network has performed well in comparison to the classical machine learning classifiers. Overall, LSTM has performed well by showing accuracy of 0.9698 with categorical loss 0.31.

Generally, the LSTM network has passes the inputs to more than one layer to capture the hidden pattern with respect to time domain. The activation in each layer facilitates to distinguish the connection records to their classes. To visualize and understand, the last layer activation values of LSTM networks are passed to t-SNE (Maaten, L. V. D., & Hinton, G. 2008) instead of FFN. This transforms the high dimensional feature vectors into two dimensional feature vectors. The newly transformed feature vectors are shown in Figure 7. The connection record belongs to ‘Normal’, ‘DoS’ and ‘Probe’ are appeared in different clusters. But, the connection records belong to ‘U2R’ and ‘R2L’ are not entirely appeared in different clusters. This infers that the LSTM network has not learnt the complete patterns associated with the low frequency attacks such as ‘U2R’ and ‘R2L’. The primary reason may be due to that the low frequency attacks contain only few connection records for each unique pattern.

CONCLUSION, DISCUSSIONS and FUTURE WORK

This paper has reviewed a comprehensive review of the effectiveness of various RNN networks to N-IDS by modeling network traffic as sequences of TCP/IP packets. In addition, the other traditional supervised ML classifiers are examined. RNN techniques have shown superior performance over the other non-recurrent networks in identifying attack and categorizing into its categories. Moreover, LSTM has performed well in comparison to the other RNN techniques. This work can be considered as a preliminary research towards the evaluation of various RNN for N-IDS. Even though RNN performed well on the well-known and widely used benchmarking synthetic datasets, applying the same on the real-time network traffic as contains more advanced recent attack types is required.

We make concrete conclusion such that the taxonomies of RNN architectures have learned a distinctive time-varying patterns for all four types of attack classes. Moreover, they are performed well for classifying the high-frequency attacks such as ‘DoS’ and ‘Probe’ in contrast to the low frequency attacks such as ‘R2L’ and ‘U2R’. ‘R2L’ and ‘U2R’ are exploit-based attacks that are very few in numbers. However, RNN architectures might require an additional training samples or additional feature sets to the existing data set to learn the distinctive time-varying patterns between ‘R2L’ and ‘U2R’.

Though RNN has performed well on the IDS data sets under different experiments in this research, we lack behind to apply on the real-time data sets. The used data sets are only a benchmark not the representation of real time traffic. They have a list of harsh criticisms. This can be mitigated through following potential way to collect traffic data from ICT systems networks in real time. However, the continuous collection of network traffic data from ICT systems is enormous, generally experiences as big data challenge. While, instead of applying feature engineering to reduce it into connection records that consists of a set of features, we really should apply deep learning concepts that facilitate the algorithms to extract hierarchical, complex feature representation from raw big network traffic data (Wang, 2015). This fundamentally avoids the feature engineering phase that requires an additional in depth subject knowledge. In addition, this might increase the efficacy of N-IDS in terms of accuracy and low false positive rate. However, a large-scale evaluation of various RNN techniques on real time big network raw traffic data set on a distributed scalable computing platform, specifically Apache Spark on top of Hadoop platform will be one more direction towards future work.

The discussed RNN models are all same except the computational unit in the recurrent hidden layer. RNN are fundamentally complex networks that consist of many interactions between the computational units in the recurrent hidden layers to carry out a certain task from one layer to the other. Despite the fact that the effectiveness of various RNN has analyzed on IDS data sets under different experiments, the information about the internal procedure of the operation in the network is partly demonstrated. This can be explored by transforming the state of network to linearized dynamics and compute, analyze the structure of Eigen values and Eigen vectors from them across many time steps (Moazzezi, 2011). This analysis provides which Eigen vector actually carrying out application specific information and it will be orthogonal to the invariance of the network. So overall the context of Eigen vector associated with the linearized weight matrix enables to understand the overall provenance of the network’s performance in each time step. Additionally, studies related to the malleability of discussed deep learning mechanisms in an adversarial environment are required. This will be one of other future direction towards ID research.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Information System Modeling and Design (IJISMD), 8(3); edited by Remigijus Gustas, pages 43-63, copyright year 2017 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).

*   Mitsuo Wakatsuki

ABSTRACT

The authors are concerned with a card game called Daihinmin (Extreme Needy), which is a multi-player imperfect information game. Using Marvin Minsky’s “Society of Mind” theory, they attempt to model the workings of the minds of game players. The UEC Computer Daihinmin Competitions (UECda) have been held at the University of Electro-Communications since 2006, to bring together competitive client programs that correspond to players of Daihinmin, and contest their strengths. In this paper, the authors extract the behavior of client programs from actual competition records of the computer Daihinmin, and propose a method of building a system that determines the parameters of Daihinmin agencies by machine learning.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Games are used in artificial intelligence research as test environments for formulating internal models of the human mind. This is because the activities for problem solving of human in the real world can be considered as the activities of players in a gaming environment.

Marvin Minsky proposed a number of theories as an approach to the problem of how the human mind works in his book “The Society of Mind” (Minsky, 1988). He defined processing units called “agents” that execute small, mindless processes, and put forward the hypothesis that a mind can be created by complex interactions between agencies which are groups of these agents.

In situations where the human mind resolves problems in the real world, such as in politics, economics, or society, it is impossible to obtain perfect information about the surrounding conditions, and the actions of an unspecified number of other people will affect the results of the actions of each person. It is therefore expected that it will be possible to analyze the human decision making process by using Minsky’s “Society of Mind” theory to model the workings of the minds of players in a multi-player imperfect information game. Grimbergen presented some ideas about how to implement Minsky’s “Society of Mind” theory in game-playing domain, especially board games (Grimbergen, 2007).

We are concerned with a card game called Daihinmin (Extreme Needy), which is a multi-player imperfect information game. The UEC Computer Daihinmin Competitions (UECda) have been held at the University of Electro-Communications since 2006, to bring together competitive programs that correspond to players of Daihinmin, and contest their strengths (UECda-2015 Project Team, 2015). These competitions have spurred on the implementation of various different client programs, as well as research (Fujimura, 2013; Yoshiwara et al., 2012; Ito et al., 2013; Okubo et al., 2015; Tajima & Tagashira, 2015).

In this paper, we regard the Daihinmin agencies as neural networks such as deep learning machines (Asoh, 2013). We extract the behavior of client programs from actual competition records of the computer Daihinmin, and propose a method of building a system that determines the parameters of Daihinmin agencies by machine learning.

2\. DAIHINMIN

Daihinmin (Extreme Needy) is a card game which originated in Japan and which is also called Daifugo (Grand Millionaire). Daihinmin uses a pack of 53 cards, 13 cards per suit plus one Joker, and is normally played by 2 to 5 players. At the start of a round of the game, the same amount of cards is dealt to each of the players. The players take it in turn to play a card or cards from their hands, and the person who plays all his cards quickest wins, but the round continues until all the players’ titles are determined.

Each time a round ends, the players are given the titles of “Daifugo (the grand millionaire)”, “Fugo (the millionaire)”, “Heimin (the commoner)”, “Hinmin (the needy)”, and “Daihinmin (the extreme needy)” (when five people are playing), in the order in which they finished that round. Immediately after the initial deal of the next round, cards are exchanged as follows:

*   1\. The daihinmin hands over the two strongest cards in his hand to the daifugo who returns any two worthless cards to the daihinmin; and
*   2\. The hinmin hands over the strongest card in his hand to the fugo who returns any one worthless card to the hinmin.

After the exchange of cards, the round of the game repeats as described above.

In Daihinmin, card strengths are determined by their face values, usually in the sequence: 2, A, K, Q, J, .., 5, 4, 3. The Joker is used as a wild card that can replace any other card, and is the strongest card when played alone, with some exceptions.

When a player places a number of cards at a time, they must fulfill a “role”. Any one card in his hand has the role of “single”. The role played by a number of cards of the same face value is called a “pair” (or “group”) and that of a straight of three or more cards of the same suit is called a “sequence”.

In case where no card has been played, the player can place cards of any type of role from his hand. In case where a card or a group of cards has been played, the player can play a card or cards of the same type of role as the current card(s) if he has stronger cards in his hand. The selectable cards that can be played from that hand, based on the decision made by this player, are called “legal moves”. If the player does not hold suitable cards, he plays “pass”. Here, the player may pass even if he has cards in his hand that can be played. However, once a player has played pass, he cannot participate in the trick of the round until the cards in play are cleared. If everyone passes, the cards are cleared and the next trick starts with the last player’s turn.

Daihinmin is known to be a game having many house rules. In this paper, we adopt the house rules used for the UEC Computer Daihinmin Competition (UECda-2015 Project Team, 2015). The house rules other than those described above are as follows:

*   • Three of Diamonds Start: The round starts from the player who holds the three of diamonds;
*   • Eight Enders: When cards that contain the card of eight are played, that trick ends and the next trick starts with that player’s turn;
*   • Tight: When cards of the same suit are played consecutively, only cards of the same suit can be played until the end of the trick;
*   • Revolution: When a “group of four or more” or a “sequence of five or more” appears, the strengths of subsequent cards are reversed. This status continues until the end of the round or until another revolution occurs;
*   • Three of Spades: When the Joker has been played alone, the cards can be cleared by playing this card. The next trick starts from the player who played this card.

3\. THE “SOCIETY OF MIND” MODEL FOR DAIHINMIN

The assumption in the “Society of Mind” is that a mind can be constructed from a large number of processing units called agents which execute small, mindless processes. An agent is a part of the workings of the mind. By activating it, only behavior that does not require mind or thought is performed. Complex behaviors are implemented by interactions between agents.

In the previous study (Fujimura, 2013), we implemented the modeling of a part of the “Society of Mind” of a Daihinmin player. In the “Society of Mind” theory, an entity that implements only a simple reaction is called an agent, and a function of a group created by combining such agents is called an agency. The agencies in the Daihinmin player are as follows:

*   • Input/Output: Inputs the hands that have been played and outputs the hand that it will play;
*   • Recognition (K-line): Retains and updates information on cards in response to their input and output, and information on its own rank and judgement on the opening and the end of the round, in order to recognize the game status, and has the following lower-order agents: 
    *   o Context Recognition: Updates information on the cards retained by the players when the cards are dealt or when players, including itself, play cards;
    *   o Evaluation: Recognizes the round start/end and the status of the cards in play, and updates information when there is a change;
*   • Competition: Has the following Search and Strategy agents as lower-order agents and decides on the cards to play, according to these battles and interactions: 
    *   o Strategy: Decides on the cards to play, from the collection of legal moves, which are cards that can be played. Each agent in Strategy agents has two parameters, plus parameter and minus parameter, and it adjusts its parameters for competition;
    *   o Search: Searches for legal moves, under the current circumstances.

The correlative relationships between these agencies are shown in Figure 1. Once a game is started, the agents operating in the Daihinmin agency are activated by the intention transmission between each agent itself and the other agents linked to it. A frame structure is used in the transmission of information between agencies. For example, the frame structures of the Recognition agency and the Competition agency in Figure 1 are shown in Figures 2 and 3, respectively.

Experiments in the previous study (Fujimura, 2013) verified that a Java program which is implemented a part of the “Society of Mind” model for Daihinmin was able to correctly mimic some thought algorithms (Nakanaka and snowl) in the constrained specific situations, by adjustments of the parameters of each agent (See Figure 4). However, the parameter adjustments were done manually, so it will be necessary to enable automatic learning of the parameter adjustments in order to activate the agents in Daihinmin in response to various different statuses.

4\. A PROPOSED METHOD

The aim of this study is automatic learning of parameters of agents in the “Society of Mind” model for Daihinmin. However, it is very hard to implement it. In this paper, we regard the Daihinmin agencies as neural networks (Ishii et al., 2013; Deguchi et al., 2014). We extract the behavior of client programs from actual competition records of the computer Daihinmin, and propose a method of building a system that determines the parameters of Daihinmin agencies by machine learning. The overall configuration of the system is shown in Figure 5.

| Figure 5. Overall system configuration |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch019.f05](i/ch019.f05.png) |
| --- |

The method is as follows:

*   1\. Extract the log data for the player program in question, from the actual competition records of the computer Daihinmin;
*   2\. Extract the information that is thought to have made the Recognition agents of the Daihinmin agency react and activate as shown in the left side of Figure 5, from the log data of the entire game, and turn it into some string. For each string, add the output label of the Strategy agent (a, b, c, .., x, y, z) as shown in Table 1 that was activated with respect to the recognition information and won the competition;
*   3\. Convert into image data by mapping onto a 28x28-pixel bit map as shown in Figure 6, in order to use the library Pylearn2 (LISA Lab, 2015) of deep learning implemented by Python and to process the string of the recognition information to which was added the output labels of the Strategy agents as pseudo visual information;
*   4\. Design a learning device and learn using a learning dataset that we have created.

Here, the input data is the activation status of the Recognition agent at the time that each move is played in Daihinmin, and the output data is taken to be the Strategy agent that won the competition, with weighting added according to the activated Recognition agent.

5\. DESIGN OF LEARNING DEVICE BY DEEP LEARNING

We designed the learning device by deep learning (Asoh, 2013), which is a machine learning technique. A deep neural network (DNN) that has been designed by deep learning is a hierarchical stack of neural networks which learns the parameters of a model by prior learning and fine tuning (See Figure 7). A neural network such as that shown in Figure 8 is called an autoencoder. In our experiments, we designed a stacked denoising autoencoder (SdA) as shown in Figure 9, that consists of an input layer, which corresponds to the data set as described in the left side of Figure 5, with 784 units, an output layer, which corresponds to Strategy agents in Table 1, with 44 units, and three hidden layers having 100 units per layer.

In this learning device, learning data in the second and third layers is converted by the former layer, and the results obtained by adding noise are used. In addition, we use a model in which the layers are linked together for fine tuning. For the output layer having 44 units, the value of each unit having output labels from 0 to 43 can be regarded as being the probability of that output label. Batch learning and prior learning of parameters by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) are done in the first and second layers, and fine tuning of the entire network is done in the final layer.

6\. EXPERIMENTS AND DISCUSSION

6.1. Comparison of Learning Performance with Respect to Client Programs

We selected three types of Daihinmin client program that are based on completely different thought algorithms (default, Nakanaka, and snowl), and extracted 60,000 items for a learning dataset and 10,000 items for an evaluation dataset from competition records for those client programs.

Learning was done using an SdA as described in the previous section, on training data obtained from the above dataset. The results of the recognition rates of the learning data and the evaluation data after the learning are shown in Table 2. Here, the recognition rate is the rate of correct outputs (i.e., output labels) identical to the learning data or the evaluation data.

Table 2. Recognition rates for learning models by deep learning

| Client Program || Recognition Rate of Learning Data (%) || Recognition Rate of Evaluation Data (%) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| default || 84.27 || 84.5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nakanaka || 84.06 || 83.97 |
| snowl || 83.97 || 82.25 |

The recognition rates for the learning models obtained from each of the client programs exhibited values of at least 80%. The recognition rates of “default”, which is thought to have the simplest algorithm, were the highest. The recognition rates of “snowl”, which implements the Monte Carlo method and won the UEC Computer Daihinmin Competition, demonstrated slightly lower results. It is believed that this result indicates the complexity of thinking of the algorithm.

In order to compare the performance of a learning model that incorporates the deep learning described in Table 2, we designed a model that learns by using the nearest-neighbor method (1-NN method) (Dasarathy, 1991), with the results of our experiments being shown in Table 3. Here, the nearest-neighbor method does not perform abstraction of the learning data and is a learning method based on example.

Table 3. Recognition rates for learning model by nearest-neighbor method

| Client Program || Recognition Rate of Evaluation Data (%) |
| --- | --- |
| default || 69.65 |
| --- | --- |
| Nakanaka || 71.05 |

The learning model using deep learning that is proposed in this paper showed a higher level of recognition performance in comparison with the learning results using the 1-NN method, for all of the client programs.

6.2. Comparison of Learning Performance by Level of Addition of Noise

In this study, we used a denoising autoencoder as an unsupervised learning device. A denoising autoencoder causes data to drop out by applying noise to part of the input data, and then learns so as to reconstruct the original data. We confirmed changes in recognition rate and determined the optimal noise addition rate by changing the parameters of the noise addition rate in the hidden layers. As the results of our experiments, we found that the relationship between the noise addition rate and the recognition rate of the learning data was as shown in Figure 10.

| Figure 10. Noise addition rate and data recognition rate |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch019.f10](i/ch019.f10.png) |
| --- |

This result shows that the recognition rate of the learning data is improved by gradually lowering the noise addition rate, but since generalization decreases, the recognition rate of the evaluation data (test data) became lower. In addition, if a high noise addition rate is set, the data recognition rate drops significantly due to the high probability that pixel values will invert. In these experiments, it can be seen that when the noise addition rate has been set to between 0.04 and 0.05, the recognition rates increase for both the learning data and the evaluation data.

6.3. Comparison of Learning Performance According to Number of Learning Data Items

We performed experiments to see how the recognition rate changes for the evaluation data (test data), by varying the number of learning data items. The relationship between the number of learning data items and the recognition rate with respect to the evaluation data for the Daihinmin client program “snowl” is shown in Figure 11.

| Figure 11. Number of learning datasets and data recognition rate |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch019.f11](i/ch019.f11.png) |
| --- |

The recognition rate rises as far as the point at which the number of data items used for learning is 60,000, but no further improvements were seen when the data was increased further. To improve the learning performance, it is considered necessary to make changes to factors such as the number of layers of the autoencoder, the learning frequency, the numbers of units in the hidden layers, and the learning rate, and so on. The datasets used for learning in this study were extracted at random from actual competition records. As a result, more learning data was obtained for the selection action of “pass”, which is common in situations in which most games are won, but little learning data was obtained for selection actions which are played less often, such as revolution or sequence, so the learning performance in those situations did not improve, and such a high recognition rate could not be obtained. When creating a dataset, it is thought effective to extract data in such a manner that the numbers of labels are equal, and then perform the learning.

7\. CONCLUSION

In this paper, we used deep learning, which is a type of machine learning, to implement a decision making method for a program that plays Daihinmin, based on the “Society of Mind” theory proposed by the previous study. For implementation, we used image recognition techniques in the design of a learning device, by substituting the activity status of the Recognition agent into image data represented by a bit map, and adding the output label of the Strategy agent that won the corresponding competition.

The learning model obtained by the learning device we designed can identify the activity statuses of the input and output agents of the Daihinmin player programs with a high probability, hinting at the usefulness of emulator design using the “Society of Mind” theory.

It is thought that the use of the technique proposed in this paper will enable humans to perform easy-to-understand rationalizations of player programs using the Monte Carlo method, where the reason for selecting an action such as “Why did you play this move?” is unclear, even though they have a high winning rate, or in the analysis of the decision-making techniques of player programs when it is impossible to ask about the designer’s thoughts directly.

For future work, we try to implement the “Society of Mind” model for Daihinmin, whose parameters of all agents can be learnt automatically.
