ABSTRACT

In the present study an attempt has been made to investigate the effect of cutting parameters (cutting speed, feed rate, and depth of cut) on surface roughness and material removal rate (MRR) during dry turning operation of AISI H13 tool steel as per Taguchi’s experimental design technique using an L9 orthogonal array. Signal to noise ratio (S/N) results and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) were employed in order to investigate the optimal and significant cutting characteristics of H13 tool steel respectively. This paper focuses on optimizing the cutting parameters for minimum surface roughness and maximum MRR of H13 tool steel using high speed steel (HSS) as the cutting tool during turning. The results indicated that feed has a significant influence on surface finish and depth of cut on MRR when turning operation was carried out with HSS cutting tool. An artificial neural network model and regression equations were also developed to obtain minimum surface roughness and maximum MRR at different cutting conditions.

INTRODUCTION

Surface finish is a major factor in the functional performance of machined components. The main aim in today’s manufacturing industry is to enhance production efficiency and safety of the products. Product quality and production efficiency can be obtained through lower surface roughness and higher material removal rate while machining. Thus, it is very important to identify the factors affecting surface quality. Among these factors machining conditions play the most significant role.

Harnessing and precise prediction of machining parameters have been a major challenge in manufacturing sector over the years. Hence, it is evident that numerous research have been conducted till date in order to study the machining characteristics influencing the quality parameters of machined products. It is also known that Taguchi’s design of experiments reduces the number of experiments required and also offers a systematic yet efficient approach for optimization of various parameters with regard to performance, quality and cost. Earlier, Yang & Tarng (1998) used Taguchi method to optimize the turning operation of S45C steel bars using tungsten carbide cutting tools and reported that cutting speed, feed rate and depth of cut are the significant cutting parameters which affect surface roughness. They deduced that the maximum contribution towards affecting the surface roughness was by the feed rate, followed by depth of cut, and subsequently, the cutting speed. Lin (2004) used the Taguchi L9 orthogonal array followed by grey relational analysis to compute the optimal cutting parameters (cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut) in order to obtain the desired output in terms of tool life, cutting force and surface roughness. Nalbant et al. (2006) also used a Taguchi L9 orthogonal array to demonstrate that the insert radius and feed rate are the main parameters amongst the three controllable factors (insert radius, feed rate and depth of cut) that influence the surface roughness in turning AISI 1030 carbon steel. Subsequently, Asilturk & Akkus (2011) used an L9 orthogonal array in formulating the Taguchi method based optimization of cutting parameters (cutting speed, feed rate and depth of cut) in dry turning operation on hardened AISI 4140 with coated carbide cutting tools in a CNC turning machine. The results showed that feed rate had the most significant effect on surface roughness. Additionally, the effects of two factor interactions of the feed rate-cutting speed and depth of cut-cutting speed appeared to be important. In another study, Davis et al. (2013) used Taguchi method to compute the optimal cutting parameters such as pressurized coolant jet, rake angle, depth of cut, spindle speed and feed rate to obtain the minimal surface roughness in EN19 steel. Taguchi’s experimental design was also used in various other researches for optimizing the machining parameters to obtain minimal surface roughness values (Kirby et al., 2006; Selvaraj & Chandramohan, 2010; Tzeng et al., 2009, Asiltürk & Neşeli, 2012).

Taguchi method uses generic Signal-to-Noise (S/N) ratio to quantify the variation in output with respect to input parameters. Taguchi method treats optimization problem in two categories: static problem and dynamic problem. There are several S/N ratios available depending on the type of characteristics, including smaller-the-better, larger-the-better and nominal-the-better (Savaş & Kayikci, 2007). The three S/N ratios of common interest for optimization of static problems:

*   1.
    
    Smaller-the-better
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch030.m01](i/ch030.m01.svg) (1)
    
*   2.
    
    Larger-the-better
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch030.m02](i/ch030.m02.svg) (2)
    
*   3.
    
    Nominal-the-best
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch030.m03](i/ch030.m03.svg) (3)
    

where y[i] - i^(th) observed value of the response, n - number of observations in a trial, y - average of observed values (responses) and s - variance. Selection of S/N ratios are based on the nature of the desired output parameter viz. in order to compute minimal surface roughness desired, smaller-the-better S/N ratios are employed while larger-the-better S/N ratio are used to find the best level for maximum material removal rate.

It is also imperative to quantify the effect of various input (machining) parameters on the final output in order to compute the most significant and sensitive input parameters affecting machining. The percentage contribution of process parameters on performance characteristics can be found out using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). Ramanujam et al. (2011) used ANOVA in determining the percentage contribution of cutting speed, feed rate and depth of cut on specific power and surface roughness during turning operation of aluminium silicon carbide particulate metal matrix composite (Al-SiC –MMC) using polycrystalline diamond (PCD) 1600 grade insert. They found that depth of cut was the most significant machining parameter affecting the multiple performance characteristics (32.23%). In another study, ANOVA results were formulated for turning operation of AISI 1030 steel bars using TiN coated tools which revealed that the percentage contributions of insert radius, feed rate and depth of cut on surface roughness were 48.54%, 46.95% and 3.39%, respectively (Nalbant et al., 2006). ANOVA analysis during turning of AISI 304 stainless steel showed that feed had a contribution of 38.38% and nose radius showed 11.77% contribution in surface roughness while in case of material removal rate, depth of cut and feed showed contributions of 87.62% and 10.31% respectively (Kaladhar et al., 2012).

Artificial neural networks (ANN) are widely used in forecasting, data control etc as they provide an alternative approach to model and analyze a set of data by inferring patterns in the data. This has led to the use of ANN modelling in predicting the output parameters (surface roughness, material removal rate etc.) based on any given cutting parameters (cutting speed, feed and depth of cut). The ANN can be trained through the data taken from the conducted Taguchi orthogonal array. Various researchers have developed ANN models in the predictive modelling of surface roughness and tool wear during hard turning (Özel & Karpat, 2005); modelling thrust force and surface roughness during drilling (Tsao & Hocheng, 2008); and prediction of surface roughness during turning (Asiltürk & Cunkas, 2011). Moreover, Sharma et al. (2008) created an ANN for prediction of surface roughness by considering factor such as cutting speed, feed, and depth of cut. Moghri et al. (2014) modelled an ANN for prediction of surface roughness of polyamide-6/nanoclay nanocomposites with hyperbolic tangent sigmoid transfer function for the hidden layer and a linear transfer function for output layer. The training algorithm used was feed forward back-propagation and after trials they found out that the proposed 3-5-1 ANN network was optimum for proper prediction.

Additionally, regression analysis can be also be conducted for prediction of output responses (surface roughness, material removal rate) as a function of input parameters (cutting speed, feed and depth of cut). Hascalik & Caydas (2008) created regression equations for surface roughness and tool life with R² values of 92% and 96% respectively for turning operation. Gopalsamy et al. (2009) modelled regression equations for finding surface roughness and tool wear during machining of hardened steel. Das et al. (2013) modelled multiple second order regression equation with 95% confidence level during hard turning of AISI 4340 steel using coated carbide inserts and found the R² value to be 90.97%. Kulkarni et al. (2013) established a first order regression equation for cutting force and average flank wear with variables as cutting speed, feed and coating thickness and the R² was 98.9% and 95.8% respectively for machining AISI 304 austenitic stainless steel. Moreover, Singh et al. (2014) derived a multiple regression model for prediction of surface roughness on turning operation of Al-6061 with CNMG 120408EN-TM insert.

The present study employs systematic procedure of using Taguchi‘s orthogonal array design in process parameter (cutting speed, feed and depth of cut) control during turning operation in order to compute the optimum cutting conditions for minimum surface roughness and maximum material removal rate in turning H13 tool steel material with HSS cutting tool. Experimental values of surface roughness and material removal rate are transferred to signal-to-noise (S/N) ratios to analyze the variation of each response. Subsequently, ANOVA was conducted to investigate the quantitative effect of process parameters during turning of H13 tool steel material. Additionally, an ANN model was developed based on the experimental values obtained. Moreover, first order linear regression equations were formulated to represent the surface roughness and material removal rate as a function of the three cutting parameters used. The ANN model and regression equations were formulated for predicting the surface roughness and material removal rate at any set of cutting parameters.

EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES

Experimental Equipment Used

Turning operation for the experiments were conducted on a Precision Lathe (HMT make; model no. N26). After each turning operation, the cutting tool was ground on a grinding machine (EIFCO make) to re-sharpen the tool in order to maintain a constant nose radius. A surface roughness tester (Mitutoyo make; model no. SJ-210) was used to determine the surface roughness of the workpiece. After each machining operation, the weight of the workpiece was measured on digital weighing balance (Wenser make; model no. TTB 3). Precision lathe machine and the surface roughness tester are shown in figures 1 and 2 respectively.

Cutting Tool and Workpiece Material

HSS cutting tool are the most common and less costly as compared to other cutting tools in machining in addition to lesser power requirement, higher ability to withstand cutting forces for intermittent cutting operations in lower rigidity set ups. Moreover, HSS cutting tool with 18% W, 4% Cr and 1% V composition facilitates machining at lower cutting speeds but at higher feed and depth of cut values as compared to carbide tools. Hence, HSS cutting tool was chosen for dry turning of H13 tool steel for the present study. H13 tool steel is the most popular and versatile chromium based hot work tool steel. It has a good resistance to abrasion at both low and high temperatures, high level of toughness and ductility, uniform and high level of machinability and polishability, good high-temperature strength and resistance to thermal fatigue. Time to time grinding of cutting tool was done on the grinding machine. The workpiece was in the form of a cylindrical rod with 50 mm diameter and 100 mm length. DESIGN OF EXPERIMENT

The design of experiment (DOE) observes the variation in performance parameters from all possible combinations of process parameters. A strategically planned and executed DOE provide a great deal of information about the effect on a response variable due to one or more factors. Design of experiments is applicable to both physical processes and computer simulation models. They are mainly used to discover interactions between factors, establish and maintain quality control, to optimize a process etc. The DOE models are aimed to optimize the machining conditions for minimum surface roughness and maximum material removal rate. It was observed from various literatures that the cutting speed, feed and depth of cut were the most significant parameters affecting the surface roughness and material removal rate (Lin, 2004; Hascalik & Caydas, 2008; Gopalsamy et al., 2009; Asiltürk & Akkuş, 2011; Asiltürk & Cunkas, 2011). Hence, these parameters were selected as the input parameters for optimizing surface roughness and material removal rate. The process parameters were varied at three discrete levels as shown in Table 2.

Table 2. Levels of process parameters

| Symbol || Factors || Level 1 || Level 2 || Level 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A || Cutting speed (m/min) || 24 || 35 || 56 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B || Feed (mm/rev) || 0.1 || 0.2 || 0.32 |
| C || Depth of cut(mm) || 0.5 || 1 || 1.5 |

The comparative study of cutting performance for HSS tool was made for dry turning which was carried out on a sampling length of 50 mm. Machining time was measured for each cutting operation. After each operation of turning, the work piece was allowed to cool for a period of 15 - 20 minutes. The surface roughness (Ra) values were then measured at different positions over the machined surface. A set of three readings were taken after every pass and average surface roughness value was calculated from the obtained set of readings. After each machining the weight of the material was measured to determine the MRR.

TAGUCHI METHOD

Genichi Taguchi developed a statistical method in order to improve the quality of manufactured goods and to minimize production time thereby reducing the number of experiments (Taguchi, 1987). This method reduces the variation in a process through robust design of experiments. The Taguchi Robust Design method uses orthogonal arrays (OAs) to study a large number of process variables with a small number of experiments (Bagchi, 1993; Singh & Kumar, 2005). The parameters affecting a process and the levels at which they should be varied have to be chosen initially. In order to select the correct orthogonal array, it is necessary to find out the total degree of freedom (DOF). DOF may be defined as the number of comparisions to be made between process parameters to determine the better levels. If interaction between process parameters are taken, then the corresponding DOF gets multiplied. Array can be selected by considering the fact that the DOF of the array should be greater than the DOF of the process parameters.

It have been observed from literature that various researchers have employed the Taguchi’s L9 orthogonal array with 3 cutting parameters each with three levels thereby providing 9 possible combinations of the selected parameters during machining (Nalbant et al., 2006; Asilturk & Akkus, 2011; Kirby et al., 2006; Hascalik & Caydas, 2008; Selvaraj & Chandramohan, 2010; Tzeng et al., 2009). Moreover, an L9 orthogonal array also facilitates saving of resources in terms of money, time and raw material. Hence, in this present study, an L9 orthogonal array was selected with three process parameters (cutting speed, feed and depth of cut) varied at three different levels with the assumption that interactions between process parameters are neglected. Therefore, six DOF were found corresponding to the three process parameters which was less than the DOF of an L9 orthogonal array. In the present study, smaller-the-better \[Eq. (1)\] criterion was considered for calculation of S/N ratios in case of surface roughness values as a surface with minimum roughness was desirable. On the other hand, larger-the-better \[Eq. (2)\] criterion was employed for maximizing the MRR.

ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORK

Amongst various contemporary soft computing techniques, artificial neural network (ANN) is considered to be one of the most potent techique which has found its importance in many fields of engineering for modeling complex structures. Neural networks are simplified models of the biological nervous system and therefore have drawn their attention from the kind of computing performed by human brain. Neural network architecture is made up of an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer. The hidden and output layers have processing elements and interconnections called neurons and synapses respectively. The number of hidden layers and the nodes in each layer have to be decided very carefully, because the system cannot model the given information if it has too few hidden layer units. However, too many hidden units also hampers the network’s ability to generalise the results, which hinders the model to perform efficiently for the new incoming data. Neural networks learn by examples and hence, they have to be trained with known examples of a problem to acquire knowledge about it.

Madhu et al. (2012) modelled ANN with different hidden layer neurons and found out that 3-25-1 ANN structure with neurons 25 was considered to be optimum for predicting surface roughness. Asilturk & Cunkas (2011) used an L27 orthogonal array to train a feed forward back propagation network consisting of one hidden and one output layer and the training function used was scaled conjugate gradient and levenberg-marquardt for determining surface roughness in turning. Grzesick & Brol (2003) modelled 7-72-72-72-7 feed forward neural network with transfer function as logarithm sigmoid and training function as gradient descent with momentum and adaptivelearning rate back propagation to predict surface roughness. Prasad & Bharathi (2013) modelled a feed forward back propagation network with 5 hidden layer and training function used was Levenberg-Marquardt for predicting surface roughness and material removal rate. The number of neurons for the hidden layer was determined by trial and error method. Although the number of hidden layers may vary depending on the nature, complexity and non-linearity of the data at hand, in most of the cases, a single hidden layer was able to deal with problems.

The main objective of modelling the surface roughness and material removal rate was to quantify the relationships that exist between process and performance parameters, in order to identify the optimal cutting conditions. For this research, a feed forward back propagation network was used and an ANN model was developed using MATLAB. The ANN architecture consisted of three process parameters as input layer. In the input layer, the inputs of the problem were received and then it was forwarded to the hidden layer and subsequently, the output layer. The error signals generated due to the difference between the networks predicted values and the actual values were back propagated from the output layer and as a result it produced the output. The knowledge presented by the interconnection weight was adjusted during the learning stage using back propagation learning algorithm in order to minimize the mean square values between the actual and the desired output.

In the present scenario, various combinations for feed forward back propagation neural network were created initially using logarithmic sigmoid, hyperbolic tangent sigmoid and linear transfer functions in the hidden and output layer and also by varying the number of neurons in the hidden layer. It was observed that a single hidden layer with 10 neurons with a logarithmic sigmoid transfer function and an output layer with hyperbolic tangent sigmoid transfer function was able to predict the best results. Therefore, 3-10-1 ANN structure was selected for performance parameter modelling. In order to stabilize ANN training, the input and output data was normalized in the range \[-1,1\]. Training procedure consists of adjusting the weights and biases of a network that minimize selected function of the error between the actual and desired outputs; and thus, had to be selected by trial and error method for each performance parameters to be estimated (Gareta et al., 2006). The training function ‘gradient descent with momentum and adaptive learning rate back propagation’ was used for surface roughness and ‘Levenberg-Marquardt’ for MRR. The learning function ‘gradient descent with momentum weight and bias learning function’ was used for this model. The ANN training process performance was followed according to the mean squared error (MSE) (Sumathi & Surekha, 2010):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch030.m04](i/ch030.m04.svg) (4)

where N is the number of data, d[i] is the experimental value (target) and y[i] is the predicted value of ANN for the i^(th) training sample. The learning rate (α) of the network was kept at 0.01 and momentum (μ) at 0.9. The MSE for Ra in ANN model was obtained as 0.04682 and 0.067156 for MRR.

ANALYSIS OF VARIANCE (ANOVA)

ANOVA facilitates determination of the percentage influence of each process parameters upon the performance parameters. A series of experimental results obtained from design of experiments provides the data set for ANOVA. Herein, breaking down of higher dimensional function into lower subsets takes place. ANOVA partitions total variation into its appropriate components. Total sum of squares term can be defined as:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch030.m05](i/ch030.m05.svg) (5)

This can also be written as,

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch030.m06](i/ch030.m06.svg) (6)

where, SS[m] = nM²and SS[e] = Σ(y[i] - M)² are mean sum of squares and error sum of squares respectively, with M = 1/n Σy[i] (i = 1,2,…n) (Gopalsamy et al., 2009). While performing ANOVA, degrees of freedom should also be considered with each sum of squares. The data which are obtained are used to estimate F value of Fisher test (F-test). Variation observed in an experiment is attributed to each significant factor or interaction is reflected in percent contribution (P), which shows relative power of a factor or interaction to reduce variation. Factors and interactions with substantial P value plays an important role (Gopalsamy et al., 2009). ANOVA analysis has been used in conjunction with Taguchi’s experimental design in numerous researches related to optimization of machining parameters in order to quantify the effects of each cutting parameters on the performance responses (Selvaraj & Chandramohan, 2010; Tzeng et al., 2009; Asiltürk & Neşeli, 2012; Ramanujam et al., 2011; Nalbant et al., 2006).

Experimental and ANN Model Results

Initially, nine experiments corresponding to Taguchi L9 orthogonal array were conducted in dry condition on a sampling length of 50 mm of a cylindrical H13 bar. It was evident from figures 3 and 4 that the ANN results of Ra and MRR showed promising compliance with the experimental results as target values. Hence, it may be stated that the 10 hidden layers and nine experiments conducted to train the set were sufficient in the present case. However, more number of experiments may be conducted in future in order to justify the robustness of the present network.

ANOVA of S/N Ratios

In any machining operation, minimizing the surface roughness and maximizing the material removal rate constitute two very important criterions. It was observed that surface roughness increases with an increase in feed rate and a decrease in cutting speed. Surface roughness decreases upto a critical value of cutting speed which is attributed to the reduction in size of built up edge. Hence, surface roughness depends on feed rate (Kuttolamadom et al., 2010). The main aim of analysis of variance (ANOVA) was to determine the individual contributions of process parameters on the performance parameters. From the present study, ANOVA was carried out at 5% significant level and 95% confidence level. Table 8 and 9 show the ANOVA tables based signal to noise ratios of surface roughness (S/N[Ra]) and material removal rate (S/N[MRR]) respectively.

According to the results obtained from the analysis of variance of S/N[Ra] (Table 8) it was observed that the feed has 59.818%, cutting speed has 27.425% and depth of cut has 0% contributions towards minimizing the surface roughness. This states that feed rate is the most significant factor on surface roughness followed by cutting speed. The expected reason behind this is that the theoretical surface roughness is primarily a function of feed for a given nose radius and changes with the square of the feed rate (Chou & Barash, 1995). It may be mentioned that the cutting tool was ground to re-sharpen the cutting tool to its original nose radius after each machining operation. Hence, the dependence of surface roughness on the feed rate may be considered based on a constant nose radius value.

ANOVA of S/N[MRR] revealed that the DOC has 43.665%, cutting speed has 27.655% and feed has 26.242% contributions towards maximizing the material removal rate. Depth of cut is the most significant factor on material removal rate as larger volume of material is removed with increased depth of cut.

Regression Analysis

Multiple linear regression equations were modelled inorder to develop a relationship between process parameters in a bid to evaluate surface roughness and material removal rate. The regression equation were modelled in MINITAB software.

Ra = 5.21 – 0.0537(CS) + 16(F) + 0.695(DOC), R² = 76.3% (8)

MRR = – 11485 + 187(CS) + 25948(F) + 6122(DOC), R² = 79.2% (9)

where, CS = Cutting speed (m/min), F = Feed (mm/rev) and DOC = Depth of cut (mm). The equations 8 and 9 can be used to obtain surface roughness and material remmoval rate at any combination of cutting speed, feed and depth of cut. Figure 7 and 8 show the probability plots of Ra and MRR respectively. The normal probability plot of the residuals for surface roghness and material removal rate shows that the residuals lie reasonably close to the straight line as seen in figures 9 and 10.

The confirmation experiments are used to determine the improvements in the Ra and MRR using optimal level of machining parameters. Therefore, confirmation experiments were performed using optimal conditions (A[2]B[1]C[1]) i.e cutting speed – 35 m/min, feed - 0.1 mm/rev, DOC - 0.5 mm for Ra and (A[3]B[3]C[3]) i.e cutting speed – 56 m/min, feed - 0.32 mm/rev, DOC - 1.5 mm for MRR. CONCLUSION

The present study investigates the machining performance of AISI H13 during turning operation with HSS cutting tool. Taguchi design of experiment (L9 orthogonal array) was employed to determine the optimum cutting conditions in terms of cutting speed, feed and depth of cut for obtaining minimum surface roughness and maximum material removal rate. Optimal cutting conditions were determined using smaller the better S/N ratios for surface roughness and larger the better S/N ratios for MRR. ANOVA was employed to investigate the effects of each process parameter on the performance parameters. ANN and regression models were developed based on experimental results inorder to predict the response parameters (surface roughness and material removal rate) at different cutting conditions. Based on the conducted experiments, the following conclusions were made:

*   1\. Taguchi analysis revealed that the optimal combination for minimum surface roughness was A[2]B[1]C[1] (cutting speed – 35 m/min, feed - 0.1 mm/rev and depth of cut - 0.5 mm) and for maximum material removal rate is A[3]B[3]C[3] (cutting speed – 56 m/min, feed - 0.32 mm/rev and depth of cut - 1.5 mm).
*   2\. ANOVA results showed that feed rate had the highest influence on surface roughness with a contribution of 59.818% followed by cutting speed i.e. 27.425%. Depth of cut had no contribution in surface roughness.
*   3\. Depth of cut plays the most significant role in maximizing material removal rate with a contribution of 43.665% followed by cutting speed (27.655%) and feed (26.242%).
*   4\. The ANN model that was designed was able to promisingly predict the output for different cutting condition with MSE values of 0.04682 for Ra and 0.067156 for MRR.
*   5\. The regression equation that was developed had R² values of 76.3% for surface roughness and 79.2% for material removal rate. Second degree regression equations may be derived in the future for obtaining even higher percentages of R² values in each case.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Materials Forming and Machining Processes (IJMFMP), 2(2); edited by J. Paulo Davim, pages 47-65, copyright year 2015 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).

# Chapter 31

*   Maria Gkovedarou  
    Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece
*   Georgios N. Aretoulis  
    Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece

ABSTRACT

Over the last few years, a plethora of public works have taken place, focusing towards urban renewal, in the greater Thessaloniki district. Municipality of Thessaloniki, provided data for twelve public projects of urban renewal. Mathematical models have been proposed for cost and time prediction based on regression analysis. Furthermore, the Fast Artificial Neural Network (FANN Tool) was applied, to predict the duration and the final cost of the project, using volume of earthwork, as input variable. Both approaches could facilitate project stakeholders, to forecast the projects’ final delivery date and cost and provide early warnings for any deviation from the initial budget. The results indicate that neural networks perform better than regression analysis’ models, in the case of urban renewal projects.

INTRODUCTION

According to the Greek Urban Project’s Legislation, the definition of Urban Redevelopment is all these residential, social, economic and architectural amendments, which aim at the improvement of both the constructed area and residents’ standard of living and the preservation of the cultural elements. The Urban Redevelopment Projects were regarded necessary after a period of time, when the quality of life in cities gradually decreased. The major participants in the above procedure of realizing the project are the owner, also known as the client, the design consultant, the contractor and the construction manager (Antoniou et al. 2013).

Kim et al. (2011), cited in Tsaousoglou et al. (2013) suggest that construction industry plays an important role in leading the national economy and macroeconomic fluctuations substantially influence the construction business. Therefore, time and cost forecasting become even more essential for public projects’ control. Variation in project costs usually results in exceeding the initial estimated cost (Aretoulis et al. 2006). In the construction industry, a company’s success can be directly related to its ability to estimate project’s parameters accurately and to control costs and complete the project within budget (Popescu et al. 2003) as cited in Aretoulis et al. (2007). In general, projects that span over a long period of time tend to present time and cost overruns (Eyers, 2001). According to Park (2005) construction management is nothing but resource management. For this reason, resources are recognized as a key to meeting project schedule. Therefore, during the construction phase one important factor that facilitates project cost monitoring and control is the selection of the appropriate construction material suppliers (Aretoulis et al. 2009). Prediction models based on regression analysis and neural networks facilitate this effort. Different cost models have been developed that contribute to a more efficient financial project management. Cost models give a more vivid picture of the costs for the various elements of the project, they help to identify the most appropriate subheadings to monitor the cost reduction and they allow comparison between different approaches to select the optimal solution according to Mitten (1997) as cited in Antoniou et al. (2011). Historical data of similar projects, including final cost or time or the area of the project, are used to predict any required variable. Therefore, availability and access to historical data from similar projects is essential. Research has used statistical methods and neural networks to forecast projects’ parameters. The application of such approaches in public urban redevelopment projects has not been found to the best knowledge of the authors. This paper, firstly, describes the sample of the twelve public urban redevelopment projects from the Municipality of Thessaloniki using descriptive statistics. Thessaloniki is the second largest city in Greece, with approximately one million citizens. Prediction models of time and cost are produced via regression analysis. Alternatively, data are analyzed using the FANN Tool 1.2 (Fast Artificial Neuron Network) program. In this way duration and cost prediction of this type of projects becomes feasible, with different reliability measures, associated with each approach.

The paper firstly, presents a number of similar research efforts through a detailed review of the international literature. Methodological approach is analytically depicted, which included: projects’ description, correlation and regression analysis and application of neural networks. Then follows a brief discussion on the analyses’ results and finally, conclusions and further research are presented.

LITERATURE REVIEW

Cost analysis, project performance, cost and schedule deviations and management have attracted the interest of a plethora of researchers (Aretoulis et al., 2006; Rozenes, 2011; Bellah, Li, Zelbst, & Gu, 2013; Frei, Mbachu, & Phipps, 2013; Kimoto, Yoshizaki, & Ikeda, 2013, Mills, 2013; Ramabodu & Verster, 2013; Phadtare, 2014; Vukomanović & Radujković, 2014; Aretoulis et al., 2015; Larsen, Ussing, Brunoe, & Lindhard, 2015, Antoniou et al., 2016b).

Furthermore, a considerable amount of research has been devoted to prediction models based on regression analysis and neural networks. The main focus of such research initiatives is on time and cost overrun (Motaleb and Kishk, 2013). Such models have focused on the prediction of highway construction duration. In this context, Antoniou et al. (2016a) proposed an easy to apply cost pre-estimating and material quantities formulation method for overpass bridges. This proposed approach was based on the processing of data from fifty-seven existing bridges. The aim was to assist stakeholders in the bridge construction industry, when choosing the most cost-effective design solution, in order to reduce the risk of failure and loss of funding.

In each case of prediction models, researchers must first identify the critical factors, influencing projects’ time and cost. In this context, Williams (2008) applied in his dissertation, statistical regression analysis, in a similar research problem. His research, firstly, identified the project factors that influence the duration of highway construction projects by using past data from the Virginia Department of Transportation. He then applied the multiple linear regression analysis and he was able to find out that the influential factors were: Traffic Volume and Geometric Standards. Jiang and Wu (2007) predicted the final duration of a highway construction project applying the same methodology. The main influential factor for contract time, as defined by their research, was the estimated duration.

Irfan, Bilal, Anastasopoulos, Labi, and Moavenzadeh, (2010) used the same method for similar projects and found that the main factors were the planned cost, the expected duration of the project, the type of project and the contract type.

A similar study was developed in Thailand by Pewdum, Rujirayanyong, and Sooksatra (2009) in which prediction was focused on final duration, and final cost using Artificial Neural Network (ANN). In this case the influential parameters of the final cost were: topography, traffic volume, estimated duration, weather conditions, construction budget, contract duration, percent of as planned completion, and percent of actual completion, while the influential factors of the project’s final duration include: estimated duration, work starting date, contract duration, percent of actual completion and percent of as planned completion.

In his thesis, Attal (2010) using ANN and regression analysis and the data from the Virginia Department of Transportation, found out that ANN analysis is more accurate than regression on both cost and duration prediction and that the parameters that influence the duration are the project size and the type of geotechnical design.

Furthermore, Apanavičienė and Juodis, (2003) thoroughly examined the effective factors in construction management using Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) and conducting a questionnaire survey with contractor companies in Lithuania and USA. Prediction models have been applied not only in highway projects, but also in other types of construction projects as well. In an Australian survey, it was found that through cross-validation regression analysis, the influential factors of construction time and cost are the estimates of contact time and cost respectively (Skitmore & Ng, 2003). Research in Taiwan concerning school reconstruction, pointed out that ANN method is more accurate than regression analysis and that floor area is the influential factor of the cost and time prediction (Chen & Huang, 2006). In addition, Hoffman, Thal, Webb, and Weir (2007) compared the Bromilow’s Time-Cost (BTC) model and the regression analysis which gives more accurate predictions of time and cost.

Anastasopoulos, Labi, Bhargava and Mannering (2012), used data from 1722 projects from Indiana and the variables selected as influential were: project time delay (the difference between the actual and planned project duration), project cost (estimated as the contract bid amount for the project), project type (bridge, road construction, resurfacing, maintenance, traffic, and traffic maintenance), weather (measured as the percentage of adverse weather days in the planned project period), level of competition (defined as the number of contractors who submitted a bid for the contract), difference between the winning bid amount and the engineer’s estimate, difference between the winning bid amount and the next lowest bid, project-completion information (number of work days available for project completion, number of calendar days for project completion and whether the contract specified a fixed deadline date for project completion).

Fragkakis, Lambropoulos and Pantouvakis (2014), collected past data from recently constructed bridges and developed through statistical analysis, models, which estimate different costs of a bridge construction for the designer, the owner and the contractor. Furthermore, another research predicts the cost of pre-fabricated housing using neural networks (Vukomanović, Kararić and Radujković, 2014).

Sharma, Bansal and Parti from the National Institute of Technology Hamirpur in India, studying Linear Scheduling method and using location based planning as a depended variable, achieved cost and time scheduling of Highway projects (Sharma, Bansal and Parti, 2014). A different approach of cost estimation based on Geographic Information System (GIS) has been proposed by Bansal and Pal from National Institute of Technology Kurukshetra in India which aims in the reduction of manual work, extracting the necessary dimensions from the design drawings (Bansal and Pal, 2013). Larsen, Ussing, Brunoe and Lindhard from the Aalborg University in Denmark have reached to a conclusion that too early decision making is the main factor that affects time and cost scheduling (Larsen et al., 2015). By realizing the benefit and difficulty of project planning, Rahman, Wittman and Thabet made an overview of the commonly used project planning practices (Rahman, Wittman and Thabet, 2016). Haque and Hasin from the University of Engineering and Technology in Bangladesh using Simulated Annealing (SA) technique based on fuzzy logic theory facilitated time and cost optimization (Haque and Hasin, 2014).

As it was already mentioned, this paper deals with projects in the public sector. Due to this complexity that these projects entail, Jaafar and Chung King from the University Sains in Malaysia, gathered data through face-to-face interviews and concluded that the lack of knowledge and the involvement of inexperienced parties, either clients or consultants are the major hindrances during the construction of a public project (Jaafar and King, 2011). Similar problems are confronted by the project managers in Greece concerning the public sector which lead in extreme delays in the project schedule. This is the main problem of a public project, as it is also highlighted and emphasized by Motaleb and Kishk (2013), who used questionnaires, and distributed them, to 50 construction companies. The results indicate that parameters causing the delays in public projects are related to various groups of stakeholders, such as clients, project managers and to the projects’ financing aspects.

Abdel Aziz (2007) developed a tool, based on statistical regression relationship, which except from predicting the cost and time of a project would, also, help to evaluate the project’s performance during construction. In this study, three methods of analysis were used (Ridge Regression Analysis, General Regression Analysis and Non-Linear Partial Least-Square Regression Analysis). Data collected from completed projects included type of the pavement, contract value, duration and project miles.

Williams, Hildreth and Vorster (2009), used 311 projects’ data from Virginia and Texas and followed the notion, that construction time is independent of the cost and thus they established two different models with variables considering time, uniform project code, district, scope of work (work type), contract execution date, contract acceptance date, highway description (state, primary, federal etc.) and contract setting (urban, rural). For the cost prediction model, the incorporated variables were: project length, annual daily traffic, geometric design standard, four lane length, two lane length, bridge length, bridge type, length of loop/ramps, bridge width, length of curb and gutter, shoulder or curb and gutter, median length, median type, number of new signals, row length, row width, percentage of residential/commercial/industrial/agricultural use.

Finally, Sweis, Sweis, Al-Shboul and Al-Dweik (2015), through a questionnaire survey, distributed in construction companies, concluded that Information Technology systems are rather beneficial concerning the quality of a project and the associated cost.

METHODOLOGICAL APPROACH

Initially, a total of twelve urban redevelopment projects were recorded. Then, the identification of required variables for the proceeding analyses followed, encompassing SPSS application and Neural Networks. Statistical analysis included correlation analysis and regression analysis. Both methods make useful predictions. The whole methodological approach can be depicted in Figure 1 in the Appendix.

Project Sample Description

The department of Urban Redevelopment of the Municipality of Thessaloniki contributed to the provision of the twelve projects’ data. Table 1 in the Appendix presents the projects that stretch throughout all regions of the greater Thessaloniki district and highlights the most important common variables among all 12 projects.

Most of these projects have ran out of budget. With regards to the repair and redevelopment projects, these have been executed without delays, as they do not entail specialized work approaches. It is worth mentioning that the project with the maximum “Earthwork Cost”, also has the maximum Estimated Budget, Final Cost and Final Duration.

Prediction Models based on Statistical Analysis

Collected data were used to produce an SPSS database. The latter included 12 cases and 6 variables: Earthwork Volume and Cost, the Estimated and the Final Cost, the Estimated and Final Duration. The above-mentioned variables were selected as they were the common data among all twelve urban redevelopment projects. Descriptive statistics, are evaluated via SPSS and are presented in Table 2 in the Appendix.

As far as the Descriptive Statistics are concerned, according to Table 2, the mean value of the variables are the following: Earthwork Volume is 19,180 m3, Earthwork Cost is 455,718 Euros, Estimated Duration is 287 days, Final Duration is 418 days, Estimated Budget is 5,507,600 Euros and Final Cost is 8,610,937 Euros.

Correlation Analysis

The first aim of the research focuses on the prediction of projects’ final duration. Therefore, research identifies variables that could affect and forecast project’s final duration. Correlation Analysis, is used to determine the required variables. To establish correlation among the variables, significance should be less than .05. Strength of correlation is indicated by the Pearson value ranging between 1 and -1. Table 3 in the Appendix presents the results. When the Pearson value ranges from .5 to .65, then the correlation between the variables is mediocre and when the Pearson value ranges from .65 to 1, then the correlation between the variables is strong (as indicated with the use of bold letters in highlighted cells and the inclusion of asterisks, in Table 3).

The results of the correlation analysis (Table 3) suggest the following:

*   • Earthwork Volume is associated with most of the variables. It presents extremely high correlation with Earthwork Cost, then follows Estimated Budget, Final Cost and finally Estimated Duration.
*   • Earthwork Cost is correlated with Estimated Budget, Final Cost and Estimated Duration.
*   • Estimated Duration is correlated with Final Duration, Final Cost and Estimated Budget.
*   • Final Duration is correlated with Final Cost
*   • Final Cost is correlated with Estimated Budget

More specifically, Table 3 indicates that there is strong positive correlation between the Earthwork Volume and the Earthwork Cost, Estimated Duration, Estimated and Final Cost respectively.

Regression Analysis

Database includes information from twelve public projects of urban redevelopment –in terms of cost, and time of completion. These projects reveal the greatest possible uniformity of the values that were included in the analysis. In this way, a database was created using Microsoft Excel to proceed in the subsequent analyses. The values of the database were inserted in the IBM SPSS Statistics, so the correlation between the independent and dependent variables could be examined. Firstly, the correlation analysis was developed and the correlation between the quantitative variables was identified. Furthermore, the Bivariate correlation’s analysis took place, which is the tool to investigate the correlation between quantitative variables. Pearson correlation coefficient was chosen along with a two – tailed test of significance. Field (2009) identified Pearson correlation coefficient and the Significance value, as the most significant factors for the evaluation of the results. The Pearson correlation coefficient takes on values close to 1 for strong relationships and -1 for adverse strong relationships. In addition Significance values less than .05 (<.05) reveal strong correlation and those values between 0.06 and 0.05 demonstrate the tendency that the variables correlate.

Having identified the potential correlations among the selected common variables, the current paper applies the linear regression analysis. The selected method is the stepwise. The aim is to predict the final duration and cost. The employed variables are the Earthwork Volume and Cost which were also the most common variables in the urban redevelopment projects. The analysis provided certain results. Table 4 in the Appendix, indicates the correlation rate between the dependent variable and the independent variables. The R Square is the proportion of variance in the dependent variable, which can be explained by the independent variable.

The corresponding model for the Final Duration is:

F.D. = 95,358+ 1,124\* E.D.

Where: F.D.: Final Duration (days) and E.D.: Estimated Duration (days). It becomes obvious that the model indicates that there is an extensive increase in the duration of the completed project (Table 5 in the Appendix). Similarly, prediction model of the Final Cost, the Table 6 in the Appendix indicates that the 82% of the Final Cost’s value is interpreted by the Earthwork’s Cost value.

The produced prediction model, according to Table 7 (Appendix), is:

F.C. = 2533125, 68 + 13,337 \* E.C.

Where: F.C.: Final Cost (in Euros) and E.C.: Earthwork Cost (in Euros). It becomes obvious that the model indicates that there is an extensive increase in the budget of the completed project.

Application of Neural Networks

An Artificial Neural Network (ANN), is a mathematical model or computational model that tries to simulate the structure and/or functional aspects of biological neural networks. Research predicts the variables “Final Cost” and “Final Duration” by means of the FANN Tool program.

In this case, the variables Final Cost and Duration and Earthwork Volume from twelve projects of urban redevelopment are inserted in the form of text file. Earthwork Volume is the only common value among the twelve projects and also a contributory factor concerning the time and the cost of a project. Data are converted and scaled through the function: \[(Input Value – Minimum Value) / (Maximum Value – Minimum Value)\] and the final values range from 0 to 1.

The neural network is trained through the process “FANN\_Train\_Prop” and the termination criterion is the “FANN\_Stopfunc\_MSE” which uses the (Mean Square Error: MSE) for the termination of the training process. The number of the repeat cycles for the training program has been set to 1000. The number of the neurons’ layers is three and there is only one hidden layer. The activation function is termed “FANN\_Sigmoid\_Symmetric” which is the optimal choice as it encompasses the rule of no linearity, which makes the network even more powerful and accurate. This program is employed in this paper for the approximate prediction of the variables Final Cost and Duration (output=2), if the variable “Earthwork Volume” is inserted by the operator (input=1). All the above options are depicted in the Figure 2 and Figure 3 in the Appendix.

DISCUSSION

The approach included, implementation of statistical analysis and more specifically correlation and regression analysis and alternatively application of neural networks in order to predict the project’s final cost and duration. Statistical analysis provided a linear approach to the problem whereas neural networks adopted a non-parametric view to the problem at hand. FANN Tool program provided an almost accurate time and cost prediction as the deviation from the target value is almost 0.03% for the project duration prediction and 0.06% for the cost prediction. As a result, the time and cost prediction via FANN Tool program is quite promising. From the two presented approaches the most successful one is the implementation of neural networks, which seems to provide a better adjustability to the available data. The legislative framework, which defines the implementation procedures for such type of projects, guarantees that especially a neural network based system will be delivering reliable estimates.

CONCLUSION

Over the last few years, in the greater Thessaloniki district, a plethora of public works have taken place, focusing on urban redevelopment. Public works are conducive to the economic, social and cultural upgrade of each respective region. Depending on the category of the project and the need which they serve, the life span and the construction costs can vary dramatically. The variations presented can be caused also by a number of additional factors such as the funding method.

Works of public infrastructure redevelopment affect, on a great extent, the daily lives of the residents; therefore, a carefully planned time-frame combined with a tightly managed budget is of vital importance. As a result, the meticulous study of the potential means of forecasting the cost and the duration of those projects is definitely beneficial.

In the current study, the Municipality of Thessaloniki provided extensive data for twelve public projects of urban redevelopment. The given paper initially produced proper mathematical prediction models of cost and time span through the method of Regression Analysis. The aim of those models is to aid, not only the Authority that delegates those projects but also the rest of the participants, citizens included, to forecast the final date of delivery but also to identify and quantify any divergence from the original budget.

Secondly, the paper focused on the use of the FANN Tool 1.2 Software, which caters the ability to predict the timeframe and the total cost of a certain project, through the use of Volume of Earthworks as an input variable.

Descriptive Statistics (Table 2, Appendix), highlight that the projects’ Final Duration values (mean value 418 days) are almost double the projects’ values in comparison to the Estimated Duration (mean value 287 days). Moreover, the values of the Estimated Budget (mean value 5,507,600 Euros) are also much lower than those of Final Cost (mean value is 8,610,937 Euros). As a result, the Time and Cost prediction before the project construction is not very accurate as it is highlighted by the final project performance.

With regard to the correlation analysis, (Table 3, Appendix), increased Earthwork Volume leads to an increase of the previous variables. Respectively, there is strong positive correlation between the Earthwork Cost and the Estimated Budget and Final Cost, also, between the Estimated Duration and the Final Duration. Strong positive correlation exists between the Final Duration and the Final Cost and between the Final and Estimated Budget.

As far as the regression analysis is concerned, the prediction model of the Final Duration depends mainly on the Estimated Duration. Table 4 in the Appendix refers to the coefficient of multi-definition R². This factor indicates the variability percentage of the dependent variable in connection with the independent. The value of R²\=0.69 means that the 69% of the Final Duration’s value is interpreted by the Estimated Duration’s value. In the same context, Table 6 (see Appendix), presents a strong association among the Earthwork Cost and the Final Cost. In fact, 82% of the Final Cost’s value is interpreted by the Earthwork Cost value (R²\=0.82). It could be noted that in the case of the project duration, the deviation of the actual duration from the corresponding estimated value is extensive. In the case of cost, the facts are better, as estimated and actual project cost are more closely associated. Furthermore, the values of adjusted R square, for both models, either in comparison to R square values or as standalone values, indicate that the models could be generalized.

At the same time, the FANN Tool program, employs the input scaled value (from 0 to 1), is the Earthwork Volume. After the program having been trained using the recorded project data, it provides two output scaled values: Final Duration and Cost. Through this analysis, it can be concluded that the cost and time prediction of FANN Tool program is far more accurate than the models of the Regression Analysis. This finding is in agreement with the international literature.

There is no doubt that more data and information from relevant urban redevelopment projects lead to more accurate prediction models through the regression analysis and the FANN Tool program. For further research these data could be enhanced by more relevant projects and more variables like the concrete quantity or the total area of the project. Concerning the FANN Tool program, the output values have limited deviation which is normal. More input variables are needed to increase the accuracy of the prediction. Therefore, FANN Tool forecasting capabilities will be tested using simultaneously as input variables: earthwork volume, estimated duration and earthwork cost.

Furthermore, the prediction of the delays in public projects is of the utmost importance and ought to be further investigated. Finally, the prediction of the duration and the final cost of each and every stage of the project are also a focus of future research. However, many difficulties emerge as these projects are public and obstacles exist such as bureaucracy, and strikes incommoding the progress of the project.
