# Chapter 32

*   Xinyao Sun  
    University of Alberta, Canada
*   Anup Basu  
    University of Alberta, Canada
*   Irene Cheng  
    University of Alberta, Canada

ABSTRACT

Hand pose estimation for a continuous sequence has been an important topic not only in computer vision but also human-computer-interaction. Exploring the feasibility to use hand gestures to replace input devices, e.g., mouse, keyboard, joy-stick and touch screen, has attracted increasing attention from academic and industrial researchers. The fast advancement of hand pose estimation techniques is complemented by the rapid development of smart sensors technology such as Kinect and Leap. We introduce a hand pose estimation multi-sensor system. Two tracking models are proposed based on Deep (Recurrent) Neural Network (DRNN) architecture. Data captured from different sensors are analyzed and fused to produce an optimal hand pose sequence. Experimental results show that our models outperform previous methods with better accuracy, meeting real-time application requirement. Performance comparisons between DNN and DRNN, spatial and spatial-temporal features, and single- and dual- sensors, are also presented.

INTRODUCTION

Hand gesture is a powerful communication mechanism and hand pose estimation has been a popular research topic in the area of computer vision, image processing and Human Computer Interaction (HCI). While sign language plays an essential role in human-to-human communication, hand gestures have often been used in HCI applications, replacing a variety of traditional input devices (e.g., mouse, keyboard, joystick, touch pad, and touch screen). The use of hand movements allows users to interact with computer interfaces directly and naturally without the restriction imposed by mechanical devices. There are more and more smart-sensor based contact-free input systems available to enhance this touch-free experience. Compact smart sensors have become consumer products and are commonplace for home entertainment systems (Blaha & Gupta, 2014). High precision sensors also benefit medical and clinical applications, where touching mechanical input device requires a re-sterilization step before continuing the operation (Ebert, Flach, Thali, & Ross, 2014) (Chng, 2012). Touch-free input systems based on hand gestures have advanced HCI technology to a new era and their performances are improving.

Motion detection based on smart sensing is commonly seen in consumer applications (e.g., games). The trend of touch-free HCI is strongly supported by two technologies. First is the release of new optical sensors such as Microsoft’s Kinect and Leap Motion Controller (LMC). Kinect is able to provide both color and depth information by using an RGB camera and a depth sensor. The Kinect technology has been successfully applied to analyze rigid human body movement. Researchers (Tang, Lu, Wang, Huang, & Li, 2015) (Oikonomidis, Kyriazis, & Argyros, 2011) combine both color and depth information to precisely detect the location of human hands and predict joint positions, and then construct a hand skeleton following an Inverse Kinematics process (Sridhar, Mueller, Oulasvirta, & Theobalt, 2015). Compared to Kinect, LMC is a higher precision but shorter detection range consumer-grade Infrared Radiation (IR) based optical sensor developed by Leap Motion Inc. LMC is primarily designed for hand gesture and hand finger position detection. LMC offers precision at millimeter level and is able to capture fully articulated hand skeleton at a sampling rate of over 120 per second. Both Kinect and LMC sensors enhance the 2D hand motion image features with a third dimension – depth information. The depth data accelerates hand detection and increases the accuracy of hand pose estimation.

The second complementing technology is the rapid development of deep learning algorithms. Deep Neural Network (DNN) has shown its capability in feature extraction by simulating the functionalities of the human brain with layers of neurons. A classical DNN model can be used to automatically extract and analyze features from raw data. The model has been successfully applied in many pattern recognition problems relating to speech signals and images (Lic, Seide, & Yuc, 2011) (Seide, Li, & Yu, 2011). Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), as a standard architecture of Deep Learning, shows excellent performance when solving many computer vision problems. Researchers applied CNN to predict the 3D joint locations of a hand with a depth map, or with a depth map and 2D RGB image combined (Oberweger, Wohlhart, & Lepetit, 2015) (Tang, Jin Chang, Tejani, & Kim, 2014).

Despite these technological advances of hardware and algorithms, accurately tracking the articulation of hand poses in real-time is still an open research problem. A sensor has a limited viewing volume and there is noisy sensor data caused by the complex and fast finger movements (Von Hardenberg & Bérard, 2001). The uncontrolled environment can lead to possible background cluttering, which adversely affects image-based detection techniques (Chen, Georganas, & Petriu, 2007). Too many degrees of freedom of the human hand push the pose analysis process into a very high dimensional space. Computational complexity for a fully articulated hand model is often high, leading to real-time performance issues. Fingers’ similarity and out-of-plane transformation lead to full or partial occlusion with each other (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016). The limited and static viewpoint of a standalone sensor reduces the effective user interaction space (Supancic, Rogez, Yang, Shotton, & Ramanan, 2015) in HCI applications.

In this work, we focus on improving hand pose estimation and enhancing existing single-view based tracking systems. We propose using multiple sensors and fuse the estimations from multiple sources in order to predict hand pose motion more accurately. We apply Deep Learning techniques to intelligently decide which sensor generates the best pose estimation. In our experiments, we tested the proposed DNN model on a set of sensor data in the spatial domain with good results. Furthermore, we applied a Deep Recurrent Neural Network (DRNN) model to perform a cross domain analysis by integrating temporal information with spatial information, which allows us to compare the performances of the DNN and DRNN approaches. We tested our motion fusion technique by setting up a dual LMC system, but our fusion technique can be generalized to multi-sensors composed of other types of sensors. We make the following contributions in this work: 1) We establish a multi-sensor fusion architecture to improve the classical single-view based tracking systems. 2) We demonstrate the principle system’s performance and feasibility with different fusion strategies. 3) We propose and evaluate two Deep Learning based models to improve the accuracy of continuous hand pose estimation in a dual-sensor setup, showing competitive performance with other fusion algorithms. Our proposed method can be used offline or in real-time and can benefit applications where hand motion is the focus of performance efficiency and assessment.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews computer vision based hand movement analysis techniques, including our earlier work on hand motion fusion. Section 3 describes the proposed multi-sensor system and motion fusion algorithm. Section 4 presents and analyzes experimental results. Section 5 gives the conclusion and future directions.

RELATED WORK

Computer vision techniques have been applied to analyze human hand movements for decades. Traditional vision-based methods focus on hand pose estimation via processing camera-captured images. Early techniques often require extra markers or colored gloves to help the image processing task, but marker and glove setup are complex and cumbersome for users to wear. In recent studies, researchers incline to explore marker-free hand tracking systems for HCI applications. In general, hand pose estimation techniques can be divided into two categories: model-based (generative) and learning-based (discriminative) (Zhou, Wan, Zhang, Xue, & Wei, 2016). Model-based approaches rely on observing the hand geometry and quantify the discrepancy between the synthesized and observed images to obtain the hand pose (Andrea et al., 2015). These methods could generate accurate hand poses but need effective optimization and always require intensive computation, which degrades real-time performance (Sridhar, Mueller, Oulasvirta, & Theobalt, 2015). Learning-based methods apply a regression function to classify the image appearance by labeling hand pose. Learning-based approaches have been shown to be more efficient than model-based approaches (Keskin, Kıraç, Kara, & Akarun, 2012). Most learning-based methods simply represent a hand pose with independent joints without physical interpretation of the hand. However, the tracking of an articulation hand with physical properties is essential because of the presence of the kinematic correlation between joints.

In pace with the recent sensor device development and the study of deep learning techniques, more and more researchers try to use DNNs to learn features automatically from sensor data. CNN has shown its effectiveness in the image and video analysis (Ciregan, Meier, & Schmidhuber, 2012) (Karpathy et al., 2014). Some researchers (Sinha, Choi, & Ramani, 2016) evaluated the different architectures for CNNs in order to predict the hand joint locations via a given depth map. To generate more valid hand poses, (Zhou, Wan, Zhang, Xue, & Wei, 2016) proposed a model-based deep learning approach to exploit the hand geometry via a layer for mapping the joint angles to joint locations, using non-linear forward kinematics. Recently, the Microsoft Kinect sensor has been routinely used by researchers and developers to analyze human hand postures. (Tompson, Stein, Lecun, & Perlin, 2014) and (Tang, Lu, Wang, Huang, & Li, 2015) used a neural network to process both color and depth images captured from Kinect, to recognize a number of hand poses without too much constraint imposed on background or color, and is able to achieve real-time performance.

We believe that the current hand pose estimation techniques can be improved by fusing tracked data from multiple sensors and applying enhanced DNN learning. Although we use dual sensors in the current implementation, our work also focuses on how to build an ultimate tracking system with multi-sensors in general and fuse all sensor data to generate reliable hand pose estimation at each time step. For sensor data fusion, the optimally fused result can be a combination of data from the same acquisition device, or derived from individual sources (Elmenreich, 2002). The sensor data fusion problem can be addressed as uncertainty reduction. The analysis of fused data based on multiple sources reduces uncertainty inherent to taking individual sources separately. In the last few years, applying deep learning techniques to merge sensor samples has increased rapidly. In (Giering, Venugopalan, & Reddy, 2015), researchers employed a Deep CNN to fuse 2D video and 3D LiDAR data sequences unsupervised for estimating the perception of an automated vehicle's physical surrounding. (Weichert, Bachmann, Rudak, & Fisseler, 2013) employed a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model to provide an estimation of the current camera pose based on previous poses and inertial measurements. The proposed sensor fusion system provides a robust final pose estimation, leading to better immersion and accuracy for augmented reality applications (e.g. games).

The authors of (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), used data from a LMC sensor array to obtain the optimal hand pose estimation. In this method, a SVM model is trained as a classifier to identify what kinds of hand positions and orientations are likely to generate lower estimation error. However, only features in a discrete spatial domain are trained and the algorithm does not consider continuously hand motions in the temporal domain. In a subsequent method (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), the authors incorporate selected spatial sensor parameters used in (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), but also combine the analysis of temporal motion features calculated as Sided Stable Factor (SSF) to assess the performance of individual sensors. Authors tested SSF on effective flow analysis in the temporal domain. Experimental results show that the temporal features are essential for assessing the performance of each sensor’s performance in a multi-sensor system. To improve the accuracy and address the limitation imposed by occlusion, we introduce a multi-sensor fusion technique, applying deep learning to focus on both spatial and temporal analysis. Experiments demonstrate that our new techniques perform better than previous work in a real-time application.

MULTI-SENSOR SYSTEM AND HAND DATA FUSION

Overview of Proposed System

The obstacles in developing an efficient and robust hand tracking system for HCI include the high dimensionality of motion data, the chromatically uniform appearance of the target region and finger self-occlusion that frequently occurs during hand movements. LMC is an IR based optical sensor, offering precision at millimeter level, and is able to capture fully articulated hand skeleton at a sampling rate of over 120 frames per second. Unfortunately, the tracking volume of LMC is limited to only a small area above the sensor, and the performance gets worse when the target is moving close to the boundary of the trackable area (Weichert, Bachmann, Rudak, & Fisseler, 2013). In fact, these issues are common in all single-view based tracking system. We propose a multi-sensor tracking system with a motion fusion strategy to combine the motion data captured from each sensor based on finger-tip error estimation, and generate a final optimal fused hand pose sequence. In an earlier work (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), the authors have proved that a more accurate pose estimation at each time step can be obtained based on a subset of the pose data from each sensor. In another work (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), it is shown that analyzing the temporal features across frames can reveal the accuracy of each sensor’s pose estimation. In this work, we set up a dual-sensor system with a user interface for capturing and visualizing the hand motions. The two LMCs are placed at different viewing positions as shown in Figure 1. Note that occlusion of the thumb and index fingers by other fingers can occur for the sensor on the right, leading to a worse hand pose estimation if only the right-hand side sensor is used. The left sensor has a direct view of the thumb and index finger, and thus can produce better hand pose estimation than the right sensor, for this given hand pose.

| Figure 1. Using two sensors combined provide a better view of all fingers than using just one senor |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f01](i/ch032.f01.png) |
| --- |

| Figure 2. Illustration of dual-sensor motion fusion work flow |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f02](i/ch032.f02.png) |
| --- |

Different sensors placed at appropriate positions should alleviate the occlusion problem because there is a possibility that at least one of the sensors has the desired view; in other words, the sensors can complement each other’s viewpoint. Once the data is collected from multiple sensors, the next step is fusion. The fusion work flow is shown in Figure 2. Our goal is building an intelligent classifier to determine the optimal pose estimation from a sensor array at each time step. In this work, we implement and evaluate two deep models as the classifier. We build the models offline with a training set, which uses a feature vector composed of each sensor’s sensory data. We also compare our work with other up-to-date techniques in following of the paper.

Multi-sensor Communication Interface

The officially released Leap Motion driver and SDK only support a single host at one time. To construct a multi LMC tracking system, we explored the Linux Containers (LXC) (Seo, 2014) to create multiple stand-alone Linux systems on a single Linux host. Each guest LXC is connected to one LMC device via USB port pass-through. The sensor data is streamed via local socket connection from each guest system to the host system and synchronized. This software design allows us to capture and visualize motion data from a scalable sensor array on a single computer as shown in Figure 3. The software records and outputs the captured motion data from each sensor, which is used for data integration and evaluation later in our fusion algorithm.

| Figure 3. Screenshot of our multi-sensor tracking system’s graphical user interface |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f03](i/ch032.f03.png) |
| --- |

Sensor Placement

We use the same setup as described in (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), which is depicted in Figure 1 and Figure 4. Two LMCs are aligned horizontally on a table surface with a 40cm distance in between. This configuration minimizes the interference between the two LMCs’ IR projections, which can affect each other's performance. The LMC has a field of view of about 150 degrees. A 40cm separation distance ensures that both sensors have a good viewing angle within the interaction space. The interaction point is at 10 cm above the sensors. This placement ensures a reasonable large tracking volume for the whole system, which provides a reasonable interaction height above the sensors as well.

| Figure 4. Illustration of a dual-sensor setup |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f04](i/ch032.f04.png) |
| --- |

Pose Error Estimation

To evaluate the accuracy of the hand pose estimation, we use the metric described in (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), which defines the error as the mean of Euclidean distances (in millimeters) of each estimated fingertip from its ground truth position. The computation is shown in Equation 1:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.m01](i/ch032.m01.svg)

where f[i] and g[i] denote respectively the estimated position and ground truth position of the i\-th fingertip in 3D vector representation. Each finger’s estimation error is defined as Euclidean distance between f[i] and g[i] as ||f[i]‑g[i]||. The final pose estimation error E for one hand at each time step is represented as the mean of total five finger’s estimation errors. We use this metric for sensor selection so that each data point is labeled with the sensor generating the minimum error E. The evaluation of hand motion fusion is also based on this error.

Spatial-Temporal Features

We observed that even in situations with high occlusion and bad pose estimation, the LMC still tracks palm position and orientation accurately. The study in (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016) confirms the hypothesis that positions and orientations of the hand dictate the pose estimation error. Therefore, the following twelve floating point values given by the sensors associated with positions and orientations are used as feature vector for each sensor:

*   1\. Three (X, Y, Z) values of the palm position relative to the sensor.
*   2\. Three (X, Y, Z) values of the palm plane normal relative to the sensor.
*   3\. Three (X, Y, Z) values of the forward direction of the hand.
*   4\. Local Roll rotation of the hand. The value is the roll angle of the palm with respect to the horizontal plane of the sensor
*   5\. The dot product between the palm normal and the direction the sensor is facing
*   6\. Sensor confidence estimation. The value is generated by the LMC internal algorithm in the range of \[0,1\]

The above 12 feature values represent the palm characteristics in the spatial domain which are generated by LMC API. Our motion capture software described in Section 3.2 is able to record all the feature data from each sensor concurrently. We use a pre-trained SVM classifier to select optimal hand pose from a sensor array, with these features input as a discrete hand motion dataset. However, HCI applications always involve hand pose estimation in a continuous hand movement sequence. Thus, we follow our previous finding and integrate temporal flow analysis with the spatial information, to increase the accuracy of hand pose estimation. In (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), we used Sided Stable Factor (SSF) to assess how well the hand pose estimation in the current frame fits the flow within a time segment. Temporal features have been used in motion prediction by researchers (Tian & Zhou, 2013) (Anagnostopoulos & Hadjiefthymiades, 2013), but integrating Spatial-temporal features in hand and finger pose estimation is still not fully explored. In our previous work, we handcrafted a temporal domain feature – SSF, to assess how well the current spatial data fits the continuous motion flow of each sensor. Interested readers can refer to the detailed computation in (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016). In order to assess the quality of a continuous motion flow, each sensor’s feature vector is enriched with 7 new (floating point) temporal features:

*   1\. SSF for three (X, Y, and Z) values of the palm position relative to the sensor.
*   2\. SSF for three (X, Y, and Z) values of the forward direction of the hand.
*   3\. SSF for the value of the dot product between the palm normal and the direction the sensor is facing.

All 19 elements are combined as a spatial-temporal feature vector to represent each sensor’s state at each time step. A SVM classifier is then trained with a labeled dataset. The classifier is used to intelligently select pose estimation and the associated sensor. In order to explore the feasibility of applying deep learning in our classification process, we implemented and tested a DNN model instead of using a SVM classifier. We built DRNN model to learn temporal features instead of pre-defining a windows size and handcrafting features as in the SSF computation (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016). Detail of the neural network is explained below.

Optimal Hand Pose Selection using Deep Neural Network

Deep Neural Network (DNN) on Spatial Domain

DNNs have been widely used in various research fields (Schmidhuber, 2014), and shown to be effective in feature learning. The DNN approach provides a feasible solution on feature extraction and selection, where it can automatically analyze and extract useful information from input data. We first tried a simple DNN architecture and input the spatial data selected from the LMC sensor output as described in Section 3.4. The structure of this DNN is shown in Figure 5.

| Figure 5. Illustration of our deep neural network classifier |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f05](i/ch032.f05.png) |
| --- |

The input data has a vector length of 24, which is a combination of two sensors selected spatial information. We normalize each value in the input vector to the range \[-1, 1\]. The sensor with more accurate hand pose estimation has index value “1” while the other sensor has index value “0.” Thus, the target output is a “one-hot” vector (length of two in our dual-sensor setup). If at a certain frame, the first sensor generates the lower pose estimation error than the second sensor. The target output vector is \[1, 0\]. The size of each layer is labeled in the graph, i.e., 24, 200, 200, 300, … (number of neurons). Information received from the dual-sensor system is passed to the network and forwarded to seven fully connected layers (“FC” in graph) composed of Rectify Linear Units (ReLU), which is a nonlinearity activation module of a neuron with activation function defined in Equation 2, where x is the input to a neuron, and f(x) is this neuron’s output. This formulation has been shown to have improved training speed and better discriminative performance compared to other standard units (e.g. classical sigmoid units) (Krizhevsky, Sutskever, & Hinton, 2012).

f(x) = max(0,x)

Lastly, we use a softmax activation function (Equation 3) in our final layer for classification, where K is the number of sensors representing two distinct classes, x is the input of a neuron and f[j](x) is the output of j\-th neuron’s output in final layer which also represent the score of j\-th class. The output of the last softmax layer represents a distribution used to estimate the probability of which sensor likely generates more accurate pose estimation. To train the DNN, we considered an average cross-entropy error over batched training samples as shown in Equation 4, where n denotes the batch size and f[j] denotes the j\-th class score relating to Equation 3. During training, the error measure is used to update the weights in the DNN by back-propagation.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.m02](i/ch032.m02.svg) for j\=1,…,K

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.m03](i/ch032.m03.svg) for j\=1,…,K

Generally, stacking too many fully connected layers will cause overfitting to the training data. To tune the network to be less sensitive to some specific weights of neurons, we apply Dropout regularization technique to our learning model (Figure 5). This can achieve better generalization and reduce the overfitting issue on training data. Dropout is a technique where it randomly ignores some neurons during training to prevent units from over co-adapting (Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, & Salakhutdinov, 2014). In real-time, the pre-trained DNN reads input data from both LMC sensors and output a probability distribution to determine which sensor’s estimation is expected to have minimum pose estimation error.

Deep Recurrent Neural Network on Spatial-Temporal Domain

Our DNN model described above only focuses on a single frame at each time step and analyzes a set of selected skeleton sensor data from each LMC. In (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016), it was demonstrated that the temporal information is also essential to assess the performance of each single sensor. In this respect, our DNN model can be enhanced by incorporating the information in the temporal domain. Although our earlier SSF technique has shown the capability of describing the temporal flow in a frame segment, it requires a pre-defined segment windows size, which is a hyper-parameter and can affect the classifying accuracy if an inappropriate size is used.

| Figure 6. Illustration of our deep recurrent neural network classifier |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f06](i/ch032.f06.png) |
| --- |

To analyze the temporal features, we take advantage of the RNN architecture, which is a powerful deep learning structure widely used for learning sequential tasks (Sutskever, Vinyals, & Le, 2014) (Graves, Mohamed, & Hinton, 2013). We embed 4 layers of stacked RNN with LSTM (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) units into a fully connected DNN model to form a DRNN as shown in Figure 6. The input and output are kept in the same format as explained in our DNN model. The key advantage of LSTM is its ability to learn how much previous memory should be retained.

| Figure 7. Illustration of unrolled stacked LSTM |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f07](i/ch032.f07.png) |
| --- |

At a given time step, the first two fully connected layers analyze the sensors’ spatial domain features. The output is forwarded to a stack of LSTMs, where each LSTM layer at time t inside the stack maintains its own state. Each LSTM layer is trained to decide what information is to be thrown away from two sources: the previous layer at time t, and its own previous state at t-1. Meanwhile, it is also trained to learn what new information should be stored in the current state. It outputs the final analyzed information to the next layer. It also outputs its state to the next time step. The ability of a LSTM layer to support further classification not only is based on the current frame, but also relies on the long-short term memory of the previous information at the t-1 step as shown in Figure 7. The network is expected to learn and extract the temporal domain features and merge them with the current frame’s spatial domain features, in order to deliver the final optimal sensor classification. We use the same Dropout regularization technique and cross-entropy loss function in this model as described in Section. 3.6.1.

EXPERIMENTS AND EVALUATION

Experiment Setup

Since this work represents a more in-depth research following our earlier work, we used the same experimental environment. We set up an artificial hand and manually modeled three hand poses commonly used in HCI applications: 1) grab; 2) open hand, and 3) pinch, as shown in Figure 8(a). The articulated artificial hand model has similar dimensions to the real human hand. There are a large number of usable hand poses in real that could be created, we used above known fixed hand poses to demonstrate the feasibility of our deep model in this work. To evaluate our technique on tracking continuous hand movements, we placed the hand model above the center of two sensors’ common field of view, and then slowly rotated the artificial hand counter-clockwise 360 degrees around the axis of the wrist, followed by clockwise 360 degrees as shown in Figure 9. These steps constitute one round of motions. To build our dataset, three rounds of motions were recorded for each hand pose. Two separate datasets were recorded containing a total of 5,134 entries for training and 5,392 for testing.

| Figure 8. (a) Illustration of hand poses used in our experiments, and (b) Snapshots for one of the hand poses |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f08](i/ch032.f08.png) |
| --- |

To define the ground truth of each hand pose, we placed the palm of the articulated hand directly facing the LMC in order to obtain high pose estimation accuracy (Weichert, Bachmann, Rudak, & Fisseler, 2013). We took snapshots from a single sensor as shown in Figure 8(b), and then computed the mean value of fingertip positions relative to the palm center. This procedure generated the ground truth for each hand pose.

| Figure 9. Artificial hand model is rotated along the axis of the wrist |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.f09](i/ch032.f09.png) |
| --- |

Each entry in the dataset was labeled with the ID of the sensor that generated the lower estimation error. We trained the SVM model with C-SVC type using radial basis kernel function method with 10-fold cross-validation procedure. Each feature vector in the training data set for both SMV model is labeled with the sensor generating the lower estimation error. The input of (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016) SVM model are 12 floating points feature vector described in Section 3.5. The SSF-7 SVM model is trained on extra pre-calculated 7 SSF values with previous 7 frames windows size explained in (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016). All weights in the DNN and DRNN models were initialized using Xavier initialization (Glorot & Bengio, 2010), which could solve the gradient vanishing problem. Both models were trained via an Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam) (Kingma & Ba, 2014) optimizer that could compute the adaptive learning rate for each parameter in the network. The Dropout probability was set to 0.5 during training and 0 during testing. The “forget bias” of the LSTM units in DRNN was initialized to 1, which was shown by (Jozefowicz, Zaremba, & Sutskever, 2015) to deliver better performance compared to other methods. The “state” value input to each LSTM layer for the first frame was zero, because there was no prior information. All experiments were implemented and evaluated on a computer equipped with an Intel Core i7, 32GB of RAM, and a nVidia GeForce GTX980M GPU. Two SVM methods were implemented with Matlab 2015b and our DNN and DRNN methods were implemented in Python using Tensorflow library (Abadi, et al., 2016).

In real-time testing, the classifier outputs the label of the sensor that generated the lower hand pose estimation error. The optimal fused hand pose sequence was obtained by appending the pose estimation of the labelled sensor at each time step. Our DNN and DRNN models are fast with up to 3,000 frames per second when using a single GPU, achieving real-time application requirement.

Performance Analysis

For fair comparison, we apply the same evaluation metric described in (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016) and (Sun, Cheng, & Basu, 2016). The mean pose estimation error (Equation 1) is used to evaluate the final optimal fused pose over all frames in the test database. In Table 1, we compare different methods’ mean estimation errors (in millimeters). The Best Case assumes that the smaller estimation error is always chosen at each time step. The Worst Case assumes the worst pose estimation is chosen every time. Random Case assumes that the method randomly selects a pose between the two sensors every time. The % of accuracy is calculated as a normalized performance of each algorithm using Equation 5, where ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch032.m04](i/ch032.m04.svg) denotes the mean pose estimation error. The comparison of different methods in % accuracy is shown in Figure 10.

As shown in the comparison between (Rossol, Cheng, & Basu, 2016) and our DNN model, we can see that our DNN model has 8.26% higher accuracy and the result is also better than the SSF-7 method for continuous hand movements. As expected, the DRNN approach achieves the highest accuracy attributed from the analysis of both spatial and temporal features. Although the DRNN model only has 2.83% accuracy increase over SSF-7, note that as mentioned earlier, the DRNN model has the ability to learn and extract temporal features without precomputing all of the SSF values. In addition, it does not need to pre-define a window size for movement flow evaluation. The window size is a hyper-parameter and needs to be adjusted for different types of sensor with various sampling rates. Moreover, the DRNN model uses LSTM units populated with a large number of neurons for automatic feature extraction, which is better than using the handcrafted SSF features.

CONCLUSION

In this work, we introduce two new models, based on deep neural network and deep recurrent neural network architectures, to accurately estimate continuous hand poses in a dual-sensor setup, which can be generalized to a multi-sensor environment. Experimental results demonstrate that our new models outperform earlier methods. The DRNN model has 2.83% accuracy increase over SSF-7, and has the advantage of intelligent learning without using pre-defined parameter values. While hand pose estimation using a single-view sensor is widely discussed in the literature, using multi-sensor fusion to optimize continuous hand pose estimation has not been adequately studied before. Furthermore, we compare the estimation results between models based on deep neural network and deep recurrent neural network, as well as assess the performance by enhancing the spatial domain information with temporal features. In addition to outperforming other methods in term of accuracy, both proposed models achieve a processing time of less than 0.5ms per frame, meeting the real-time HCI application requirement. In particular, our DRNN model is a generic design suitable for different types of sensor with various sampling rates. Its LSTM component can discriminate and learn useful information with long-short memory over time for accurate classification.

In future work, we will test more hand-finger poses including using real human hand. We plan to use a marker-based tracking system OptiTrack (Carse, Meadows, Bowers, & Rowe, 2013) or Electro Magnetic sensors (Salazar-Alvarez, Korostynska, Mason, Tofail, & Magner, 2016) to obtain more precise pose estimation as ground truth. We will also increase the number of sensors to evaluate the scalability of our deep models. Along with working on fusion of sensory data from the same type of sensor, we also plan to fuse the sensory data from different modalities such as integrating Leap and Kinect sensory data.

# Chapter 33

Building Classroom Practices that Work

*   Becky Boesch  
    Portland State University, USA
*   Candyce Reynolds  
    Portland State University, USA
*   Judith Patton  
    Portland State University, USA

ABSTRACT

ePortfolios are being used throughout the world as a way to engage students more deeply in their learning, encourage integrative learning, and provide more authentic assessment for courses, programs and institutions. While ePortfolios have great potential, instructors need to provide opportunities to create meaningful products. This chapter describes a model that provides a framework for developing classroom practices that promote integrative and deep learning. Four practices, reflection, making connections, life-long learning, and communication, serve as the base for a successful course ePortfolio assignment. Recommendations about how to introduce ePortfolios into courses and programs are offered. The chapter concludes with a discussion of recommendations for practice.

INTRODUCTION

Today, ePortfolios are becoming more common in education mainly for the opportunities they provide for promoting and assessing student learning (e.g., Stefani, Mason & Pegler, 2007; Chen, Penny Light & Ittelson, 2012). Through ePortfolios, students have the opportunity to discover and explore their role as a learner, make connections, and more intentionally integrate their learning. ePortfolios are also a plus for administrators and faculty as they provide a more authentic way of evaluating student and program success. While ePortfolios have been used more heavily to date in such areas as writing, art, and graphic design, students and educator can benefit from ePortfolios potentially in all subject areas. For example, in math, students can use ePortfolios to not only show the correct to certain math problems but also the critical process used in solving the math problems. The promise of ePortfolios is great; the promotion of learning and the assessment of learning can happen with one tool. However, as the means to create an ePortfolio becomes more available and accessible, it threatens to make the process too easy. Instead of providing enriched opportunities for students to learn and for program coordinators to use for assessment, ePortfolios can become no more than electronic depositories of information, especially if attention is on providing the technology or on creating easy-to-assess ePortfolios. Students need only take a few minutes to download some assignments, write a short reflection and add a picture or two with no significant learning involved. ePortfolios can meet the goal of advancing and documenting student learning well if instructors provide the necessary classroom supports for this to happen.

Creating deep and meaningful ePortfolios means managing the tension between teaching the technology of the ePortfolio tool, program assessment opportunities, and promoting integrative and deep learning. Making learning the center of the ePortfolio creation can be transformational for the student and faculty. When learning is at the center of ePortfolio creation, it can actually help assessment efforts by providing opportunities for authentic assessment of courses and programs, providing insight into students’ learning and guide improved practices.

The use of ePortfolios has been touted as a potential tool for integrative learning (e.g., Chen, Penny Light & Ittelson, 2012). Integrative learning has been identified as an important university learning outcome by the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching and the Association of American Colleges and Universities (AAC&U, 2007). These organizations are exploring how integrative learning can be used on college campuses to help students make more intentional connections within their learning rather than expecting it to happen on its own. This work came from an understanding that at least from high school on, students are taught that knowledge is in discrete packages called a subject or a course. Institutions of higher education teach students to learn facts, ideas, and skills associated with a course and then test them. As Huber and Hutchings (2004) note, “The very structures of academic life encourage students to see their courses as isolated requirements to complete” (p. 1). However, in this increasingly complex world, segmented and compartmentalized learning is insufficient because students will need to connect the knowledge they have learnt and apply it to solving the problems of the day.

This chapter will describe the use of ePortfolios in higher education, explaining their use in promoting student learning and for student, program and institutional assessment. It will also describe the growing interest in and literature on integrative learning. The main focus of the chapter will be on the need to develop specific pedagogical strategies for the classroom to help ensure that ePortfolios provide the opportunities for students to experience integrative learning. A framework for and examples of such strategies will be shared. Finally the chapter will discuss recommendations for the future, including the need for ongoing research on ePortfolios and integrative learning.

BACKGROUND

ePortfolios

Hard-copy portfolios have been used for quite some time in education particularly in such areas as writing, visual arts, architecture and graphic design. Beginning in the mid-1990s, the use of portfolios went beyond these areas in higher education to address pressures by outside constituents to demonstrate the value of students’ education and to create a more learner-centered environment. This was coupled with the desire to promote more active teaching strategies and deepen student learning. These portfolios transitioned from hard-copy to digital as technology progressed. Lorenzo and Ittelson (2005) define an ePortfolio as “a digitized collection of artifacts, including demonstrations, resources, and accomplishments that represent an individual, group, or institution. This collection can be comprised of text-based, graphic, or multimedia elements archived in a CD-Rom or DVD….E-portfolios encourage reflection” (p. 2). Garrison & Ring (2013) identify the components of a true ePortfolio as work that is digital, shows evidence of the author’s experiences and accomplishments, and includes reflection on the learning demonstrated. Figure 1 illustrates how these three components fit together. It is possible for students to use the digital medium for reflection and to share accomplishments in a variety of ways. However, the ePortfolio can bring all of these together.

| Figure 1. Digital presence |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch033.f01](i/ch033.f01.png) |
| --- |

It has been noted that ePortfolios go beyond the capability of hard-copy portfolios in several areas. ePortfolios allow for the development of a wider range of learner habits and skills as described by Labissiere and Reynolds (2004).

An eportfolio requires the development of several skill sets, each of which enhances the student’s ability to engage more deeply with what has already been learned. For example, hyperlinking, which is the primary activity of building a website, forces students to make new connections with what has previously been learned. Such hyperlinking practices, we argue, encourage metacognitive skills development. (pp. 2-3)

This is just one example of the ways that ePortfolios allow for the expansion of learning.

Labissiere and Reynolds (2004) further outline the added benefits of electronic portfolios. They can be collaborative rather than individual, can be seen by a wider audience which can navigate the portfolio in multiple ways and can be stored online. In addition, ePortfolios develop students’ critical thinking, create opportunities for student reflection and integrative learning, and they allow students to demonstrate learning through multiple modes—visual, oral, written, video. As Reynolds and Patton (2014) state, “ePortfolios are digital representations of students’ work and accomplishments along with their reflections on learning. The ePortfolio has the potential to enhance student learning through the process of collect, select, reflect, and share” (p. 12). Table 1 provides a comparison of the differences between hard-copy ePortfolios and ePortfolios, naming several advantages for using an ePortfolio over an electronic portfolio.

Table 1. Differences in hard-copy versus ePortfolios

| Hard Copy Portfolio  || Eportfolio |
| --- | --- |
| Work done by an Individual || Work done by Individual but can be a collaborative effort |
| Limited Audience – Generally Instructor/Artificial || Students controls who can see but can be used in multiple ways for multiple audiences |
| Difficult to Keep and Store over Time || Online storage |
| Hyperlinking – critical thinking exercise in and of itself |
| Viewed usually from beginning to end, one page at a time || Reader creates own journey using links and navigation system |
| Emphasis on what students can do |
| May include student reflection on work, rarely over more than one course || Creates opportunity for student reflection and integrating learning |
| Primarily written work || Students can demonstrate learning in multiple modes – visual, oral, written, video |

(Labissiere & Reynolds, 2004).  

Perhaps the strongest endorsement for the use of ePortfolios is the current realization that in this rapidly changing world, higher education needs to produce graduates who are self-directed learners and autonomous thinkers. Current research by Bransford, Brown & Cocking (1999); Halpern and Hakel (2000), Tagg (2004) and Zull (2002) all support teaching with the goal that we develop life-long learners with the ability to apply that learning. In order to do be able to do this, Chickering and Gamson (1987) said students “must talk about what they are learning, write about it, relate it to past experiences, and apply it to their daily lives. They must make what they learn a part of themselves” (p. 4). ePortfolios provide the perfect vehicle to accomplish this.

Integrative and Deep Learning

Serendipitously, along with the rise of ePortfolios has come the promotion of integrative learning. This interest in integrative learning has developed, in part, from the realization in higher education that many students are graduating not equipped with the tools to thrive in an increasingly complex world where the ability to make connections between what we have learned to our present and future is critical. In other words, they graduate not having a chance to develop the habits of mind necessary to become life-long learners. Recognizing and promoting integrative learning as a critical part of a student’s education worthy of attention might rectify this shortcoming. Carol Schneider (2003), president of Association of American Colleges and Universities (AAC&U), states that

… \[i\]ntegrative learning is a shorthand term for teaching a set of capacities— capacities we might also call the arts of connection, reflective judgment, and considered action—that enable graduates to put their knowledge to effective use. It should also lead students to connect and integrate the different parts of their overall education, to connect learning to the world beyond the academy, and, above all, to translate their education to new contexts, new problems, new responsibilities. (pp. 1-2)

To help address this need to make connections between academics and the real life situations, AAC&U publication, Liberal Education and America’s Promise (LEAP) (2007), has recognized integrative and applied learning as one of the four essential learning outcomes of college and define integrative learning as “an understanding and a disposition that a student builds across the curriculum and co-curriculum, from making simple connections among ideas and experiences to synthesizing and transferring learning to new, complex situations within and beyond the campus” (p. 51). Still others have defined integrative learning as “developing the ability to make, recognize, and evaluate connections among disparate concepts, fields, or contexts” (Huber, Hutchings, Gale, Miller, & Breen, 2007, p. 46). Integrated learning, in essence, is helping students develop the ability to make connections and see relationships between subjects, themselves and the world around them. Taylor (2011) states that “integrative learning is, at its core, a process of synthesizing learning across multiple experiences, coalescing meaning, and also creating new learning and meaning (p. 14)” Perhaps Reynolds and Patton (2014) sum it up best when they state that “\[i\]ntegrative learning is an understanding and a disposition that a student builds across the curriculum and co-curriculum, from making simple connections among ideas and experiences to synthesizing and transferring learning to new, complex situations within and beyond the campus” (p. 31).

Integrative learning is connected to the concept of deep learning. The idea of deep learning surfaced initially with the work of with Marton and Saljo (1976) and was further developed by Ramsden (1992), Rhem (1995) and Biggs and Tang (2007). It was juxtaposed against surface learning which translates into a transitory and shallow understanding. “Students who use a surface approach to learning substitute memorization of facts for learning and use quotes to pad their papers without really interpreting their significance” (Biggs and Tang, 2007, 23). Surface learning is short-lived. Deep learning, on the other hand, leads to a genuine understanding which encourages long-term learning that can be drawn upon in the future (Millis, 2010, p. 1) Deep learning occurs when it is meaningful, significant and life changing. Mckay and Kember (1997) articulated the characteristics necessary for deep learning. They are:

*   1\. A well-structured knowledge base with a focus on concepts, integration of knowledge, and a cumulative experience.
*   2\. An appropriate motivational level, with an emphasis on intrinsic motivation and a sense of “ownership” of the material.
*   3\. Learner activity associated with active, not passive, learning.
*   4\. Interaction with others, including student-teacher interactions and student-student interactions. (p. 65)

Deep learning and integrative learning go hand in hand and ePortfolios are a perfect vehicle to achieve both.

The focus on integrative and deep learning through the use of ePortfolios is particularly important today on two fronts. First, it is aligned with the goals of higher education—the education of the whole person which can be lost when disciplines take precedence. For example, specialization in majors such as business, biology, and English, while important, become more important than gaining an understanding of the interconnection of disciplines and the application of knowledge. The culture of higher education both for faculty and students tends to reward disciplinary silos rather than the interconnection of knowledge. Higher education leaders, such as those at AACU, call for a deliberate focus on integrative and deep learning. ePortfolios is a way to promote integrative learning.

Second, ePortfolios provide authentic means for helping address accountability. It is critical at this time that a reliable mechanism be developed to demonstrate student learning as colleges and universities are being pressured more and more to “prove” student learning and achievement. At a time when governments are calling for more accountability, ePortfolios can provide an alternative to simple measures such as high stakes testing and degree attainment. So far, higher education has been able to stave off high stakes testing but for how long is unknown. Carol Geary Schneider (2009), president of AAC&U clearly articulates the answer that ePortfolios can provide to these outside pressures.

What then should we recommend? Educators around the country are pointing to an accountability strategy that can provide, simultaneously, a framework for raising student achievement, evidence of progress over time, and transparency about the extent to which students are achieving what ACC&U’s LEAP initiative calls “essential learning outcomes.”

The strategy—well attuned to the technologies of our time—uses e-portfolios or what we might call “supplemental transcripts.” Already adopted by institutions as diverse as the University of Michigan, LaGuardia Community College, Hampshire and Carleton and in development in many others, e-portfolios enable us to see what a student is working on over time, to discern an emerging sense of purpose and direction, and to review samples of writing, research projects, and creative work as well as progress in integrating learning across multiple levels of schooling and multiples areas of study and experience. An e-portfolio also opens windows into a student’s field-based assignments by creating opportunities to present supervisor evaluations or even videos about real-world performance. They can be sampled, using rubrics, for external reporting. (p. 1)

DEVELOPING ePORTFOLIOS THAT PROMOTE INTEGRATIVE LEARNING

If integrative and deep learning need to be nurtured and fostered in higher education and if ePortfolios can be a tool for this, how then does an instructor begin to incorporate integrative learning ePortfolios into their classrooms? Several institutions have begun to incorporate ePortfolios as a way to enhance students’ integrative learning and to serve as tools for assessment. These institutions include Portland State University, LaGuardia Community College, Clemson University, University of Michigan, Virginia Tech and Georgia Institute of Technology. A project funded by the United States Department of Education, Catalyst for learning, which looked at ePortfolio use and their impact on integrative learning across 24 campuses. The study reports that students report that ePortfolios allow them to make connections, learn connect more deeply, and succeed as a student (Enyon, Gambino, Torok, 2014However, as these authors note, this kind of success is only possible with good instruction and support for students creating an ePortfolio. Utilizing ePortfolios in the classroom as a key assignment is one avenue.

Integrative Learning as a Learning Outcome

So, how can one achieve integrative learning through the ePortfolio? First and foremost, integrative learning must become a goal of one’s course. Instructors should consider making integrative learning an essential learning outcome. This may seem unnecessary but if we want students integrate their learning, we must make this goal explicit and provide opportunities for them to integrate their learning in a course.

To be effective, learning outcomes should be clear and precise. Well written learning outcomes for a course and especially those directed at integrative learning provide students with many benefits:

*   • Students have a clearer understanding of what is important in the course. Students often come to a course with little background information on the subject of your course. Even if they have some background in the topic, they don’t necessarily understand how the content fits together and what is most important. Learning outcomes can help focus students on what is most important about a subject. If integrating one’s knowledge is a prominent learning outcome, students will know that this is an important area to focus on.
*   • Students have a clearer understanding of what is expected of them. When learning outcomes are written clearly and specifically, students know what they need to do in the course to get that good grade but also what they need to do to become proficient in this field of study. If integrative learning is identified as a learning outcome, students can begin to see that just learning facts about a topic is not enough; making connections and applying these facts is at least equally if not more important in mastering a field of study.
*   • Students have the language for the process of integrative learning which can facilitate continuing to make these connections in other settings. Because students may not have been exposed directly to the concept of integrative learning in their previous studies, they may not have paid attention or given much credit to the fact that they were making connections between the course content and their workplace, for example. Integrative learning has often taken on the status of bonus learning for students if they’ve even recognized it as learning. Naming integrative learning as a course goal allows students to start to see the importance of being able to make connections and encourages them to continue to making these connections.
*   • Students are better able to self-assess. They can use the learning outcomes to measure what they have learned in a course. Learning outcomes provide a great opportunity for students to look back on a course or program and evaluate their progress. What did I master? What do I need to spend a bit more time on? This kind of self-assessment for integrative learning outcomes can prompt students to push even further in making connections with what they’ve learned in the course.

Faculty also benefit from well written learning outcomes:

*   • Learning outcomes help instructors organize and develop learning activities aimed at helping students achieve these outcomes. Learning outcomes provide the road map for course planning. Course descriptions and outlines give us information about what we should cover in a course but learning outcomes help an instructor be able to think deeply about what students should learn in courses. Developing integrative learning outcomes guides instructors in creating activities and assignments that directly address these outcomes. Learning outcomes not only help students to know what is important but reminds instructors what is important.
*   • Learning outcomes help assess the learning strategies employed in a course. Without clear and specific learning outcomes, it is difficult to say if one has been successful in teaching a course. Students may report they like the class. They may do well on tests. But using learning outcomes allow instructors to develop student assessment practices that can point to whether or not the classroom activities or assignments promoted the learning that one wanted for their students.

Learning outcomes are statements that specify what learners will know or be able to do as a result of a course. Learning outcomes are usually expressed in terms of what one will know (knowledge), what one will think or feel (attitude), or what one will be able to do (skills) after completing a course. It is important to note that learning outcomes are focused on what the student does, not what the instructor does. Learning outcomes aren’t about what instructors “cover” in a course but what students are able to know, think, and do after completing the course.

Well written learning outcomes should be:

*   • Detailed and specific,
*   • Measurable,
*   • Something that is done by the student and is hopefully a result of the learning experience in a course or program.

To aid in writing clear learning outcomes, many find Bloom’s Taxonomy to be a useful place to start. Measurable learning outcomes should focus on what the student is able to know, think and do after the course and should include activities that address all five levels of Bloom’s (1956) Taxonomy of Educational Objectives revised by Anderson and Krathwohl (2001). The five ascending cognitive levels are:

*   • Knowledge/remembering;
*   • Comprehension/understanding;
*   • Application/applying;
*   • Analysis/analyzing;
*   • Evaluation/evaluating;
*   • Synthesis/creating.

Using Bloom’s taxonomy can help an instructor identify verbs to describe student learning. Here are some examples of learning outcomes verbs:

*   • Knowledge/Remembering: Define, list, recognize.
*   • Comprehension/Understanding: Characterize, describe, explain, identify, locate, recognize, sort.
*   • Application/Applying: Choose, demonstrate, implement, perform.
*   • Analysis/Analyzing: Analyze, categorize, compare, differentiate.
*   • Evaluation/Evaluating: Assess, critique, evaluate, rank, rate.
*   • Synthesis/Creating: Construct, design, formulate, organize, synthesize.

Because learning outcomes are supposed to be detailed and specific, there are some verbs that one might want avoid such as: understand, appreciate, know about, become familiar with, learning about, and become aware of.

In developing learning outcomes specific to integrative learning, the categories in the integrative learning rubric developed by the AACU VALUE project (n.d.) is helpful. The categories from this rubric are as follows:

*   • Connection to Experience: Connects relevant experience and academic knowledge.
*   • Connection to Discipline: Sees (makes) connections across disciplines, perspectives.
*   • Transfer: Adapts and applies skills, abilities, theories, or methodologies gained in one situation to new situations.
*   • Integrated Communication: The presentation of material that represents appropriate types of communication, including visuals, and takes into consideration audience.
*   • Reflection and Self-Assessment: Demonstrates a developing sense of self as a learner, building on prior experiences to respond to new and challenging contexts.

These categories can help one develop specific integrative learning outcomes. Incorporating an ePortfolio assignment into a course design is one way to make integrative learning a transparent learning goal in a course. An integrative learning ePortfolio assignment makes it clear to students that making connections is an important part of learning in a course. ePortfolios are often assigned as a culminating activity for students. And while, it may be finished at the end of a course, it is imperative that activities that promote integrative learning and contribute to the development of the ePortfolio are included throughout a course. Like any skill we develop, integrative learning requires practice. The remainder of this chapter will highlight ways that activities that can encourage integrative and deep learning that can be incorporated into classroom activities and assignment that can lead to an effective ePortfolio assignment. These suggestions are based on a model developed by Reynolds and Patton (2014). This model is illustrated in Figure 2.

Integrative Learning ePortfolio Framework

| Figure 2. Integrative learning ePortfolio framework |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch033.f02](i/ch033.f02.png) |
| --- |

In this framework, four types of classroom practices and activities provide the bedrock (or the base of this pyramid) for integrative learning (the center of this pyramid). The outcome of this learning is documented in the ePortfolio (the Pinnacle of the pyramid). The figure also illustrates the roles that technology and assessment have in an institution’s use of an ePortfolio. Considering issues related to technology and teaching students how use technology, of course, aids in the creation of an ePortfolio. And through the ePortfolio, faculty, programs, and/or institutions have the ability to assess student’s integrative learning (and more). The four practices are reflection, making connections, lifelong learning, and communication and will be discussed in the following section.

Reflection

Reflection is touted as the centerpiece of ePortfolios. Without reflections, ePortfolios are just glorified file cabinets—a catalogue of work with a brief index. As such, providing students a way to learn about and practice reflection is important if students are to benefit from learning through ePortfolios. R. Rogers (2001) and C. Rogers (2002) point to the paradox in education—we value and seem to understand the centrality of reflection in education, but we really don’t seem to have an agreement about what it is and how to facilitate the process in our students. Varying conceptions of reflection make it difficult to think about how to approach teaching reflection in the classroom and its use in the ePortfolio. A thesaurus search for the word “reflection” helps one understand the difficulty; the synonyms are similar but definitely are not exact matches—terms include careful thought, assessment, consideration, soul-searching, reasoning, introspection, focus, and forethought.

Webster’s dictionary (n.d.) defines reflection as: “a thought, idea, or opinion formed or a remark made as a result of meditation” and “consideration of some subject matter, idea, or purpose” This may seem easy enough but it is far more complicated than it appears on the surface. If one looks at articles and books about reflection, you would think that it is a well understood concept in education. However, it is actually far from it. Authors have talked about reflection as a cognitive activity (e.g., Loughran, 1996), as an affective process (e.g., Boud, Keogh, & Walker, 1985), as necessitating an examination of one’s beliefs (e.g., Dewey, 1933) and even as a process requires substantial change in one’s thinking (e.g., Meizrow, 1991). One of the above, some of the above, or all of the above would be correct depending on the purpose of the reflective activity for the student. The reality is that there is not one right way to reflect and, in fact, it depends on what an instructor wants his/her students to learn from participating in reflection. Having a good conceptual framework to use to guide your classroom practice can help determine what an instructor wants his/her students to learn from reflective activities and guide the development of classroom practices and course assignments. Carol Rogers (2002) provides a framework she developed for teachers for thinking about reflection that is helpful in creating environments and activities that promote the kind of reflection instructors would like their students to engage in. These principles are derived from her synthesis of Dewey’s (1933; 1938; 1944) ideas about reflection. Rogers (2002) notes these principles:

*   1\. Reflection is a meaning-making process that moves a learner from one experience into the next with deeper understanding of its relationships with and connections to other experiences and ideas. It is the thread that makes continuity of learning possible, and ensures the progress of the individual.
*   2\. Reflection is a systematic, rigorous, disciplined way of thinking…
*   3\. Reflection needs to happen in community, in interaction with others.
*   4\. Reflection requires attitudes that value the personal and intellectual growth of oneself and of others. (p. 845)

Using these principles, instructors can craft activities and assignments that encourage reflection. However, the activities outlined below are ones that can be used in helping students develop ePortfolios but could be used in any classroom. The trick to helping students develop a reflective practice and ultimately demonstrate high levels of insight is just that—practice. One might notice that many of these activities are ones that don’t seem directly related to ePortfolio reflection but practicing the process of reflection is the key.

The suggested activities in this chapter are organized by these general categories:

*   • Set the Tone: Reflection is learning.
*   • It is the small things that count.
*   • Know Your Goal: Reflect on what matters.
*   • Consider various forms of reflection.
*   • Make it more complicated.
*   • Learning Is Social: Make reflection a conversation.

Set the Tone: Reflection Is Learning

If you want your students to become reflective practitioners, students need to

*   1\. Understand the connection of reflection to their learning,
*   2\. Harness their innate ability to reflect and use it in a variety of ways and contexts, and
*   3\. Model or show good reflective practice.

One activity that has been useful to one author (Reynolds) in setting the tone is the use of an Opening Letter to students in a class. This activity provides an early opportunity to engage in reflection and model reflective practices. The instructor writes a letter to the class, introducing him/herself and shares the particular goals for the course and invites the student to dialogue about their hopes and fears for the course. This can be the first writing assignment and students can be given points for this assignment to emphasize its value. Often, instructors share these kinds of things at the beginning of a course and often have a discussion with students about why they are taking a course, asking how this particular course fit into their academic pursuits. However, these attempts can fall short of one’s expectations. Students may participate in the discussion but the responses can be lackluster or pro-forma. Writing students an opening letter can serve as a model of reflective practice; students can see an instructor’s thought processes and biases in a more personal and transparent way. The letter creates the expectation that reflection will be an important part of their learning in the course. And finally, the letter invites students to take the time to share their thoughts, connecting personally with the instructor in an academic setting. This assignment can change the tone of one’s courses. Students get to know an instructor early on. The instructor get to know students early on (instructors can even gain an early sense of students’ ability to write from this assignment). And it sets the tone that there will be more than learning content in the course; the instructor’s intent is that students engage and reflect on their own learning process as well as what they are learning in the course.

This assignment can be incorporated in the course as a blog post, by email, or even part of a discussion thread in an online course. However, students from this era report that they find the idea of a physical letter as “quaint” and are thus intrigued by the notion of doing something that many of them have never done. The instructor can give the letter to students on the first day and the response from them is expected at the next class meeting. The instructor should write them. The notes can usually be quite brief and for the most part encouraging. It is a great opportunity to make connections between what students are hoping to get in the class and what the instructor’s plans are for the course. If there appears to be a disjunction between what the students expect to learn and what the instructors hopes they will learn, this disconnect can be addressed early on. It also provides an instructor with a way to push those who did the assignment in a half-hearted way with encouragement and a low score.

It’s the Little Things That Count

Setting the tone doesn’t mean doing one activity in the beginning of a class and then forgetting about a focus on reflection. To help students develop practices and put reflection in forefront, one must continue to provide ways to engage in reflective practice. Below are some examples of activities you can use to encourage reflective practice in the classroom. A small but simple way to do this is to point out reflection when it happens. It happens in classroom discussions, in conversations with students, and in written work. Humans reflect constantly but don’t always recognize that is what is happening or how or why it is important. Naming and acknowledging this natural phenomenon can help students more consciously engage in the process.

Know Your Goal: Reflect on What Matters

There is no right way to reflect. However, for students to benefit from the process of reflecting, instructors need to be clear about what we want them to do and why. Following the principles of reflection discussed earlier is helpful, but the focus of reflective activities can be very different, dependent on an instructor’s goals for the course or program. For example, for certain topics, one may want to have students focus on a more cognitive task, reflecting on making connections between concepts they learned in a pre-requisite course and the ideas present in the syllabus. In a service-learning course, one might want students to take a more affective stance, and ask them to reflect and write or even draw something representing their reactions to the first visit to their service site.

Writing effective reflection prompts is important. It is easy to make the assumption that students can read and can follow instructions but it is often the case that students are not able to read between the lines and clearly understand an instructor’s expectations. Getting students to engage in reflective activities is difficult. It requires the instructor to think (reflect) and develop thoughtful prompts, motivate and reward students for engaging in the activity, and give students the time necessary to make this kind of reflection occur. Students have to see it as a valuable activity (either intrinsically or extrinsically or both hopefully) and commit the time and mind power to make it happen. The first step is for an instructor to let students know what is expected explicitly.

Make It More Complicated

Reflection is a skill. And like all skills it takes time and practice to learn how to do it well. One way instructors can help students learn new skills is to scaffold their learning of the skill. Just as one would teach children in steps to learn to ride a bicycle, one can also do this in helping students learn to become reflective practitioners. Start students out with simple and easy to answer reflection prompts to begin this process. For example, one might begin a series of reflection assignments with asking students to describe what they know or have observed using who, what, and where questions. Subsequent prompts will ask students more complex questions once they have mastered the ability to respond to that level of questions. The idea of scaffolding learning is that instructors provide lots of support in the beginning of learning a task and as students begin to master the task, instructors can pull out the supports as students begin to understand what needs to be done and can meet (or begin to) the challenges instructors set out for them.

Learning Is Social: Make Reflection a Conversation

Often instructors are initially excited to assign reflective activities, like a weekly journal, but can be ultimately disappointed by the results. A common concern is often the lack of depth in student reflections. Sometimes instructors assign journals or reflective writing activities but then do not have any interaction with the students’ writing throughout the term. Reflection is a communication process and thus requires an audience. Often, the audience for reflective writing is oneself. Writing helps us get ideas, thoughts and feelings out and provides us an opportunity to clarify our ideas. It would be great if all students were self-directed learners who took full advantage of reflective activities, engaging fully and using what they discover in their learning. However, being our own audience may only go so far for many students. Students may need an outside audience to react to their communication to help the ideas keep flowing and to help the students improve on the depth of their reflection.

In addition, this is a reminder too that all reflection is not written. Reflection happens easily in class discussions, face to face and online, especially if instructors provide discussion prompts that facilitate student reflection. It also helps to remind students that the discussion is actually a reflection activity. As part of the discussion process, take the time to let students think about what they have learned from the discussion.

In conclusion, reflection is a complex process that educators have long recognized as an essential part of learning. While it is important to learning, it is also a difficult skill to teach and cultivate.

Making Connections

When discussing ePortfolios and integrative learning, the phrase, “making connections” will inevitably be part of the conversation. Connection is the nexus of the issue with integrative learning and with ePortfolios. Making connections means intentionally building relational links between prior understanding of material and the material that is currently being learned. Included in connections then, is setting future goals and identifying needs to forward the growth in understanding and use of that material. The most straightforward way to achieve this linking is to create activities that ask students to find the relationship between:

*   • Assignments,
*   • Assignments and students’ lived experiences,
*   • Courses within programs of study,
*   • Disciplines, and
*   • Assignments and experiences as they relate to the learning outcomes and goals for courses or programs.

The more students retrieve information from their memories and use it to make those connections, the deeper and longer lasting the learning will be (Halpern and Hakel, 2000). Also, reflective practice is an important strategy to help students make those connections. Reflection is the way students connect learning and make it meaningful. Designing student experiences to make learning accessible and usable in their lives and careers and to help students develop those habits will enable them to continue to engage in rich and lasting learning after graduation.

One such student experience would be to ask students to keep journals as one strategy for helping students make connections. Journals can take many forms. For example in the sciences, faculty use lab reports and include ending questions that connect experiments to class concepts and to scientific work that is happening in the world today. Humanities faculty use reflective journals as part of the ongoing structure of their classes. In these ways, weekly prompts ask students to think about what they have read and learned that week and to relate that learning in any number of ways to past understanding and to current events. It is important that the practice is regular, ongoing and offers a structure that collects and makes visible the students’ growing understanding of the course material over time.

Providing verbal, written or visual reflection prompts is also useful in helping students make connections. What it does in every case is to ask students to think about what they know, and are just learning, and relate it to something in order to embed it into their ongoing and growing understanding of that material.

Making connections is not only a verbal process. Mind maps are visual maps of assignments, ideas, concepts and bits of knowledge that allow students to connect disparate activities and experiences to each other and to their past understanding. Mind maps are a graphical way to structure information making the connections clear and helping students remember what they have done, capture their relationships and generate new understanding and ideas. Mind mapping can be done individually or in groups, online using software, or on small pieces of notebook paper with pens and pencils or on large pieces of butcher paper with markers, colored post-it notes, crayons and stickers. Students can bring laptops to class to create the mind maps in groups or in a computer lab. Mind mapping is a critical thinking and reflective activity that is also an art activity. Maps can be simple or complex, rudimentary or very artistic.

Another activity could be the creation of inventories. Inventorying is a list-making activity that provides an opportunity for students to catalogue what they already know about a topic and determine what they need to know in addition.
