The main task of Big Data Analytics is to extract meaningful and knowledge patterns from huge volume of input data for much purpose like decision making and prediction. There various challenges facing Big Data Analytics such as fast moving streaming data, highly distributed input sources, noisy and poor quality data, high dimensionality, scalability of algorithms, unsupervised and un-categorized data, limited supervised/labeled data and format variation of the raw data (Beebe, Nicole, Clark, 2005) so that there is a need to solve these challenges through using extension of machine learning techniques such as Deep Learning.

Machine learning is an important domain in artificial intelligence that aims to representation of data to generate machine learnt patterns that captured from the data to be used in future for unseen data. The performance of machine learnt depends on the quality of data representation so that if the data representation good the performance of the machine learnt will be high else the performance will be low. Feature engineering is an essential element of machine learning that concern with constructing features and data representations from raw data. In Machine learning task a large effort is consuming in feature engineering that allow to extract features automatically without direct human input. There are many feature engineering such as Scale Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) and Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) which are used in computer vision area.

Deep learning is a branch of machine learning techniques based on automated extraction of complex data representations or features at high levels of abstraction using multiple processing layers, with complex structures or otherwise, composed of multiple non-linear transformations. Deep Learning algorithms are beneficial when dealing with learning from large amounts of unsupervised data. Using Deep Learning to obtain data representations and features can achieve many benefits such as improved classification modelling, better quality of generated samples by generative probabilistic models and the invariant property of data representations (Najafabadi et al., 2015) at based on supervised and unsupervised methods to automatically learn hierarchical representations in deep architectures. Deep Learning algorithms can extract high-level and complex abstractions as data representations through a hierarchical learning process. Complex abstractions are learnt at a given level based on relatively simpler abstractions formulated in the preceding level in the hierarchy. A key benefit of Deep Learning is the analysis and learning of enormous amounts of unsupervised data, making it a valuable tool for Big Data Analytics where raw data is largely unlabeled and un-categorized. Recently, there are some problems in Big Data Analytics that includes extracting complex patterns from enormous volumes of data, semantic indexing, data tagging, fast information retrieval, and simplifying discriminative tasks. There are several useful characteristics of the learnt abstract representations using Deep Learning as follows (Najafabadi et al., 2015):

*   • Relatively simple linear models can work effectively with the knowledge obtained from the more complex and more abstract data representations.
*   • Relational and semantic knowledge can be obtained at the higher levels of abstraction and representation of the raw data. While there are other useful aspects of Deep Learning based representations of data, the specific characteristics mentioned above are particularly important for Big Data Analytics.
*   • Increased automation of data representation extraction from unsupervised data enables its broad application to different data types, such as image, textural and audio.

Digital Forensics Based on Big Data Analytics using Deep learning

Digital Forensics is a topic that is becoming increasingly important in computing and often requires the intelligent analysis of large amounts of complex data extracted from crime scene. Digital forensics investigation is the process of extracting, analysis digital evidence for use as admissible proof about committed crimes. This process can help to reconstruct the crime events. Big Data analytics (BDA) is a process of analyzing Big Data. The objective of Big Data Analytics is to extract knowledge patterns from massive volume of input data. Recently, there are several challenges led to use Big Data Analytics for digital forensics investigations. Some of these challenges are (Mohan, Salisu, 2015):

*   • Storing and Backups of Large Volume of Data: Traditional data storage not suitable for large amount of data that created as a result of big data concept. These large amount of data that generated from different data sources need high size storage capacity to store for the digital investigation purpose.
*   • Faster Indexing of Enormous Amounts of Data: In recent time, data become big so faster indexing of the data is a challenge for digital investigators. In order to rapid indexing to analysis of large size of data there is a need to faster methods and devices that have the ability analysis data within a given time frame.
*   • Presentation and Visualization of Large Amounts of Data to the Court of Law: Presentation and visualization of finding from analysis of digital evidence is an important for presenting the results in a court of law. Presentation and visualization of large of data is a problem faced digital practitioners and examiners in the digital forensics area so that there is a need for new techniques and methods to deal with massive size of data that generated from crime scene in forensically and timely fashion way.

Machine learning can considered as an ideal approach to deal with many problems that currently exist in various areas such as multimedia processing, pattern recognition and computer security. Machine learning techniques also can use in digital forensics to solve complex problems in extracting and analysis digital evidence from crime scene. There are several areas in digital forensics where machine learning techniques can be used as follows:

*   • Authorship Identification: Attackers and criminals can use fake E-mails for performing activities without tracing them through hiding their identity. Authorship Identification is an important technique which used to solve this problem by identifying the authors of these fake E-mails that can help digital investigators and examiners to perform investigation process in timely fashion manner. The authorship identification process involves many sub-process as authorship attribution, authorship characterization and similarity detection (Nirkhi, Smita, Dharaskar, 2015). Authorship attribution is known as Authorship identification that determine the probability that a piece of writing produced by a particular person by examining the other writings from that the same person. Authorship characterization method is used to determine the personal attributes of author like age, gender and other personal attributes by using existing writings from that author. Similarity detection is a popular technique that used in plagiarism detection. This technique can use to compare different pieces of writing and determines if they were produced by the same person or not.
*   • File Fragments: Detection of data from disks is challenging faced by digital investigators to recover the data from disk. The data when deleting from disk is not permanent where they simply mark each block of the file as unallocated and available for use. The process of recovering unallocated data known as ‘file carving’. Machine learning provide a methods to recognizing the file types of file fragments for the purpose of file carving for the reconstruction of partially erased files on disk into whole files. In (Duffy, 2014) they used different type of classification techniques such as Support Vector Machine, Multinomial Naive Bayes, and Linear Discriminant Analysis models to apply them for file fragments. They used 257 calculated features of an input fragment then applied the three above techniques to choose the most accurate method of classification where was Support Vector Machine with accuracy 75.03%.
*   • Pattern Recognition: Pattern recognition is an important domain in machine learning that working on extracting patterns from input data. Supervised data that trained from labeled data and unsupervised learning that discover unknown patterns. Both of them can used in the Pattern recognition. It is used to identify pattern or feature in data through determine and specify types or clusters of data. The pattern recognition can help in digital forensics for performing detecting a pattern in an e-mail message which indicates malicious code like spam or virus. Also can be used to discover identities in digital evidence that are extracting from crime scene. In (Henseler, Hans, Hofste, Keulen, 2013), they proposed an algorithm to extract, merge and rank identities that are encountered in the electronic evidence during processing. This algorithm can assist with the identification of frequently occurring identities so that investigators can prioritize the investigation of evidence units accordingly.

Using techniques that can automatic extraction of complex data representations or features in digital forensics can improve and enhance the process of analysis large amount of digital evidence in short time with high quality and accuracy of results. These techniques motivated by digital investigators and examiners to use in the forensic analysis phase. One of recently become popular as extension of machine learning is Deep learning. The Deep Learning algorithms are beneficial when dealing with learning from large amounts of unsupervised data to automatically learn hierarchical representations in deep architectures. The combination of Deep Learning with Big Data Analytics can use for many areas inside digital forensics as follows:

*   • Image Region Forgery Detection: In recent time, the number of tampered images is increased incredible way due to the use of social networks like Facebook and Flicker, Instagram and Twitter. These tampered images can be shared easily by the users that may lead serious consequences so the authenticity of digital images is urgently needed. The presence of tampered images is an important topic in digital forensics. There are many work done to cover this area but to identify certain tampered image using tampering methods. In (Zhang, Ying et al, 2016), they proposed a two stage deep learning approach to learn features in order to detect tampered images in different image formats. In the first stage, they utilized a Stacked Autoencoder model to learn the complex feature for each individual patch while in the second stage; they integrated the contextual information of each patch so that the detection can be conducted more accurately. This work utilized deep learning approach for feature learning in the field of tampered region localization. The experiment results of the proposed method detect tampered regions well with an overall accuracy of 91.09%.
*   • Data Indexing: Large-scale volume of data such as text, image, video, and audio are being extracted and collected from different sources that can make investigation process harder especially when crimes related to environment like social networks and cloud computing. These massive amounts of data needs semantic indexing rather than being stored as data bit strings. Semantic indexing presents the data in a more efficient manner and makes it useful as a source for knowledge discovery and understanding. Deep Learning can be used to generate high-level abstract data representations which will be used for semantic indexing of data rather than using raw data for indexing. An example for using Deep Learning for indexing is document representation that increase the process of retrieval information in a given frame time that can useful for digital investigators during the investigation process.
*   • Data Tagging: Data tagging task can be performed through Big Data Analytics using Deep Learning algorithms for help in performing the search process. Data tagging is another method to semantically index of data. The difference between data tagging with semantic data indexing where semantic indexing, the focus is on using the Deep Learning abstract representations directly for data indexing purposes while the abstract data representations are considered as features for performing the discriminative task of data tagging. Here it possible to tag massive amounts of data using simple linear modeling methods on complicated features which extracted by Deep Learning algorithms. For example, Microsoft Research Audio Video Indexing System (MAVIS) that uses Deep Learning with aids of Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) to enable search of audio and video files speech (Najafabadi, Maryam et al, 2015).

CONCLUSION

Fighting cybercrimes has become an important topic for individuals, organizations and governments for protecting them from severe attacks. Nowadays, massive amount of generated data from Social Media, Cloud Computing and Internet of Things which contain vital and valuable information that can help to detect, prevent and predict cybercrimes in a given time frame. Managing and analyzing these data cannot be done using traditional tools and techniques so that there is a serious need for new tools and solutions. Big Data solutions will be the best for handling these type of data. Digital investigators, practitioners and experts are leveraging big data tools to identify the potential threats and prevent cybercrime incidents. One of important area in information security is Digital Forensics. Digital forensics is the process of collecting, extracting and analysis digital evidence about committed crimes and incidents. Using machine learning techniques such as deep learning with Big Data Analytics can help to improve the existing Big Data Analytics techniques and tools to fight different type of crimes. A key benefit of Deep Learning for Big Data Analytics is the analysis and learning of massive amounts of unsupervised data, making it a useful tool for Big Data Analytics where data is largely un-categorized or un-labeled. This chapter introduce a study on the use of Big Data Analytics in the digital investigation field to help digital practitioners and experts to design and develop new techniques and methods to cope with new technologies like Internet of Things that generated enormous amount of data. The chapter contents includes Big Data attributes, digital forensics definition and process, cybercrimes definition and categories, Big Data Analytics classifications and workflow, Deep Learning techniques and applications, Big Data Analytics using Deep Learning and finally the use of Big Data Analytics using Deep Learning in the digital forensic area to perform the investigation process in efficient and timely fashion manner.

This research was previously published in Deep Learning Innovations and Their Convergence With Big Data edited by S. Karthik; Anand Paul; and N. Karthikeyan, pages 79-101, copyright year 2018 by Information Science Reference (an imprint of IGI Global).

# Chapter 35

*   Rostom Mennour  
    Constantine 2 University, Algeria
*   Mohamed Batouche  
    Constantine 2 University, Algeria

ABSTRACT

Big data analytics and deep learning are nowadays two of the most active research areas in computer science. As the data is becoming bigger and bigger, deep learning has a very important role to play in data analytics, and big data technologies will give it huge opportunities for different sectors. Deep learning brings new challenges especially when it comes to large amounts of data, the volume of datasets has to be processed and managed, also data in various applications come in a streaming way and deep learning approaches have to deal with this kind of applications. In this paper, the authors propose two novel approaches for discriminative deep learning, namely LS-DSN, and StreamDSN that are inspired from the deep stacking network algorithm. Two versions of the gradient descent algorithm were used to train the proposed algorithms. The experiment results have shown that the algorithms gave satisfying accuracy results and scale well when the size of data increases. In addition, StreamDSN algorithm have been applied to classify beats of ECG signals and provided good promising results.

INTRODUCTION

In the recent few years, big data has been one of the most attractive fields for both industry and academy. This is due to the vast opportunities that big data can give to several sectors in real life. Big data refers to the amounts of data that exceed the storage and computation capacities provided by traditional databases and data processing engines. The size of data has considerably grown in the last decade, with the emergence of social networks, internet of things, cloud computing and other technologies that have led to what is called the data explosion. In 2011, the size of data had grown nine times in just five years (Gantz & Reinsel, 2011), and will soon (by 2020) reach 35 zettabytes (10^(21) bytes) (Gantz & Reinsel, 2010).

Those massive amounts of data generated continuously at unprecedented scale have to be exploited. Machine learning and data mining techniques have been used for many years to extract useful information from complex data generated in several fields like bioinformatics, healthcare, economy, social media, and so on. Now, it is harder to apply those techniques in the actual conditions. As mentioned before, the size of data has considerably grown, and the conventional learning methods were not designed to deal with this kind of phenomenon. It is imperative to rethink the way we develop our models and algorithms so that they will be able to meet the requirements of big data. This will considerably improve the quality of life, and bring big advances in science and engineering.

Recently, a new learning technique has emerged. In the machine learning field, deep learning is one of the most popular research areas nowadays. It uses deep hierarchical architectures inspired from the neocortex in the human’s brain, to learn from large amounts of supervised and/or unsupervised data. These techniques have won the most important places in the world of machine learning, and have managed to achieve the best performance rankings becoming the state of the art in this field (Chen & Lin, 2014). Due to the high performances of the deep learning algorithms compared to classic ones, more and more academicians have turned to them for diverse applications like image processing, speech recognition, text and language analytics, bioinformatics and drug discovery and even more (Min, Lee, & Yoon, 2016). For instance, Google’s DeepMinde (Hassabis, Suleyman, & Legg, 2014) has created the Deep Q-networks algorithm that can play Atari games (Mnih, Kavukcuoglu, Silver, Graves, & Antonoglou, 2013) successfully. The same company has also created a program (AlphaGo), based on deep learning, that has, for the first time, won a Go game versus a professional human player.

One of the most challenging issues for machine learning, especially for deep learning, in the era of big data, is the inability to use all of the data available (Najafabadi, Villanustre, Khoshgoftaar, Seliya, Wald, & Muharemagic, 2015). One good solution is to scale up those algorithms and use distributed and parallel paradigms to design them. Engines that are designed for processing massive datasets, like MapReduce (Dean & Ghemawa, 2008) and Spark (Zaharia, Chowdhury, Franklin, Shenker, & Stoica, 2010) are very suitable for this task. Their high ability to scale to large clusters of machines and to tolerate faults when the program is running makes them the best way to face the data size challenge. Also, the algorithms have to be parallelizable and fit well with these models. Given present circumstances, this task is considered to be crucial.

Another big challenge for deep learning in the big data context is velocity; data arrive at high speed to be processed on time (Najafabadi, Villanustre, Khoshgoftaar, Seliya, Wald, & Muharemagic, 2015). The fact is, current machines cannot hold all the data in memory, especial when it comes to big data applications. The solution for this problem consists of online learning, where one instance is learned at a time. Only a few works have been done in this context (Chen & Lin, 2014) and it’s imperative to adapt deep learning to handle big streaming data, as the need for such approaches is becoming very significant.

On the other hand, Clinical databases have accumulated huge quantities of information about patients and their medical conditions. The danger of heart diseases requires an extremely fast analysis. A diagnosis at the right time can save a patient's life, while a delay could prove to be very dangerous. The health information of a patient, especially those related to his heart, are most relevant and valuable at the time of their arrival, that’s why on the fly predictions must be done immediately. Also, it is time for the healthcare industry to move from the era of analyzing our health history to the age of managing its future (Agneeswaran, Mukherjee, Gupta, Tonpay, Tiwari, & & Agarwal, 2013). In this context, streaming analytics are the best solution to get an immediate result and to predict future of patient’s heart condition.

In this paper, the authors propose two novel distributed deep learning algorithms to deal with the challenges of big data and deep learning. The first algorithm LS-DSN (Large-Scale Deep Stacking Networks) is a deep discriminative algorithm for big data analytics on large-scale cluster based on the Spark platform. LS-DSN needs the data to be stored on a stable storage system like HDFS and uses the full dataset in its training phase. The second algorithm proposed in this paper is StreamDSN, an online learning algorithm that, in contrast to LS-DSN, doesn’t require the data to be stored and learn from arriving streams of data instead. The Algorithms have shown good accuracy on the MNIST dataset and good scalability when the size of data rises. Finally, StreamDSN has been applied to ECG processing, StreamDSN has been chosen because of the nature of the application, and it has shown good results.

The rest of this paper is structured as follow, in the next section, the authors give at first an overview of tools and platforms used for big data processing, secondly, deep learning is introduced, and different algorithm classes are presented, and finally, the DSN algorithm is presented. The third section gives an overview of existing and related research works in the fields of large-scale deep learning, and ECG processing. LS-DSN and StreamDSN algorithms are presented in the fourth section, and their results are shown in the fifth section. The sixth section shows the experiment on ECG data, with data preprocessing, features extraction and results of StreamDSN when applied on ECG data. Finally, a conclusion is given in the seventh section with some future work.

BACKGROUND

Big Data and Tools

We are now living in an era where old storage and processing techniques are not enough to solve actual real-world problems. The size of data is clearly the most important and challenging characteristic of the big data, but they are also often associated with other characteristics that are commonly named the 5Vs (Ozkosea, Ari, & Gencer, 2015) (López, del Río, Benítez, & Herrera, 2015) The term big defines the first V; we are talking here about volume; the huge quantity of data that we have to deal with. In addition to volume, velocity is the second big challenge that big data technologies have to face; it refers to the speed at which data arrive. Real-time stream computing is gaining significant attention in the context of big data. In theory, streaming processing is a powerful way to manage big data by offering low latency processing platforms and highly distributed processing engines in real-time data analysis (Sun, Zhang, Zheng, & Li, 2015). This paradigm is vital for real world applications where batch processing is not sufficient to get fast good results, essentially those where a data stream changes frequently. Streaming analytics have opened a new era of future approaches in the world of big data. They occur when the data is too large, fast, dispersed and beyond the ability of available hardware and software facilities. Variety, veracity, and value complete the 5Vs. Each one has its meaning, its challenges and a set of techniques that are specifically made to deal with it.

While MapReduce platform and its well-known implementation system Hadoop have gained a large place in the domain of big data analytics, many limits have been brought to light. MapReduce has shown poor performance when performing iterative analytics like graph processing, data mining algorithms, etc. the fact that Hadoop uses HDFS to store intermediate results has considerably decreased its performance. To ameliorate iterative algorithms, which are very important in data analytics, in-memory programming models have emerged. Spark is one of the most important in-memory platforms, and experiences show that it surpasses the MapReduce-based models significantly.

Spark, like Hadoop, is an open source platform specialized in large data analytics developed in AMPLab at University of California, Berkeley. It can work on top of the HDFS system, but it’s not related to the MapReduce model. Spark started as an Apache incubator project in 2013, and it became a high-level project rapidly in 2014. Up to now, more than 30 companies have contributed to the project, including Yahoo, Intel, etc.

Spark uses the cluster memory to load the necessary data. In contrast to Hadoop, that requires loading data in HDFS at every iteration. It applies calculation directly in memory which results to high-speed analytics for iterative processes making it much faster than the Hadoop paradigm. Besides its performance, the popularity of spark is due to several other characteristics. Spark is easy to use, a user can write its program on spark using four high-level standard programming languages: Scala, Java, Python and recently R. Also, Spark is a general big data platform, it supports a large set of high-level applications, and a set of libraries and platforms have been built on top of it, like Spark SQL, Spark Streaming, MLLib and GraphX.

Experiments and evaluation of this processing engine have shown its superiority compared to Hadoop and other big data processing system like illustrated in Figure 1. Spark has been tested for several types of algorithms, like iterative machine learning, Page rank, and interactive tasks. For certain kinds of applications, Spark can surpass other platforms 100 times which shows clearly that it’s the most suitable platform for these types of big data analytics.

As mentioned before, streaming analytics for big data has gained a large place and importance. Spark Streaming (Zaharia, Das, Li, Shenker, & Stoica, 2012) is an extension of the Spark platform that has the objective of taking care of this aspect. Internally, spark streaming divides the streaming inputs data into batches; then they are processed on top of the Spark engine. This extension provides a high-level abstraction named Discretized Stream (DStream). The DStream represents a continuous stream of data, where the key idea is to treat the data streams as series of deterministic batches in small time intervals. The input data received at each interval is stored in the cluster memory, then it’s processed via deterministic parallel operations after the time interval is finished. Spark streaming has shown better results than other big data streaming engines like Storm and S4.

| Figure 1. Performance comparison between spark and Hadoop on K-means and logistic regression algorithms (Zaharia M., 2014) |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.f01](i/ch035.f01.png) |
| --- |

By supporting a wide range of workloads that previously required separately distributed systems, including batch applications, iterative algorithms, interactive queries, and streaming in the same engine, Spark makes it easy to combine several processing types, which is often necessary for production data analysis pipelines. Besides, it reduces the management burden of maintaining separate tools (Karau, Konwinski, Wendell, & Zaharia, 2015).

Deep Learning

The recent few years have viewed the emergence of machine learning techniques in much of real world fields. In the same context, deep learning algorithms are now the best ones in term of performance, they surpass classic algorithms very much. Inspired by the human’s neocortex, deep learning algorithms show very good results by automatically learn hierarchical representations using deep architectures in supervised or unsupervised mode. Due to their performance, deep learning technics has attracted the attention of academic researchers in several fields like speech recognition, language processing, computer vision, etc.

The basic idea of deep learning is stacking up nonlinear transformation layers. Deep learning refers to architectures that use consecutive layers. Each layer performs a nonlinear transformation on the data input and generates a representation of output. The primary goal of this approach is to pass data through multiple transformations to get a high-level data abstraction. The initial input data are given to the first layer. Consequently, the output of each layer is provided as input to the next one. This model can efficiently lead to representations of high abstraction level because each layer generates a more abstract representation by using a less abstract one.

In the literature, deep learning can be classified into three major categories, namely generative deep architecture, discriminative deep architectures, and hybrid architectures (Deng, Three classes of deep learning architectures and their applications: a tutorial survey, 2012), according to what the architectures are intended to be used.

*   • Generative deep architectures: This class of deep architectures generally has the goal of describing the dependencies between visible variables. This kind of architectures is often used for unsupervised feature selection purpose. They can also be used for supervised learning tasks, but with an unsupervised pre-training phase. A high set of deep algorithms has been developed in this category, the energy based one are the most common, such as deep autoencoders. Others algorithms are also very famous for deep unsupervised models with generative capabilities, like RBM, DBNs, DBM,…etc. One important type of generative deep architectures is the Deep Boltzman Machines (DBM). DBM is a set of multiple layers, with no connections between nodes in the same layer. Each layer computes complicated correlations between activities of the hidden features in the layer bellow. The DBM is widely used for applications like speech recognition because of its capability to learn representation that becomes more and more complex;
*   • Discriminative deep architectures: Often used for supervised classification and learning where target labels data are always available in a direct or indirect way. Most supervised learning algorithms are based on shallow architectures, like HMM, or CRF. The discriminative deep architectures are basically based on stacking lower layers output, together with the original input onto higher ones. In this paper, we focus our attention on this kind of deep architectures, in particular on the Deep stacking networks that we give details at the end of this section;
*   • Hybrid architectures: This category makes reference to architectures that take advantage of both generative and discriminative model components. The final goal of this kind of architectures is to exploit generative components to help with discrimination. The first point of view for this help is optimization, where an initialization points are provided by generative model trained in an unsupervised manner (pre-training). Secondly, the help can be viewed as regularization, where a prior on the set of function responsible for the model is provided by unsupervised learning.

Deep Stacking Network

Deep stacking network (Deng, Yu, & Platt, Scalable stacking and learning for building deep architectures, 2012) is a deep learning algorithm based on the stacking concept proposed initially in (Wolpert, 1992). Simple learning modules are trained first, then they are stacked on top of each other to learn complex functions. Firstly, DSN was named deep convex network (DCN) (Deng & Yu, Deep Convex Network: A scalable architecture for deep learning, 2011) this refers to the convex nature of the algorithm used for training the model. Modules of the DSN take the simplified form of the multi-layer perceptron, where the outputs are linear, and the hidden layers are sigmoidal. The choice of linearity in the outputs units was made with the learning scalability problem in mind, in contrast to other algorithms that have proven to be difficult to parallelize and scale-up to large clusters of machines. The DSN is highly efficient, scalable and allows closed-form estimation due to the linearity choice.

DSN architecture, as shown in Figure 2, contains a variable number of layered modules, each one consists of a simple multi-layer perceptron with a single hidden layer. Each layer in every single module has two trainable sets of weights. The lowest module contains naturally three layers, the first one is made by the set of inputs units, they correspond to the raw data in a vectored form. Secondly, there is a non-linear layer that corresponds to sigmoidal hidden units. And finally, a linear output layer with the values of output units. Above the bottom module of the DSN, all other modules are constructed in a similar way with one exception compared to the lowest one. In contrast to the first module, input layers are the result of lower(s) module(s)’s output vector and the raw data vector concatenation. The augmented vector serves as the effective input for the immediately higher layer.

Let’s say that X = \[x[1], x[2], .., x[i], …, x[N]\] is the set of all training data, where each x[i] = \[x[1i], x[2i], …, x[ji], …, x[Di]\]^T is a vector of input units for the bottom layer. N is the size of the training set of data, and D is the dimension of the initial input vectors. Let L be the number of hidden layer’s units hi = σ(W[m]^T .x[i]) where W[m] is an D\*L trainable weight matrix at the layer number m, and σ(.) is the sigmoidal function defined by:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.m01](i/ch035.m01.svg) (1)

The output layer of each module consists of a set of C linear output units. The output values y[i] are calculated by: yi = U[m]^T .hi where U[m] is an L\*C trainable weight matrix associated with the upper layer of the module number m. The output units correspond to the targets of the classification.

| Figure 2. Basic architecture of DSN algorithm with three layers, in each 3000 hidden units,784 input units and 10 output units (MNIST dataset) (Deng, Yu, & Platt, Scalable stacking and learning for building deep architectures, 2012) |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.f02](i/ch035.f02.png) |
| --- |

The dimensionality D[m] of the input vector in each layer is a function of the module number m. This is a result of the concatenation process between each two adjacent layers. D[m] is calculated from bottom up by:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.m02](i/ch035.m02.svg) (2)

Given the target vector T = \[t[1], t[2],…, t[i],…, t[N]\] where each target t[i] = \[t[1i], t[2i],…, t[ji],…, t[Ci]\]^T correspond to the input entry x[i], a supervised learning process is applied to train both of the trainable weight matrices W and U. The loss function of mean square error is used to learn the weight matrix U assuming W is known. The objective here is to minimize: E = Tr\[(Y - T)(Y - T)^T\], where Y = \[y[1], y[2],…, y[i],…, y[N]\]. It is important to notice that the fact W is known, the hidden layer values H = \[h[1], h[2],…, h[i],…,h[L]\] are also determined, the weight matrix U can be determined by setting the gradient in (3) to zero:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.m03](i/ch035.m03.svg) (3)

This optimization problem is well-known and has a close form solution known as pseudo invers and given in (4):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.m04](i/ch035.m04.svg) (4)

The weight matrix W needs to be set empirically across all DSN modules before the application of equation (4). For this end, the close-form expression of the gradient ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.m05](i/ch035.m05.svg) is derived by considering the relationship between W and U expressed in (4) and its effect on loss E:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.m06](i/ch035.m06.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.m07](i/ch035.m07.svg) (5)

where ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.m08](i/ch035.m08.svg) and ο denote the element-wise matrix multiplication. The weight matrix W can be then trained using the batch-mode gradient descent (Zhang, Deng, He, & Acero, 2011) and the equation (5). In contrast, weight matrix U can be updated with no iterations using equation (4). The initialization task for the matrix W in gradient descent in stacking modules is presented in (Deng, Yu, & Platt, Scalable stacking and learning for building deep architectures, 2012).

RELATED WORK

Deep learning requires large sets of data to accomplish the training task efficiently, thus the big data analytic paradigm is a natural way to do that. Many challenges have emerged for deep learning in big data, and researchers gave it more and more importance. In the last few years, deep architectures, algorithms, and software have been proposed for analyzing big data using specific platforms.

Recently, parallelization of deep architectures for learning from very large sets of data has gained much attention. DistBelief (Dean et al., 2012), a distributed software framework that can work on thousands of machines using tens of thousands of CPU cores was developed. The main purpose of this software is to efficiently train deep models. It was used to parallelize successfully deep network thirty times larger than reported in the literature and achieve state-of-the-art performance. A parallelism model was used to train a distributed deep sparse autoencoder on a cluster with 1000 machines and 16000 CPU cores on a dataset of 10 million images with good results (Le, 2013). A distribution on convolutional neural network with Q-learning variant has been proposed in (Ong, Chavez, & Hong, 2015), this approach has used the DistBelief software to accomplish the distribution mode of the algorithm. The distributed deep Q-learning algorithm has shown good results and a reasonable success on a simple game, it has also shown well scalability capacity.

Large scale GPU based approach for deep learning was proposed in (Rajat, Anand, & Andrew, 2009). Two deep algorithms have been implemented on GPU processing paradigm, namely deep belief networks and sparse coding. The motivation of this work is that the GPUs are much faster than multicore CPUs. The implementation of DBN has shown amelioration 70 times faster than dual-core CPU. This shows the great importance of parallelizing deep architectures for the executing time. The problem of GPU processing paradigm is its poor scalability for significant amounts of datasets due to the limited memory.

A large scale DBN has been presented in (Zhang & Chen, 2014). Distributed versions of RBMs for pre-training and the backpropagation algorithm for fine-tuning using the MapReduce platform are presented. Proper key-value pairs for each level RBM level were designed on MapReduce, they have used MRJob to run multi-step MapReduce jobs automatically. The learning of this distributed DBN version is accomplished by stacking up multiple MapReduce RBMs for pre-training and also MapReduce back-propagation for fine-tuning. MapReduce is not adapted for iterative algorithms due to HDFS I/O at each iteration, which is the case in the DBM, this can considerably reduce the perforce of the algorithm especially in regard to enormous datasets.

On the other hand, machine learning algorithms have been widely used for ECG analytics and processing. Many approaches have been proposed in this context, neural networks have been used for cardiac arrhythmia disease classification in (Malay & R.K, 2013) with good results. An SVM based approach for ECG beats classification was presented in (Banupriya & Karpagavalli, 2014). In (Kim, Hang, Shin, & Lee, 2009) Morphology Filtering, Principal Component Analysis and Extreme Learning Machine have been used to classify heart beat types. The approach has shown good results in term of sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy. Clustering also has been employed for ECG analytics purpose (Balouchestani & Krishnan, 2014) with good results. Other works in the context of using machine learning algorithms for ECG analytics have been published in the last few years, like (Dilmac & Korurek, 2015) and (Andrysiak, 2016). Surveys of methods for ECG analytics have been presented in (Jambukia, Dabhi, & Prajapati, 2015), and (Luz, Schwartz, Cámara-Chávez, & Menotti, 2016).

It is very important for hearts diseases to be detected early, this allows medical staff to plan and begin the treatment before it’s too late. With the fact the medical data are generated in a near real time is a big challenge for processing them. Approaches based on streaming and incremental analytics are highly suitable for this kind of purpose. In (Andreãoa, Mullerb, Boudyc, Dorizzic, Bastos-Filhob, & Sarcinelli-Filhob, 2008) an incremental HMM algorithm base on expectation-minimization strategy to analyze ECG signal has been proposed. Another arrhythmia prediction system has been presented in (Rashmi & Dipti, 2014). This work was based on online random forest algorithm and was applied on ECG signals.

In the big data context, machine learning for ECG analysis starts to gain a great importance in batch and streaming processing. A decision tree approach on MapReduce platform was proposed in (Li, Ma, & Zhao, 2016). A streaming approach based on random forest algorithm and implemented on the storm platform for ECG signal processing has been presented in (Agneeswaran, Mukherjee, Gupta, Tonpay, Tiwari, & & Agarwal, 2013). In (Mohammed, Far, & Naugler, 2014) a survey of applications of the MapReduce platform in the context of big clinical data is presented. The paper includes a section of clinical signal and ECG analysis and shows significant works in this area.

All the works mentioned above were based on shallow architectures like ANN, SVM or Random Forest. Deep learning is now considered as the state of the art in machine learning field. Several works start applying those deep architectures in the area of e-health to analyze clinical data efficiently. A deep architecture was used to analyze ECG data in (Al Rahhal, Bazi, AlHichri, Alajlan, Melgani, & Yager, 2016). n this work, an unsupervised approach based on stacked denoising autoencoders with sparsity constraint for feature learning is proposed. After this phase, a deep neural network was added as a softmax regression layer. The approach shows good results for ECG processing. Another approach for electrocardiogram signals classification with deep architecture is presented in (Meng & Zhang, 2014). Deep belief networks were used with two parts, feature extraction and classification with good results compared to some shallow architectures.

PROPOSED SCALABLE DEEP LEARNING APPROACHES

In this section, LS-DNS and StreamDSN are presented on top of the Spark platform. The main designs of the distributed spark DSN algorithms for batch and streaming analysis and are described with the approaches for calculating the gradient and training the weights using large scale versions of gradient descent algorithm.

LS-DSN

Given a set of input dataset X = \[x[i], x[2], …, x[N]\] where N is too large to fit in a single node memory, the input matrix has to be distributed across multiple processing nodes. The LS-DSN algorithm is divided into multiple distributed heavy steps. Calculating the gradient described in equation (5) of the second section is one of the big tasks that LS-DSN have to deal with. Matrices processing can take a huge time when executed on a single node, especially the multiplication and inverting tasks.

Distributing the gradient calculation can be done with two approaches, distributing the dataset, or distributing the processing itself. The authors have noticed that the second method cannot be implemented efficiently on the Spark platform. This is due to the nature of RDDs themselves. RDDs are read-only immutable datasets, and each update on them generates a new RDD. For example, the gradient descent at each iteration updates the matrix H, which is a big matrix (L\*N). This will lead the algorithm to consume much memory and execution time for the garbage collecting process. Also, the distributed computation of matrices multiplications, inverse and transpose will take much time for big matrices. So, the distribution of the processing is not good for big data DSN training on spark.

To get over those limits, the authors of this paper have chosen to distribute the dataset instead of distributing computations. The input matrix X is divided to multiple mini-batches, each mini-batch represents a partition of the RDD and is processed by a single CPU in the cluster. In this approach, all updates are processed locally at slave nodes, also the matrices computations are performed locally using MTJ (Matrix Toolkit Java) with native libraries to increase the computation efficiency. This will avoid data transfer between different nodes in the cluster.

DSN evaluates two weights matrices in the training phase at each module, namely W the input weight matrix and U the output weight matrix. The original DSN uses batch-mode gradient descent algorithm to tune the input weight matrix W, because the calculation of the pseudo inverse has to be done on the entire data set for high accuracy. The large-scale version of DSN (LS-DSN) keeps this in mind and synchronizes all the distributed processes on the pseudo inverse calculation that is done on the driver like shown in algorithm 1.

In this approach, each partition will calculate its hidden matrix H, calculate HH^T by locally multiply H with its transposed matrix, then a sum of all matrices HH^T is done by the spark reduce function. The driver computes the inverse of the resulting matrix and then broadcasts it to all the slave nodes to resume the gradient calculation. Note that the pseudo inverse matrix H^+ is implicitly partitioned on the slaves when each partition performs the multiplication of its local H^T by the global (HH^T)^(\-1).

| Figure 3. Illustration of the calculation of the gradient and evaluation of W matrix in LS-DSN on a Spark cluster with four workers |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.f03](i/ch035.f03.png) |
| --- |

*   Algorithm 1. Pseudo code of evaluating W and U matrices at the first module of LS-DSN

RDD<Integer, Vector> X = readFile(data) ;  
RDD<Integer, Vector> T = readFile(Labels);  
Matrix W = Random (-1, 1);  
0 < alpha < 1;  
WHILE (not Stopping criterion)  
RDD<Integer, Vector> H = X.mapPartitionsToPair(x -> sigmoidal (W^T\*X));  
RDD<Integer, Vector> HHT = H.mapPartitionsToPair(x -> x\*x^T) ;  
Matrix globalHHT = HHT.reduceByKey((x,y) -> x+y) .collect();  
Matrix inverse = invers (globalHHT) ;  
Matrix G = X.join(H).join.mapPartitions ((x,h)->calculate gradient using equation (5)) .collect();  
W = W – alpha\*G;  
END  
RDD<Integer, Vector> HTT = H.joint(transposed(T)).mapPartitionsToPair((h,t) -> h\*t) ;  
Matrix globalHTT = HTT.reduceByKey((x,y) -> x+y) .collect();  
Matrix U = globalHTT + globalHHT;

Different matrices are calculated before the gradient. Some of these matrices are independent and can be computed in a parallel manner like the matrix HT^T and the matrix TH^+. LS-DSN calculates those matrices in a multi-threaded manner.

Each partition on the cluster calculates its partial gradient with the global hidden matrix H received from the driver in the previous step.

The distributed batch-mode gradient descent algorithm will generate three matrices as output, the fine-tuned input weight matrix W, the global HH^T matrix calculated using the best W by the same way mentioned before, and finally, the global HT^T matrix calculated in the same way as the global HH^T. The last two matrices are used to compute the output weight matrix U as shown in the equation 4 of the second section without any iteration. Figure 3 shows the data flow and data portions in the gradient calculation.

After the two weight matrices are calculated, predictions are done on the full training data in a distributed manner on Spark. Each partition calculates the Y matrix that represents the prediction on its subset of input data. The result is an RDD that contains the predictions; it is concatenated with the original input data, and the new resulting RDD represents the input for the next module.

Each module uses the W fine-tuned by its predecessor as the initial value of the batch mode gradient descent.

StreamDSN

Many big data applications need streaming analytics, especially applications where data come on line. For this end, the authors propose StreamDSN which is a streaming deep learning algorithm for big data analytics. It performs both phases, training and prediction, in an online manner. In contrast of LS-DSN that requires all the dataset to be available before analytic starts, StreamDSN acquires incoming streams of data as they arrive, analyses them stream by stream, and gives results that approaching the batch ones.

Like LS-DSN, StreamDSN has to evaluate two weight matrices, the input weight matrix W, and the output weight matrix U. Both matrices have to be evaluated on the fly, because the data are not fully available and come in the format of infinite stream of mini batches. At every arriving mini batch, StreamDSN has to give predictions approaching those given by the batch mode algorithm involving all the previous mini batches.

In the training phase, the batch mode gradient descent is not suitable for streaming analytics, so the authors have chosen the mini batch stochastic gradient descent to train StreamDSN. The algorithm has to evaluate the weight matrices incrementally. To overcome this issue, StreamDSN evaluates the two weight matrices, by using some information of the calculation over all the previous mini batches of the data stream, like shown in Figure 4, to approach the batch mode results.

| Figure 4. Illustration for StramDSN on arriving Streams of data with inputs and outputs |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch035.f04](i/ch035.f04.png) |
| --- |

Let X[i] be the i^(th) batch received from the data stream, Spark Streaming takes care to divide it into partitions that are represented as an RDD. StreamDSN stores three types of matrices that represent the global state of the algorithm at each module, like shown in Figure 4, a D\*L matrix that represents the global input weight matrix W initialized at random numbers, an L\*L matrix representing the global HH^T matrix, and an L\*C matrix representing the global HT^T both initialized at zeroes. Let’s recall that D is the dimensionality of data, L is the number of hidden units, and C is the number of output classes.

*   Algorithm 2. Pseudo code of evaluating W and U matrices at the first module of StreamDSN

WHILE (data come)  
DStream<Integer, Vector> X = readFromNetwork(X);  
DStream<Integer, Vector> T = readFromNetwork(T);  
Matrix w = Random (-1, 1);  
0 < alpha < 1;  
J =1 first module  
WHILE (not Stopping criterion)  
DStream<Integer, Vector> H = X.mapPartitionsToPair(x -> sigmoidal (W^T\*X));  
DStream <Integer, Vector> HHT = H.mapPartitionsToPair(x -> x\*x^T) ;  
Matrix globalHHT = HHT.reduceByKey((x,y) -> x+y) .collect();  
Matrix inverse = invers (globalHHT) ;  
Matrix G = X.join(H).join.mapPartitions ((x,h)->calculate gradient using equation (5)) .collect();  
w = w – alpha\*G;  
END  
DStream<Integer, Vector> HTT = H.joint(transposed(T)).mapPartitionsToPair((h,t) -> h\*t) ;  
Matrix globalHTT = HTT.reduceByKey((x,y) -> x+y) .collect();  
Update: State.W(j) = State.W(j) - alpha\*G;  
Update: State.HHT(j) += globalHHT;  
Update: State.HTT(j) += globalHTT;  
Matrix U = State.HHT(j) + State.HTT(j);

At every arriving stream of data, the gradient is calculated and used to update a local w matrix iteratively, and the sum of gradients calculated over all iterations is obtained to update the global input weight matrix W of the current module. In addition to the sum of gradients, the algorithm outputs from the iterative process the matrix H. HH^T and HT^T are calculated and used to update their associated global matrices by doing the addition between the global matrix and the newly calculated one. The updated global HH^T and HT^T are used to derive the new output weight matrix U at the current module like shown in algorithm 2.

New updates are performed on the three state matrices for each new arriving batch. At the lower modules of the first arriving stream of dataset, W is initialized with random numbers, and at every other module, the fine-tuned W of the previous one is used as the initial input weight matrix for the current one. The predictions Y[i] are done on every data stream X[i] by using the resulting W and U matrices, as in LS-DSN, Y[i] are concatenated with Xi and given to the next module in the deep architecture as input data.

PERFORMANCE EVALUATION

In this section, LS-DSN and StreamDSN are validated, and their performance on big data sets are evaluated. For the experimentations, the MNIST (LeCun & Cortes, 1998) data set are used. It consists of 60,000 images of handwriting digits for the training set and 10,000 images for the testing set. All images were normalized to the size of 28x28 pixels that are represented as a vector of dimension 784. The labels are integers in \[0, 9\] representing the digits in the image. The labels set is transformed to a 60,000x10 matrix, each entry in the matrix has 1 in the ith case where i is the label of the image, and 0 in all other cases. The file containing the data has the size of 100Mb, for the evolution of LS-DSN and StreamDSN this file is duplicated 10, 20, 30, and 40 times. Table 1 shows the sizes of duplicated files.

The goal of this section is to validate and evaluate the performances of the algorithms. For this end, the authors compare the accuracy and the executing time of the proposed algorithms with their sequential version. For accuracy evaluation the same conditions are used to evaluate each algorithm in order to provide fair results, all algorithms are run on the same dataset (MNIST) with the same network configurations (3000 hidden units). The initialization of the input weight matrix for the first module was done randomly. Also, the same learning rate and number of epoch were used to train the model. Figure 5 shows that LS-DSN is as efficient as the sequential DSN algorithm by providing the difference of only 0.03% error rate on the MNIST testing set. Both algorithms were superior to their shallow version. StreamDSN shows comparable accuracy compared with batch versions, this is due to the non-availability of all the data set when training the model, but the algorithm still provides high accuracy reaching 98.9%. Note that with other initialization politics, the result could be better as shown in the original paper when the input weight matrix was initialized by using RBM.

Figure 6 shows the evolution of the error rate of StreamDSN algorithm as data stream arrive. In this experiment, the training set was randomly divided to 12 subsets sent to the algorithm one by one in a streaming manner, the algorithm learn from each subset on the fly and the results are plotted. The experiment demonstrates that the error rate decrease as more data arrive, this demonstrate the incremental nature of StreamDSN that don’t have to retrain over all of the data but only use the new one to improve the accuracy of the algorithm. Also, it shows the importance of the size of training set for high accuracy classification.

Scalability of the LS-DSN has been evaluated by studying running time on different data sizes using various numbers of CPUs. The number of CPUs used in the experiments varies from 8 to 40, Figure 7 shows the running time taken by running LS-DSN algorithm on different data sizes for each number of CPUs used. The results show that the running time increases with the data size and decreases when the number of CPUs increases. It is also observed that the benefice of raising the number of CPUs decreases when data are small, this is due to the communication overhead of the reduce operation.

STREAMDSN APPLIED TO ECG ANALYTICS

Electrocardiograms are important information sources about human health and heart state, efficiently analyzing them will give a better understanding of heart conditions. Beats classification is a major step in arrhythmia detection and diagnosis, where knowing the classes of sequential beats in the signal leads to detect the type of some heart diseases. For this end, StreamDSN has been used to classify heartbeats in an ECG signal on streaming efficiently. The authors have chosen StreamDSN over LS-DSN because of the data nature where ECG signals are recorded over time, and new data are available from time to time.

The ECG is a graphical representation of the electric activity of the heart; this activity is related to the electric potential of some heart cells. ECG is recorded using electrodes on the skin surface. A regular beat in an ECG waveform consists of three different wave shapes; P, QRS, and T waves. The P wave is due to atrial excitation, the QRS corresponds to the ventricular electric excitation, and the T wave corresponds to the repolarization of ventricles.

The dataset for the experiment on the ECG signal was extracted from the MIT-BIH ECG arrhythmia database (Moody & Mark, 2001). This database consists of 48 half-hour two-channel ECG signal recordings obtained from 47 patients and having different types of arrhythmia. Each record in the database has a description file that contains the kind of each beat identified by an expert. Beats can be classified into six classes, namely normal beat (N), atrial premature beat (A), ventricular premature beat (V), right bundle branch block (RB), left bundle branch block (LB), and paced beat (P).

In this experiment, 9000 beats (1500 of each class) were randomly selected from 18 records for the training phase and 4196 for testing. The records used in this experiment are 100, 101, 102, 103, 104, 107, 109, 111, 118, 124, 200, 207, 208, 209, 212, 222, and 232. The data were preprocessed by the MF (Morphology filter) method that removes noise from a signal and at the same time preserves the ECG morphology. The resulting ECG signal after this phase is a signal without high-frequency noise components and baseline drift that were present in the original ECG. After the preprocessing stage, features extraction is performed to obtain input vectors to give to the classification algorithm. For this end, discrete wavelet transform (DWT) method is used to extract features from each ECG beat.

The idea behind the wavelet transform is to represent any function as a superposition of wavelets. Wavelet Toolbox on Matlab was used to perform DWT, Daubechies db2 was used in this work because of its good accuracy when used for classification. 265 coefficients are obtained for each ECG segment and used to form the input vector of the algorithm.

StreamDSN has shown good accuracy compared to existing algorithms when training on ECG data, reaching almost 98.5% global accuracy. The results are demonstrated on the confusion matrix illustrated by Table 4, and Figure 8 with true positives of each beat class. The authors believe that more data will improve the accuracy of the algorithm like when it was used for the MNIST data set.

CONCLUSION

In this work, the authors have presented two discriminative deep approaches based on DSN algorithm. The first approach LS-DSN is a scalable deep learning algorithm conceived for big data analytics on large clusters. LS-DSN requires data to be available on a stable storage system before the training phase. A distributed version of the batch-mode gradient descent algorithm on Spark is presented to train LS-DSN. In contrast, StreamDSN is an online deep learning algorithm that trains from arriving streams of data. Stochastic mini-batch gradient descent is used to train the algorithm, and the gradient is calculated on streaming on top of Spark Streaming platform. Experiments show that the two approaches not only can achieve similar accuracy but also scale well when the data size increase considerably. Finally, StramDSN has been tested on ECG beats classification since significant ECG signals arrive on streaming, the algorithm shows good results. This paper presents two potential solutions for two of the most famous deep learning challenges in the big data era, namely volume and velocity. In the future, the proposed approaches will be experimented on larger datasets from different fields like bioinformatics, drug discovery, or even fraud detection.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Applied Metaheuristic Computing (IJAMC), 9(4); edited by Peng-Yeng Yin, pages 33-51, copyright year 2018 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).

ABSTRACT

This article describes how machine learning (ML) algorithms are very useful for analysis of data and finding some meaningful information out of them, which could be used in various other applications. In the last few years, an explosive growth has been seen in the dimension and structure of data. There are several difficulties faced by conventional ML algorithms while dealing with such highly voluminous and unstructured big data. The modern ML tools are designed and used to deal with all sorts of complexities of data. Deep learning (DL) is one of the modern ML tools which are commonly used to find the hidden structure and cohesion among these large data sets by giving proper training in parallel platforms with intelligent optimization techniques to further analyze and interpret the data for future prediction and classification. This article focuses on the use of DL tools and software which are used in past couple of years in various areas and especially in the area of healthcare applications.

INTRODUCTION

Machine learning (ML) is a field of study which learns the behaviour of functional relationship among data without considering the detail underlying characteristics present in them. These techniques are applied to derive the functional attributes of underlying data which do not contain precise definition about them. In real cases, the datasets which are available do not have a precise definition and functional co-relation. So, ML algorithms are used appropriately for these types of data which are capable to infer the useful features of the data and their functional co-relationship so that they can be used in the problems of classification, clustering and prediction etc. Deep learning (DL) is a field of study under the umbrella of Machine learning (ML) which is constituted on the algorithms inspired by the structure and utility of human brain. This study is coherent to artificial neural network (ANN) and can be called as advanced ANN having higher set of problem solving capability and utility. DL refers to a special type of ANN which is constituted by multiple numbers of hidden layers. The hidden layers are responsible for handling nonlinearity and complexity of underlying data. These are mainly useful for giving training to network exhibiting complex co relational functions and behaviour and are mostly suitable for large data sets. Due to this reason these are very successfully applied to big data domain. In this contemporary era, data is highly scalable and growing exponentially. There is a parallel growth in data reproduction, availability and access and abundance high speed computers. So, the need of the hour is to develop high speed large neural network which are scalable enough to deal with plethora amount of big data. The input to the conventional shallow learning algorithms are known features from the data, but DL algorithms possess the potential to extract the representative feature available from the raw data whose sources are social media, transactional data, business houses, etc.

In most application of data like classification, clustering and prediction the common work flows for machine algorithms are built on some basic steps like: (i) data cleaning (ii) pre-processing (iii) training which build the learning model and (iv)testing which will evaluate the built model. For these problems the input space contains a set of input data sample x[i] (i = 1, 2, ..., n ; where n is the number of input instances which is a vector of ‘m’ dimension where m is the number of features) and output y[i] . In supervised algorithms the artificial model learns to derive a mapping function f(x) = y from a priory known pair of (x[i], y[i]). After the model is duly trained on the basis of known input-output pairs (x[i], y[i]), it is evaluated against the unknown samples to infer the target output which is called as testing.

In the case of unsupervised model, the model has to explore the pattern exhibiting in input x[i] to find out y[i.]. In the training phase output y[i] is not provided to the model, it has to find itself. Clustering and principal component analysis are some of the examples of unsupervised learning.

Deriving feature sets x[i] to build an input dataset is very time consuming and problem specific. These are less available and difficult to create for every problem. This is the reason for unsuitability of supervised and unsupervised algorithm in all problems. But deducting the principal feature from a data set is directly associated with the performance of a learning algorithm. If features are correctly fetched from the data, then learning will take less time and the model shows higher level of accuracy. In the other hand for high dimensional data containing big data components, it is almost impossible to find out all the informative and relevant features from the raw data. This is a major limitation behind using conventional machine learning algorithms in big data possessing high dimensional feature data. This limitation is overcome by the emergence of deep neural network (Bengio et al., 2013; LeCun et al., 2015). Deep neural network contains many layers containing more than one hidden layer (Oliveira et al., 2016). The input layer takes the high dimensional raw data and extracts the relevant representive features from them. These abstract features are regenerated in subsequent hidden layers to incorporate the complex and nonlinear functions exhibited in high dimensional big data. The potential of deep learning algorithms to handle high dimensional raw data make them popular in the field of data analysis to deal with data having components like volume, variety, veracity, versatility of data (Aye & Thein, 2015).

BACKGROUND

Apart from health care, the application domains of DL are in various sphere such as: speech and audio processing, natural language processing, acoustic modelling, speech synthesis, language modelling, object recognition, computer vision, etc. (LeCun et al., 2015). Some specific task may include colorization of black and white images, classification of objects in still photographs, auto generation of handwriting, automatic system for gaming, generation of appropriate captions for images etc. In last couple of years DL has been widely used in the area of public health care and life science (NVIDIA corp. (2016). The data analyst from NVIDIA has recently disclosed in a report about the estimation of possession of AI components is 80% in applications by the year 2020. They have discussed about the recent advancement of medicine world and pointed the role of DL in bringing transformation in medicine world. Some of the focused areas in health care which indulge DL are discussed below.

Mining Clinical Data for Faster Treatment

The medical records of a patient which may include prescription details, medical images, MRI scans and clinical test reports are the useful information for a doctor. Maintain all these data for all the patient is a cumbersome job. Extracting useful information on time will help the doctor for diagnosis and detection of a disease. In these cases, GPU accelerated DL tools can be used to process these data and finding relevant information of a patient data for quicker treatment.

Quicker Diagnosis Process

Doctors rely greatly on medical images like MRIs, CT Scans, X-Ray reports, Ultra sound reports, ECG signals to detect and diagnose some diseases. Sometime these data are hard to analyse and consume a lot of time. In this case DL can be used as an automatic tool to analyze the data, which can further help the medical practitioners to make the diagnosis process faster.

Prescribing Personalized Medicines

The genomic data are responsible for causing disease in living body. Identifying and studying the genomic data causing disease is very difficult. Because genomic data are voluminous and extracting genetic parameters from huge genomic data are computation intensive jobs and require faster processing. DL can be employed to handle voluminous genetic data to do processing on these to mine information of disease causing genetic materials. So that personal medicines can be prescribed to individual patient according to the genetic structure and analysis. A GPU accelerated project taken over by a class of researchers from University of Toronto are working on a project named as” genetic interpretation engine”. Their work is focused on identifying cancer causing genes present in individual patient.

Helping Disabled People

Visually impaired people face a lot of difficulties while doing routine tasks such as road crossing, recognising people, reading tags and labels of different products. For this segment of people wearable devices are being developed containing embedded prior programmed chips. DL algorithms with the help of other techniques like image processing, computer vision is employed as embedded programs to perceive and understand the surroundings and transform these perceptions to words so that the blind people can get help to know their surrounding and accomplish the task.

Prediction of Pharmacological Properties of Drugs

Experimental gene expression data collected from human cells are applied as input data for studying the functional changes by using chemical and drugs. These study focuses on the reaction of different newly designed drugs by exploiting them to gene expression data. These types of data are voluminous and hard to compute with conventional methods. Deep neural network is used in these cases to forecast properties of drugs on various diseases (Mamoshina et al., 2016).

OBJECTIVE OF PRESENT WORK

Different types of DL architectures are: Deep neural network; Deep Auto-encoder; Deep Belief network; Deep Boltzmann machine; recurrent neural network; convolution neural network. Among these the widely used is deep neural network. The available software to implement and deploy DL models do not support all mentioned types. Some tools are specific, and some are generic. Some have fixed architecture, and some have customizable modules. The deployment of DL models can be done through two parts: (i) Frame work or (ii) Library. These are responsible for model different layers as a building block of the network and the architecture of the network is fully dependent on the problem domain. Figure 1 presents the available DL libraries and framework.

The limitations of these tools are studied and depicted. The results are taken from studied literatures from reputed article, industry white papers and product documentations.
