EXPERIMENT AND RESULTS

Preprocessing

Pre-processing is one of the critical tasks in the area of text classification or Natural Language Processing (NLP). To prepare the data various steps are performed like removal of special characters, stop word removal and tokenization. Twitter data need additional pre – processing like removal of hyperlinks and twitter handle.

Hyperparameters

Hyperparameters are the high-level concepts about the particular model that are learned directly from the data while training process. Once the hyperparameter are optimized, they can be used to achieve best results for the model. The subsections below specify certain important hyperparameters of CNN.

Padding

For convolution operation in CNN, the input sentences need to be of equal length. Therefore, the maximum length of the sentence (maxlength) is specified which is based on the average length of the text sentence. All the sentences smaller than maxlength are padded with zeros to make it equal to maxlength and the larger sentences are truncated to make it equal to maxlength.

Word Vector Initialization

The text data is converted into vector form so that it can be processed mathematically. Therefore, they are randomly initialized into word vectors using the uniform distribution in the interval \[-0.25, 0.25\]. In current work, the word vectors are pre-trained with word embedding from Google’s Word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013). They are the vectors with the size 300.

Filter Size and No. of Filters

The filter size helps in learning the local features from the text. They act as the n-gram feature learner. The activation function when applied on these feature maps gives the best features as an output. The filtering process is repeated with the different filter size sliding along the different windows of the sentence matrix.

Dropout Rate

Most of the neural networks suffer from the problem of overfitting especially when the amount of data is less. One way to reduce the extent of overfitting is to decrease the size of the network rather than increase the amount of data. This can be done through one of the regularization technique known as a dropout. In the dropout layer specified part of the network hidden nodes is deleted or dropped. Therefore, the co – adaptation of the nodes is prevented and thus reduces the overfitting of the network.

No. of Epochs

The epoch refers to the number of times the training process is repeated using the same training data. The number of epochs depends on the training data. The complex and noisy data require more training iterations. A careful choice of the number of epochs is needed since a very large number might lead to overfitting of data and that would result in increased training accuracy but lower test accuracy.

Dataset and Evaluation Measures

The model is evaluated on two datasets – SMS spam collection dataset, available in UCI repository and Twitter dataset, created by scrapping the public live tweets from the micro blogging site Twitter using Twitter API. These tweets are manually classified as ham or spam. The class wise tweets distribution is shown in the Table 3.

Parameter Settings and Results

Two datasets were used to evaluate the SCNN model along with the baseline methods. The model was implemented using Keras 2.0 API with python 2.7 on the Ubuntu 16.04.2 platform. The performance of SCNN was considered by carrying out experiments with various configurations. The mean accuracy is calculated via 10-fold cross-validation. Initial experiments were performed by keeping all the variables constant. Since, the dataset consists of SMS data and Twitter data in which the size of text is limited, the maximum number of characters in a sequence is taken as 160 and the batch size of 32 is considered. The filter size of (2, 3, 5) is considered for the creation of feature map and the number of filter taken is 64 with a dropout rate of 0.1. For gradient descent, the Adagrad (Duchi, Hazan & Singer, 2011) update rule is used with the learning rate of 0.01. Max-pooling strategy is used with the pool size of 4 and ReLu activation function is used. The final softmax layer uses the sigmoid function that classifies the text as spam or ham. For creation of word vectors, Google’s Word2Vec (Mikolov et al, 2013) is used. This word embedding has the dimension of 300. To support the use of word2vec for every word, WordNet and ConceptNet were also used. The performance in the Table 5 shows that the word2vec word embedding increases the performance of the model since, it can better correlate with the similar words.

CONCLUSION

In this paper, extensive experiments were performed for spam detection using a well-known deep learning technique known as a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). The CNN is generally used in the area of computer vision, but in this research, it is used for Natural Language Processing (NLP) task specifically for spam detection. The work in chapter proposes to add a semantic layer above the CNN layer which results in enriching the word vector semantically. This is done with the help of word2vec, WordNet and ConceptNet. The word2vec maps the word to the pre-trained word vectors from Google’s Word2Vec. While WordNet and ConceptNet gives the alternate word for the words that does not exists in Word2Vec. The resultant word vector is used by CNN to give the model is known as Semantic CNN. The local features are captured with the help convolutional layer. They are phrase level features and the length of the phrase is equivalent to the length of the filter. Since these features are better initialized and semantically related, they gave better than state-of-the-art results for spam detection.

Future work includes the experimentation of SCNN on Big data which could not be carried out in the present work due to hardware limitations. The work can also be extended for spam detection on languages other than English.

ABSTRACT

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are best known for being the state-of-the-art in artificial intelligence (AI) applications including natural language processing (NLP), speech processing, computer vision, etc. In spite of all recent achievements of deep learning, it has yet to achieve semantic learning required to reason about the data. This lack of reasoning is partially imputed to the boorish memorization of patterns and curves from millions of training samples and ignoring the spatiotemporal relationships. The proposed framework puts forward a novel approach based on variational autoencoders (VAEs) by using the potential outcomes model and developing the counterfactual autoencoders. The proposed framework transforms any sort of multimedia input distributions to a meaningful latent space while giving more control over how the latent space is created. This allows us to model data that is better suited to answer inference-based queries, which is very valuable in reasoning-based AI applications.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Often in real-world applications such as multimedia, NLP, and medicine, large quantities of unlabeled data are generated every day. This surge in data gives rise to the challenging semantic gap problem (Lin, Shyu & Chen, 2012; Chen, Lin & Shyu, 2012; Zhu & Shyu, 2015; Sadiq, Yan, Shyu, Chen & Ishwaran, 2016) which is to reduce the gap between high level semantic concepts and their low level features (Sadiq, Tao, Yan & Shyu, 2017a; Sadiq, Zmieva, Shyu & Chen, 2018; Yan, Chen, Sadiq & Shyu, 2017). Despite rigorous research endeavors, this remains one of the most challenging problems in information sciences where we have overwhelming quantities of all sorts of fast, complex, heterogeneous and unstructured data. To handle such data, conventionally we have been utilizing descriptive models that try to find deterministic features and build probabilistic models (Chen & Kashyap, 1997; Chen, 2010; Lin, Shyu & Chen, 2013; Sadiq et al., 2017b). However, the problem with discriminative models is that they, generally, estimate a hyperplane. For example, when categorizing images of cats and dogs, data points on one side of the hyperplane are categorized as cats and everything on the other side as dogs. Discriminative models follow a condition in logistic regression that relaxes the computation of a joint probability p(x,y) to a conditional probability p(x|y) which is much easier to calculate because it maps directly to the hyperplane that divides between two clusters. This problem gets exacerbated in deep learning models due to the increase in dimensionality and boorish memorization of patterns. Mere rotations or color-inversions in the trained images can easily confound very deep neural networks even though the modified images share the same semantics and structures as the original images (Hosseini & Poovendran, 2017).

Recently, there has been a growing concern of this shortcoming, resulting in a soaring interest in Knowledge Representation and Reasoning (KRR) (Liu, 2017) and reasoning based deep learning (Andreas, Rohrbach, Darrell & Klein, 2016; Santoro et al., 2017). We believe that the next generation of AI systems will need to have the ability to understand problems at a deeper level rather than just based on memorization of data. However, discriminative models fail completely in inferencing problems because they do not capture the underlying relationships in the input space. Figure 1 shows how the addition of an adversarial noise can completely fool the classification while the L2 loss between the original and modified images was minimal. The discriminative models considered them as identical images while producing completely different results. All images were classified with 99.9% confidence.

| Figure 1. Classification results produced by state-of-the-art deep learning models, but fooled by simple noising up of the images (Nguyen, Yosinski & Clune, 2015) |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.f01](i/ch040.f01.png) |
| --- |

There has been a growing interest to uncover such deep representations by mapping the observed data to latent spaces (Blei, Ng & Jordan, 2003; Neal, 2000; Roweis, 2003; Lei & Rinaldo, 2015; Koren, Bell & Volinsky, 2009). Thus, for reasoning applications, we have to look into generative models such as Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) (Kingma, Mohamed, Rezende & Welling, 2014) and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) (Goodfellow et al., 2014). This paradigm shift in training machine learning methods uses latent relationships and generative models and has proven to be successful in inferring relationships (Makhzani, Shlens, Jaitly, Goodfellow & Frey, 2015; Wetzel, 2017). Inference based training can open access to some interesting AI reasoning applications including: (1) Aiding users in understanding their surroundings or social media content (AI: ‘Mike just sent you a picture from his vacation in Thailand’; Human: ‘Great, is he at the beach?’; AI: ‘No, on a mountain’). (2) Aiding in decision making based on surveillance data (Human: ‘Did anyone enter this room last week?’; AI: ‘Yes, several instances found’; Human: ‘Were any of them carrying a black bag?’). (3) Health and safety applications (Human: ‘Can you see the baby in the baby monitor?’; AI: ‘Yes, I can’; Human: ‘Is he sleeping or playing?’). (4) Search and rescue missions (Human: ‘Is there smoke in any room around you?’; AI: ‘Yes, in room B6’; Human: ‘Look for people in room B6’).

Extending our previous work in semantic representation (Chen, Shyu & Kashyap, 2000; Chen, Zhu, Lin & Shyu, 2013; Yan, M. Chen, Shyu & Chen, 2015; Zhu, Lin, Shyu & Chen, 2011; Li, Chen, Shyu & Furht, 2002; Chen, Sista, Shyu & Kashyap, 1999; Chen, Rubin, Shyu & Zhang, 2006; Chen, Shyu, Zhang & Kashyap, 2001), here we propose a generative model that becomes the source for multimedia based inferencing frameworks. The proposed model implies the structure on the latent space in generative models and can be used for clustering, latent space arithmetic, semantic hashing and dimensionality reduction to make information retrieval faster. We can also use the proposed generative VAE with semi supervised learning to get very close to the state-of-the-art performance. Similar methods such as in (Makhzani et al., 2015) reported with good performance with MNIST data while using10 labels instead of 5000 labels.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows, Section 2 describes the previous work done in generative models. The foundations of VAEs and statistical inferencing are presented in Section 3 to get an understanding of knowledge representation with the generative models. Section 4 provides the details about the proposed framework and performs the experiments in Section 5. Section 6 concludes the findings of this paper and identifies the future opportunities to extend this work.

2\. PREVIOUS WORK

Without statistical inferencing, we are simply confined to the bounds of our data and cannot infer new knowledge that extends beyond our data. Statistical inferencing in the reasoning paradigm is the process of generating conclusions about a population from a noisy and complicated sample. Until recently, deep generative models, such as Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), Deep Belief Networks (DBNs) and Deep Boltzmann Machines (DBMs) were trained primarily by Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC)-based algorithms (Hinton, Osindero & Teh, 2006; Salakhutdinov & Hinton, 2009). In these approaches the MCMC methods compute the gradient of log-likelihood which becomes more imprecise as training progresses. This is because samples from the Markov Chains are unable to mix between modes fast enough. In recent years, generative models have been developed that may be trained via direct back-propagation and avoid the difficulties that come with MCMC training.

Some notable mentions of the existing methods include Knowledge-Based Artificial Neural Network (KBANN) (Towell, 1990), a hybrid learning method that leverages domain-knowledge and maps reformulated knowledge theories into neural networks. KBANNs proclaim promising results on biological applications with shallow encoding rules. Others have combined neural networks with Markov logic networks by learning the weights of the probabilistic logic clauses (Lippi & Frasconi, 2009). This technique requires structured equation modeling of background knowledge (e.g., bioinformatics and time-series forecasting) that suffers from the assumptions of model correctness and feature distributions. Bayesian Deep Learning (BDL) (Wan & Yeung, 2016) improves not only the perception tasks such as understanding of content (e.g., from text or image) but also the inference/reasoning tasks using principled probabilistic frameworks. However, BDL necessitates prior distribution information and assumes Gaussianity that restricts the input datasets and consequently restricts the applications. GANs (Radford & Chintala, 2015) are able to train the Question-Answering (QA) models but still lack the relationships between the black box features. Other noteworthy mentions include Memory Networks by Facebook AI Research (Sukhbaatar, Weston & Fergus, 2015), Neural Turing Machines by Google DeepMind (Graves, Wayne & Danihelka, 2014), and Watson by IBM (Gliozzo, Biran, Patwardhan & McKeown, 2013). These large architectures do promise the reasoning capability, but they are proprietary systems that are not intended for public release. Our primary target is to propose a novel generalized open-source framework that imbeds the spatio-temporal data collinearities in the neural networks and activates the data flow invariant to sparsity and imbalance in the data. There are several other methods offering improvements on various dimensions such as the rate-distortion theory perspective presented in β-VAEs (Burgess et al., 2018). Their approach represents variational factors of data under a modified Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) bound by a β condition. It creates the disentangled representations of the latent variables without a considerable loss in the reconstruction accuracy.

Another variant of the VAEs was proposed in (Dilokthanakul, 2016), where a Gaussian mixture was used as the prior distribution. This is helpful in performing uncluttered unsupervised clustering without over-regularization of the generative model. Walker, Doersch, Gupta & Hebert (2016) proposed a pixel-level dense trajectory prediction of given data frames. These frames were taken from a moving video scene where the algorithm estimates the changes over the time duration of one second using a conditional variational autoencoder setup. Another interesting approach was proposed by Sønderby, Raiko, Maaløe, Sønderby & Winther (2016) where a recursive inference model called the Ladder Variational Autoencoder was proposed. Their model corrects the generative distribution by using likelihood approximations. Their predictive log-likelihood claims superiority over the bottom-up inference in conventional VAEs.

3\. VARIATIONAL AUTOENCODERS

Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are related to an unsupervised learning model called autoencoders. VAEs are used to learn a lower-dimensional feature representation from the unlabeled training data. The input data x is converted to a latent space vector z by a mapping function p(x|y). The encoder can take many forms, but neural networks usually outperform all other methods in learning the complex mapping functions. The hidden space z is usually smaller than x to avoid trivial solutions and serves as a form of dimensionality reduction as well. Then, z represents the most important features in x that can capture meaningful factors of the variation in data. The latent feature representation z is utilized to reconstruct the original data by decoding them using an identical network to the encoder called the decoder to get the same dimensionality as x, thus the term autoencoder – encoding itself. The data likelihood p(x) is defined as taking the expectation over all possible values of z, which is continuous, and the expression with the latent space z can be obtained:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m01](i/ch040.m01.svg) (1)

However, we are unable to take the gradient and maximize the likelihood p(x|y) for every possible value of z because the integral is intractable. Here, p[θ](z) is a simple Gaussian prior, p[](x|y) is a decoder neural network, and θ are the distribution parameters of the encoder and decoder. Similarly, the posterior density also becomes intractable due to the intractable data likelihood p[θ](x) in the denominator:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m02](i/ch040.m02.svg) (2)

The solution that will enable us to learn this model is to define an additional encoder network q[ϕ](z), with a different set of parameters ϕ, that approximates p[θ](x|z), in addition to the decoder network modeling p[θ](x|z). This allows us to derive a lower bound on the data likelihood that is tractable and can be optimized. Since we are modeling a probabilistic generation of data in variational autoencoders, the encoder and decoder networks are probabilistic. Our encoder network q[ϕ](z) with parameters ϕ will output a mean ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m03](i/ch040.m03.svg) and a diagonal covariance ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m04](i/ch040.m04.svg). This will be the direct output of our encoder network. A similar method can be performed for the decoder network ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m05](i/ch040.m05.svg) which is going to start from z and outputs the mean ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m06](i/ch040.m06.svg) and diagonal covariance ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m07](i/ch040.m07.svg) as shown in Figure 2(a).

3.1. KL-Divergence

It is important to note that dimensionality reduction by latent space representation works only if the inputs are highly correlated, for example, images from the same domain or texts from the same corpus. If completely random inputs are given each time while training an autoencoder, it will not be able to create a sound latent representation. This is because the encoded latent space will not cover the entire 2-D latent space and will have a lot of gaps in its output distribution. Hence, if we enter some values that the encoder has not fed to the decoder during the training phase, weird looking output images will be generated. This can be overcome by constraining the encoder output to have a random distribution, i.e., ~N(0,1), when producing the latent code. Thus, KL divergence is used as a weighted sum on some similarity measure to add the constraint on the latent space to match a normal distribution ~N(0,1) as shown in Figure 2(b):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m08](i/ch040.m08.svg) (3)

Here, p(z) is the original latent distribution and q(z) is the normal distribution ~N(0,1). Using variational inferencing, the Kullback-Leibler divergence can be reduced to the following:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m09](i/ch040.m09.svg) (4)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m10](i/ch040.m10.svg) (5)

It is a distance measure between distributions (Hoffman, Blei, Wang & Paisley, 2013). However, p(z|x) cannot be calculated. Thus, applying the power of logarithms to Equation (5) transforms it into:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m11](i/ch040.m11.svg) (6)

The first two terms on the right-hand side are equivalent to maximizing the ELBO, which only requires to calculate the joint distribution p(x,z). Please note that the third term does not involve q and thus this distribution can be ignored because it is just a number in optimizing the variational distribution. There is, however, always a trade-off between how accurately the latent space can fit into the desired Gaussian shape and how well informative new data can be generated.

3.2. Reparameterization

Autoencoders are generally simpler to train because we simply have to backpropagate the reconstruction loss across the weights of the network. However, VAEs are not as simple to optimize because the sampling operation is not differentiable. This means that the gradients from the reconstruction error cannot be propagated to the encoder. The reparameterization trick is to stretch the encoded standard deviation with an additional random noise as shown in Figure 3. This is equivalent to random but becomes a linear equation:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m12](i/ch040.m12.svg) (7)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m13](i/ch040.m13.svg) (8)

Here, i represents the batch and ε[i] is the random noise that helps us backpropagate the network. With the reparametrized form, we changed ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m14](i/ch040.m14.svg).

4\. FRAMEWORK

In this paper, a novel object correlation model that uses VAE for feature translation to the latent space is proposed (as illustrated in Figure 4). We start with our minibatch X[i] that is passed through the encoder network which can be a Convolutional, Bi-LSTM or a fully-connected network depending on the data type. Two vector outputs μ[θ] and Σ[θ] (i.e., the mean and the covariance matrix) can be obtained. After applying the reparameterization trick, we sample the actual latent stochastic representation of the image z|x. The K dimensional latent encoding is decoded using the decoder network, which is similar to the encoder network, to get the replica of our minibatch X[i]. The network trains in three steps. The first part is the reconstruction phase where we train the VAE to reproduce the minibatch X[i] using the L2 loss and Adam optimizer. The K\-dimensional latent vector obtained from the first phase is called z[C]. The second phase is to train and produce the counterfactual latent representation denoted by z[T]. The counterfactual latent encodings are produced by our proposed Shallow Randomized Backpropagation (ShRB) networks. The ShRB networks, explained in the next subsection, allows us to produce Gaussian versions of the original latent encoding with the capability to manipulate the latent space. The final step is to backpropagate on the loss of these two counterfactual terms and train the encoder to minimize the KL divergence between z[C]||z[T]. There will be two losses. The first one is the reconstruction loss to train the horizontal pass of the variational autoencoder; while the second one is the KL loss that will help train the ShRB networks.

| Figure 4. The proposed counterfactual autoencoder framework |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.f04](i/ch040.f04.png) |
| --- |

4.1. Shallow Randomized Backpropagation (ShRB)

It is interesting to note that VAEs are very bad at disentangling and separating the clusters or subgroups of data in the hidden space. Thus, we propose an unsupervised subgrouping method, called Shallow Randomized Backpropagation (ShRB) networks, which completely removes the subsampling / pooling layers and maximizes the diversity of the hidden space variables. The ShRB networks primarily takes the latent space created by VAEs and additionally separates the variance of the feature covariance matrix by sampling the features of the minibatch. The ShRB networks create disjoint Gaussians. That is, each latent dimension z[k]∈K is trained on each ShRB network.

Suppose that each ShRB network is represented by the function ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m15](i/ch040.m15.svg), and z[k] is the univariate continuous valued outcome vector, and ε is the error term. Then for an i^(th) input batch X[i] and the latent vector z, the goal is to closely predict the latent vector z[k].

If ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m16](i/ch040.m16.svg) predicts z=f[0](X)+ε, where ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m17](i/ch040.m17.svg) is the predicted z, and f[0]()is the learned functions, then:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m18](i/ch040.m18.svg) (9)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m19](i/ch040.m19.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m20](i/ch040.m20.svg) (10)

Here, PE () is the prediction error, ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m21](i/ch040.m21.svg) is the expectation over the learning dataset, ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m22](i/ch040.m22.svg) represents the expectation over the test dataset, and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m23](i/ch040.m23.svg). The first term σ² is the internal noise and this is the lower bound on the generalization error. The second term ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m24](i/ch040.m24.svg) is the bias, described as the difference between the true predictor and the mean of the learned predictor. The final term is the variance ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m25](i/ch040.m25.svg), described by the difference between the predictor and its mean value. It is basically a mean-squared error decomposition. There are two observations from this. The prediction error for each predictor is always bigger than the averaged predictor and the amount is equal to the variance. Thus, by taking the average, we can completely remove the variance, and it drops to zero. Moreover, if our original predictor is unbiased, then taking the average of it will also be unbiased. Hence, it is in some ways a very effective predictor, taking an average of an unbiased high variance predictor and turns it into a stable and accurate ensemble learner. In cases where we have high dimensional latent spaces, then the perturbation would not be enough to decorrelate the predictors and to reduce the variance. Thus, we further sample from the feature set and pass only 1/3^(rd) of the features for every sample. This is another form of randomization in the process to reduce the variance.

4.2. Tensor Slicing and Conversion to Gaussian

We assume that z[1],…,z[K] are all independent latent vectors, thus giving us only a diagonal variance matrix. Instead of calculating O(n²) computations, we trade the complexity for the bias and calculate only O(n) steps through variational approximation. This is done by slicing the latent tensors and estimating them individually through the ShRB networks. By this approach, we know that we do not estimate the true Gaussian nature of the latent tensor, but we will get the best answer under the complexity constraints that the application can tolerate. The tensors need to be sliced along each dimension of the latent vector z such that, given the vector ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m26](i/ch040.m26.svg) the notation z[k] ∈ R[K] denotes the k-th dimension of z. Each predicted z[k] is scaled between 0 and 1 values using sigmoid activation and converted to Gaussian using probabilities to z-score transformation activation:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m27](i/ch040.m27.svg) (11)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m28](i/ch040.m28.svg) (12)

4.3. CounterFactual Approach

Conventionally in VAEs, almost all methods attempt to force the latent variable to match a normal distribution ~N(0,1). This approach forces a distribution that brings the latent vector mean towards zero, imbalancing the underlying data relationships such that, the outliers and imbalanced data points are also conditioned to be generated under a zero mean restriction. Our proposed counterfactual approach takes the original latent variable distribution as a prior and generates a counterfactual Gaussian of the latent variable z without forcing any prior conditions on it. This allows us to learn a latent distribution that allows better disentanglement between each latent vector along all dimensions. Formally, let {(x[1],z[1]),…,(x[i],z[i])} denote the minibatches where x[i] is a minibatch and z[i] represents the latent vector for that minibatch. After learning the latent representation, we call the non-transformed z[i] as z[i,C] (where C indicates no transformation) and the ShRB estimated latent vector ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m29](i/ch040.m29.svg) is denoted by ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m30](i/ch040.m30.svg) (where T represents being transformed). Our goal is to train on the loss incurred by the differences between z[i,C] and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m31](i/ch040.m31.svg). The loss is defined as:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch040.m32](i/ch040.m32.svg) (13)

Equation (12) relies on what is so-called the counterfactual framework or the potential outcomes model (Neyman, Dabrowska & Speed, 1990). In this framework, one models what an individual vector would look like if it were generated as a Gaussian although the observed vector is non-Gaussian. This modification allows us to use a broader set of distributions as priors for the latent code as follows:

*   1\. Preserves the distribution giving better manifold;
*   2\. Removes the gaps between the latent representations;
*   3\. We can switch to the variance as a loss function and get the maximized separation;
*   4\. It does not matter how high dimensional we treat each z[k] individually; and
*   5\. It can be scaled without affecting the Gaussian conversion.

5\. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS

In this section, we perform several experiments using the proposed Counterfactual Autoencoders and the MNIST and Fashion MNIST datasets. One of the advantages of using the ShRB networks is that they create disjoint estimates of the sliced latent dimensions. For example, in any given image, some ShRB networks will see the top part of an image while other ShRB networks will see the bottom part of it. Based on what each ShRB network sees, it will create a different set of μ and σ estimates for each z[k]∈K. This increases variability in the z estimates and gives us the benefit of scalability and the ability to manipulate the z-space easily.

5.1. Performance Comparison

The experiment was compared with the original VAE (Kingma et al., 2014) and a comparative approach called the Maximum-mean discrepancy VAEs (Zhao, Song & Ermon, 2017). The results of the comparison are shown in Figure 5.

While comparing the learned manifold spaces, we see a near circular 2-D Gaussian shape with good disentanglement achieved by the proposed counterfactual autoencoder in Figure 5(c). The learned manifold depicts sharp transitions between data points indicating that the coding space is filled and contains no gaps. By contrast, Figures 5(a) and 5(b) illustrate the coding space of the MMD and vanilla VAE with almost similar architectures to that of the proposed counterfactual autoencoder. However, it can be observed that the two methods roughly match the shape of a 2-D Gaussian distribution and there are several gaps in the manifold. These points map to no data and end up creating garbage data. The methods were not able to capture the manifold as good as the counterfactual autoencoder. Similar observation is found when comparing the three methods when trained on the Fashion MNIST dataset as illustrated in Figures 5 (d), (e) and (f). The Fashion MNIST dataset is more ambiguous than MNIST, thus we see bizarre distributions for MMD and vanilla VAE. Whereas the proposed counterfactual autoencoders achieves perfect 2D Gaussian shape with good disentanglement between classes. 6\. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

Deep Learning puts forward some of the most sophisticated machine learning solutions to the current state-of-art Artificial Intelligence (AI). However, these methods are based on a monolithic approach of being confined within the data. This results in an array of non-interpretable and high dimensional features that cannot be reasoned or used in any methodical framework. In spite of all the success and power of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), AI is still far from how a human analyzes the data. The answer may lie in an inference-based approach that looks at the problem in a reduced heuristics space, like humans, and uses the power of the latent space arithmetic to put 2 and 2 together. Current reasoning frameworks are either too narrow or require too much human assistance that renders them un-scalable. In this paper a novel approach called counterfactual autoencoders is proposed that regularizes hidden space representations using randomized shallow learners and trains the generative network using a counterfactual loss. The proposed approach transforms the hidden representations to near perfect Gaussians with good disentanglement and provides wide-ranging control to manipulate and explore the latent space. This provides us with opportunities to use the Counterfactual Autoencoder in order to solve semantic learning, reasoning and inferencing problems. The algorithm was tested only on the prior mentioned two datasets, but the proposed framework’s capability can be easily extrapolated to other multimedia datasets. As a future prospect, further specific use-cases will be explored and presented in upcoming publications.

ABSTRACT

Recent years, textual semantic similarity measurements play an important role in Natural Language Processing. The semantic similarity between concepts or terms can be measured by various resources like corpora, ontologies, taxonomies, etc. With the development of deep learning, distributed vector models are constructed for extracting the latent semantic information from corpora. Most of existing models create a single prototype vector to represent the meaning of a word such as CBOW. However, due to lexical ambiguity, encoding word meaning with a single vector is problematic. In this work, the authors propose a knowledge-augmented multiple-prototype model by using corpora and ontologies. Based on the distributed word vector learned by the CBOW model, the authors append the concept definition and the relational knowledge vector into the target word vector to enrich the semantic information of the word. Finally, the authors perform the experiments on well-known datasets to verify the efficiency of the authors’ approach.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Semantic similarity or relatedness, a basis for textual analysis in natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR), is commonly used to quantify the degree of the likeness of semantic content and lexical meaning. Textual semantic similarity measurements have been widely applied to a variety of applications, such as web service discovery (Paliwal et al., 2012), word sense disambiguation (Resnik, 1999), text clustering (Song et al., 2009), question answering (Ramprasath and Hariharan, 2012), as well as detection and correction of malapropisms (Hirst and StOnge, 1998). In addition to linguistics, the semantic similarity computing also emerges in other research fields, such as Biomedicine (Pedersen et al., 2007) and Geoinformatics (Schwering and Raubal, 2005). Some studies use the notion of semantic similarity and semantic relatedness interchangeably. Actually, the connotation of semantic relatedness is more general than semantic similarity, which represents a special case of relatedness. Two semantically dissimilar concepts may be related to each other in certain contexts. For example, “bank” and “interest”, whose meanings are apparently dissimilar, have some semantic relatedness since generally co-occur in a financial article. In terms of lexical resources, existing semantic similarity measurements are generally classified into knowledge-based methods and corpus-based methods. Knowledge-based measures rely on inherent structure and information content of priori knowledge bases or semantic lexicons such as WordNet (Miller, 1995) and Gene ontology, however, it is limited by the size of knowledge base; While corpus-based measures employ distributional properties of occurrence of words in a given corpus, such as British National Corpus, Wikipedia, and web search. Knowledge-based measures are considered more useful for evaluating the semantic similarity with predefined semantic relationships between words, on the contrary, corpus-based measures are more helpful for assessing the semantic relatedness using the co-occur statistics, but it is hard to show the relationships between words.

Nevertheless, most of existing works employ either knowledge base or corpora, which may suffer from the insufficiency of semantic information and the ambiguity contained in raw corpora. Therefore, some works combine knowledge bases with corpora for extracting the accurate semantic of words and measuring the semantic similarity. In the article by (Jiang and Conrath, 1997) extended WordNet-based method by adding the information content from corpus, and indicated the structural information sources from the lexical taxonomy WordNet, which consists of edge, depth, density and link type. The work by (Li, 2003) replaced the local semantic density in WordNet by the information content derived from corpus for measuring semantic similarity with distinct lexical sources. Moreover, due to polysemy and homonymy, there is other works conduct multiple sense-specific vector representation per word in distributional vector space or distributed vector space. In these multi-prototype vector representations, semantic similarity between two words is then computed as the max similarity or the average similarity of all pairs of prototype vectors.

Most of existing works employ either knowledge base or corpora, which may suffer from the insufficiency of semantic information and the ambiguity contained in raw corpora, to solve this problem, in this work, the authors proposed a knowledge-augmented multiple-prototype vector representation model which represents each word by a set of distinct vectors. The semantic similarity between two words is therefore computed as the max among the similarity values of multiple vector pairs. Inspired by the emerging distributed word representation in deep learning, the authors primarily leverage the corpora to train distributed word vector via neural network language model. Then the authors use WordNet as additional knowledge with unambiguous semantics to augment the semantic information of corpora and conduct multiple prototype vectors per word in low-dimensional vector space. This work contributes to propose a knowledge-augmented multiple-prototype model to enrich the semantic information of the word vector. The contributions include: 1. This work leverage both the corpora and knowledge base to train the language model; 2. The language model is multiple-prototype, which means the word is represented by set of distinct vectors.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 gives related background on distributed vector space and the works on semantic assessment which combine corpora with knowledge base. Section 3 presents the main attributions of semantic knowledge. Section 4 presents our knowledge-augmented word sense model and multi-prototype distributed vector representation. Our experimental evaluations and discussion are presented in Section 5, and Section 6 concludes the paper.

2\. RELATED WORK

Distributed vectors, namely word embedding, are commonly used knowledge representation of words in corpus-based semantic similarity measures. The representation vectors are learned via unsupervised neural network language model such as HLBL (Mnih and Hinton, 2009), SENNA (Collobert et al., 2011) as well as loglinear CBOW (Mikolov et al., 2013a). As an effective expression of word semantics, distributed vector has dramatically improved traditional distributional vector in terms of latent semantics (Huang et al., 2012) and syntactic features (Mikolov et al., 2013c) as well as morphology (Luong et al., 2013). And it has been applied to many semantic cognition tasks such as word similarity (Yogatama et al., 2014), sentiment analysis (Maas et al., 2011) and machine translation (Mikolov et al., 2013b). For improving the corpus-based semantic similarity measurement, some works leverage knowledge bases to make up the insufficient of semantics in corpora, which provide valuable complement for the semantic information derived from corpora.

The related works based on distributed vectors are classified into two groups depends on how external knowledge is used. In these works, semantic knowledge contributes to modify the neural network model or construct relation-constrained model. As for the former, knowledge is incorporated into neural network model as either additional input or auxiliary supervision to improve the quality of distributed word vector. The work by (Bian et al., 2014) added syntactic and semantic knowledge of words to extend the input in CBOW model. In the work by (Xu et al., 2014) leverage both the relational and categorical knowledge in the deep learning framework. In the article by (Yu and Dredze, 2014) only use the relational knowledge as constraints to extend the neural language model. As for the latter, the semantic relations between words in knowledge base are taken as constrains for modeling an objective function and retrofitting the word embedding. In The article by (Faruqui et al., 2014) propose belief propagation on knowledge graph where the word embeddings of are expected to be closer to construct a relation constrain of objective function. This method based on retrofitting is simpler than other methods, which use knowledge while training neural network. However, the aforementioned studies assume single sense for each word in raw corpus as the single-prototype vector per word learned via neural network training. The single distributed vector representation cannot solve the polysemy and homonymy problem, and possibly leads to semantic ambiguity in semantic similarity measurement.

In addition, for capturing the different meanings of polysemy, some existing studies propose multi-prototype vector model of words where each prototype corresponds to a one word sense. In the related works, the context of word or bilingual knowledge is used to distinguish word senses. In the article by (Reisinger and Mooney, 2010) propose context-aware multi-prototype vector space models for per word by simply clustering the surrounding words of the word. Huang et al. (Huang et al., 2012) combine global context with local context of words to word sense disambiguation. In the article by (Tian et al., 2014) leverage the diversity of local context under different sense of the same word. Moreover, in the article by (Guo et al., 2014) exploit bilingual lexicon to determine word senses and learn sense-specific distributed word vector. However, in this works, the authors use WordNet (Miller, 1995) as our knowledge base since its rich semantic definition and relationship. The authors propose a knowledge-augmented multiple-prototype word representation model, which represents each word as a set of distinct vectors. For semantic property, the gloss is considered, and for relations, the authors us the hypemyrn/hyponym relation and the synonymy relation.

3\. WORDNET

WordNet is an online semantic dictionarya lexical database of English words, developed at Princeton University, which partitions the lexicon into nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs as the format of sets of synonym (namely, synset which is a group of words sharing the same meaning). In WordNet, there are many semantic properties of concepts, and various relationships between concepts include: hyperonymy/hyponymy, synonymy, antonym, meronymy (the part-whole relation), Cross-POS relations.

In this work, the gloss semantic property is considered, and for relations, the authors use the hypemyrn/hyponym relation and the synonymy relations.

3.1. Gloss Semantic Property

Each synset contains a brief definition called “gloss”, in most cases, one or more short sentences illustrating the use of the synset members. The authors also use the “gloss” property to strengthen the semantic component of the word in our work. For example, when given the word “bank”, it is difficult to distinguish that it is a word about “river bank” or a word about “banking and finance”, one gloss of “bank” in WordNet is “sloping land (especially the slope beside a body of water)”, and the other is “a financial institution that accepts deposits and channels the money into lending activities”, it is obviously that when incorporated the gloss we can distinguish polysemous words more clearly.

3.2. The Hyperonymy/Hyponymy Relation

The most frequently encoded relation among synsets is the super-subordinate relation (also called ISA relation). It links more general synsets like {wood} to increasingly specific ones like {pine, maple}. The hyperonymy/hyponymy relation is an asymmetrical relationship, generally, a synset only has one hypemyrn, this means the hyponym is inherited from the hypemyrnmore generalized nature of a concept, and the hyponym will have more properties than the hyperonymy. Taking an example as {willow}, it is the hyponym of {tree}. And {willow} has all the properties that the {tree} has, and it has more concrete knowledge to discriminate from other trees. In Wordnet, all noun hierarchies ultimately go up the root node {entity}.

3.3. The Synonymy Relation

Synonymy is the most important relation among words in WordNet is, as between the words shut and close or car and automobile. In WordNet, synsets are used to represented lexical concepts in which all words have similar words and word sense together. Words that denote the same concepts are interchangeable in many contexts–are grouped into unordered synsets. There are 117798 noun words organized into 82115 synsets in WordNet 3.0 with a maximum depth of 20, which formed a huge concept semantic knowledge network.

4\. METHODOLOGY

The concept definition and relational knowledge are extracted from WordNet to enrich the semantic information of the target word. The authors design two steps to achieve our aims, in step I, the authors try to search for relational knowledge of the synset, and mix them as a word prototype; In step II, theses knowledge-relational words are incorporated into the target word to get the word prototype. In this work, words are represented by a distributed vectors trained by an unsupervised neural network language model named CBOW (Mikolov et al., 2013c).

4.3. Strategy

The authors design two parts of experiments, one is to search some relational knowledge and mix them to replace the target word; the other is incorporating the relational knowledge into the target word to rich its semantic definition and relationship. The number of hyperonymy or hyponymy of a synset in WordNet is always different. In order to balance the relational knowledge infomation, the authors use pooling operation to incorporate them together.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch041.m05](i/ch041.m05.svg)

where ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch041.m06](i/ch041.m06.svg) is the set of the relational knowledge in WordNet of the synset S[i](w), and vec(w[r]) is the vector of word w[r] trained by the CBOW Model.

4.3.1. Replace the Original Vector

In the experiment part I, the authors search the corresponding knowledge of target word from WordNet, and then the authors replace the original word vector delivered from CBOW. The authors deign four strategies as follows:

*   Strategy 3 Hyponym Pooling: A synset in WordNet may have several hyponym, these concepts contains more detail knowledge that the synset. The authors incorporate the hyponym together.

4.3.2. Append the Relational Knowledge

In the above 4 strategies, the prototypes are composed of the relational knowledge from WordNet, and the target word vector is not kept. However, the vector of target word trained by CBOW contains the semantic information, so in the experiment part II, the authors will incorporate the above semantic knowledge, the authors add the target word vector to the Equation 1-4, respectively, based on the four strategies 1-4, the four strategies in part II include: the vector of Equation (1) add the target word vector, the vector of Equation (2) add the target word vector, the vector of Equation (3) add the target word vector, the vector of Equation (4) add the target word vector.

4.3.3. Measuring the Similarity

After learned the multiple prototypes of the word, the authors then calculate the similarity value to check our model. Give two words, for example, there are 2 synsets of “automobile” and 5 synsets of “car” in WordNet, so we have 2 word prototypes of “automobile” and 5 word prototypes of “car”. Then the similarity value between two words in our multiple prototype model is computed by the “MaxSim” method (Reisinger and Mooney, 2010).

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch041.m11](i/ch041.m11.svg)

where d()can be any standard distributional similarity measure. All the experiments in this paper the authors use cosine similarity¹. The MaxSim method will produce only one value to represent the similarity of two words (e.g. automobile and car) at the cost of lower robustness to noisy clusters that might be introduced when K is large.

5\. EXPERIMENTS

In our experiments, three unlabeled corpora are integrated and pre-processed to train the distributed word vectors using word2ve², which include the BNC³(346,592 word types, 10⁷ tokens) and the Brown Corpus⁴ (14,783 word types, 10⁵ tokens), as well as a Wikipedia Corpus⁵ that is current to August 2014 (3,483,254 word types and 10⁹ tokens). To evaluate our methods, three benchmark databases are taken to compare our approaches with others.

5.1. Pre-processing the Corpora

The authors first combine three corpora to one file as the input. Once the input corpora are available, the authors start to carry out pre-processing as following steps:

*   1\. Remove the XML tag and other special symbols.
*   2\. Join adjacent pairs of words with a “\_” character, for example, word “new” and word “york” will be “new\_york”.
*   3\. Remove the duplicate sentences.

Abbreviations are taken as named entities or special terms that contain uppercase letters in this work. Hence, the authors remove them from the corpora file since they may significantly impact the training of words around it in a window size. Besides, the stop words such as “a” and “the” are removed to avoid over-training and make the remaining lexical meaning clearly represented. Finally, we get a vocabulary of 1221971 word types and over 0.8 billion tokens.

5.2. Benchmark Databases

The authors use three benchmarks to evaluate our methods:

*   • RG-65 (Rubenstein and Goodenough, 1965) Rubenstein and Goodenough established synonymy judgments for 65 pairs of nouns. They invited 51 human judges to assign every pair a score between 0.0 and 4.0 to indicate semantic similarity.
*   • MC-30 (Miller and Charles, 1991) Miller and Charles follow this idea and restricted themselves to 30 pairs of nouns selected from Rubenstein and Goodenoughs list, divided equally amongst words with high, intermediate and low similarity.
*   • WS-353 (Finkelstein et al., 2001) The WordSimilarity-353 Test Collection contains two sets of English word pairs along with human-assigned similarity judgments. The first set (set1) contains 153 word pairs along with their similarity scores assigned by 13 subjects. The second set (set2) contains 200 word pairs, with their similarity assessed by 16 subjects.

5.3. Results

The experiments have two parts, in the first part the authors want to find some relational knowledge in WordNet to replace the target word itself and the authors use CBOW Model as our baseline. In part two, the authors use the relational knowledge and incorporate them into the target word. The goal of our experiments is to find various combination of semantic knowledge to get the multiple-prototype word representations and improve the performance on word similarity task. The authors use Pearson correlation coefficient to evaluate whether the method performs well or not. Pearson correlation coefficient define as follows:

Although the authors incorporate relational knowledge to represent the target word, the authors are not keeping the semantic information of target word. Table 2 are the results of experiments part II, It demonstrates that incorporating the Gloss, Hyponym or Hypernym relational knowledge into the target word vector delivered from CBOW can significantly improve the performance of word similarity task. Notice that the Synonym fells the results. The authors argue that adding the words of synonym relation will bring more ambiguity and reduce the performance of word similarity task. Results on the WS-353 dataset are shown in Figure 2, the authors also add CBOW Model as a comparison. It shows that our best result has reached 0.7, which is better the CBOW model (0.63).

Results of related work on MC-30 dataset that are available for us are shown in Figure 3. Resnik (Resnik, 1995) consider the semantic similarity by comparing the concepts in the WordNet and their result has reached 0.80. Jiang and Conrath (Jiang and Conrath, 1997) consider the IC value of words and their result reaches 0.83. However, they only consider the WordNet as their semantic resource. Li (Li et al., 2003) considered the local semantic density derived from the brown corpus and the minimum length of path and depth from WordNet, their results on MC-30 datasets have reached 0.89 which is much higher than former. It indicates that combining knowledge bases with corpora can improve the performance in word similarity task. However, in the method of Li (Li et al., 2003), each word is represented by only one single prototype vector, which can be illogical. Different from their works, we consider the synsets of the word to build a multiple-prototype model to represent the word. Meanwhile, we append the concept definition and the relational knowledge into the target word trained by the CBOW model in order to enrich the semantic knowledge of the word, and our approaches have reached 0.90.

6\. CONCLUSION

In this work, we propose a knowledge-augmented multiple-prototype word model, which represents each word as a set of distinct vectors. We leverage the corpora to train distributed word vector via a neural network language model. Then we conduct an empirical study on the capacity of appending the concept definition and relations into the target word trained by the CBOW. The relations consist of the hyperonymy/hyponymy relation and the synonymy relation. The target word finally is represented by the multiple prototype vectors in low-dimensional vector space. The experiments on RG-65, MC-30 and WS-353 datasets indicate the efficiency of our approaches. For the future wok, we plan to find a group of optimization parameters and combine different relational knowledge.

ABSTRACT

Low-cost, flexible, easily maintainable and secure traffic management support systems are in demand. Internet-based real time bi-directional communication provides significant benefits to monitor road traffic conditions. Dynamic route computation is a vital requirement to make the traffic management system more realistic and reliable. Therefore, an integrated approach with multiple data feeds and Backpropagation (BP) Neural Network (NN) with Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) optimization is applied to predict the road weights. The results indicate that the proposed traffic system/tool with NN based dynamic weights computation is much more effective to find the optimal routes. The BP NN with LM optimization achieves 96.67% accuracy.

INTRODUCTION

Traffic jam is an on-going challenge, and is not showing any signs of improvement. It results losing valuable time being stuck in traffic jams and increases CO2 emissions due to the present traffic situation. As a result, an up-to-date technological based traffic management support system/tool has become a need for metro cities.

A new internet-based (WebSocket (HTML5 Web Sockets, 2015) over HTTP) traffic management support system with real time bi-directional communication is implemented in Rahman et al., (2015a; 2015b; 2015c) to assist the traffic system to reduce the traffic and create a more sustainable environment. It also supports low cost implementation, flexibility, maintainability and infrastructure security. Thus, provides significant benefits over the existing surveillance technologies in use to monitor road traffic condition. However, this work is based on static or manual weight updates. Optimal paths/routes are calculated from the given static weights.

Weights are calculated from current road situations including-construction status, damaged status, accident status, traffic status, environmental disaster status etc. The value of the statuses are intelligently crawled by search engine, with metadata indexing (title, description, keyword etc.), directly from the multiple data feeds (like web site, RSS feeds, web service etc.). Crawled data are simplified (structured) and stored in a historic table. The decision to update the weights is decided by the DT (Rahman & Akhter, 2015a; 2015b; 2015c) and Dijkstra algorithm (Dijkstra’s Algorithm, 2015) is applied to calculate the optimal path/route using the dynamic route weights. However, DT takes long time to be trained for large data sets. It is also not good for online learning as continuous data needs frequent updating/changing in the model. Since any data includes some exceptional situation will force the DT model to be fall apart and needs to be constructed again. In addition, ID3 (Rahman, 2012) does not apply any pruning procedures nor does it handle numeric attributes or missing values (Rokach, & Maimon, 2011).

Evolutionary searching techniques e.g., genetic algorithm (Goldberg, 1989) can perform a directed search of the solution space and takes a long time to find an acceptable solution for each testing. However, when we have a number of items in different classes, NN can learn to classify items it has not seen before. In addition, NN takes some time to learn, but then it can almost instantly classify new inputs. In addition, NN is capable of reflecting the information of new instance on a model very efficiently by just changing the weight values. Thus, the DT model is replaced by the Backpropagation (BP) Neural Network (NN) and is implemented over the simplified data to adjust the route weights in database. Moreover, the Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) optimization is applied on BP to reduce the number of hidden layers as well as the training iterations. In addition k-fold cross validation and confidence interval is used to trace the NN overall performance.

BACKGROUND STUDY

The traditional traffic information services available through the radio and television, several web sites offer on-line current traffic information, not predicting traffic condition. Over the time different solutions in (Verma, 2012; Aloul et al., 2012; Dhar, 2008; Romão, 2006; Angel et al., 2003) have been proposed to solve the traffic management problem. The solutions vary in their core technologies, as some of them used infrared sensors, CCTV cameras, machine vision (image processing), GSM and/or cellular towers, RFID gateways, sound sensors, aerial surveillance and remote sensing etc. In (Romão, 2006), high quality CCTV cameras were used to capture vehicle images and machine vision technique was applied to process them on a terminal for necessary information. The procedure was very expensive due to high cost of CCTVs and also required heavy installations and regular maintenances. In addition, machine vision had limitations during heavy snowfall, sand storm, rainfall, and foggy weather. In (Aloul et al., 2012; Dhar, 2008), RFID Sensor was used. This technology required RFID gates to be installed and vehicles were needed to pass through the gates. This was ineffective if the vehicles go around the gates for any reason. Surveillance Drone and aerial imagery techniques were used in (Verma, 2012; Angel et al., 2003). They were effective during the normal weather condition. Nonetheless, could not be an option during bad weather. Also the deployment and maintenance cost was very high.

Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals can be reliably used for measuring travel times (Reporter, 2013). Wireless connections, particularly in urban areas, are steadily getting worse. In addition, Bluetooth based solution can be used for unidirectional monitoring traffic flows only. Automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems (ANPR, 2014) are using ever more sophisticated control systems and more sensitive imaging technologies. However, ANPR systems require high quality cameras with fast frame rates to capture an image of the number plate with enough definition for the system to define the vehicle’s registration number. Such cameras are relatively costly to install and maintain. Thus, many of those solutions are either very expensive or difficult to install and maintain over the periods of time. Moreover, their coverage zones are limited and most of the existing technologies use unicast communication (client to server only).

Bi-directional communication is already in use for different purposes like Named Data Networking (Almishari et al., 2014), video conferencing (Panagiotakis et al., 2013), chatting, telecommunication, etc. However, the benefits and the results of real time bi-directional communication are yet to be discovered especially for moving agents (i.e. the road traffic system).

Questions are raised - whether any approach or technique would bring low operational-cost but flexible internet-based solution for road traffic system. Therefore, a new internet-based (WebSocket (HTML5 Web Sockets, 2015) over HTTP) traffic management support system with real time bi-directional communication is implemented (in Rahman & Akhter, 2015a; 2015b; 2015c) to assist the traffic system. It also supports low cost implementation, flexibility, maintainability and infrastructure security. Thus, it provides significant benefits over the existing surveillance technologies in use to monitor road traffic condition.

WebSocket was developed as a part of the HTML5 with JavaScript interface, and represents the next evaluation of Comet and Ajax (HTML5 Web Sockets, 2015). It simplifies much of the complexity around bi-directional web communication and connection management. HTML5 WebSocket is not just another incremental enhancement to conventional HTTP communications. Once a client and a server have opened a WebSocket connection, both endpoints may asynchronously send data to each other. Thus, WebSockets represent a standard for bi-directional, massively scalable, and real-time communication across multiple platforms (servers and clients) (Rakhunde, 2013). As a result, we integrated Web Socket technology (HTML5 Web Sockets, 2015) over HTTP with real time bi-directional communication. The main reason behind the selection of this technology is low cost implementation, flexibility, maintainability and infrastructure security (Erkkilä, 2012).

BI-DIRECTIONAL TRAFFIC MANAGEMENT SYSTEM (TMS)

In this section, a generic architecture for the proposed real time system has been presented. Figure 1 illustrates the components of the proposed architecture along with their involved signaling. The vehicles are referred as clients and have access to GPS (Global Positioning System, 2015), which allows them to gather their current location in terms of latitude and longitude. GPS is a space-based navigation system which provides location information in all weather conditions. The clients are also equipped with devices (GPRS, EDGE, 3G, 4G, and etc.) and capable to handle the web request/response over the HTTP. The clients are also equipped with WebSocket protocol RFC6455 supported device and capable to handle the web request/response over the HTTP. Thus, clients are capable to pinpoint their locations from anywhere and can send/receive data over HTTP.

The architecture comprises a WebSocket server. At the starting point of the application, client requests the server for necessary scripts. The scripts utilize a proxy connection and initiate a WebSocket connection. The scripts also inform the server about the methods available on the client side. Server accepts the WebSocket connection. The connection remains open for the whole session, until any endpoint requests to disconnect. In our implementation, the WebSocket server hosts the logical parts of our web services, and responsible to maintain a list of client peers with active WebSockets and session management.

The server application has the real-time location plotting system on region based available data. The server application is also responsible for data mining and business logic execution based on the collected data from various clients. This process has been described in detail in our previous works in (Rahman & Akhter, 2015a; 2015b; 2015c).

Test Zones/Study Area

The traffic jam is unfortunately an on-going old problem and is not showing any signs of improvement. This problem is resulting in air pollution, sound pollution, accidents, late arrival at destination etc. In addition, the demand for a feasible solution to the above mentioned problems is very high for a metro city- like Dhaka, Bangladesh. Losing valuable time (approx. 200%) being stuck in traffic jams and increases CO2 emissions (approx. 300%) due to the present traffic situation. As a result, an up-to-date technological based traffic management support system/tool has become a need for such metro cities.

The Banani area (Banani Intersection) is the heart of Dhaka road network system and thus has been selected as test area for vehicle routings. Like other intersections at Dhaka city it follows the all way stop control intersection resulting in a huge congestion of vehicles at peak hours which makes it almost impossible for the traffic police to control the vehicle flow in a nimble way. In addition the road networks inside the Banani area shape as quadrangle and suitable for our test simulation.

All the roads (at simulated test site) are divided into segments depending on the junctions to test the effectiveness of the vehicle routing and present in Figure 2. Each segment is marked as a rectangle and has five points – the four corners and the midpoint. The four corners are required to identify the proper road segment and the midpoint of a road is used to define a read marker. Client can decide the nearest road segment by using the difference between its location and segment’s road marker. Thus, segment location is stored (in database) in terms of latitude and longitude of the five points and placed on the Google Map (Google Map, 2015).

Static Road Weight Matrix

The road weights (arbitrary numbers) are stored in a table at the database server using From-To format to support both directions. One way roads are not considered here. In real test bed the weights must be dynamically calculated (discussed in the next section) based on external data coming from weather forecast, traffic congestion, road condition, and other sources. Present application is capable to work with the resulted weights for each of the roads stored in the weight table. Table 1 shows part of the weight matrix from database.

Few simulated clients are created with their test routes (as if they are driving on the road) and stored in a test route table. When the application is active, each test client logs in and transmits the corresponding test route to the server. The server application has the capability of mapping any transmitted location to an existing test location and plots that on an aerial map.

Decision Tree (DT) Based Road Weight Calculations

The application uses data scraping technique to extracts data from the predefined external data sources (like web site, RSS feed, web service etc.). For test purpose -three dummy weather web pages are created. A scheduler runs in the background and scraps data for each of the road segments in a regular interval (e.g. every six (6) hrs.). Then, it stores the scrapped data in a historic table. At the same time, the weights for the road segments are also updated in the weight matrix (Table 1). The decision to update the weights is decided by the DT (in Rahman & Akhter, 2015a, 2015b, 2015c). DT has an easy to follow natural flow. The top node in the tree is the most influential piece of data that affects the response variable in the model. Because the tree is so easy to understand, they are very useful as modeling techniques and provide visual representations of the data. For this test purpose four weather attributes are considered– rain fall, temperature, humidity and wind to determine the environmental status. However, the number of attributes can be changed according to the system requirements. Rainfall is one of the most influential weather attributes to determine the road congestion in Dhaka city as the road segments are submerged due to the heavy rains and makes slower traffic movements (Reporter, 2015). The heat released from the engines, air-conditions of the traffic stacked vehicles, and may increase the overall temperature of the area. Thus, the current temperature can classify the traffic congestion status of a particular road segment. Gusts of wind have direct influence on road safety and that pushes to slower vehicle movement. In addition, temperature, wind and humidity have direct influence to predict the future rainfall in a particular area. Thus, these four (4) weather attributes have direct or indirect relationship on traffic congestion as well as vehicle movement issues and influence to choose them as decision making parameters. Increased weights by DT will reflect lesser chance for the road segment to be in the optimal path.

The interpreted data (Table 2) is then evaluated against the generated decision tree (Figure 6) and based on the result; the application either increases or resets the weight of a road (segment) and reflects in the road weight matrix accordingly. Figure 3 and Figure 4 highlight the fact that the application is changing the route suggestion dynamically based on the resulted weights from the external data sources. For example in Figure 3, the point ‘D’ is adjacent to point ‘C’ and is on the right side of the point ‘C’. This is the suggested route before the weight for the point ‘D’ is increased. Now the weight for the point ‘D’ has increased (according to decision tree). So this road segment is going to be omitted. Thus, Figure 4 presents alternate route with relocating the point ‘D’. This is the resultant of the dynamic weight adjustments or dynamic routing.

Road Weight Forecast

Weight Prediction

The future weight prediction module utilizes the structured data from the historic database to predict the future road weights. First and foremost, the module predicts the factors like Rain Fall, Temperature, Road Status etc. and those values have direct influences to the road weight calculation. To predict the factor values Weighted Moving Average algorithm (Moving Average Algorithm, 2016) is used and this algorithm allows the most recent data to have higher impact on the prediction. Different factors influence the road weights in different ways and thus, factor values are predicted and later decision tree uses them to calculate the estimated road weights. The estimated road weights are stored in “Predicted road weight” matrix. Thus, the application is capable to simulate and suggest future routes based on the road weights from the “Predicted road weight” matrix.

Prediction Statistic

To analyze the performance of the prediction module, one of the weight influencing factors – Temperature is considered. The temperature data for December 10^(th), 2015 to December 29^(th), 2015 (20 data) are collected from the AccuWeather site (AccuWeather, 2016). Weighted Moving Average algorithm (Moving Average Algorithm, 2016) is used to calculate the next (future) five expected data and compared with their actual values. Average of absolute difference represents the error rate.

Figure 7 highlights the accuracy of the predicted data for two different Alpha (α) values (0.4 and 0.8). The X axis represents the # of predicted values and Y represents the corresponding error rates. The first experiment counts the fifteen (15) data as seed data and remaining are the testing data. Testing data are used to evaluate the error rate. The second experiment includes the sixteen (16^(th)) as the most recently known data and estimates the 17^(th) – 20^(th) to evaluate the error rate and thus, continue for 3^(rd), 4^(th) and 5^(th) experiments. In usual condition, the higher value of Alpha includes more weight to the latest data and directs the future trends. However, for exceptional conditions- latest known data holds much smaller or higher value than the previous and thus inclusion of higher weight affects significantly on the error rates. Our experiment in Figure 7 (# of Prediction Values 4 & 1) reflects such circumstances.

PROPOSED NN BASED DYNAMIC ROAD WEIGHT CALCULATIONS

Figure 8 presents the proposed work flow of NN based road weight processing and prediction system. Three dummy feed sites (provide the data/forecast of the weather, city corporation road maintenance works and road status from government roads and highways authority) are created to simulate the proposed model. The sites display Weather (Figure 5), City Corporation and Roads & Highways data in human readable format. The Search Engine referred as the web crawler visits the web sites in regular intervals. It looks for an HTML Table element with a predefined ID or class name. It does not depend on the position or the hierarchy of the HTML elements. Once the tag has been identified the crawler scraps the rows using XPath (XPath, 2016). The unstructured data is converted to structured data and stored in a historic table at the same time. Also, the new data is evaluated by the NN decision process and the road weights are adjusted as needed. In parallel the weight prediction module utilizes the historic data to predict the future factors and generate another road weight matrix (called the future weight matrix). This road weight matrix can be used to predict or simulate route suggestions. The future weight prediction module utilizes the structured data from the historic database to predict the future road weights. First and foremost the module predicts the factors like Rain Fall, Temperature, Road Status, and etc. These factors have direct influences on the road weight calculations. To predict the factor values still the Weighted Moving Average algorithm is used and in near future the algorithm will be replaced with NN based scheme.

NN Formulation

DT is replaced by the NN in the proposed model (in Figure 8) and Table 2 data are interpreted to numeric (0, 1, and 2) from corresponding linguistic (low, mid, high) formulations. Thereafter, the weight matrix value is updated/adjusted by using a multi-layer fully connected BP NN and later the NN is upgraded with LM optimization (Hagan et al., 1995). In Figure 9, the BP NN consists of one hidden layer (with 10 neurons) and one output layer (with 2 neurons). The BP NN is optimized by using LM optimization (in Figure 10) with one hidden layer (with 5 neurons), and one output layer (with 2 neurons). In both networks the output of the each neuron is in the range of \[0 ~ 1\] as we use Purelin threshold function to calculate the final output of the neurons. Later, the binary outputs are combined to reform in decimal 0-3 values (four decision classes) to increment the weight values. For simplicity, only positive weights are considered. However, the model is adjustable to work with both positive and negative values.

To determine the number of optimal neurons in the hidden layer was the tricky part, we start with one (1) neuron in the hidden layer and test the performance of the neural network on the basis of a fixed test set, and then we increase the number of neurons as factor of five (5) till 45, the number of neurons in the hidden layer is chosen based on the best performance. The accuracy curve is illustrated in Figure 11. In both networks, Logsig is used for transfer function of each neuron in hidden layer this is differentiable and squashes the output into the range 0 to 1 (Hagan et al., 1995).

Mean square error is used as performance function. The learning rate in Widrow-Hoff algorithm is 0.05. Weights and biases are randomly initialized. Convergence reflects the disparity or maximum error in the actual target output and network generated output and is set to 10^(\-3). The BP NN requires more than 8,000 epochs to reach the convergence and successfully train the network; whereas LM based NN requires only 14 epochs to reach the convergence.
