NN Performance

Four attributes–Rain Fall, Temperature, Road Status, and Road Works are considered for training and testing networks. However, the number of attributes can be changed according to the system requirements. External feed data (e.g. weather data) is first interpreted from numeric to an attribute in the data set. The interpreted data is then evaluated against the NN and based on the result; the application either increases or resets the weight of a road (segment) and reflects in the road weight matrix accordingly. DT implemented in (Rahman & Akhter, 2015a; 2015b; 2015c) has two decision classes (Yes/No weight updates); however, NN considers four decision classes (3-0) to increment the weight values.

The NNs are trained with 30 samples (12 from class 3, 9 from class 2, 5 from class 1, 4 from class 0) and tested with 15 samples (5 from class 3, 3 from class 2, 3 from class 1, 4 from class 0). BP NN achieves 93.33% accuracy and LM based NN achieves 96.67% accuracy. The training process performs several times to analyze the confidence interval of training, testing, validation to the measure the overall performance. Table 3 shows the training, testing, validation and overall performance of training algorithms are shown. The Levenberg Marquardt (LM) shows higher confidence in training, testing, validation and overall network performance than BP (gradient descent) training technique.

However, overfitting is a major problem to train NN with small set of data. Train multiple NNs or single NN multiple times and average their outputs are used to improve the generalization. For instance, five (5) neural networks are trained with similar data set and their mean squared errors are computed as the means squared error of their average. Next, each network is tested on the testing dataset with both individual performances and the performance for the average output calculated. In addition, a k-fold cross-validation (Wiki-1, 2016) is applied to estimate the LM based BP model’s true errors. First the total data set (108) is divided into three (3) subsets (2-37, 38-74, 75-110) and two (2) sets are used for training and the remaining data set is for testing. The same procedure is repeated three (3) times with different testing sets as Table 4. Then estimate the true error through average the overall errors on the testing sets. Thus, overall LM based BP achieves 94%- 96.67% accuracy.

| --- | --- | --- |
| 2-74 || 75-110 || 4.87 |
| 38-110 || 2-37 || 3.475 |
| 2-37 and 75-110 || 38-74 || 6.755 |
| Total average error || 5.033 |
| Accuracy || 95.34% |

DISCUSSION

In 2000, BBC reported that pollution due to road traffic is to be blamed for the death of tens of thousands every year across Europe (Kunzli, 2000). Another research published in The Lancet Medical Journal estimated that 6% of deaths in several countries in Europe were due to air pollution; where half of these deaths (around 20,000) were linked to toxic fumes emitted from vehicles stuck in traffic (Romm, 2009). In 2007, MSNBC reported a U.S. study stating that traffic pollution is affecting children who live near busy roads by preventing their lungs from developing properly (MSNBC, 2007).

A new internet-based traffic management support system with real time bi-directional communication was implemented and assists the traffic system to reduce the traffic and create a more sustainable environment. Decision tree based logic is implemented over the simplified data to adjust the route weights in database. Dijkstra algorithm is applied to calculate the optimal path/route using the dynamic route weights. However, DT is generated by ID3 (Rahman, 2012) algorithm and does not apply any pruning procedures nor does it handle numeric attributes or missing values \[20\]. It is also inefficient for online learning as continuous data needs frequent updating/changing in the model. Thus, another alternative decision making system is required. Probabilistic decision trees or Naive Bayes based DT is good for semi-supervised learning or something embarrassingly simple that performs pretty well. Probabilistic Neural Network (PNN) uses Bayesian network and a statistical algorithm called Kernel Fisher discriminant analysis. PNN is slower than multilayer perceptron networks at classifying new cases and requires more memory space to store the model.

Moreover, two decision making systems-weights updating and future traffic forecast are in the proposed model. The forecast model requires both time series data analysis and prediction. NN is suitable for this circumstance. With the hypothesis that similar tools can do better bridging between two decision systems and thus the choosing strengthen for weight updating decision process goes in favor of simple BP NN.

Online multi data feeds capability supports the proposed model to be connected with different social medias (face book, twitters etc.) and collects necessary information (mishap, disaster situations) and uses analytic tools to make proper decisions. However, need special consideration on internet securities as all of the information is available on the Internet. Still, the proposed TMS is in construction phase and cover small road networks. City level broader area will be considered in near future.

CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORKS

This paper demonstrated the ability of Back propagation (BP) and/or Levenberg Marquardt (LM) training method of neural network for making decision to update the road weight of bi-directional traffic management system (TMS). External feed data (e.g. weather data) is first interpreted from numeric to an attribute in the data set. The interpreted data is then evaluated against the NN and based on the result; the application either increases or resets the weight of a road (segment) and reflects in the road weight matrix accordingly. LM based NN forecast model shows better results than the BP NN. BP training technique of NN shows lower training capability of the network than improved BP NN with LM technique which avoids the neural network to trap into the local minima. LM based model (BP NN) regression analysis shows that, the network achieves 95% of confidence interval for network training, testing, validation and overall NN performance. Consequently, LM NN model proves that the higher accuracy than BP due to strong generalization capability over a large data. K-fold cross-validation technique also applied achieves 95.34% accuracy.

Future research focuses on the enhancement of accuracy by including more weather parameters with their influential statistical features (mean, standard deviation, moment, etc.), quantity of data sets (testing, training and validation) and NN structure optimization. In the proposed model data sets are classified by instinct method. Cluster based classifications (K means, Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH) etc.) will be used to find optimum number of classifications in each feature. Thus, the dynamic routing with NN based road weight calculation needs to be enhanced and tested with more advanced decision making system.

The data from the external feeds (like web site, RSS feed, web service etc.) are stored in the database and opens opportunity to analyze or predict future traffic based on the historic data. Weighted Moving Average algorithm was implemented to calculate the estimated or predicted factor values in DT based system. In near future, the estimation model will be implemented by NN based system and its performance will be evaluated.

ABSTRACT

In deep neural networks, which have been gaining attention in recent years, the features of input images are expressed in a middle layer. Using the information on this feature layer, high performance can be demonstrated in the image recognition field. In the present study, we achieve image recognition, without using convolutional neural networks or sparse coding, through an image feature extraction function obtained when identity mapping learning is applied to sandglass-style feed-forward neural networks. In sports form analysis, for example, a state trajectory is mapped in a low-dimensional feature space based on a consecutive series of actions. Here, we discuss ideas related to image analysis by applying the above method.

INTRODUCTION

According to the 2015 Telecommunications White Paper from the Japanese Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, the number of “things” related to the Internet of Things (IoT) is expected to increase tremendously; a wide variety of data will be collected and analyzed via IoT and movements to link these are expected to enhance work efficiency, among other things. Naturally, this includes the treatment of big data, and when analyzing data collected in such large quantities, their analysis could be performed interactively, allowing interpretations from many different angles. In particular, security camera images, while considering privacy, are linked to a large volume of data collected using IoT. The reason for this is exceptionally simple. For example, to monitor the daily behavioral patterns of elderly people and children, it is convenient to construct surveillance systems using data collected from IoT because it is portable and allows us to analyze and extract data in order to evaluate whether their behaviors have changed or are in danger of doing so. There are the researches in the computer network for the realization of such a system (Shintaro, Mariko, Mingrui, Yoshikazu, & Toshimitsu, 2013). However, with this simple idea, the main point is how to construct a system in which the behavior pattern data collected from IoT can be linked to actual behavior. Although the search engine to connect sensor data with an event has been already proposed (Koji, Yutaka, Takuya, Yasue, Yasushi, & Takeshi, 2010; Takeshi, Yasue, Takuya, Koji, Yutaka, & Yasushi, 2010), we believe that if a video is captured at the same time as the IoT data are collected, specification of these data is a simple matter.

In relation to the treatment of images, deep learning using deep neural networks (DNNs) has attracted a lot of attention in recent years because it successfully demonstrated automatic organization of neurons selectively reacting to images of a cat (Quoc,2013) and high recognition performance in relation to difficult tasks, such as general object recognition. In other words, this success engendered several methods to mitigate model complexity including weight decay (Stephen, & Lorien, 1989) and weight sharing (Le, Bernhard, John, Donnie, Richard, Wayne, & Lawrence, 1990; Steven, & Geoffrey, 1992) and to roughly form DNN at an early stage through prior learning (Geoffrey, Simon, & Yee-Whye, 2006). Furthermore, by creating an ensemble of multiple neural networks, such as DropOut (Geoffrey, Nitish, Alex, Ilya, & Ruslan, 2012) or DropConnect (Li, Matthew, Sixin, Yann, & Rob, 2013), which is a model assumed to have information deficiency in it, it has greatly contributed to the development of various parameter tuning for keeping generality.

Analyzing the action parameters from videos captured at the same time as data is collected from IoT, it is clear that although human eyes can specify actions easily by directly viewing them, due to issues such as their processing ability and fatigue, they soon encounter limitations when processing large quantities for long periods. Therefore, there is a demand for the automation of action pattern analysis using such images, and DNN can be used to achieve this.

In DNN image processing, if a convolutional neural network (CNN) (Alex, Ilya, & Geoffrey, 2012) or sparse coding is used, the response neurons corresponding to image input in the feature extraction layer learn to respond and become able to recognize objects. By utilizing this process on a video frame by frame, it is possible to consider a discrete feature vector corresponding to this video (Yasuyuki, Takashi, & Kuniaki, 2015). However, we have considered utilizing a continuous trajectory of an object or person moving consecutively. These trajectories are formed from a nonlinear mapping into a low-dimensional feature space by handling feed-forward neural networks without CNN or sparse coding.

In this paper, we handle form analysis of the table tennis as one example. In such a case, the series of movements from the backswing to hitting the ball and following through are important. Subsequently, if this video is provided as identity map learning data using sandglass-type feed-forward neural networks, the feature extraction function acquired in the middle layer would allow the movements to be expressed as a state trajectory of corresponding state as time proceeds. As a result, it is expected that nonlinear conversion and generality of the neural networks will work effectively in action pattern analysis. In this paper, we include the preliminary results of the data analysis and discuss the possibility of action analysis using DNN.

The second section presents a description of our concepts in this paper. The following section describes that the feature space can represent the heteromorphic degree of the target object by hand-written character data. In the next section, we present the implementation of simple video. In the section after, we explain the implementation of form analysis of the table tennis. Finally, we conclude this paper in the last section.

CONCEPTS IN THIS STUDY

For example, considering table tennis (sports) form analysis (Figure. 1), if we decode the series of captured movements frame by frame into still images and overlay these as shown in Figure. 2, we observe that the target object is continuously changing its form. In practice, obtaining a video of sports form that can be sufficiently analyzed requires the use of a high-speed camera. Then, only the player’s image must be extracted from the background. However, we do not consider these practical aspects at present.

In 1995, Usui et al. (Shiro, & Shigeki, 1995) demonstrated that spectral reflectance data could be used for identity map learning using multilayered neural networks. In fact, reducing the number of neurons in the middle layer to three, these neurons could be captured by a Munsell hue ring. These results suggested the continuously changing feature expression of the target data can be captured by a sandglass-type (the number of neurons in the middle layer being narrowed down at once) structure when performing identity mapping with feed forward neural networks.

In the table tennis form analysis, the still images processed frame by frame reveal the constantly changing human form, as data Figure 2 shows. If there is a (low-dimensional) feature quantity expression that captures these continual changes, it should be possible to extract these features in the same manner using sandglass-type neural networks.

To verify this, we used the Mixed National Institute of Standards and Technology database (MINST) handwritten character (numbers) image data often used in DNN. By including a large quantity of handwritten character data, it is possible to find continuous features in the way that the characters break down.

We performed an experiment in which a continuous feature quantity was extracted from a handwritten character (image) using multilayered neural networks.

FEATURE EXTRACTION USRING MNIST HANDWRITTEN CHARACTER

Hierarchical Neural Networks

The neural networks used in this study are handled within the normal Back-Propagation (BP) learning (David, Geoffrey, & Ronald, 1986) without performing pre-training with Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) or Auto-encoder, as used in deep learning in a broad sense.

In other words, a training data was randomly chosen from the dataset, and the synapse weights were repeatedly updated according to the following equation. An online-type BP system with inertia terms was adopted as shown by Equation 1.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch043.m01](i/ch043.m01.svg) (1)

Here, E represents the error function obtained from the square error of the actual output and the target signal, and while expanding the second term in Equation 1, the back-propagation process of the error was derived.

The actual operation in this study involves deep neural networks. Therefore, as already known, as synapse weights become away from the output layer, their learning efficiency reduces. Nevertheless, the objective of this study is to confirm the appearance of feature layer that expresses the consecutive nature of the changes in the image input in the middle layer. Consequently, learning was stopped without waiting for a sufficiently small error value to be reached.

Learning Using a Seven-layer Neural Network

In this study, we investigate continuous feature extraction when performing identity mapping on feedforward neural networks using a part of the MINST handwritten character data set.

Normally, learning could be conducted using all the handwritten digits from 0 to 9. However, we placed emphasis on the scale of the problem to the extent of visually understanding the expression created through learning in the feature extraction layer. Hence, we chose three random characters before learning and analyzed them through principal component analysis. The level of difficulty was determined from the linear mapping on the low-dimensional space. The characters 0, 1, and 4 could be easily classified, whereas 2, 5, and 8 were more difficult to separate.

| Figure 3. A Sand-glass type Neural Network |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch043.f03](i/ch043.f03.png) |
| --- |

As shown in Figure 3, we prepared 500 patterns with each of the three types of handwritten digits on a seven-layered (784-100-30-2-30-100-784) feedforward neural network and carried out identity mapping learning with these data. With a learning coefficient ε = 0.005 and a stability constant α = 0.8, the number of learning steps was set at 10000. Afterward, the feature extraction is performed in the fourth layer (two neurons). Thus, the result was evaluated by observing the feature layer in relation to the input (learning) data and the output image when values from 1.0 to 0.1 in 0.1-steps were forcibly input into the two neurons of the feature layer. Figures 4 and Figure 5 show the results from learning the handwritten characters for 0, 1, and 4. Using the feature expression layer neuron output, a two-dimensional state space was formed, and the corresponding state within the state space for each of the handwritten characters used as learning data was plotted as shown in Figure 4.

Figure 5 shows the points in the feature state space, which correspond to the handwritten characters. However, when a decoding operation is applied to these correspondence relationships, from the feature layers of Figure 3, to reproduce the handwritten characters, there may be discrepancies between the represented image and the points mapped onto the actual feature space.

In the feature extraction, using both handwritten character with 7-layrered feedforward neural networks, we observe that the feature space expressing the character image deformation state is qualitatively learned and that the character deformation corresponds continuously to the feature space.

Furthermore, the classification based on the principal component analysis reveals that it is not very difficult to capture continuously projected feature spaces.

Effect of Preprocessing using a Gaussian Filter

Figure 8 shows an example of an image in the learning data and an example of an image to which a 5 × 5 pixel Gaussian filter is applied. The result of performing feature extraction using the previously described a 7-layered feedforward neural network after filtering the learning data is shown in Figure 9. Through comparison to the corresponding Figure 4, we can see that this method can be used to expand the learning dataset over a wider area of the feature space.

Using sports form analysis as the target, mapping the difference from the ideal form into the feature space is easier, although some fluctuation occurs even after repeating the ideal form. When this feature extraction learning including the fluctuation is placed in a low-dimensional space, it is desirable for the learning to bury the area showing the fluctuation from the ideal form more deeply in the feature space. It has been considered that preprocessing using the Gaussian filter improves the processing.

FEATURE EXTRACTION PROCESSING USING A SIMPLE VIDEO

Next, we will consider feature extraction processing using hierarchical networks aimed at expressing a simple video image. Figure 10 shows the example of a simple video in which the letter Z is drawn by moving 9 × 9 dots on a screen of 32 × 32 pixels, giving a static image for each frame.

| Figure 10. An example of each frame which makes a video of character Z (16 frames) |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch043.f10](i/ch043.f10.png) |
| --- |

For the learning in this case, we performed feature extraction using the same method as that for the previous MINST handwritten character, changing the number of frames required to draw the letter Z by moving dots at a fixed speed.

The learning coefficient was set at ε = 0.01 and the stability coefficient was set at α = 0.9. The network structure consisted of five layers made up of 1024-200-3-200-1024 units. In this neural network, feature expression was performed in three neurons in the third layer.

| Figure 11. Changing trajectories in a feature space at each learning steps |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch043.f11](i/ch043.f11.png) |

Figure 11 presents the results for 32 frames mapped in the three-dimensional feature space; the learning steps have progressed from 10,000 times to 60,000 times. Based on these results, in the initial stages of the learning, each frame is mapped in a close state, and the features of the movement cannot be grasped. As the learning progresses, the path of the movement is enlarged and smoothed within the feature space.

The results of the spatial relationships are not included in this paper. Nevertheless, it has been confirmed that for a low number of frames, the trajectory of the movement cannot be expressed in a smooth way, and pattern overlaps between the still images greatly affect the smoothness. This is probably related to the Gaussian filter preprocessing described in the previous example of the MNIST handwritten character.

APPLICATION TO A FORM OF THE TABLE TENNIS

Preparations for Data

As a concrete problem, we tried the application to the form of the forehand of the table tennis. One set was the rally of 100 strokes and we recorded 10 sets per a day. We carried these out twice. The recording used a video camera fixed to tripod with 1920x1080 pixels, 30fps and mpeg 4 video format. However, I didn't prepare for the special illumination and so on for picture improvement. Figure 14 shows the image processing of recorded pictures. We cut a fixed domain of 100x100 pixel out of a video and then convert it into a static image of gray scale every frame.

As Figure 15 shows, the target of this research is one swing. A subject returns it after a table tennis ball made a landing to a stand, then it lands again. This period thinks with 1 swing and has from 27 to 33 frames. This period, which is between 0.9 and 1.1 second, thinks with 1 swing and consists of 27 to 33 frames.

Response to Data Using the Deep Neural Network

In this section, the network structure consisted of seven layers made up of 10000-100-30-3-30-100-10000 units. In this neural network, feature expression was performed in three neurons in the fourth layer. The learning coefficient was set at ε = 0.005 and the stability coefficient was set at α=0.8, the number of learning steps was set at 100,000.

Figure 16 shows the trajectories mapped from swings in the fifth rally of first day after learning. The left side figure shows a result of 20 swings used as training data, the right side shows a result of other 80 swings.

We can think that this domain is general trajectories mapped from the normal forehand of the subject, because both trajectories pass through a domain almost same. The trajectory extremely outside on the right side is related to the disturbance of the swing, we can see it from a recorded video too.

Figure 17 shows three orbital examples from 100 swing. They are an approximately normal form (left side), a form leaning forward (middle) and a form leaning backwards (right side). If you pay your attention to the position of the foot of the subject of each image, the differences may be understood easily.

Although the difference between a left side video and a middle video is hardly recognized, the difference of these trajectories in the feature space become appears conspicuously. Furthermore, the difference in right form is the level that we can judge on the video easily, so the disorder of trajectory grows bigger.

In the case of a neural network learning, it is expected that the response of neighboring of training data is connected smoothly by ability for generalization. Hence, though a trajectory of middle video is smooth, it is understood that the trajectory is greatly turbulent, if the data far from training data are input. This property may be available in a judgment of the good or bad from a standard form.

Emphasis Learning Using an Inter-Frame Difference Method

Here, we try to apply a method to emphasize a movement object through preprocessing, because what we should intend for is the movement of the subject. When a direct image is inputted into a DNN, not only subject image but also background image must be fed, so that there is the worry that ability of a DNN is consumed. This method is that the pixel of the movement object is decided by inter-frame difference method and then we emphasize error values of this pixel with weight coefficient.

This new error function is shown by Equation 2.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch043.m02](i/ch043.m02.svg) (2)

Here, a[i] is additional coefficient to emphasize an error by a pixel. In case of a conventional BP, a[i] is equal to 1.

Figure 18 shows a procedure of inter-frame difference method of this experiment, and the image is gray scale of 8 bits. To binarize this image, the threshold value was defined as 20 which was determined by trial and error. A pixel shown with white in a figure of the right-side end is moving, the coefficient a[i] of this pixel is set as 2.0. Other coefficients are set to 1. Structure of DNN and other parameters, the end condition are similar to a former experiment.

| Figure 18. An inter-frame difference method |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch043.f18](i/ch043.f18.png) |
| --- |

Figure 19 shows results by the emphasis BP learning corresponding to Figure 16. We can obviously see a region where the trajectory uses. Moreover, the left figure shows that the trajectory corresponding to training data comes more smooth. We consider that it was improved by decreasing the influence of the background of the subject.

Figure 20 shows results by the emphasis BP learning corresponding to Figure 17. The trajectory of average form (left side) becomes more smooth, and difference among 3 trajectories corresponding to 3 swing spreads more. Since we can detect difference among forms more easily, our proposed emphasis BP learning is useful.

CONCLUSION

We are continuing our investigations into whether feature space functions of sandglass-type hierarchical neural networks can be effectively used when analyzing a series of continuous movements.

In this paper, we focused on how the target object is continuously deformed in videos of objects or people when there is a series of continuous movements. First, we concentrated on the same continuous deformation of the target object, for example, in the case of handwritten characters, and applied identity mapping learning using a seven-layered sandglass-type neural network.

Based on the results, we confirmed, in low-dimensional (two dimensions in this study) feature spaces, that feature extraction processing expressing the level of continuous deformation in the target object could be achieved. Furthermore, we confirmed that if a Gaussian filter is applied to overlapped learning data as a form of preprocessing, the expression space for the state captured in the feature space could spread. In addition, using a five-layered feedforward neural network in relation to a simple video, we verified that a continuous trajectory corresponding to the movement of the input image could be drawn in a three-dimensional space.

Next, using a rally of the table tennis as a practical problem, we performed an experiment by seven-layer DNN. As a result, trajectory of every swing was drawn to the three-dimensional feature space. Because orbit exists in a limited domain, we could catch a trajectory space which characterize normal swing of the subject. Furthermore, the difference among forms appeared as a change of trajectory.

Finally, we proposed an emphasis BP learning. This idea is that the processing places more weight on to a movement object of animations. By this method, we could achieve to spread the trajectory space.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Cognitive Informatics and Natural Intelligence (IJCINI), 11(2); edited by Kangshun Li, pages 25-40, copyright year 2017 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).

*   Goutam Kumar Bose

*   Pritam Pain  
    Haldia Institute of Technology, India

ABSTRACT

In the present research work selection of significant machining parameters depending on nature-inspired algorithm is prepared, during machining alumina-aluminum interpenetrating phase composites through electrochemical grinding process. Here during experimentation control parameters like electrolyte concentration (C), voltage (V), depth of cut (D) and electrolyte flow rate (F) are considered. The response data are initially trained and tested applying Artificial Neural Network. The paradoxical responses like higher material removal rate (MRR), lower surface roughness (Ra), lower overcut (OC) and lower cutting force (Fc) are accomplished individually by employing Cuckoo Search Algorithm. A multi response optimization for all the response parameters is compiled primarily by using Genetic algorithm. Finally, in order to achieve a single set of parametric combination for all the outputs simultaneously fuzzy based Grey Relational Analysis technique is adopted. These nature-driven soft computing techniques corroborates well during the parametric optimization of ECG process.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Our modern lifestyle is improving day by day because of the swift improvements and developments in modern technology. To overcome our daily life problems, it is important to achieve more efficient solution. Mathematical dynamics of the related solution based on nature has a remarkable impact. Nature servers various possible approach to think about solution and helps to develop efficient scientific methods.

Eventually, the connection between science and nature has made several possibilities for new research work. There is countless nature inspired techniques which can be utilize for the modern intelligent solution approach. As these nature-inspired techniques are very much effective on forming efficient algorithm, they are quite popular amongst modern Artificial Intelligence research. This is also remarkable that these techniques can easily use with other associated intelligent techniques in order to form new hybrid techniques. Mostly, correlative characteristics by the swarm in the nature had given researcher to develop various types of algorithm methods inspired from swarm such as bat, bee, firefly, cuckoo etc. Then again it is similarly possible to generate new nature-inspired techniques based on the theory of evolution. It is also remarkable that efforts are always given for optimizing the pre-deigned techniques to accomplish a more possible ideal solution to the real life problems. Genetic Algorithm is one such nature-inspired technique which is developed based on the theory of survival of the fittest by Darwin.

The ever-increasing precision machining requirements ultimately call for optimized machining process to sustain in the competition in the global market. To sustain in this competitive business industries are introducing several modifications by altering the traditional manufacturing process to non-traditional manufacturing process. Electrochemical Grinding (ECG) is one such non-traditional machining process which is a collective process of electrochemical dissolution and mechanical grinding. This method is generally applied for generating complex shape with high surface finish of high strength electro conductive material, low machinability alloy with high brittleness. In ECG process a small gap between conductive cathode grinding wheel and anode work piece is filled with flowing electrolyte through which dielectric current passes. The main factors affecting ECG process are Electrolyte concentration (C), Machining Voltage (V), Depth of cut (D), Flow rate of electrolyte (F), type of the abrasive wheel, physical properties of the work piece, relative speed in between tool and work piece, particle size on the abrasive wheel etc. As the machining process is mainly governed by the electrochemical dissolution of the work piece material, the generating surface is free from burr and residual stress as a result there is almost no chance of rejecting a material due to the surface cracks. Apparently, ECG process generate finished surface, therefore there is no need of time consuming additional finishing operations.

Some review of the past research works is presented here. Zhang et al. (2015) employed ECG process on Inconel 718. To elongate the wheel life, the brazed diamond wheel is utilised as a tool in place of the electrodeposited diamond wheel. Experiments showed that the tool durability has been improved significantly from 15 hours to 50 hours while a brazed diamond wheel is employed to replace an electrodeposited diamond wheel. Roy et al. (2007) investigated an experimental study, organized by statistical procedure, is made to calculate the effect of the major effecting parameter ‘voltage’ on the roughness of P-20 grade cemented carbide. The roughness data are investigated for different voltages. Lyubimov et al. (1998) are presented of diamond consumption in electrochemical in comparison with the routine grinding process. Initiation, development and the mutual correlation of various components of the diamond deterioration - adhesion, abrasion, diffusion, chemical wear and cracking at the electrochemical grinding - are discussed. Maksoud and Brooks (1995) investigates the electrochemical grinding process when used to machine metal-bonded diamond composite wheels. These wheels are utilise as form tools to grind ceramics. Operational parameters such as feed rate, electrolyte flow and current density, are investigated. The optimum operating conditions are evaluated. A comparison with conventional grinding methods is made also. Ilhan et al. (1992) has studied to optimize electrochemical grinding (ECG) process responses simultaneously by an off-line multi response optimization methodology. The responses considered as objectives are side and bottom overcuts, total metal removal rate, surface finish, spindle load and cutting wheel wear. It is shown in this paper that the multi-objective optimization technique can be utilise for an ECG operation, and that the optimal operating conditions for any given combination of weights can be achieved depending upon the objectives. Samanta (2009) presented to model roughness of the work surface in end milling by employing adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) and genetic algorithms (GAs). The results illustrate the effectiveness of the suggested approach in modelling the surface roughness. This article of Panda and Yadava (2012) reports an intelligent approach for the modelling of DS-ECSM process using finite element method (FEM) and then artificial neural network (ANN) in integrated manner. The ANN model is found to accurately predict Die sinking-electrochemical spark machining process responses for chosen process conditions. The primary objective of Sanjay and Prithvi is the prediction of suitable process control parameters for roughness of the work surface in drilling. Cutting force, cutting speed and machining time are taken as inputs of the adaptive fuzzy neural network and neuro-fuzzy analysis to estimate the values of surface roughness by employing 2, 3, 4, and 5 membership functions. The ideal structures are selected based on minimum of summation of square with the actual values with the predicated values by employing artificial neural-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) and neuro-fuzzy systems. Zhang el. al (2013) analyzed the work piece surface quality and the material removal rate on process parameters through machining SKD11 by medium speed wire electrical discharge machining (MS-WEDM). The trial data are utilized to model MRR and Ra at optimal parametric combination by a back-propagation neural network combined with genetic algorithm (BPNN-GA) technique. Hossaina et al. (2016) make an effort to build up an intelligent fuzzy expert system (FES) model to calculate the kerf width in CO[2] laser cutting. The employed input parameters are assisting gas pressure, cutting speed, standoff distance and laser power. The fuzzy logic is performed on fuzzy toolbox in MATLAB R2009b by employing Mamdani technique. Ding et al. (2005) presents an optimization approach for process sequencing based on multi-objective fitness: minimum machining cost, lowest possible manufacturing time and best satisfaction of manufacturing sequence rules. A newly developed hybrid approach is planned to incorporate a neural network, genetic algorithm and analytical hierarchical process (AHP) for process sequencing. Zaina et al. (2012) proposed a new approach in estimating a minimum value for machining performance. In this methodology, artificial neural network and genetic algorithm techniques are integrated in order to search for a combination of ideal cutting condition points that achieve the lowest value of machining performance. Yip-Hoi and Dutta (1996) presented various aspects of parallel machining which effect the generation of process plans are discussed. Further a process planner is described with the use of a genetic algorithm for sequencing operations. Implementation results are also included. Shie (2006) focused on finding an ideal cutting parameter setting of high-purity graphite in dry machining conditions by using an artificial neural network and then employing the Sequential Quadratic Programming method. This algorithm yielded better performance than the traditional methods for instance the Taguchi method and the Design of Experiments (DOE) approach. Du et al. (2015) proposed an improved Quantum-inspired cuckoo search algorithm (QCSA) created on the basis of self-adapting adjusting of search range known as IQCSA. The evolution speed factor and aggregation degree factor are primarily initiated into the proposed algorithm. In each iteration process, IQCSA can regulate the search step size dynamically depending on the current evolution speed factor and also aggregation degree factor, what will deliver the search process with more possible dynamic adaptability. Wang et al. (2015) proposed an improved hybrid cooperative algorithm which combines cooperative cuckoo search (CS) algorithm and particle swarm optimization (HC CS-PSO). The cooperative co-evolutionary structure is introduced in cuckoo search algorithm to implement dimensional cooperation. Yang and Deb (2010) presented a wider comparison study by means of some standard test functions and recently designed stochastic test functions. Then the CS algorithm is applied to evaluate engineering design optimization problems, including the design of springs and welded beam structures. The optimized solutions achieved by CS are far better than the best solutions obtained by an efficient particle swarm optimizer. Madi et al. (2012) aimed at investigating the possibilities of using novel meta-heuristic algorithms for example improved harmony search algorithm (IHSA) and cuckoo search (CS) algorithm for training ANNs in laser cutting modelling. The effectiveness of the algorithms is verified by comparing the outcomes with ANN model trained with real coded genetic algorithm (RCGA). Chawla and Duhan (2014) reviewed some of the applications of three newly developed algorithms, such as biogeography-based optimization, cuckoo search and bat algorithm, in various domains of biomedical engineering, i.e. biomedical instrumentation, clinical diagnosis, artificial neural networks, biomedical image processing, biological control system and biomechanics, bioelectronics, and illustrated how these fields have benefitted over the recently introduced MOA based on evolutionary computation. Ma et al. (2012) exhibited on the basis of analyzing the uncommon objectives in hazardous material transportation (HMT), a new multi-objective optimization model for hazardous material transportation (MOMHMT) is verified, which can take into account transportation risk, operation time, risks fairness, the number of sensitive population and multi-batch transportation simultaneously. Afterwards a fuzzy adaptive weighted genetic algorithm (FAWGA) is arranged in order to solve the MOMHMT by designing priority-based encoding method, fuzzy logic control with adaptive weighted assignment mechanism and partial matching crossover. Bose et al. (2011) studied on the identification of process control variables that have significant importance during electrochemical grinding of alumina-aluminium interpenetrating phase composites (Al[2]O[3]/Al IPC). The two important responses, i.e. better surface finish (Ra) along with possible maximum material removal rate (MRR) are evaluated as objectives that are to be satisfied simultaneously by a set of process control variables like electrolyte concentration, machining voltage, depth of cut and electrolyte flow rate keeping other parameters unaltered.

It is noted that few research study have been done to establish the optimum process variables so as to achieve maximum material removal rate, lowest surface roughness, minimum overcut and least cutting force. However, there is hardly any research study has been done in this field which includes comprehensive use of nature driven metaheuristic technology that can successfully optimize all the output responses simultaneously. Therefore, this is a clear case of multi objective optimization, which stands very challenging to accomplish simultaneously by a distinct set of process variables.

The current research study emphasises on machining of alumina-aluminum (Al[2]O[3]/Al) interpenetrating phase composite (IPC) material through electrochemical grinding process to reveal the effect of machine control parameters namely electrolyte concentration (C), machining voltage (V), depth of cut (D) and electrolyte flow rate (F), keeping other process control parameters unaltered, on performance responses like material removal rate (MRR), surface roughness (Ra), overcut (OC) and cutting force (Fc). A well-designed experimental combination is employed to reduce the total number of experiments in order to save both time and production cost. The control parameters are varied in three levels for twenty-seven experimental run based on the Taguchi methodology. Primarily the responses data are tested and trained by applying Artificial Neural Network (ANN) for investigating the validity of the experimental runs. This is followed by individual optimization of responses using Cuckoo Search (CS) algorithm. Next Genetic algorithm (GA) is applied to find the ideal or near ideal parametric condition which can simultaneously satisfy the contradictory objectives. Eventually, a well-known Grey relational analysis (GRA) is conducted where the weights of the responses are calculated using fuzzy set theory to full fill the multi criteria decision making (MCDM) process.

2\. PLANNING FOR EXPERIMENTATION

Here in this current research study electrochemical grinding (ECG) of Al[2]O[3]/Al interpenetrating phase composites (IPC) material (Al[2]O[3]\-68.9% and Al-31.1%) synthesized at 1150ºC (for 24 hours) has been considered. The mechanical characteristics of the work material are shown in Table 1.

The experimentation is performed in an improved (microprocessor controlled) and modified surface grinder that uses a grinding wheel having 150 mm diameter with 12.27 mm width where the surface consists of metal bonding and diamond abrasive particles. The abrasive grit size is 100 and the width of the layer comprising the diamond is 3 mm thick. The grinding wheel is mounted at the tip of the rotating spindle which is governed by a DC motor rotating at a 3500 rpm.

3\. ARTIFICIAL NEURAL NETWORK

Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is globally accepted for self-adaptive approach of non-linear experimental model. They are very powerful tool for experimental modelling, particularly when the relationship between the data are unknown. ANN can find out the interrelationship and associate pattern in between the data sets and expected target values. After training, ANN helps in predicting the result of new independent data. This algorithm is basically developed on the basis of neural network.

Each neuron takes a set of inputs (X[i], i=1, 2…., n-1, n) from associated neurons and issue the adjusted output signals (O[i], i= 1to K) to the end nodes. The function of the synapses is to multiply each input data, X[i] by the associated weight W[i] value and send the modified signal to the next hidden layer. Equation 1 displays the net input to each neuron in the hidden layer.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m01](i/ch044.m01.svg) (1)

Result Analysis

The statistical design of the data set is done by using the software Matlab R2015a. The algorithms considered in Matlab during calculating are as follows: the data has been randomly divided using the Divider and function, Levenberg-Marquardt while training, Mean Squared Error (MSE) for performance. The simulink model of ANN for considering four input parameters to optimize the outputs is shown in Figure 4. In this ANN model 27 experimental run are conducted for analysing.

| Figure 4. Simulink diagram of ANN analyse |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.f04](i/ch044.f04.png) |
| --- |

In the present work back-propagation algorithm is employed to develop the gradient and the Jacobian. The backpropagation computation is designed using the chain rule of calculus backward throughout the artificial network. Amongst the network output and target value of ANN’s model Mean Squared Error (MSE) is applied. Epoch is the demonstration in the set of training (input and/or target) vectors to a network and use for evaluating the new weights and biases for the data. Primarily the maximum number of 1000 epoch is set to terminate the training for each case. Also, for every investigation, if the magnitude of the gradient falls below 1 x10^(\-7), the training will stop.

A regression plot shows the correlation between the outputs of the network with the targets value. The four plots indicate the training, validation, testing along with overall data. The dotted line in every plot signifies the perfect result – outputs = targets. The continuous line signifies the best fit linear regression line in between outputs with targets. If R = 1, this signifies that there is an exact linear relationship in between outputs and targets. If R is close to zero, then there is a non-linear relationship in between outputs and targets.

If the number of validation check reaches 6, the training will stop. Here the number of successive iterations performed for validation checks is 2. 4\. CUCKOO SEARCH ALGORITHM FOLLOWING LEVY FLIGHTS

Cuckoo Search (CS) algorithm is a new metaheuristics algorithm which is developed based on mimicking the characteristics of cuckoo. In this algorithm each egg in a nest is represented by a possible solution and each cuckoo egg denotes a new solution. The objective is to apply the new and probably superior solutions to substitute a lower solution in the nests. More complicated cases such as multiple eggs in a nest, implying a set of solution, can be merged in this algorithm. This algorithm follows three steps as follows:

*   1\. First individual cuckoo lays one egg at a randomly chosen host nest.
*   2\. The next generation will inherit best nest with excellent quality of eggs

Finally, the number of available host nest is constant and the possibility of parasitic egg recognition by the host bird is p[a]∈\[0,1\]. The host bird can either throw away the sponging egg or ditch that nest for a better new nest. For practicality, in the later hypothesis it can be assumed that fraction p[a] of the host nests is substituted by new nests (with new random possible solutions). Generally, the quality or fitness of a solution is suggested to be proportional to the value of the objective function in case of a maximization problem.

Guided by the above three rules, the CS is abridged by the pseudo code (see Algorithm 1).

Algorithm 1. Cuckoo Search via Le'vy Flights

begin  
Objective function f(x), x=(x1, x2,………xd)^T  
Generate initial population of  
n host nests xi (i=1, 2, 3……, n)  
while  
(t<Maxgeneration) or (stop criterion)  
Get a cuckoo randomly by Levy Flights  
calculate its quality/fitness Fi  
Choose a nest among n (say, j) randomly  
if  
(Fi > F j),  
Replace j by the new solution;  
end  
A function (pa) of inferior nests  
are discarded and fresh ones are built;  
Keep the best solutions  
(or nests with quality solutions);  
The solutions are ranked and the current best solution is found  
end while  
Post process results and visualization  
end

When making new solutions x[i] (t +1) for the i^(th) cuckoo, the following Lévy flight is performed

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m03](i/ch044.m03.svg) (3)

where a >0 is the size of stage, which should be connected to the scale of the problem of interest. The product ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m04](i/ch044.m04.svg)denotes entry-wise multiplications. In this experimentation, a Lévy flight is considered, in which the step-lengths are distributed according to the following possibility spreading

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m05](i/ch044.m05.svg) (4)

It has an infinite alteration. Here, the successive steps of a cuckoo essentially outline an arbitrary walk process which obey a power-law step-length distribution to a heavy tail. It is significant that, in the real world, if a cuckoo’s egg is very alike to a host’s eggs, then this cuckoo’s egg is most unlikely to be distinguished, so the fitness must be related to the difference in solutions. Hence, it is a decent idea to do a random walk in a biased way with some haphazard step sizes.

Result Analysis

In the preliminary study, four parameters are analysed specifically on their implicit effects on material removal rate (MRR), surface roughness (Ra), overcut (OC) and cutting force (Fc). To optimize the experimental test functions, a MATLAB code is generated, by using MATLAB Version R2015a, is established based on the CS. During analysis, the numbers smaller than 4.9407e^(\-324) are taken as zero. The PC used is an Intel(R) Core i5 3230 M CPU @ 2.60GHz having 4GB of internal memory, with 64 Bit OS.

Optimization problem can be formulated as follows:

*   Find C, V, D, F
*   To Maximize: MRR and
*   To Minimize: Ra, OC, Fc
*   The cutting parameters are varied as:
    
    20≤C≤30 (5)
    
    15≤V≤25 (6)
    
    0.04≤D≤0.12 (7)
    
    0.1≤F≤0.3 (8)
    

At first each response is individually optimized applying Cuckoo Search algorithm via Levy flights. α is size of the population, i.e. number of the host nest, and Pa is the probability of the discovery rate. In this calculation, α assumed a value of 25 and Pa assumed a value of 0.25. The step size factor is calculated as L/100 and the total number of iteration is allowed up to 50,000 iterations.

Maximum MRR is obtained 0.975 gm/min for parametric combination of C = 30 gm/lit, v = 15 volts, D = 0.04 mm and F = 0.3 lit/sec. Whereas minimum Ra is obtained 0.115 μm with the parametric combination of C = 30 gm/lit, v = 15 volts, D = 0.04 mm and F = 0.3 lit/sec. Lowest OC is obtained at 0.036 mm having parametric combination of C = 20 gm/lit, v = 25 volts, D = 0.04 mm and F = 0.1 lit/sec. Finally, lowest Fc is obtained 0.054 kgf while the parametric combination is C = 20 gm/lit, v = 15 volts, D = 0.04 mm and F = 0.1 lit/sec.

Analysis of the Result for Multi-Objective Global Optimization

Multi-objective optimization of all the responses is carried out by applying Genetic Algorithm (GA). The objective functions are optimized so that four contradictory objectives i.e. maximum MRR, lower OC, lower Ra and minimum Fc are satisfied simultaneously. The control parameters are varied within a range as shown in equation 5-8.

6\. MULTI OBJECTIVE MODEL USING GREY RELATION ANALYSIS

Grey Relation Analysis (GRA) can utilize to optimize reliable responses simultaneously which opposes one another in nature. The grey system theory was developed by Deng in 1989’s and at the present time it is frequently used for analysing experimental design in which the model is undetermined or the information is not complete indicating a combination of known and unknown information’s.

GRA builds the relationship in between desired (best/ ideal) with real experimental data. Grey grade is computed by averaging the grey coefficient of respective response. In this study multiple response optimizations are found out by converting into a single grey relational grade. The calculated grey relational grade range varies in between 0 to 1, where closer to 1 values indicate its closeness towards the global possible idle solution. Finally, among all the combinations of process control variables, one that attains the maximum grey relational grade is taken to be the best parametric combination.

If higher value is for the better performance such as MRR then it is normalized as per equation,

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m12](i/ch044.m12.svg) (15)

If lower value for the better performance such as F[c], OC and Ra then it is expressed as,

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m13](i/ch044.m13.svg) (16)

The grey relational co-efficient is utilised to articulate the relationship between actual normalized experimental output with reference. This relation co-efficient can be evaluated as;

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m14](i/ch044.m14.svg) (17)

where,

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m15](i/ch044.m15.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m16](i/ch044.m16.svg)

and

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m17](i/ch044.m17.svg)

*   ζ = Distinguished co-efficient (varied with in a range 0-1)

Usually, the notable co-efficient can be regulated to fit the partial requirements. MRR and Ra both of them are given equal weights that assume a value of 0.5. The expression is as follows:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m18](i/ch044.m18.svg) (18)

where, m = Number of response parameter.

To optimize both the response at a time by single combination of process variables, GRA is performed. The combination with the rank 1 full fill multiple response parameters optimization.

Fuzzy Set Theory

Fuzzy set theory is the finest controlling tool to solve the uncertainty in decision making problem. Rarely unclear judgments of decision maker(s) makes it difficult to evaluate accurate mathematical assessment. Use of linguistic assessments values of weights of the conditions in the problem is a more valuable approach as compared to numerical values (Keufmann & Gupta, 1991). Decision matrix can be changed into a fuzzy decision matrix and associated with weighted normalized fuzzy decision matrix while considering the decision makers' fuzzy ratings. In a cosmos of discussion X, a fuzzy set ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m19](i/ch044.m19.svg)is characterized by an associated function ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m20](i/ch044.m20.svg)i.e., degree of association of x in ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m21](i/ch044.m21.svg)which maps each element x in X to a real number in the interval \[0-1\]. Triangular fuzzy number (TFN), ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m22](i/ch044.m22.svg)can be defined as a triplet (d[1],d[2],d[3]) and the membership function is defined (Dubois & Prade, 1979) as shown by equation 19.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m23](i/ch044.m23.svg) (19)

The transformation technique of fuzzy number into non-fuzzy number, that is, crisp value is recognized as defuzzyfication. In this study ‘centroid of area’ technique for determining Best Non-Fuzzy Performance (BNP) value is applied.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch044.m24](i/ch044.m24.svg) (20)

The results show that experiment number 1 has the maximum grey relational grade value. As defined above, this testing setup fulfils multiple response parameter optimizations. Hence, the experimental run of 1 which having parametric combination as C 20 gm/lit, V 15 volts, D 0.04 mm and F 0.1 lit/sec is the best among other experimental setup for having high MRR, low Ra, OC and Fc.

The confirmation experiment performed with the above optimal combination results in grey relational grade MRR, Ra, OC and Fc obtained 0.072 gm/min, 0.137 µm, 0.134 mm and 0.054 kgf respectively. It is found that MRR, Ra, OC and Fc increase considerably as appeared from computational results by using ideal machining variables combinations. 7\. CONCLUSION

The present study attempts to validate and optimize the machining parameters while machining of Al[2]O[3]/Al IPC material by ECG. Nature Inspired intelligent systems has proven their effectiveness in answering complex optimization problems. Nature driven techniques can definitely optimize a problem whose objectives are opposing in nature along with a wide variety of possible solutions. Artificial Neural Network (ANN) can simply train and validate the trial data and also test in the trained background. While analysing the experimental data using ANN in order to attain maximum MRR, lower Ra, minimum OC and least Fc the training, validation and testing data indicates that the values of R is closer to 1. This signifies that there is a specific relationship between outputs and targets.

Nature inspired techniques like Cuckoo Search (CS) algorithm can note the best parametric combination to satisfy the maximum MRR and lowest Ra, minimum OC and least Fc separately. Then the individual responses are optimized where the following parametric combinations are found: Maximum MRR 0.975 gm/min is obtained at C = 30 gm/lit, V = 15 volts, D = 0.04 mm and F = 0.3 lit/sec. Minimum Ra 0.115 µm is obtained at C = 30 gm/lit, V = 15 volts, D = 0.04 mm and F = 0.3 lit/sec. Lower OC 0.036 mm is obtained at C = 20 gm/lit, V = 25 volts, D = 0.04 mm and F = 0.1 lit/sec. Minimum Fc 0.054 kgf is obtained at C = 20 gm/lit, V = 15 volts, D = 0.04 mm and F = 0.1 lit/sec.

The contradictory objective functions can have achieved simultaneously by using Genetic Algorithm (GA) through a possible range of the control parameters. For MRR the range is 0.917 gm/min to 0.072 gm/min, for Ra it varies between 1.921 µm to 0.133 µm, for OC it is 0.477 mm to 0.046 mm and for Fc it is between 1.191 kgf to 0.054 kgf.

Finally, the results obtained from Genetic Algorithm is hybridized with Fuzzy set theory to obtain an exact parametric combination of the process control variables which satisfies these four conflicting objective function simultaneously. Weights of the outputs are considered as linguistic variables, where importance is given on Ra instead of on other parameters because ECG is mainly a finishing operation. The result of GA is approached for evaluating the best parametric combination during machining is C 20 gm/lit, V 15 volts, D 0.04 mm and F 0.1 lit/sec. Conclusively, the results are validated and the grey relation grade upgrades to 0.17.

Therefore, the experimental study as presented here for determining the optimum ECG parametric combination during machining of Alumina-Aluminium IPC materials can provide a valuable and an effective guideline for manufacturing of products of similar material.

# Chapter 45

*   Nikolaos E. Karkalos

    TEI of Western Macedonia, Greece

ABSTRACT

Solution of inverse kinematics equations of robotic manipulators constitutes usually a demanding problem, which is also required to be resolved in a time-efficient way to be appropriate for actual industrial applications. During the last few decades, soft computing models such as Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) models were employed for the inverse kinematics problem and are considered nowadays as a viable alternative method to other analytical and numerical methods. In the current paper, the solution of inverse kinematics equations of a planar 3R robotic manipulator using ANN models is presented, an investigation concerning optimum values of ANN model parameters, namely input data sample size, network architecture and training algorithm is conducted and conclusions concerning models performance in these cases are drawn.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Industrial production became highly automated from early 1900s and on. The assembly line of early automotive industries can be considered as the earliest form of automated systems in manufacturing industry. Automated systems have resulted in increased productivity, improved product quality and accurate manufacturing, lower production costs and significant reduction in production time. Furthermore, these systems are widely employed not only for monotonous or repetitive tasks but also in harsh and hostile environments or in cases when significant amount of force or other capabilities are required that man is impossible to provide. However, the design and development of automated systems requires significant research work and financial costs in order to ensure safety in the workplace and high quality of final products. Nowadays, automation components of various types are present in industrial production lines such as computer systems, employed in many stages from design to control of production line, robotic systems, used for several tasks such as welding or assembling processes, as well as other minor electronic automations.

Especially, industrial robots were first employed in the 1960’s, in automotive industry (Shell and Hall, 2000). ISO 8373 (1994) defines an industrial robot as an automatically controlled, reprogrammable, multipurpose manipulator, programmable in three or more axes. Some of mostly employed robot types are SCARA (Selective Compliance Articulated Robot Arm) robots, articulated robots and Cartesian coordinate robots. Early industrial robots were employed only to transfer various objects between different positions but nowadays they perform considerably more complicated tasks such as assembling, product inspecting, painting etc. Apart from the programming and controlling of robotic systems, the first and most fundamental analysis stage is the kinematics analysis.

Kinematics analysis is essential in order to plan the conduction of tasks efficiently and also in order to ensure the safe use of these robotic systems. Kinematics analysis is divided in two major categories: Forward kinematics and Inverse kinematics. Forward kinematics are used to compute the configuration of the robot, given its geometric parameters and inverse kinematics are employed to compute the opposite problem, which is a more laborious and complicated task. Several methods have been developed to deal with these two problems, with various shortcomings.

During the last few decades, the use of advanced methods such as soft computing has been introduced in robotic systems kinematics analysis as alternative methods with considerable potential improvement. Artificial neural networks (ANN) application in solving the inverse kinematics problem was first reported during the 1980s in works such as the work of Guez and Ahmad (1988). Hou and Utama (1992) were among the first to solve the inverse kinematics problem for a redundant manipulator using ANN. Wada and Kawato (1993) proposed a novel neural network model to calculate arm trajectory in order to overcome the deficiencies of previous models based on minimum torque-change criteria. Gupta et al. (1994) employed a neural network with dynamic neural units as computational nodes for the accurate prediction of end effector position and orientation. Tejomurtula and Kak (1999) presented solutions to inverse kinematics problem by employing various soft computing methods such as multilayer perceptrons (MLP), modified MLP and Kohonen maps. Karlik and Aydin (2000) compared the performance of two different ANN architectures concerning the prediction of motion of 6 degrees of freedom (DOF) robotic manipulator. Oyama et al. (2001) developed a novel module neural network model composed of individual expert networks. Furthermore, performance was measured in order to determine the number of expert networks and reduce computational time.

The copious problem of singularities prevention was addressed by Mayorga and Sanongboon (2005) using suitable ANN models. Bingul et al. (2005) employed ANN to compute the inverse kinematics for a 6R manipulator with offset wrist, a rather demanding case. Al-Gallaf (2006) created an ANN model for the solution of inverse kinematics of a multi-fingered robot with a view to use this model in an optimization problem concerning desired force distribution. Hasan et al. (2006) employed a novel adaptive-learning ANN model to solve the inverse kinematics for a 6 DOF serial robot manipulator. It was shown that the developed model could perform adequately for any change in the set-up of the robotic system. Chiddarwar and Babu (2010) used a less conventional ANN model, the RBF model and a fusion approach to provide a time efficient model. Shah et al. (2011) analyzed forward and inverse kinematics of a 2 DOF robot using ANN and noted the speed and accuracy of ANN models concerning this difficult task. Kumar and Irshad (2012) applied ANN to a case of 2-link serial chain manipulator. Magtanong et al. (2012) applied ANN in a case of solving the inverse kinematics of an android face. Yahya et al. (2014) compared conventional ANN and RBF networks in the solution of the problem of geometrically bounded singularities and joint limits prevention of a 3D and 6 DOF manipulator. Aggrawal et al. (2014) used ANN models to predict singularity zones for a 6 DOF PUMA 560 robot. Jha et al. (2014) investigated the characteristics of ANN models employed to solve the inverse kinematics problem of a 5 DOF manipulator and showed that the Mean Square Error (MSE) can be considered as the most suitable performance index in these problems. Ayyıldız and Çetinkaya (2016) compared four different optimization methods for the calculation of the trajectory of a 4-DOF robotic manipulator. Automated systems are also widely used in manufacturing and are an important field of study (Álvares et al., 2010; Pattanaik et al., 2015; Tamás, 2016).

In the current paper, the optimal choice of various parameters of the ANN model, used to solve the inverse kinematics problem of a planar RRR manipulator, is examined. The focus is set on parameters affecting ANN performance, namely, the size of training data, the training algorithm and the network architecture of a multilayer perceptron neural network. Conclusions concerning convergence speed and accuracy for each case will be drawn and will be further discussed. This study is considered as a preliminary step towards the implementation of an ANN-based controller for a real 3D robot manipulator, which will be employed for tasks related to manufacturing processes.

2\. ROBOTIC MANIPULATORS

In their simplest form, robotic manipulators are composed of discrete, rigid members called links, connected with each other by means of joints, with the first one of them connected to the foundation of the arm, namely its base. The joints allow a relevant movement of manipulator members and contain sensors that record the relative angular movement of two moving members. This angle is called joint angle. The types of joints are usually: linear, rotational, twisting, orthogonal or revolving joints. The number of DOF of a robotic manipulator equals the number of independent variables representing position. In a typical industrial robot, the number of DOF is equivalent to the number of joints.

At the free end of the robotic manipulator (the end of the kinematic chain) a suitable tool or other device is adapted, termed generally as end-effector, e.g. welding electrode, electromagnet etc. The position of manipulator is often described using two specific frames: the tool frame, and the base frame, as it will be explained in subsection 2.1.

2.1. Forward Kinematics Problem

The problem of forward kinematics is the problem of determining the kinematic characteristics of a robotic arm with a free end such as position, velocity and acceleration without studying the forces that cause them. Thus, it is a problem of statics and consists of determining the position and orientation (posture) of the end-effector, from given joint angles using proper transformations. These quantities are calculated in accordance to joint variables in regard to base frame, see Figure 1.

| Figure 1. Schematic depicting D-H parameters |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch045.f01](i/ch045.f01.png) |
| --- |

The joints are numbered from the base to the end-effector as 0, 1, ..., n. A joint axis is defined as the direction of the vector around which member i is rotating around member i-1 (it is described by 2 parameters). The distance between two axes is measured on a line perpendicular to both axes (link length a[i]). Another parameter is the link twist α[i], defined as the angle between two links measured in a normal plane. Apart from these two parameters, two additional parameters concerning consecutive links are defined: link offset d[i] that represents the distance between two members measured on their common axis and joint angle θ[i], i.e. as mentioned before, the relative angle between two consecutive members with respect to this axis. For the extreme members of the kinematic chain, special values are assigned to these parameters. These four parameters, also depicted in Figure 1, that can describe the kinematics of a robot are employed in Denavit-Hartenberg notation system, one of the most widely used systems to describe kinematics of robotic manipulators. An alternative way to compute forward kinematics, used in simple systems, is geometric analysis of the various parts comprising the robotic system.

2.2. Inverse Kinematics Problem

What is more important in terms of the operation of a robotic manipulator is the inverse kinematics problem. From known position and orientation of end-effector, the joint angles that produce these postures are desired to be computed. The algorithms implemented for solving this fundamental problem are embedded in the control system of robots. It is essentially a problem of mapping positions from a Cartesian space to the space of joint angles. In older times, robots were taught to resolve this problem for predefined final points but nowadays it is required that solutions are provided for complex and demanding problems. This problem is particularly difficult in that it leads to a non-linear system of equations for which a closed form solution is often very difficult or impossible to be calculated. The points where the robotic arm can move constitute the workspace of the robotic arm and are derived as solutions of inverse kinematics equations.

Generally, when a non-linear problem arises, there are several issues to be resolved such as the existence of a solution, the problem of having multiple solutions and the problem of finding a suitable solution. The subject of existence of a solution is related to the robotic manipulator workspace. In order for a solution to exist the point of interest should lie inside the workspace. Generally, robots with few DOFs have more restricted workspace, a solution is highly dependent on the actual configuration of the tool adapted in the end-effector.

Another important subject is the potential existence of multiple solutions. The choice of the optimum solution among the possible ones is based on specific criteria such as the criterion of shortest path. When two or more configurations can lead the manipulator to a desired position, the configuration with the shortest path is the most preferable unless an obstacle is preventing the robot to follow this path or due to the current position of end-effector. Another possible method of choosing the optimum solution is the assignment of weights to the joints and giving more importance on the displacement of certain parts of the robot. The number of possible solution, which can be subject to constraints, is also related to the number of joints in the manipulator.

A robotic arm is solvable when the joint variables can be determined by means of an algorithm. This algorithm should be able to provide all possible solutions. Two types of solution algorithms are usually used: algorithms that lead to a closed form solution and iterative methods. Iterative methods are usually Newton-type methods such as Newton-Raphson method. Analytical methods are either algebraic or geometric methods and are considered more traditional as they originate from the solution of various types of mechanisms.

2.3. Artificial Neural Networks

Modeling is commonly used in manufacturing technology problems (Sukaylo et al., 2004; Karthikeyan et al., 2012; Szabó and Kundrák, 2012; Grabchenko et al., 2014). Lately, soft computing methods have been also adopted. Artificial Neural Networks method is one of the most important soft computing methods. This method is employed in a large variety of scientific fields as an advanced prediction method (Sudhakaran and Siva Sakthivel, 2013; Porwal et al., 2014; Markopoulos and Kundrák, 2016). ANN models are shown to exhibit excellent predictive capabilities especially in problems when the function of studied systems is governed by complex, non-linear relationships or when no analytical description of the system is possible.

Artificial neural networks imitate the actual function of biological neural networks, especially the neurons and their interconnections or synapses as well as the learning process of senior biological species. So, a sufficient amount of input data and their corresponding outputs are recorded and then, they are given to the ANN model in order to learn the data and discover the relationship between inputs and outputs. When the training process is completed, the network should be able to predict accurately the response of the system to unknown inputs, even when they are not close to the given input data, i.e. the generalization ability of the network.

| Figure 2. Architecture of a simple multi-layer perceptron |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch045.f02](i/ch045.f02.png) |
| --- |

More specifically, conventional ANN are usually comprised of three layers (multi-layer perceptron model), namely an input layer, a hidden layer and an output layer, depicted in Figure 2. The number of neurons in the input and output layers directly correspond to the inputs and outputs of the system, respectively. The number of neurons in the hidden layer is often determined by trials and often more than one hidden layer is used. In simple ANN the information enters the network from the input layer, gets processed in the network and the outcome of the process is appearing at the output layer (feed-forward network). Each connection between neurons (synapse) is associated to a weight coefficient. Weights have a random initial value and their value is updated after each step in the learning process according to the error between desired and produced output. The error is propagated from the output to the input layer (back-propagation of the error). For the weight update, various training algorithms based mainly on the calculation of error derivatives are employed, such as gradient descent or Newton method. Further description of training algorithms is presented at Methodology section.

During the training stage, a subset of the input/output sample is used and the rest of the data are preserved for the validation and test stages. Validation stage involves updating of weights until the error is not further decreasing and improves the generalization ability of the network. Then, in the last stage, the weights are fixed and a small subset of the initial sample is presented to the network to assess its predictive capability on unknown inputs. Performance of the network is often measured in terms of MSE and coefficient of correlation (R) between target and predicted output values. Mean square error is calculated from the following equation:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch045.m01](i/ch045.m01.svg) (1)

where ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch045.m02](i/ch045.m02.svg) represents the predicted output values and Y[i] the actual output of the system. Linear correlation coefficient R is calculated as follows:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch045.m03](i/ch045.m03.svg) (2)

where, in the case of artificial neural networks, x[i] is the dataset of predicted outputs, y[i] the dataset of target values and n the size of these two datasets, as using this equation, the degree of correlation between predicted and target outputs is desired to be calculated. Finally, apart from conventional feed-forward, backpropagation ANN models, other more advanced models are nowadays in use such as RBF or recursive NN.

2.4. Methodology

In the current study, a 2D (planar), 3R robotic manipulator, depicted in Figure 3, is considered.
