BACKGROUND

Usually, the production of fruits and vegetables and their related activities face significant losses in Brazil. The use of computer-based systems to early alert, identify or predict the occurrence of tomato foliage diseases may benefit small farmers to reduce the chemical management of the disease. It may provide a reduction in the number of sprayings and diminish the total amount of pesticide residues in fresh and processed fruits (Andrade, 1997; Vale et al., 2000). According to Becker (2005) and Mahlein et al. (2012), with the aid of computer-based early alert systems it was possible to delay the beginning of the first spraying on tomato in comparison with the fixed schedule spraying method.

Pattern Recognition in Tomato Diseases

In Brazil, although broadly studied, the tomato crop suffers from a lack of investigation of integrated production strategies for disease and pest control, with the help of early alert computer-based systems. For instance, countries with smaller agriculture like Portugal and Mexico use a model named Tom-cast (based on digital data loggers) to monitor environmental variables (temperature, humidity, velocity of the wind and solar radiation) to alert the occurrence of late blight and to reduce the use of pesticide residues in the crops Mexia et al. (2003). This approach is still far from the reality of the majority of small Brazilian farmers because it is based on expensive equipment like data loggers. Furthermore, this equipment requires large devices to store ever-increasing amounts of environmental data that should be handled by specialized technical assistance. Apart from such disadvantages, it is important to stress that some crops may extend over vast areas, making this monitoring a challenging task.

According to Boch et al. (2010), Mahlein et al. (2012) and Barbedo (2013), many of the plant foliage and stem diseases can be detected by the use of digital pictures combined with some image processing. In some cases, pattern recognition or automatic classification tools are the suitable approaches. Besides, according to these authors, imaging systems are preferable to non-imaging systems because image analysis can be quick, accurate and reliable when automated. Besides, image analysis equipment is relatively inexpensive and easy to use by workers with little qualification.

So far, small Brazilian farmers have limited options of computational tools that can help them in early detection of late blight in tomato crops. The commonest approach involves naked eye observations (Correa et al., 2009; Barbedo, 2013). The procedure that uses manual classification of the disease defined by Correa et al. (2009). This key is based on schematic images of leaves of tomatoes that quantify the degree of infestation by P. infestans, allowing to evaluate the tomato contamination degree visually. However, professionals must perform early detection, which is not always a feasible option because it is an error-prone and time-consuming task. An alternative would be to computerize the process of evaluation of cultures. Such approach may accelerate the identification of strains so as to separate them into two sets: one containing specimens of plants in good condition and the other with specimens that must undergo further examination by specialists.

Digital Approaches that Investigate Vegetable Leaves

Image processing is a useful tool for analysis in various agricultural applications (Vibhute & Bodhe, 2012). The development of methods to compute digital images from crops has the purpose of improving image quality both for human analysis or to enable automatic processing by pattern classifiers. The main problems of pre-processing are those related to the quality of the image, noises, distortions, blur, variations of scale. In pre-processing tasks, it is common to perform noise suppression, image rotation, and scale normalization (Nixon & Aguado, 2008).

Usually, in image recognition applications, the extraction of features is motivated on shape extraction, which implies finding the shape position, orientation, and size. There are many techniques to extract shape and other characteristics from digital images, like first and second order edge detection, corner extraction, Hough transforms, planar curvature, change in edge detection, movement of optical flow, the differential approach and others (Freeman, 1970; Gonzalez & Woods, 2010). In biological morphology, shape recognition was conducted at increasing levels of abstraction (geometric, structural and semantic). Most machine vision works on plant species identification deals with leaf shape identification and fewer investigate methods for the identification of the whole plant (Slaughter et al., 2008).

The format used to represent the data will depend on the problem being treated. For instance, different formats can bring significant changes to the performance of the recognition system (Gonzalez & Woods, 2010). There are several ways to assess the discrimination power of the representation format. We can mention the methods of analysis by using discriminant functions, such as Fisher's, an analysis of first and second order statistics, and the evaluation of distances between data classes centroids (Afifi & Clark, 1990; Bishop, 1995).

When dealing with a region or object, compact representations can simplify measurements on the object, enhance the performance of digital communication systems and improve the accuracy of automatic systems for digital image classification (Kariya & Wasu, 2013). Feature extraction methods can reduce the dimensionality of pattern representation; different strategies have been used in image processing. Several methods have been proposed to select features. Recently, there have been several studies investigating the use of broadband color or chromaticity values, for plant species recognition (Zwiggelaar, 1998; Brown & Noble, 2005; Scotford & Miller, 2005). One of the key advantages of these techniques is that pixel-based color classifiers tend to be less computationally intensive than shape-based methods. In the first case, the computational effort is done upon each pixel of the image, where its value is replaced with a new value obtained from the first. In that way, the computational cost is proportional to elementary operations over a matrix of integers. In the case of shape processing techniques, like edge detections or corner extraction usually is necessary to use the calculation of gradients, or first and second differentials and multiplications of matrix. All of those heavy calculations require a faster processor and more memory to guarantee a proper performance of the system. However, this goes against our main objective that is to offer an affordable solution for small farmers (Nixon & Aguado, 2008).

In this paper, we deal with the issue of identifying and classifying some parts of an image by using an automatic processing system. To face such problem, we use the same classification key defined by Correa et al. (2009), the shape, size or texture of tomato leaves were not essential, but the tones of color that occur in leaves are crucial. Thus, we have selected features based on the broadband colors of images, as will be discussed in next sections.

RELATED WORK

The semi-automatic recognition of diseases and pests with the assistance of algorithms supported by neural networks has been addressed in several works. However, these works used different species of plants other than tomato. As far as we know, this is an open research question because tomato crops and its leaves have particularities that cannot be found in other vegetables.

Becker (2005) proposed a manual alert system based on integrated production system as indicative for the spraying in the controlling of late blight compared with a fixed calendar system used in conventional production by the tomato growers of the region of Vale do Rio do Peixe, with reference to the town of Caçador, Santa Catarina State, in the South of Brazil, where environmental conditions are very different from Rio de Janeiro.

Sanyal & Patel (2008) analyzed the texture and color of the leaves of rice (Oryza sp.) to identify diseases as brown spot and blast diseases. The simulation presented by the authors was based on 400 images, and a Multilayer Perceptron network performed the ranking. Images of healthy and infected leaves were used; the authors reached a performance of about 89.26% of accuracy in the classification of individual pixels of the images (considering either injured leaves or not injured ones). We stress that neither the leaves as a whole nor the plants were evaluated. Such work is different from our approach since the authors investigated individual pixels while we examined the entire amount of pixels of affected tomato leaves.

Camargo & Smith (2009) defined a classifier that uses support vector machine to operate on color images of cotton (Gossypium sp.). The authors used 127 pictures of the cultures. The best classification of their model was found when using 45 different characteristics, reaching a performance of 93.1%.

Vieira et al. (2011) used an MLP neural network to detect the lesions in tomato leaves. However, his success rate was about 77.8% in the identification of late blight wounds. The author reported in his work that he used a small amount of images of infected leaves. For instance, only nine images of leaves with wounds of a total set of 65 of wounded leaves of three different types of illness were used. Vieira´s digital images were captured using semi-professional cameras in a laboratory (controlled environment) and had manual pre-processing. Besides, the end-user must define the relevant areas of the original image wounded by the disease, and only those subsets of images are analyzed. This work used a manual contour-based approach to select the images that were used by the MLP neural network.

Xu et al. (2011) described a method to detect potassium and nitrogen deficiencies in tomato plants, causing the yellowing of leaves. The algorithm extracts some features from colored images. The author considers texture functions that are extracted by using three different methods (Fourier Transform and Wavelet packet decomposition). The selection and combination of the features were carried out with the use of genetic algorithms. Finally, the optimized combination of features is used as the input of a fuzzy K-nearest neighbor classifier, which is in charge of the final identification. The experiments showed that the accuracy of this diagnostic system is above 82.5%, and it can diagnose disease from 6 to 10 days before experts could determine its occurrence. Such work uses image processing but is different from the method we used because the authors used fuzzy logic to detect a nutritional deficiency and employed an elaborate and expensive imagery apparatus.

Gastélum-Barrios et al. (2011) developed a method based on pattern recognition and image segmentation to improve tomato production and fruit quality through tomato fruit measurements. This method has a low impact factor on the fruit and plant during measurements. We stress that this work is different from our work because it is tailored to detect healthy fruits instead of injured tomato leaves.

Some papers describe works in the field of plant automatic recognition, using the RGB color values as a central discrimination feature. Franz et al. (1991) studied the use of broadband reflectance in the visible (blue, green, red) and infrared for plant species recognition of a variety of mixed greenhouse grown plants. Woebbecke et al. (1995) evaluated the values of RGB color as well as red and green chromaticity values, a number of color indices and hue in color images taken in greenhouses for identification selected species from weeds and soil. The authors evaluated, in a laboratory study, five potato plants, 12 sugar beet plants, and 25–30 plants of each of three weed species. Borregaard et al. (2000) achieved a classification accuracy of 89–94% when performing an automatic crop-weed discrimination.

MATERIAL AND METHODS

Despite the economic importance of the tomato in the Brazilian economy, there have been few studies focused on the automatic detection of diseases and pests in Brazilian tomato crops. Our approach is quite different from related works. We have used digital images obtained directly by low resolution built in cell phone cameras that are accessible to small Brazilian tomato farmers. Furthermore, the images have been achieved in a controlled experimental open field that had 66 different kinds of genotypes and the typical environmental conditions of Brazilian tomato crops. Besides, to simulate a real situation where workers will take images to be further analyzed, the images were collected in situ, having details of leaves, soil, fruits and sometimes parts of the sky and the environment. Such characteristics reinforce the value of the filtering and the pattern recognition system approach that we proposed to detect the late blight. Finally, this study used a larger number of real images and the rates achieved are greater than those reported in similar works.

The experimental setup is composed of a digital camera in the field and desktop computers at the computer science lab; no color sensors or filters were used to acquire the digital images in the visible spectrum. Besides, we did not use sophisticated machinery or proprietary software packages because small farmers and workers may not be willing to afford expensive equipment or might be unable operate it properly.

The initial set of pictures available encompasses 226 color digital images of leaves collected from tomatoes plants, grown on the principles of organic agriculture. The pictures were taken in the open environment of the experimental area under sunlight conditions. No backgrounds or additional sources of light or shadows are necessary to take the images from tomatoes leaves because the images should be as close as possible to the ones captured by small farmers on his crops. The tomatoes plants were cultivated in the experimental fields of the horticulture sector of the Horticultural Department of the IA/UFRRJ in a cropping area historically linked with the natural occurrence of late blight. The genotypes include a commercial cultivar susceptible to the illness, two which are resistant to it and 63 cultivars still under review at the UFRRJ (Correa et al., 2009).

Figure 2 shows the sequence of processes performed on the original images, collected from the field. For instance, in the example shown in step (1), an image (063.jpg) had its definition diminished to achieve a 70% of reduction in its size in order to speed up the performance of further procedures. Next, in step (2), the reduced colored image was converted into a black and white image. That reduced color image was used to generate a picture containing only red, green and black pixels step (3) as we will explain further.

In this work, the shape, size or texture were not important to the pattern recognition, but mostly the relative percentage of some color patterns. Over the images created by the steps (2) and (3), we conducted a counting of pixels from different color bands. In step (5), these counters are then stored in a table that contains the absolute number of pixels of each color (red, green, black and a gamma of gray tones). Next, data are then linear-normalized, generating a new table containing the same variables, but now varying from 0 to 1. Finally, these variables were evaluated for the selection of the most significant, in the final step that will be discussed in the next sections.

We evaluated 160 neural network distinct configurations with a learning rate changing from 0.2 up to 0.8 (with steps of 0.2), the momentum changing from 0.1 up to 0.9 (with steps of 0.2), and the number of hidden neurons varied from 2 up to 16. Despite the existence of many heuristics in the literature about how choose the best size for the hidden layers of an MLP networks. Our previous work (Vianna & Cruz, 2013a) presented the algorithms and search method used to define the optimal number of hidden neurons for our application. Features of the architecture of all verified networks were identical: eight input neurons, one output neuron, and sigmoid transfer function.

Our approach was developed to be as simple as possible. This goal was a requirement to satisfy the target users, i.e., families of small farmers that could not have the enough funds to buy an expensive computer-based apparatus. Thus, the proposed approach used standard hardware. We used an Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-2430M CPU @ 2.40GHz, with an onboard Intel(R) HD Graphics Family card for running the system, a) and free license software. We used the Eclipse IDE for Java and free packages such as Neuroph (Sevarac, 2012), AWT Image, Java Advanced Imaging (JAI), plus the MySQL as the relational database system. The images were taken from the experimental field using a cell phone camera; the resolution of the images has been reduced to only 0,3 Megapixels, and each image files is less than 100 KBytes, to increase the performance of the recognition process.

Red/Green Filtering

For the identification of the leaf area affected by the late blight, we used a set of real images of young and adult tomato plants; each image was initially submitted to a red/green color filter. The red/green filtering process consists of an automated procedure developed by previous works (Vianna & Cruz, 2013a, 2013b); it considers that healthy tomato plant is bright green colored. The brown or yellow tones may indicate the occurrence of an injury and all different tones are regarded as part of the environment (background) and must be discarded (examples of unhealthy leaves and backgrounds are depicted in Figure 3).

According to this definition, the examination of the tones of each pixel of the image was accomplished by sorting it according to the values of their R, G and B components of the RGB color system. Over 200 different labeled pixels were selected, from various images. For each pixel, we divided the R, G, and B component values and created three data sets. The first containing the three values for pixels extracted from regions of lesions on tomato leaves. The second containing the R, G and B values for pixels extract from parts of healthy areas of leaves and the last contains the pixel values of the background. After that, we calculated the mean and standard deviation values of each color band for each pixel type. Finally, we defined the following rules:

*   I.
    
    If a pixel is classified as an injury, it will be converted to solid red (255,0,0), in case it is yellowed or browned, which indicates the occurrence of the lesion (necrotic area). For the tone calculation, we used the following:
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m01](i/ch061.m01.svg) (1)
    
*   II.
    
    If a pixel is classified as healthy, it will be converted to solid green (0,255,0) in case it has a green tone, from any bright to dark green hue, according to the formula:
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m02](i/ch061.m02.svg) (2)
    
*   III. A pixel of any different tone will be considered as part of the background image and will be converted to solid black (0,0,0).

As soon as the filtering process ends, all images had its pixels counted. This first process counts the amount of Red, Green and Black pixels. We stress that it is interesting to notice that the proposed method keeps its performance in discriminating brown spots, even when the focus of the image was poor (blurred images). Figure 3 shows an example of the pixel classification strength of the proposed method.

Relevance Analysis

Further, the pixels counting over the Red/Green and Grayscale images, the mean values of the original images RGB components are also counted. The average value of R, G and B components were calculated in a similar way as the MeanGrayTone (4); The MeanRed value was obtained by calculating the arithmetic mean of all R (red) components, from the RGB representation, among all pixels that form the image. A similar procedure was used to calculate the MediumGreen and MediumBlue values.

During the analysis, we detected that the order of magnitude of each variable was quite heterogeneous, as some variables represent absolute amounts of pixels that can be over 200,000 while others represent a mean of values that only can vary from 0 to 255, for example. To homogenize the interval of possible values of the variables, they were normalized by applying a linear normalization process. The equation (5) was used for this purpose, being attributed to each variable, a linearly distributed value between 0 and 1.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m05](i/ch061.m05.svg) (5)

Normalization was carried out before the relevance analysis of variables commenced. Only after the normalization process was concluded, the data set was made available for the training of the neural networks.

A crucial point in the developing of automatized classifiers is the selection criteria for the most relevant characteristics. The first experiments used all data extracted from the whole set of images, but their performance was not good. The solution was to reduce the dimension of each image representation, by applying a relevance analysis of extracted variables, leading to a subset of the most significant ones (Vianna & Thomé, 2000). Thus, to do that, the first step considered the separation of the normalized set of variables into two different groups. One group have the examples belonging to the original images that showed visual evidence of foliage disease and the other group containing the ones that were considered healthy. The two groups were identified as G[1] and G[0].

Subsequently, we evaluated the statistical moments of the first and second order of each variable of the groups G[1] and G[0], to check the discriminative capacity of them (Spiegel, 1978). The use of pre-processing can often improve the performance of a pattern recognition system, and the evaluation statistical moments could lead to the selection of the variables with the greater discriminative power for a classifier, as a neural network system. In many practical applications, the data pre-processing will be one of the most significant factors for the final performance (Bishop, 1995). We evaluate the discriminatory capacity of each variable by considering the spatial separation of sets G[1] and G[0]. For example, given a variable X, to be regarded as a discriminative variable, X must observe the following condition:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m06](i/ch061.m06.svg)

where:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m07](i/ch061.m07.svg) (6)

Figures 4.a and 4.b shows the Gaussian curves that represent the statistical distribution of variables BlueMean and MediumGrayTone, inside each group G[1] (continuous line) and G[0] (dashed line). It could be observed in Figure 4.a that the intersection between curves is relatively small, especially when compared with the one at Figure 4.b, which is considerably bigger. A bigger curve separation suggests a bigger discriminative capacity. The selected variables are those that presented the smaller intersection between the distribution curves.

In order to a variable be considered discriminative, the confusion area between its distribution curves G0 and G1 must be as minimum as possible. In equation (6), only those variables which the mean values of G0 and G1 are separated by a distance bigger than one standard deviation, plus the tolerance value, represented by the tol parameter, will be considered discriminative. In the automated evaluating procedure, only the variables with curves separated by a measure with beyond the minimum distance, controlled by tol, will be considered. As a consequence, tol depends on the general characteristics of the set, and its definition is an empirical process. Moreover, different sets could select different discriminative variables, depending on image quality (regarding light, contrast, noise).

It could be noticed that as the tol values increase, the size of the selected variable set decreases. For the available image set, we analyzed some tol values, within the range \[0,1\] and the selected variables, in each case, are described in Table 1. It can be verified that no new variable will be selected for tol values below 0.1. This occurs because the distribution curves have the same type as Figure 5.b. In other words, the sum of parameters μ(X[0]) + δ²(X[0]) will always be bigger than μ(X[1]) and no new variable will be selected, no matter the value of tol changes. After this initial investigation, we defined the value of tol as 0.1, which conducted to the selection of eight variables, a 30% discard rate of the original variable set.

NEURAL NETWORKS FOR PATTERN RECOGNITION

Perception becomes one of the most complex human skills by engaging analog signals, with high degree of noise, and a large number of variables that need to be understood simultaneously (RICH, 1988). Pattern recognition via machines involves tasks of learning and classification, resulting in the association of each point in space to an existing class. Frequently, this is not a trivial task, requiring the classifier module some advanced abilities, such as separating overlapping classes, establishing non- linear boundaries, or having dynamic adaptability to changes in the input data patterns.

The simplest way to implement a classifier is through the use of discriminant functions or classifiers. In this approach, if a pattern ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m08](i/ch061.m08.svg) belongs to the class C[i], then the discriminant function D[i](![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m09](i/ch061.m09.svg)), associated with the class C[i], i =1, 2, ..., k must have the highest value of all D[i](![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m10](i/ch061.m10.svg)). Furthermore, over the decision boundaries, D[i](![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m11](i/ch061.m11.svg)) \= D[j](![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m12](i/ch061.m12.svg)) (Duda, 1973). The calculation of D[i](![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.m13](i/ch061.m13.svg)) could be made supervised or non-supervised. Common supervised techniques are maximum likelihood Bayes classifier and the rule of Perceptron while clustering algorithms such as nearest-neighbor, k-means, and the ISODATA implement unsupervised classification (PAL, 1999).

Neural networks are powerful tools for pattern recognition tasks. The separation boundaries of classes are estimated during the training phase where the network weights are changed by comparing the values produced by it with the expected output values for each entry. In particular, a network with more than one layer is capable of learning any continuous mapping. The addition of layers allows the network to extract higher-order statistics data, which is particularly useful when the size of the input layer is large (Fausett, 1994).

Neural networks possess the ability to store information and make it available for later use. His knowledge is acquired and consolidated by a learning process, and they have the ability to generalize, producing consistent outputs for inputs not seen during the training process. They can be trained to perform non-linear mappings of an n\-dimensional space to another m\-dimensional. Main applications of neural networks are mapping activities, and optimizing clustering (HAYKIN, 1999; ZURADA, 1992). In a neural network, the outputs can be interpreted as posterior probabilities of existing classes. Thus, Bayes' theorem can be applied to decision-making criteria classifications made by neural network systems (Johnson, 1992).

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this section, we present the results of the experiments based on neural networks experiments and discuss it results.

For each configuration of the neural network, we did a batch of 50 training and testing cycles, a total of 8,000 batches of training and testing, using a 10-fold cross-validation of the calculating of mean performance of each configuration had statistical validity. After the training phase, we tested the performance of each distinct neural network configuration. For each architecture, we calculated the average performance of the classification task and also calculated the architectures that have the highest classification power were identified (Table 2). These results were acquired, during the testing phase, only with validation examples that had not been presented to the network during the training phases.

Table 2. Best recognition performances among all different neural networks configurations tested, using a 0.5 class separation threshold, and tol=0.1. The third column shows the worst recognition score found with the respective amount of hidden neurons. In parenthesis, it is shown the learning rate, and the momentum used when the worst recognition score was found. Similarly, the last column shows the best recognition score obtained, and the respective learning rate and momentum used

| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch061.g02](i/ch061.g02.png) |
| --- |

As the majority of the neural networks presented a higher performance with a learning rate of 0.2, this value used for the further calculations of the ideal separation threshold. The calibration of the outputs threshold of the neural networks could affect the performance of the whole system. During the tests, we used the value of 0.5 for the frontier between the outputs: for a given input example, if the network output were lower than 0.5, the case would be considered as belonging to the G[0] class. The values above this threshold were classified as belonging to G[1] class.

To calibrate and configure the threshold of the network and to raise the hit rate in the classification, each network was presented to 50 test subsets, each subset consisting of 20 images of tomato leaves, randomly chosen from the testing set. All answers provided by each group of networks (with the same configuration) was separated into two subsets. The first containing the answers for images of affected plants leaves (S[1] class) and the second providing the answers for images of healthy plants (S[0] class). Once more, we calculated the mean value and the standard deviation for each subset of outputs and analyzed the curves of the graphs.

We use the subsets of outputs described above to determine the optimal threshold for classes’ separation as illustrated in Figure 6. The vertical line indicates a possible decision boundary for the scheme. If the decision boundary is located at the intersection of the curves, the probability of erroneous classifications can be minimized. The graph was constructed by taking the total set of outputs from the 50 networks trained with two hidden neurons, the learning rate equal to 0.2, and the momentum equal to 0.7. Based on such distribution analysis, each threshold was defined as being a point inside the intersection area between the distribution curves that would best select the sets. In this example, the optimal threshold value is 0.67, which increased the classifying performance from 73.55% to 82.24% of hits.

The same analysis of the outputs of the distribution curves were performed for all networks selected in the former step (Table 2). For each configuration, we defined another discrete threshold value. Now using these new thresholds values and the same trained networks, we reached the results described in Table 3. It can be seen that the threshold adjustment for already trained networks improved the average performance for all configurations.

Finally, we chose the configuration with the best performance. The best configuration was the 8-14-1 network, with training rate equal to 0.2, momentum equal to 0.3, and threshold equal to 0.63. When we analyzed each network of the total amount of 50 networks with this configuration, we detected networks that have achieved the best accuracy rate with values of about 94.12%.

Table 3. Best recognition performances among all different neural networks configurations tested. The results emphasize that a different threshold can change the accuracy of the final classification. For all neural networks, we have used tol=0.1

A sensitivity analysis of the results attained to each network configuration can bring more information about the performance. For instance, Table 4 shows the details of the classifications, it took into account the fraction (percentage) of correct answers for each network in each category of the example. For instance, the percentage of correct responses for the cases labeled with value 0 (no evidence of late blight) or 1 (with evidence of the disease). The table also shows the percentage of false positive and false negative classifications. A false positive classification is an image of healthy tomato plant that were classified as having the disease, and a false negative is an opposite.

The results depicted in Table 4 were calculated based on the previously described tests (each network was presented with 50 testing sets, where each set consisted of 20 randomly selected images). Furthermore, we done the evaluation using the finest classification thresholds for each configuration. That table is not balanced. Nevertheless, we decided not to apply any artificial balancing algorithm on the dataset, as we are waiting for the next late blight seasons to collect more novel images to balance the set of examples. Nevertheless, there is no significant difference between the system performance during classification of healthy or injury examples.

CONCLUSION

Tomato has become one of the most important vegetable crops worldwide. This paper presented a computational approach aimed at detecting the commonest tomato disease on Brazilian small properties. The experiments were based on real world crops. The pattern recognition of late blight through the use of techniques of MLP Neural Networks showed to be effective, with its best accuracy rate with values of about 94.12%.

The red/green filtering process that prepared the digital images was effective even if compared to more sophisticated digital image algorithms such as image segmentation (e.g. boundary detection, trimming the bottom, contour detection, among others) (Bock et al., 2010). The filtering process showed to be valuable enough to overcome issues such as low focus, image blur, bright and little definition of the digital images.

The MLP model is a well-known approach. Despite its simplicity, we estimate that the approach is a suitable contribution to help the small farmer to detect late blight early. The easy of use, low cost and simplicity were targets in our research. We believe that a large number of Brazilian tomato workers have neither the expensive computers resources nor the time or the expertise to spend on digital processing with sophisticated programs.

Some possible benefits of this work can be evaluated in two dimensions:

*   I. Economic: The computational approach may aid farmers to increase the volume of the vegetable production; reduced operational costs of the tomato crops and improved its quality. Besides, the software can assist in automating the process of conducting on-farm research. This will allow small farmers to utilize novel precision agriculture technologies for improving management decisions and to overcome the issues of food safety regulations and food traceability. Finally, the approach may offer to small farmer’s greater access to expert information, services, and best practices;
*   II. Environmental: The approach is an effort to contribute to the conservation of the soil and groundwater and even the health of tomato workers. Besides, it may also result in the reduction of the use of pesticides in tomato crops, allowing a better risk mitigation (pests, diseases, weather).

We stress that all the experiments, from the digital image pre-processing to the training and testing of neural networks, were developed by the research group on the open-source technologies and inexpensive computers. The module of neural networks used classes and methods from the public library Neuroph, and all other pieces of software were developed at the Laboratory of Databases at UFRRJ.

As future work, we intend to evaluate improvements in algorithms for digital image processing, to extract more significant information from the input data and improve the performance of the recognition system based on Neural Networks. We will consider the use of fuzzy logic to enhance the performance of intelligent recognition and automating procedures for some minor modules that are performed manually, such as the definition of thresholds for each color band (R, G and B), the proper value of the tol variable and the optimal output thresholds of classification.

Another future work will be guided to evaluate the paths to turn our research into an open source software released under the GPL 3.0 license. Where small farmers or local entrepreneurs will have the freedom to change the software to suit new needs and the freedom to share it with neighbors to empower and increase the incomes of small communities and create new job opportunities with growth potential.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Natural Computing Research (IJNCR), 5(4); edited by Nilanjan Dey and Vikrant Bhateja, pages 24-44, copyright year 2015 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).

# Chapter 62

*   Jony Haryanto  
    President University, Indonesia
*   Luiz Moutinho  
    Dublin City University, Ireland

ABSTRACT

Chapter 5 explores the main features contributing towards the formation of living brand among children within the age 10 to 12-year-old by using a fuzzy logic analysis. From this methodological approach, several interesting insights emerge with regard to children’s consumer behaviour, especially the factors of future anticipation, ritual, and autobiographical memory in the priming of the development of a living brand. In this chapter, we are going to expand on the discussion by identifying the antecedents of a successful product using Indonesian market segment from the same age group as the research subjects in Chapter 6. Some of the important elements for success in the children’s segment that we identify here include brand personality, brand trust, and brand salience, particularly on how each of them affect brand relationship. When combined with autobiographical memory and buying habituation, this emotional bonding results in brand loyalty. Finally, we utilised a neural network topology in order to fully understand the antecedents of brand loyalty construction within the children’s market.

Box 1. Orienting questions

| • What are the antecedents of product success and longevity in children’s market segment?  
• How can neural network topology be utilised in order to fully comprehend the antecedents of brand loyalty construction within the children’s market?  
• What is the importance of brand relationship in the context of children?  
• How do brand personality, brand trust, and brand salience affect brand relationship?  
• Why and how should marketers involve children as their key information sources to anticipate their future needs? |
| --- |

INTRODUCTION

The importance of children’s market as a substantial opportunity for marketing research has been recognized by researchers from both developed and developing economies. In the U.S. alone, the market value for products and services aimed at the children’s market is estimated at USD 51.8 billion.

Children is still considered to have high purchasing power due to the support of parents and other relatives (e.g. the children pester power), although these children do not spend their own money. This becomes a notable characteristics of children market since the market is both large and highly susceptible to promotional messages (Yusuf, 2007). It also appears that when children are hooked to a particular brand or product, they develop an intense emotional attachment. This attachment leads to greater chance of securing customer loyalty. These children may undeniably become an ambassador as the persuade their friends of the value for such a brand/product. It means that the children then act as a promotional tool themselves.

There are three identified distinct segments within the children’s market, i.e., the primary market, the influence market, and the future market (McNeal, 1992). In the case of the primary market, children are targeted as end users; which makes its appeal to parents, people involved with children, and children themselves. On the contrary, the future market targets children as a potential market in a not so distant future.

In this chapter, we focus our study on children between 10 and 12 years old. This group of age is categorised as within school age (Erickson, 1950). During this stage of life, children are considered to be generally familiar with their social obligations and tend to behave properly. When this is seen from moral perspective, children are considered to have developed such maturity that enables them to distinguish between good and bad, and can recognise the differences among peoples and cultures.

Acuff and Reiher (1997) explained that children within this group of age are at the beginning of their brain neuron development. The consider that during this range of age is a crucial stage in the development of children’s capability to perceive their environment and to adjust their own thoughts and behaviour. This results in children’s ability to fit into an environment. Children, at this point, are prone to influence from role models such as teachers, parents, spiritual leaders, celebrities, and sporting figures. In other words, the children’s susceptibility also means they can be easily impressionable. At the same time, when the children asked simple questions, they are considered to be sufficiently mature to understand such questions, and able to give answers. It shows that they are capable of participating in a research.

Children in this group of age are able to remember previous events and to take their memories into adulthood (Acuff & Reiher, 1997), which suggests that marketers should create positive feelings towards their products if they seriously want to promote future loyal customers. Lindstorm and Seybold (2007) observed that since this particular behaviour of children occurs through a shift in the dominance of the right brain to the left brain, it makes them capable of reasoning, and can provide an explanation for all of their actions, good or bad. Consequently, similar to our approach in the previous chapter, the research sample for the study reported in this chapter are children within this age group of 10-12 years old.

This age group undoubtedly serves as a significant market segment and it is essential, therefore, to perform a research on children’s intention to buy, how they influence their parents, and the features that act as antecedents of long term memories. Marketing strategies adopted by service providers and other sources of appeal to children as customers are some other substantial dimensions. These are the areas of intelligence required to determine how brand loyalty is developed in the children’s market.

One of the characteristics of the children’s market is that some products demonstrate exceptional longevity; while others fall short in maintaining their successful venture, and despite the exorbitant advertising campaigns, they swiftly fall into oblivion. This is a clear sign of the underlying dynamics within this market, and raise the need for identifying the factors that enable products to sustain their popularity and to optimise their presence.

In this chapter, the antecedents of product success in the Indonesian children’s market segment are identified. A preliminary study was undertaken to explore the potential influences of such success and consequently, brand loyalty, adopting a qualitative methodology in the form of in-depth interviews with 12 children within the age range of 10 to 12-year-old. From this preliminary work, brand personality, brand trust, and brand salience emerged to be seen as important ingredients for success in the children’s segment. The reasons are these features create the desired emotional bonding between the child and the product. Further, when this emotional bonding is combined with autobiographical memory and habituation, it results in brand loyalty.

From this understanding, a neural network topology is then employed in this research to fully comprehend the antecedents of brand loyalty construction within the children’s market. Some interesting findings concerning the consumer behaviour of children are then produced through a computer modelling approach. It is identified that emotional authenticity, brand partnerships, brand relationship, brand salience, and brand personality all play key roles in generating brand loyalty.

Through these outcomes, it is hoped that the study in this chapter can contribute to the existing literature and appreciate the various inter-relating factors that are relevant for product longevity in the children’s market.

THEORETICAL BACKGROUND

Brand-Relationship in the Context of Children

The concept of brand relationship is concerned with the tenet that customers can relate to particular brands, and as such develop a liking or disliking for those brands (see for example, Fournier, 1998; Smit et al., 2008). This idea is important for organisations, especially when such relationships are established, certain benefits will ensue. These benefits include reduced marketing costs, improved ease of access, the acquisition of new customers, customer retention, brand equity and, ultimately, more profit (Blackston, 2000; Dowling, 2002; Reichheld, 1996; Winer, 2001).

Organisations need to ensure that their brand(s) have a strong personality, in their efforts to develop brand relationships. This is especially true in the case where children become their targets. Brand personality, essentially, refers to the relationship between the brand and the personality of the consumer (Rangkuti, 2004). Brand personality is less concerned with the nature of the product, but the way in which the customer’s personality influences his/her perception of the product. Additionally, in this interaction, the degree of satisfaction experienced by the customer operates as an antecedent of the strength of the consumer-brand relationship (Park & Lee, 2005).

Self-image is an important construct, since consumers are seen to demonstrate positive responses towards brands that apparently reflect their self-image (Chang et al., 2001; Yi & Law, 2002). The consonance between brand personality and self-image, therefore, promotes a positive orientation in those consumers who rate highly on hedonistic and symbolic values. Aaker et al. (2004) suggest that one reason for this outcome is that consumers are able to express themselves through the brand relationship personality.

Children, therefore, are clearly predisposed to those brands that suit their personalities, and that such predisposition nurtures a brand relationship between them and the brands. Further, a longitudinal research demonstrated that at least 23% of brands used in childhood carry through to adulthood, thereby supporting the notion that early childhood experiences have a definite impact upon later choices (Guest, 1944; 1964). Consequently, the following hypothesis is formulated:

*   H1: The stronger the brand personality, the stronger the child’s relationship with that brand.

| Figure 1. Conceptual framework |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch062.f01](i/ch062.f01.png) |
| --- |

Trust is an important component of brand relationship, and Moorman et al. (1992) defined it as a willingness to rely on an exchange partner with whom one has confidence. There are two underlying facts that shows the importance of trust, i.e., firstly, it has been conceptualised as a dimension of relationship quality, and secondly, it is considered as a determinant of relationship quality.

Chaudhuri and Holbrook (2001) contend that brand trust can be considered simply as the amount of trust that customers place in a particular product or service provider. It results from the degree of congruence between what customers expect and what they receive, and not surprisingly, it plays a vital part in establishing any relationship. Various scholars noted that trust is an antecedent of commitment in business-to-business relational exchanges (see for example, Moorman et al., 1992; Morgan & Hunt, 1994). Additionally, in their measurement of brand relationships, Smit and Toolbom (2007) considered trust as a crucial element. As a result, this chapter argue that brand trust contributes to the development of the consumer-brand relationship, in a way that the brands in which consumers place their trust are more frequently purchased than others. Thereby, it demonstrates a greater degree of brand relationship.

Children’s confidence in a brand, therefore, can be argued to breed positive orientations towards that brand. Further, those positive orientations underpin the development of a cordial brand relationship. Based on the given understanding, hypothesis 2 is formulated:

*   H2: The stronger the brand trust, the stronger the child’s relationship with that brand.

Although it may be true to say that what a person believes about a brand will influence the amount of thinking accorded to it, Miller and Berry (1998) observed that brand salience refers to the priority of a brand in the mind of the consumer. It is simply a ranking concept rather than one that embraces ideas held by the consumer about the brand. Brand salience, therefore, can refers to the prominence or level of activation of a brand in memory (Alba & Chattopadhyay, 1986). This is also similar to ‘top-of-mind awareness’ that essentially is estimated according to the ranking of the demonstrated brands (Johnstone and Dodd, 2000; Miller & Berry, 1998). Furthermore, the brand which competes on price is likely to appear top or high on the list of salience.

In this connection, Raggio and Leone (2007) identified that brand usage or purchase salience resulted in salience, and that usage produces positive markers which in themselves translate into more positive responses about brands. These responses can be seen in the amount of consideration given to a brand, in the amount of word-of-mouth recommendation, and in loyalty, attitude, and commitment. A high level of brand awareness and association, therefore, is likely to produce a high level of brand salience in the minds of consumers, and a high level of commitment. Hence, the greater the brand salience, the more that brand is purchased, and the greater the extent of the brand relationship developed.

In the specific case of children, Moore and Lutz (2000) established that children become committed to brands when the brand salience is strong, and consequently, children or their agents are loyal to them. This loyalty is reflected in the establishment of robust brand relationships, and consequently, hypothesis 3 is formulated as follows:

*   H3: The stronger the brand salience, the stronger the child’s relationship with that brand.

Buying Habituation in the Context of Children

Hoyer (1984) contend that buying habituation is a strategy that facilitates choices since it prompts the consumer to choose what has previously been purchased. This habitual behaviour, in fact, does not necessarily represent the outcome of a positive orientation towards a particular brand, but is rather a product of the selection process. Further, several researchers have observed that the experience of previous purchases underpins this selection procedure (see Deighton et al., 1994; Hoyer, 1984).

The separate studies of Chakravarti and Biehal (1990) and Oliver (1993), in this respect, demonstrated how previous experience was used as an evaluatory mechanism. From a positive brand assessment, it is undeniable that a commitment to continued use emerges (Nicholls & Cullen, 2003). Commitment, then, represents a lasting intention to sustain a valued relationship (Moorman et al., 1992), the existence of which prompts people to prolong their buying habits.

Consumer habits are those repeated habits in daily life, often with a degree of unconsciousness, which removes choice processes (see Deighton et al., 1994; Hoyer, 1984). A favourable assessment of a brand, therefore, will result in a positive commitment to it. This, in turn, will cause memory formation in children that predisposes them towards always purchasing that brand. It is the relationship between memory and action that leads to the habit formation (Ji & Wood, 2007; Robbins, 1997). From this discussion, the following hypothesis is created:

*   H4: The stronger the brand relationship, the stronger the child’s buying habituation towards that brand.

Autobiographical Memory in the Context of Children

Braun et al. (2002) noted that autobiographical memory is memory that has been stored as long-term memory and this memory has been developed from past experience. A distinction is made between autobiographical memory and long-term memory, where distinction depends upon the role of past experience in forming the memory. In relation to long-term memory, it is considered as a process of obtaining information and storing it over time, so the memory is available when needed (Solomon, 2007). In autobiographical memory, however, this is a process of remembering a particular occurrence with a certain image (Rubin, 2006), e.g., it might happen with a child recalling an event that occurred when eating at McDonald’s. When recalled, this event would be accompanied by the various associations of McDonald’s, for example, cheerfulness, or a relaxed atmosphere.

Researchers have indicated that a product is assessed according to previous use and performance (see Oliver, 1993; Dick et al., 1990), and in this evaluation, favourable outcomes lead to commitment and negative ones to a reluctance to re-purchase. A positive brand assessment clearly promotes a positive autobiographical memory in children (Rubin, 2006; Rubin & Bernstern, 2003), and this memory underpins the willingness to form a brand relationship. This in turn will feature within the child’s autobiographical memory.

Consequently, the chapter suggest that brand relationship contributes to the development of positive autobiographical memory. The trusted brands will be purchased more frequently, in so promoting habituation, and supporting the development of more positive autobiographical memories that are relate to the brands. The following hypotheses is, therefore, formulated:

*   H5: The stronger the brand relationship, the stronger the child’s autobiographical memory of that brand.
*   H6: The stronger the buying habituation, the stronger the child’s autobiographical memory of that brand.

Brand Loyalty in the Context of Children

Brand loyalty can also be considered as the degree of closeness felt by a consumer towards a brand (Aaker, 1997). An emotional relationship then develops, where the consumer experiences a sense of brand attachment. Mugge et al. (2008) suggest that product awareness can be seen in the amount of emotional bonding between the consumer and the product (triggered by the consumer’s experience of using it). Specifically, Mugge et al. (2008) demonstrate in their research that memories of the past influence the extent of satisfaction with the product. The same goes with Lynch et al. (1988) and Chakravarti and Biehal (1990) who conclude that customer choice is established on the evaluation of past experience.

Fournier (1998) has identified that enduring relationships can be formed by nostalgic means. In one case, due to the memory of having a mother who used a certain brand of perfume, a mature woman was observed to keep on using the same perfume although she hated it. The case shows that the woman had formed a ‘childhood friendship’ with the perfume, which is how early nostalgic memories are considered to form.

It can be asserted, therefore, that favourable circumstances help to create positive memories, and in turn foster children’s buying habits that continues into adulthood, where these historic memories influence how the brand involved is perceived (Rubin, 2006; Nicholls & Cullen, 2003). Children’s assessment of their purchases, then, represents the antecedents of their later loyalty, and their childhood consumer patterns. This is supported by Kurniawan and Haryanto (2011), who demonstrate how autobiographical memory and buying habituation affect children’s brand loyalty. The greater the satisfaction experienced, the greater the influence on the establishment of brand relationship and loyalty. Consequently, the following hypotheses are formulated:

*   H7: The stronger the buying habituation, the stronger the child’s brand loyalty.
*   H8: The stronger the brand relationship, the stronger the child’s brand loyalty.
*   H9: The stronger the autobiographical memory, the stronger the child’s brand loyalty.

METHODOLOGY

Data were gathered through a survey approach in several elementary schools in Jakarta (an urban area) and Salatiga (a rural area) in order to test the hypotheses. This research decided to test parts of the model before testing it as a whole due to the complexity of the relationships between the various constructs in the model. The research in this chapter undertook extensive qualitative research (focus group discussion \[FGD\] and in-depth interviews) with 12 children in Jakarta as an initial stage to validate the questionnaire and the construction of the model. This was done before the research since it was assumed that not only this strategy would generate the constructs familiar to the children, it would also assist in the formulation of new measures of the key emergent constructs, and in the refinement of existing ones.

Two children’s specialists and one child psychologist were consulted as professional experts to help in evaluating the questions, constructs, and the logic underpinning the questionnaire. The questions presented and the vocabulary used, therefore, were suitable for and comprehensible to the children in the sample. Furthermore, where existing scales were used, they were pre-tested to ensure the validity of any adaptation made.

Pre-Test Study

Survey data was gathered from a convenience sample of 30 elementary students in Salatiga and 30 elementary students in Jakarta for the pre-test study. The taken measures are related to McDonald’s, chosen as the proposed object due to children’s familiarity with McDonald’s is high compared to other fast food industries. McDonald’s also focuses on children, as it can be seen from the availability of play areas for children, the familiar character of Ronald McDonald, special gifts for children, and special products for children.

McDonald’s, in this context, is a bundle of products consisting of every offered facility and variance of the products. From the FGD (Focus Group Discussion), is identified that McDonald’s can create memory for children with certain circumstances, i.e. when children are highly involved with McDonald’s due to their strong preferences toward its products. This pre-test aimed to examine the planned scales used to test the model.

MEASUREMENT

In examining the children, a construct measurement using scales from Cook (2000) was adapted. The measures will use ’emotion pictures’ (Figure 2) with a four-point Likert scale (from strongly disagree to strongly agree), so the children find it easy to answer the questions for the empirical test. There are two sets of show cards, each to describe boys or girls.

These show cards were adapted from Cook (2000). The original cards consisted of seven points (strongly disagree, moderately disagree, disagree, neutral, agree, moderately agree, and strongly disagree). However, during the pre-study and FGD, the children could not differentiate between moderately agree and agree, or moderately disagree and disagree. That is why a four-point Likert scale is devised for this research.

Following Nunnally’s (1978) standard, the reliability of all scales was adequate based on the results of the pre-test. Also, from the pre-test respondents’ comments, some questions were paraphrased for the main study since they appeared to be problematic.

RELIABILITY MEASUREMENT TEST

Reliability is the extent of which the results of a measurement can be trusted or relied upon. A measuring instrument is considered reliable when the instrument can provide measurement results that match with what has been measured. The reliability of brand personality, brand trust, brand salience, brand relationship, autobiographical memory, buying habituation, and brand loyalty were measured using a Cronbach Alpha reliability formula. Reliability testing using Cronbach Alpha coefficients indicates how well the items used in the instrument positively correlate with one another (Sekaran, 2003).

*   • Brand Personality: Brand personality was measured based on Phau and Lau’s (2001) developed scale, used with some modifications. The six items used are those focused on the personality of the brand used in this study. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient is 0.807.
*   • Brand Trust: Brand trust was measured based on Riana’s (2008) developed scale. This scale composed of five items focusing on the degree of trust between customer and brand. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient is 0.799.
*   • Brand Salience: Brand salience was measured based on Suroija’s (2010) developed scale, used with some modifications for children to understand it better. The six items emphasized the level of activation of a brand in memory. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient is 0.723.
*   • Brand Relationship: Brand relationship was measured based on Aaker, Fournier, and Brasel’s (2004) developed scale, used with modifications. The five items used are those focusing on the relationship between brand and consumers. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient is 0.854.
*   • Autobiographical Memory: Autobiographical memory was measured based on Braun’s (1999) developed scale. The six items used are those focusing on the long term memory a consumer has with a specific brand. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient is 0.889.
*   • Buying Habituation: In measuring this variable, some adjustments were made in the scale developed by Kurniawan (2011). The five items focused on repeat purchases by consumers. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient is 0.847.
*   • Brand Loyalty: Brand loyalty was measured based on Ji & Wood’s (2007) developed scale, used with some modifications. The focus of the four items was on the commitment to re-buy a preferred brand. The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient is 0.888.

VALIDITY MEASUREMENT TEST

A validity test of an instrument means the extent to which the accuracy and precision of a measuring instrument can exactly measure the function. This research performed an item analysis to determine the quality of the items used. It was done to set as the benchmark to be measured from each scale. A validity test was done on listed items in the instrument. The purpose of the validity test was to find the items whose declared function was in accordance with the desired function in the study. An analysis of factors was performed in this research to test the validity.

Constructs Used in the Study

For this chapter, seven constructs were used in this study: brand personality, brand trust, brand salience, brand relationship, autobiographical memory, buying habituation, and brand loyalty. Each construct had 5 indicators respectively.

Artificial Neural Networks

Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are named based on their attempt to reflect the nerve cells networks inside the human brain (Haykin, 2008). Kohonen (1988) concurs that the ANNs consist of an interconnected number of simple units, also called neurons, cells or nodes, intended to interact with the real world objects of in the same way as biological systems. The ANNs reproduce the network of neurons that carry out the lower level computational actions against the high level cognitive operations in the human brain. ANNs, more specifically, are pattern recognition algorithms that capture prominent features from a set of inputs and map them to outputs (Bishop, 1995; Swingler, 1996).

Neural networks do not require a knowledge base to be constructed, nor they need an explicit inference procedure to be developed and subsequently encoded. A neuron executes two operations on the receiving values: the first is the combination function that consists of summing its inputs weighted by the correspondent links of the neuron. The second applies a function to the value obtained in the former operation and produces the output of the neuron, designated by the activation function. The activation function or sometimes called the squashing function, as it limits the amplitude range of the output signal to some finite value, can be classified into three groups: Threshold, Piecewise-linear, and Sigmoid (S-shaped) function.

For the study in this chapter, the sigmoid function is used because it is by far the most common form of activation function implemented in the construction of a neural network (De Tienne et al., 2003) and it is a bounded non-decreasing and non-linear function that exhibits smoothness and asymptotic properties. This function, in particular, is able to find patterns of non-linearity that cannot be modelled by linear statistics such as regression analysis (De Tienne et al., 2003). When compared to regression models, ANNs are much better for dealing with the modelling of non-linear relationships. The comparison between ANNs and regression models depends on the nature of the modelling approaches in terms of prediction and classification. For example, un-nested regression models can be outperformed by neural networks. On the other hand, nested generalized linear models (GLMs) can sometimes perform very well when compared with a more complex ANN topology, depending on the type of response variable (e.g. multinomial logit, proportional odds).

An artificial neural network is usually composed of an input layer, used to represent the independent variables in the study, hidden layer(s), and an output layer used to represent the dependent variables. Each layer comprises a predetermined number of neurons, which generally define the topology of a neural network. The mapping, however, occurs in the intermediary layers (hidden layers) where the number of neurons is unrestricted (DeTiene et al., 2003; Somers and Casal, 2009). These interior layers of neurons are not directly observable from the inputs and outputs system. Each hidden layer neuron is connected to each input layer node and each output layer neuron, with the network neurons evaluate the values for each computing unit as a weighted sum of the neurons in the preceding layer, according to the connection weights. In this architecture, the Neural Networks are generally denominated by feedforward networks. Figure 3 illustrates the topology of this neural network.

| Figure 3. A feedforward network with one hidden layer |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch062.f03](i/ch062.f03.png) |
| --- |

Further, the network is able to extract high-order statistics, with the addition of hidden layers, as it acquires a global perspective despite the extra set of links and the extra dimension of neural interactions. Previous researches have also showed that feedforward networks using arbitrary activation functions are universal approximators (see Stinchcombe & White, 1989; Hornik et al., 1989). In an organisational context, hidden layer neurons can be regarded as latent or unobservable variables and the neural network can be used comprehend these variables through their links, identifying communal behaviours or feelings that cannot directly be measured. Then, the hidden layer neurons can be labelled by considering the weights of the connections from the input nodes feed into the neurons (Moutinho et al., 1996).

Learning algorithm – or the method of modifying its weights – is another important definition in the specification of an ANN. It is paramount to point out that neural networks only require a minimum understanding of the problem’s structure. Prior knowledge of the statistical distribution of the data is not required because the network develops an internal relationship between the variables. Neural networks, therefore, are particularly suitable for complex classification problems in which the mapping rationale is either fuzzy, inconsistent, or completely unknown. The majority of business and marketing applications can be considered as fuzzy classifications, and this is the area where neural networks can be of service. More importantly, the most common learning algorithm for feedforward networks is the backpropagation (BP) algorithm.

One of the common complaints about BP, however, is that when dealing with complex problems it can run considerably slow. To overcome this difficulty, a number of BP variations have been proposed to accelerate its speed of convergence, and also to improve the capacity of the resultant network to be generalized. In addition, a new neural network architecture, called a multiple feedforward (MFF) network, and a new gradient-based method, the multiple back-propagation (MBP) have been developed by Lopes and Ribeiro (2003).

Multiple Feedforward Networks

MFF networks are obtained by integrating two feedforward networks. The main network has selective neurons and its activation role is detained through space localization of input pattern data. In this sense, only the neurons fired by a particular data point become relevant while retaining the capacity to approximate closely, more general, non-linear features in localized regions. The other is space network, which is responsible for determining the importance factor of the main network neurons to the extent that each pattern is presented to the MFF network.

THE USE OF ANNs IN MARKETING AND CONSUMER BEHAVIOUR

Although several fields of study have used neural networks for many years in, their use is a fairly recent development in the business world. As researchers realize their flexibility and the wide range of problems for which they can be used, applications are increasingly appearing. Artificial neural networks have also been applied to numerous marketing problems including modelling consumer responses to market stimuli (Curry & Moutinho, 1993), evaluating the effect of gender on car buyer satisfaction and loyalty (Moutinho et al., 1996), predicting consumer choice (West et al., 1997), new product development (Thieme et al., 2000), marketing strategy (Li, 2000), sales forecasting (Kuo, 2001), market segmentation (see Boone & Roehm, 2002a, 2002b; Philips et al., 2001; Davies et al., 1996a), target marketing (Zahavi & Levin, 1995) and modelling the effect of market orientation on firm performance (Silva et al., 2009). Various researchers have also applied NN in other marketing problems including consumer behaviour.

Customer requirements, elicitation, and evaluation have held a crucial position in the early stage of product conceptualisation with the increasing interest and emphasis on customer demands in new product development. It is highly desirable, therefore, to devise a systematic strategy for soliciting customer requirements effectively, and, subsequently, analysing customer orientations quantitatively. Chen et al., (2002) proposed and investigated a customer-oriented approach with this objective. Further, to enable customer requirements elicitation, the laddering technique has been employed.

In addition, the adaptive resonance theory, particularly the ART2 neural network, has been applied as a toolkit for further customer and marketing analysis. Davies et al. (1996b), on the other hand, employed a neural network model to analyse how customers develop positive or negative attitudes towards bank automatic teller machines (ATMs): different consumer groups are expected to show different expectations of this service so that a clustering strategy should be beneficial for the bank.

Davies et al. (2001) present another study that is worthy of discussion. The authors applied the same statistical approach to look into the decisive factors in consumer supermarket shopping behaviour. Kuo et al., (2002) have also integrated a self-organizing feature map and a K-means algorithm providing a more sophisticated way to analyse consumer behaviour. Meanwhile, Gan et al. (2005) used the probability neural network, a special class of neural networks, a multiple feedforward network, and a logistic model to analyse the major factors that influence consumers’ choices between using electronic banking or non-electronic banking.

Moreover, their investigation allowed them to conclude that both ANN models display a higher overall percentage of correct consumer choice predictions than the logistic model. Hu and Tsoukalas (2003) used neural network models and the ensemble technique of stacked generalization to investigate the relative importance of situational and demographic factors on consumer choice instead. Further, Chiang et al. (2006) offered another study to predict and explain patronage behaviour towards the Web and traditional stores using neural networks.

In addition, Athappilly et al. (2010) employed three data mining techniques: cluster analysis, neural network, and market basket analysis methods, with the purpose of understanding consumers’ buying patterns and behaviours. This multi-technique approach provides a comparative analysis between sales of infant items at baby centres and non-baby centres. It also helps understand the buying patterns at these centres, and analyses items most frequently purchased together by consumers.

The rapid development of Internet usage has paved the way for the use of online shopping. In this sense, Majhi et al. (2010) investigated the behaviour of Indian consumers towards online shopping using a functional link of artificial neural network. The result is then compared with that obtained from the discriminant analysis. The simulation study reveals that the first model provides better classification of consumers compared to other approaches.

Despite of the growing interest in applying artificial neural networks to explain consumer behaviour and to model the consumer decision-making process, this modelling approach is still unknown in children’s consumer behaviour.

THE NEURAL NETWORK APPROACH

Due to the purpose of the study in this chapter, the analysis of the principal factors that influence the success of products in the children’s market segment in Indonesia within the age group of 10-12, several multiple feedforward network architectures were implemented and trained with the MBP algorithm, online mode. As explained earlier, one advantage of neural network (NN) models is their ability to serve as ‘universal approximators’. Additionally, the use for NNs in several other reasons was decided. First, the input data was judgmental rather than factual, so there was some ‘fuzziness’ in the data - the numbers used in the analysis were indicators of feelings or perceptions rather than exact observed values. Looking for overall patterns in the data becomes more important than making effort to formulate equations that relate inputs to output.

Second, a high degree of correlation existed between the different inputs. Although the performance of a neural network or the validity of its results is not affected, a special consideration when a multivariate analysis is being conducted is still needed. Finally, the use of a neural network allows the labelling of hidden layer neurons (Davies et al., 1996a; Mitchell et al., 1999) – thus, clusters of factors contributing to each hidden neuron can be examined to see whether they indicate an underlying management philosophy that would otherwise impact on brand loyalty either positively or negatively.

The data set comprised 230 examples and was divided into training and test subsets. Training data were employed to estimate weights used by the neural network to subsequently generate predicted outcomes. The presentation of the training patterns was random. Test data represented a holdout sample. Weights derived from training were applied to test validity and the predictions compared to known outputs, and a significant decrease in performance indicated that the network was over-trained and uncovered patterns unique to the data set (Bishop, 1995). The training data included 161 cases or 70% of the sample, where the remaining 69 were used for the test set. provided the best fit between inputs and outputs, A multiple feedforward network with one hidden layer of three neurons was then identified; this was thought to be a reasonable number of intermediate variables that could be identified and labelled, and the network did not significantly give better results by increasing the number.

It has been mentioned that the activation function used for the hidden and output neurons of the main and space networks was the logistic function. The main network had six input nodes corresponding to the following explanatory variables: Brand Personality (BP), Brand Trust (BT), Brand Salience (BS), Brand Relationship (BR), Autobiographical Memory (AM), and Buying Habituation (BH). The output node corresponded to brand loyalty (BL). The space network had only one layer responsible to determine the relevance of the selective neurons placed in the hidden layer of the main network.
