PARKINSON’S DISEASE DIAGNOSIS SYSTEM IMPLEMENTATION AND EVALUTION

Server component of Parkinson’s disease diagnosis system is implemented in Java which is a robust, secure, object-oriented, multi-threaded programming language. Inference engine of the system is developed (using ANN feed forward back propagation algorithm), trained, tested and validated in MATLAB (version 7.8.0 R2009a) which is a high-level language and provides an interactive, synergistic environment for numerical computation, programming and visualization.

Inference engine’s working is based on gait data of the subjects which are extracted going through sequential stages of video processing, image processing and segmentation. For training of inference engine of the system three data sets GA-dataset, Ju-dataset, Si-dataset have been used which are collected by Yogev et al. (2005), Hausdorff et al.(2007), Frenkel-Toledo et al. (2005a, 2005b) respectively keeping data sampling rate 100 Hz. A mixed dataset is also prepared which consists gait data of 71 normal person (mean age 66.3 years, 55% male) and 103 PwP (mean age 66.3 years, 63% male).

ANN feed forward back propagation algorithm is used to train the inference engine which is a supervised learning method, so, training data set requires both input data set and corresponding target data set to train the system.

*   • Input Set: It is an nX19 matrix, where, n is a number of subjects including both PwP and normal/healthy persons, 19 is number of gait features (as specified in Table 1) extracted from each of these subjects.
*   • Target Set: It is an nX1 matrix and consists either 0 or 1, where, 0 denotes PwP, 1 denotes normal/healthy person.

Table 1. Extracted gait features about a person

| Column No. || Attribute |
| --- | --- |
| 1 || Time in seconds |
| --- | --- |
| 2-9 || Vertical Ground Reaction Force (in Newton) on each of 8 sensors located under the left foot |
| 10-17 || Vertical Ground Reaction Force (in Newton) on each of 8 sensors located under the right foot |
| 18 || Total force under the left foot |
| 19 || Total force under the right foot |

Feature Vector Optimization using Genetic Algorithm (GA)

Training of the neural network (used in inference engine of the system) with large feature vector may consume more time and can make the system inefficient. In order to reduce processing time and make the system more efficient keeping recognition accuracy at acceptable range it is required to optimize (reduce) feature vector to have prominent features only. In current research work feature vector of size 19 is reduced to optimized feature vector of size 10 using GA.

Training, Testing, and Validation

Pattern recognition is a way of spotting a pattern in the stored information so as to predict the future event based on the current and past available information. For it, first of all a feed forward neural network is generated as per specifications stated in Table 2.

Table 2. Neural network parameters used for training

| Factor || Value |
| --- | --- |
| Number of Input Neurons || 15 |
| --- | --- |
| Number of Hidden Layers || 1 |
| Initial Weights and Bias Term values || Randomly generated values between 0 and 1 |
| Training Function || Trainlm |
| Transfer Function in Hidden Layer || Tansig |
| Transfer Function in Output Layer || Purelin |
| Mean Square Error (MSE) || 0.01 |

Now, in order to train, test, validate the neural network complete data-set is divided into three sub-sets named training, testing and validation sub-sets as below:

*   • Training Data Subset: It is used mainly for training the neural network and ultimately adjusting the weights and biases of the neural network in such a way that output error gets minimized. This data subset consists of large portion (70%) of total data in order to train the network in best possible way and minimize output error.
*   • Testing Data Subset: It is used to check the final solution in order to confirm the predictive power of the neural network and make sure the neural network model is fit to detect Parkinson’s disease. 20% of total data set is used for testing the neural network.
*   • Validation Data Subset: It is used to validate the neural network against new (unexposed) independent data set. It helps to overcome/minimize the problem of over fitting in the neural network. The network is called over fitting if the accuracy over the training data subset increases, but, the accuracy of validation data subset remains same. Over fitting is very dangerous because it can lead to prediction which is far beyond the range of the training data with much common type of NNs. 10% of total data set is used for validating the neural network.

Confusion Matrix

Pattern classification tool is used to find out how many of data are correctly detected and how many are not in given dataset and confusion matrix is prepared which includes value of important parameters like True Positive (TP), True Negative (TN), False Positive (FP) and False Negative (FN). TP decision occurs when a Parkinson’s disease patient detection of the classifier coincides with a decision of the physician. TN decision occurs when both the classifier and the physician suggests the absence of Parkinson disease. FP occurs when the system diagnoses a normal person as a diseased one. Finally, FN occurs when the system diagnoses a diseased person as a normal. Confusion matrix for the mixed dataset with 10 features is specified in Table 4.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

Currently proposed system based on ANN for Parkinson’s disease diagnosis yields classification accuracy of 97.11% using 19 features of gait, and 95.55% using optimized feature vector having 10 features of gait obtained using GA. In future, the system can be further enhanced by:

*   • Identification of better supervised algorithm which can reduce diagnosis time while maintaining the classification accuracy in acceptable range.
*   • Integration with video and image processing tools, so that, based on gait video input of the person, the disease can be diagnosed directly.
*   • Increasing size of gait dataset covering more cases of Parkinson’s disease and use it to train the inference engine of the system to obtain better classification accuracy.
*   • Identification of better feature vector optimization technique to reduce count of features used in Parkinson’s disease diagnosis, while, maintaining the system classification accuracy in acceptable range.
*   • Developing robust mobile application which can capture gait of the person in home environment, de-noise it and extract features needed for Parkinson’s disease diagnosis.

CONCLUSION

Parkinson’s disease is a very common disease among elder population worldwide which reduces quality of life due to motor and non-motor complications. The cost of illness rises as the disease progresses; the largest share of the cost comes from inpatient care, while, the share of medication cost is substantially lower. The proposed system based on ANN can be used for diagnosis of the disease using person’s gait features, and thereafter management of the disease can be started appropriately. The system is trained, tested and validated by gait dataset retrieved from Parkinson’s disease patients and healthy persons. For the proposed system classification accuracy is observed 97.11% using 19 features of gait, and 95.55% using optimized feature vector having 10 features of gait obtained using GA. Finally a client-server architecture based pervasive automated Parkinson’s disease diagnosis system is implemented which can be accessed through web browsers and mobile android applications.

This research was previously published in Optimizing Assistive Technologies for Aging Populations edited by Yosry S. Morsi; Anupam Shukla; and Chandra Prakash Rathore, pages 357-377, copyright year 2016 by Medical Information Science Reference (an imprint of IGI Global).

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Artificial Neuron: It is a mathematical function conceived as a model of biological neuron and used as a constitutive unit in an artificial neural network.

Basal Ganglia: Basal ganglia comprises multiple subcortical nuclei, of varied origin, in the brains of vertebrates, which are situated at the base of the forebrain. Basal ganglia are strongly interconnected with the cerebral cortex, thalamus, and brainstem, as well as several other brain areas.

Chromosome: In genetic algorithm, a chromosome is a set of parameters which defines a proposed solution to the problem that the genetic algorithm is trying to solve.

Dopamine: It is primary chemical messenger of the basal ganglia.

Freezing of Gait: It occurs in Parkinson’s disease when a person’s feet become suddenly ‘frozen’ while walking or turning.

Gait: It is pattern of movement of the limbs in humans.

Supervised Learning: It is a machine learning task of inferring a function from labeled training data. In supervised learning, training data is fed in a pair of input values and corresponding target values.

ABSTRACT

Type-One Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) is a chronic disease characterized by the elevation of glucose levels within patient’s blood. It can lead to serious complications including kidney and heart diseases, stroke, and blindness. The proper treatment of diabetes, on the other hand, can lead to a normal longevity. Yet such a treatment requires tight glycemic control which increases the risk of developing hypoglycemia; a sudden drop in patients’ blood glucose levels that could lead to coma and possibly death. Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) devices placed on a patient body, measure glucose levels every few minutes. These devices can also detect hypoglycemia. Yet detecting hypoglycemia sometimes is too late for a patient to take proper action, so a better approach is to predict the hypoglycemic events ahead of time and alarm the patient to such occurrences. In this research, the authors develop a system that involves a special type of Artificial Neural Networks (ANN), the Time-Sensitive ANN (TS-ANN), to predict hypoglycemia events ahead of time and within a prediction horizon of thirty minutes. This period should be long enough to enable diabetic patients to avoid hypoglycemia by taking a proper action. A TS-ANN based system that is able to predict hypoglycemia events have been developed and tested with high accuracy results (average specificity of 98.2%, average accuracy of 97.6% and average sensitivity of 80.19% with a maximum value reaching 93%).

1\. INTRODUCTION

Type-One Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) is a chronic disease characterized by the elevation of glucose levels within patient’s blood. Controlling the blood glucose level in diabetic patients and keeping it within the normal range is the biggest challenge facing physicians nowadays (Wach, Trajanoski, Kotanko, & Skrabal, 1995). The improper control of diabetes can lead to many serious complications, including blindness, renal failure and foot disorders to name a few (BOUNDLESS, 2014; Gibbons, & Shaw, 2012). Nevertheless, tighter glycemic control increases the risk of patients experiencing acute hypoglycemia (Bergenstal et al., 2010). Hypoglycemia is a condition that occurs when blood glucose drops dangerously low. This leads to starving the brain -from glucose- which may result in coma and possibly death (Cryer, 2007). Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) concluded in (Diabetes Control and Complications Trial Research Group, 1993) that the occurrence of hypoglycemia is three times higher in intensively treated group of diabetic patients over those of the group receiving standard treatment (Dassau, et al., 2010). For intensive treatment of diabetes, Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM) devices are used. These devices are placed on patient body and measure glucose levels every few minutes. The development of CGM devices is considered a breakthrough in diabetes treatment and management field, due to the wealth of useful information they supply to the diabetic patients and their doctors (Georga, Fotiadis, & Protopappas, 2011).

During the last decade there has been an explosion of interest in medical machine learning, due to the trillions of data elements collected from patients and stored in databases, yet not being effectively utilized (Canlas, 2009). Moreover, machine learning techniques proved their effectiveness in many fields including medicine (Barakat, & Bradley, 2010; Canlas, 2009; Patil & Kumaraswamy, 2009). The study presented in this paper aims at developing a machine learning based system suitable for predicting future occurrence of hypoglycemic events within a prediction horizon of thirty minutes. The prediction is carried out using the recent history of CGM subcutaneous glucose measurements, simulated rate of appearance of glucose in plasma following a meal intake, and simulated plasma insulin after administering subcutaneously infused insulin. Our study, presented in this paper, follows the case study technique, namely, the study starts with collecting data from Type-1 diabetic patients, analyzing the data, and then generating the results (highly accurate prediction of future hypoglycemic events).

In this paper, section II reviews recent research on glucose and hypoglycemia predictions in Type-1 diabetic patients. Section III, on the other hand, presents some background information about machine-learning and in specific Artificial Neural Networks and their use as predictors. Section IV describes our proposed prediction system. Section V discusses the results obtained from applying such a model to a group of type-1 diabetic patients, and finally, section VI presents some concluding remarks.

2\. STATE OF THE ART IN GLOCUSE AND HYPOGLYCEMIA PREDICTION

During the last decade, plenty of research efforts went into developing machine learning algorithms suitable for predicting events in the healthcare field. Two types of research can be identified, namely, blood glucose predication and hypoglycemic events predication. Both of these research types are presented next.

Table 1. A sample of blood glucose prediction studies using machine learning techniques

| Study Reference || Year || Number of Involved Patients || Input Variables || Machine Learning Method || Performance RMSE |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Georga, Fotiadis, & Protopappas, 2011 || 2011 || 7 || CGM data, insulin, carbohydrate || SVR || 16.02 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pérez-Gandía, et al., 2010 || 2010 || 9 || CGM data || ANN || 17.45 for group I |
| Pappada, Cameron, & Rosman || 2008 || 18 || CGM data, insulin, carbohydrate and others || ANN || Varied results |

2.1. Blood Glucose Level Prediction Techniques

Many research efforts went into blood glucose level prediction using machine learning techniques (Georga, Fotiadis, & Protopappas, 2011; Pérez-Gandía, et al., 2010; Bellazzi, & Abu-Hanna, 2009; Pappada, S.M., Cameron, B., Rosman, P., 2008; Yamaguchi, Kaseda, Yamazaki, & Kobayashi, 2006), a sample of which is summarized in Table 1. Most of this research has been able to design precise predictors in the euglycemic/normal range (70 mg/dl -120 mg/dl) but not as precise when forecasting the glucose levels in the hypo- (< 70 mg/dl) and hyperglycemic (> 120 mg/dl) ranges (Pappada, Cameron, & Rosman, 2008). The study presented in (Georga, Fotiadis, & Protopappas, 2011) used both mathematical models along with a machine learning ones, namely, the Support Vector Machines for Regression (SVR) to predict the blood glucose levels. They simulated three compartmental models that are already available in literature. Firstly, a meal model which simulates the consumption and absorption of carbohydrates by the human body (Lehmann, & Deutsch, 1992). Secondly, the insulin model that simulates the absorption and the pharmacokinetics / pharmacodynamics of subcutaneously administered insulin (Tarin, Teufel, Picó, Bondia, & Pfleiderer, 2005). Finally, the exercise model which simulate the impact of exercising on glucose – insulin metabolism. The dataset used in (Georga, Fotiadis, & Protopappas, 2011) is composed of seven diabetic patients who used Guardian Real-Time CGM device (Mastrototaro, Shin, Marcus, & Sulur, 2008) to measure subcutaneous glucose concentrations continuously. The glucose Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), which measures the difference between the predicted and actual values of a series, for prediction horizons of 30 and 60 minutes were 16.02, and 24.85, respectively.

Another study, conducted by (Pérez-Gandía, C. et al., 2010), uses an Artificial Neural Network (ANN) for predicting the subcutaneous glucose concentrations. The inputs to the ANN are the preceding subcutaneous glucose concentrations obtained from CGM device during the last 20 minutes. Their dataset consists of 9 subjects who used the Medtronic Guardian (Mastrototaro, Shin, Marcus, &Sulur, 2008) and 6 subjects that used the Abbott Navigator (Weinstein, et al., 2007). Regarding the structure of ANN, it is composed of two hidden layers with the first hidden layer of 10 neurons and a second layer of 5 neurons; the transfer function in both layers is sigmoidal. The output layer has one neuron with linear transfer function. The ANN was trained using back-propagation Levenberg-Marquardt optimization training algorithm (Yu, &Wilamowski, 2011). The RMSE results for group I are 17.45, and 25.08 for the prediction horizon of 30, and 45 minutes, respectively. The RMSE results for group II, on the other hand, are 19.51, and 29.07 for the same prediction horizons of 30 and 45 minutes, respectively.

A third study reported in (Pappada, Cameron & Rosman, 2008) has investigated the development of Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) suitable for predicting subcutaneous glucose levels within prediction windows of 50, 75, 100, 120, 150 and 180 minutes. The inputs to the ANNs are the preceding subcutaneous glucose values obtained from CGM device readings, insulin dosages, meals intake and a multitude of other factors. Their dataset consists of 18 subjects. An electronic diary has also been implemented and used by these subjects in collecting the needed information. As a result, this study concluded that the developed neural network models performs adequately when predicting blood glucose in the normal (> 70 mg/dl and < 180) and above normal (>= 180 mg/dl) ranges, however, predicting glucose levels in the hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dl) range was found to be inadequate since the developed ANNs tends to overestimate such a prediction.

2.2. Hypoglycemia Prediction Techniques

Smaller amount of research went into developing hypoglycemia prediction techniques. These techniques can be grouped into two types. The first group uses mathematical models for prediction, whereas, the second group uses pure data driven models to predict hypoglycemic events using input-output data. Our proposed system, to be presented in section IV, combines both of these techniques to predict hypoglycemic events in diabetic patients.

The study presented in (Zhang, 2008) is an example of a pure data-driven model’s development to predict hypoglycemia. It uses a classification tree technique to predict hypoglycemia within a prediction horizon of one hour. The used dataset is extracted from the Multi-Parameter Intelligent Monitoring in Intensive Care (MIMIC II) database which stores the blood glucose measurements of Intensive Care Unit (ICU) patients measured each one hour for patients under intravenous (IV) insulin infusion. Data is collected from 3116 ICU patients (MIMIC database II, 2014, August). A classification tree was built using See5tool set (“Data Mining Tools See5.”, August 29, 2014) to predict future hypoglycemic events. The classifier input features were the glucose measurement along with insulin infusion rate in a time series. The output class was “1” for experiencing hypoglycemia within the next hour, “0” otherwise. For evaluation, 70% of data records were used for training the classification tree, the rest (30%) were used for evaluation. The classification tree accuracy for predicting hypoglycemia was 86% and specificity was 89.87%.

3\. BACKGROUND

3.1. Artificial Neural Networks

Artificial neural networks (ANNs) represent a type of machine learning structures that are inspired by the way human brain performs computations. Neural networks are good at fitting non-linear functions and recognizing patterns (Hagan, Demuth, Beale, & De Jesús, 1996). ANN consists of interconnected group of artificial neurons that use a computational model for information processing based on a connectionist approach to computation (Melin, & Pedrycz (Eds.), 2009). The structure of the neuron is defined by the number of its inputs, and the transfer function used. During the training process weights and biases of the neurons are adjusted to give the most accurate output. Neural networks are organized in a single or multi-layer of interconnected neurons. A given neural network is defined by the number of its layers, number of neurons per layer and the type of connections between them. MATLAB Neural Network Toolbox (“Neural Network toolbox documentation”, August, 29, 2014) that contains several neural network architectures, multiple training algorithms, and various transfer functions, is used as an important component of our proposed hypoglycemia prediction system to be presented in section IV of this paper.

3.2. Performance Measures: Root Mean Squared Error, Sensitivity, Specificity, and Accuracy

3.2.1. Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)

RMSE is a measure pertains to numeric/series prediction situations. It's the averaged squared error between the actual values of a series and its predicted ones. The error has the same dimensionality as the quantity being predicted. Equation 1 shows the way to calculate such a measure,

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m01](i/ch069.m01.svg) (1)

where p1, p2, …, pn are the predicted values on the test instances; the actual values are a1, a2, …, an, and n is the number of test instances.

3.2.2. Sensitivity, Specificity, and Accuracy

Sensitivity, specificity and accuracy are statistical measures of binary classification performance. Sensitivity measures the percentage of hypoglycemic events that are correctly classified. In contrast, specificity refers to the proportion of non-hypoglycemic events that are predicted as such. Accuracy is the proportion of the testing set examples that is correctly classified by the model. These measures can be calculated using the following formulas,

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m02](i/ch069.m02.svg) (2)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m03](i/ch069.m03.svg) (3)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m04](i/ch069.m04.svg) (4)

where, the true positive (TP) and true negative (TN) are the number of instances with correct classifications. Specifically, TP refers to the number of instances that were predicted as hypoglycemia, when they are as such. Likewise, TN represents the number of instances that were predicted as non-hypoglycemic when they are as such. A false positive (FP) is when the outcome is incorrectly predicted as positive (hypoglycemia) when it is actually negative (non-hypoglycemia). On the contrary, false negative (FN) is when the outcome is incorrectly predicted as negative (non-hypoglycemia) when it is actually positive (hypoglycemia); thus decreasing FN is the focal goal in this study. 4\. THE PROPOSED HYPOGLYCIMIA PREDECTION SYSTEM

Figure 2 presents a proposed system suitable for predicting hypoglycemic events. Such a prediction is divided into two steps; during the first step, a Time-Sensitive Artificial Neural Net (TS-ANN) is utilized to predict subcutaneous glucose measurements at several points in the future. Then during the second step, these values are used to predict the occurrence of hypoglycemia events within the given prediction horizon. The inputs to TS-ANN, as shown in Figure 2, are the subcutaneous glucose measurements, insulin, and carbohydrate intake. The effect of these input variables on the accuracy of the developed hypoglycemia prediction method is investigated later in this paper.

| Figure 2. A system for predicting hypoglycemic events |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.f02](i/ch069.f02.png) |
| --- |

Two mathematical models, the meal and insulin ones shown in Figure 2, developed and implemented in literature, are used to compute “the rate of appearance of glucose in plasma after a meal (Ra)”, and “plasma insulin concentration (Pin),” respectively. Thus the input to the predictive (TS-ANN) model is Ra, Pin, as well as the current and past subcutaneous glucose measurements. The output generated by TS-ANN predictive model is the future 6 subcutaneous glucose measurements (glucose[t+1], glucose[t+2] … glucose[t+6]), generated once each 5 minutes. A comparator (<=) block, as shown in Figure 2, is used to compare the predicted subcutaneous glucose measurement with the hypoglycemia threshold (60 mg/dl). If the value is below the hypoglycemia threshold, one is stored in the corresponding cell of the output array, zero otherwise. The values of the array cells are ORed using the binary OR function, thus at least one occurrence of a hypoglycemia event within the prediction horizon will result in Hypo output equals to one. Figure 3 illustrates the preprocessing stage for subcutaneous glucose input, as well as the corresponding Hypo output. In this figure, the horizontal line crossing the figure at 60 mg/dl represents the hypoglycemia threshold. Any glucose value below this line corresponds to a hypoglycemic event, and is represented by 1 in the corresponding ORed cells. On the other hand, the 0 value represents non-hypoglycemic event with a glucose values above the line. A sliding window, the prediction horizon, of size 30 minutes is used to calculate the occurrence/non-occurrence of a hypoglycemia event within such a window, as shown in Figure 3.

4.1. The Meal Mathematical Model

The amount and time of carbohydrates (Carb) in a patient’s meal is logged in the file of that patient; mainly there are three meals a day yet the snacks between the meals are also recorded. A Meal model is used to describe the ingestion and absorption of carbohydrate intakes. The model, developed by Lehmann and Deutch (Lehmann, E. & Deutsch, 1992), is used in this paper for that purpose. Specifically, the Meal model calculates the “rate of appearance of glucose in plasma” (Gin) assuming that the rate of gastric emptying, Gempt (mmol/hr), is a trapezoidal function. In this paper, we reproduced the equations of (Lehmann, & Deutsch, 1992), to calculate the input Ra of the predictive model of Figure 2.

Using equations 5, Gempt(t) calculates the Carb (in millimoles) of carbohydrate in a meal greater than Carbcrit.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m06](i/ch069.m06.svg) (6)

Tasc and Tdesc are the duration time of ascending and descending of Gemp curve where the default value for Tasc, and Tdesc is 0.5 hr (30 min) for both of these parameters. However, for Carb value below critical level Carbcrit, Tasc and Tdesc are defined as follows:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m07](i/ch069.m07.svg) (7)

where Carb[crit] is calculated using equation 8 presented next.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m08](i/ch069.m08.svg) (8)

4.2. The Insulin Mathematical Model

The insulin model is used to simulate the subcutaneous absorption and the pharmacokinetics / pharmacodynamics of insulin following subcutaneous injections; moreover, it describes how insulin enters plasma after absorption. In literature, models for two types of insulin were developed, namely, Soluble (regular, hexameric) insulin and Rapid-acting insulin analogs (monomeric insulin). Most research efforts went towards modeling soluble insulin; however, few researchers analyzed the novel monomeric insulin that is administered through the CGM pump; our focus in this study. The developed insulin models are used to quantify two processes, namely, the absorption of insulin, and the transportation of the insulin to plasma after subcutaneous injection. The different available models vary mainly in the first process, where plasma insulin is assumed to be single compartment in all developed models. As mentioned earlier most of the developed models are suited for soluble insulin, contrariwise two researches mainly analyzed monomeric insulin (Shimoda, et al., 1997; Wach, Trajanoski, Kotanko, & Skrabal, 1995). We have used the proposed model of (Wach, Trajanoski, Kotanko, & Skrabal, 1995) to simulate the plasma insulin after subcutaneous insulin injections. The research reported in (Wach, Trajanoski, Kotanko, &Skrabal, 1995) has simplified the proposed model of (Mosekilde, Jensen, Binder, Pramming, &Thorsteinsson, 1989) for subcutaneous insulin absorption, and estimated the models' parameter values.

*   •
    
    Subcutaneous Insulin Absorption: According to the model proposed by (Wach, Trajanoski, Kotanko, & Skrabal, 1995), the subcutaneous absorption of insulin analogues in spherical coordinates can be calculated using the partial differential equation 11.
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m11](i/ch069.m11.svg) (11)
    

where m is the monomeric insulin dose, D is diffusion constant, and B is the absorption rate constant. Equation (11) is solved numerically, by spatial discretization of subcutaneous region into fifteen spherical shells, where the center of these shells is the injection point. Constant insulin fluxes between two consecutive shells are assumed.

*   •
    
    Plasma Insulin: Subcutaneous insulin, after its absorption, is transported to plasma. According to (Wach, Trajanoski, Kotanko, &Skrabal, 1995) plasma insulin can be calculated using the following Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE),
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m12](i/ch069.m12.svg) (12)
    

where Vp, B and Ke, are the distribution volume for insulin, absorption rate constant, and insulin elimination rate constant, respectively. The values for these constants are defined in (Wach, Trajanoski, Kotanko, &Skrabal, 1995). I, in equation 12, is the concentration of plasma insulin, and d is the concentration of monomeric insulin. The integration part of Equation 12 has computed numerically using the trapezoidal method (with unit spacing). Precisely, Z = trapz(X, Y) function of matlab was used, where Y= B\*d. Now we have the following ODE:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch069.m13](i/ch069.m13.svg) (13)

Equation 13 has been solved numerically using variable step Runge-Kutta method to solve first order differential equations.

4.2.1. The Glucose Predictive Model

In this paper, a Time-Sensitive Artificial Neural Network (TS-ANN) is employed, as shown in Figure 2, to predict the subcutaneous glucose concentrations. The neural network is trained for each patient separately to reflect the diverse lifestyles and insulin regimens of the different patients. The dataset is divided into three parts. First part is 70% of the dataset used for training, second part is 15% used for validation, and finally the remaining 15% is used for testing. The division is carried out in blocks, where the first 70% consecutive instances are in the training block and the following 15% consecutive instances are in the validation block and so on, such that the order of the time series values are maintained.

In this study, MATLAB Neural Network Toolbox, which contains several time-sensitive neural networks architectures, is investigated. These networks are the Time Delay Neural Network (TDNN), Nonlinear Autoregressive Network with exogenous inputs (NARX), Distributed Time Delay Neural Network (DTDNN), and Nonlinear Autoregressive Network (NAR). During the training process of these neural networks, we utilized several training functions in order to produce the most accurate output. The MATLAB Neural Network Toolbox contains various functions/algorithms suitable for training neural networks. Table 2 lists the training algorithms available in MATLAB neural network toolbox. We have used these training algorithms as they are; the details of these algorithms are outside the scope of this study.

| --- | --- |
| trainbr || Bayesian Regularization back-propagation |

It is obvious from Table 3 that both the trainlm and trainbr algorithms have outperformed all other training algorithms. Moreover, NAR and NARX networks architectures outperformed TDNN and DTDNN networks. We studied two different transfer functions in the hidden layer, “logsig” and “tansig”, but the transfer function of the output layer is kept the same as “purelin.” Moreover, different numbers of neurons in the hidden layer are implemented namely, 10, 20, 30 …, and 100 neurons are used. In conclusion and due to its good performance, the Nonlinear Autoregressive network with Exogenous Inputs (NARX) has been used in predicting future glucose values. The NARX network is a dynamic network that forecasts the future values of a time series using past values of the same series, and past values of other/exogenous inputs series. The selected NARX, as mentioned earlier, has a single hidden layer with 20 neurons and an activation function logistic sigmoid (logsig). The NARX was trained using Bayesian Regularization back-propagation algorithm. The prediction horizon (PH) used in our study is thirty minutes; six steps where each step is five minutes long. The prediction window (PW) used, is a function of the prediction horizon; namely PW size is twice that of PH.

5\. EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY

5.1. Dataset

The dataset used in this study was obtained from the American Hospital (AH) in Dubai; the first hospital in the Middle East to be awarded the Joint Commission International Accreditation (JCIA). The dataset contains the data of 10 patients who were cared for by the AH. These patients used the Medtronic CGM device (Mastrototaro, Shin, Marcus, & Sulur, 2008) for real-time monitoring of their subcutaneous glucose levels and insulin doses for extended periods of time ranging between 1 and 60 days. Collecting the patients’ data has been approved by the AH ethical committee, since the confidentiality of the patients has been maintained throughout this study. The data records of the different patients were separated into different excel files; a summary data about the generated files is presented in Table 5. Each file contains a set of readings, each reading has its own date and time (in mm/dd/yyyy and hh:mm:ss format), thus forming time series attributes. The main measurement in these files is the subcutaneous glucose level which is measured, in mg/dl, every five minutes using the Medtronic CGM device which was calibrated twice per day with a standard glucometer (“American Diabetes Association.”, August 29, 2014). The amount of carbohydrate in each patient meal, in grams, is also recorded. Finally, the infused insulin through the patient-attached pump is also recorded. Two types of insulin are recorded, namely, basal and bolus (“Basal and Bolus Insulin.” August 29, 2014).

The hypoglycemic events were not logged into the patient’s excel file directly. Instead, a binary attribute for hypoglycemia (hypo attribute) is added to each one of the data files. The value of this attribute is one when the glucose level in a given reading is less than or equal to sixty (the hypoglycemia threshold), zero otherwise. The hypoglycemia threshold was not chosen arbitrary; it was suggested by the AH physician advising this study. It is interesting to note here that only six patients out of the ten, as shown in Table 5, have experienced hypoglycemia during their monitoring period, whereas four others (patients 2, 4, 6 and 7) did not.

5.2. Results and Discussion

The neural network NARX (Nonlinear Autoregressive network with Exogenous Inputs) discussed earlier has been adopted to predict the future 6 consecutive subcutaneous glucose measurements. Those predicted measurements are compared to the hypoglycemia threshold. If one of them fell below the threshold (60 mg/dl), then this is considered to be a hypoglycemia event, and 1 is stored in the corresponding cell of the Predicted\_Hypo array, zero is stored otherwise. The Actual\_Hypo array contains the actual occurrences of hypoglycemia events. A MATLAB script was implemented for comparing the actual vs. the predicted hypoglycemia, then calculating the performance measures of such a prediction model (sensitivity, specificity and accuracy).

NARX, used in this study with subcutaneous glucose values as the main input and plasma insulin and Gin as exogenous inputs, is trained using Bayesian Regularization back-propagation training algorithm. NARX is also organized as a single hidden layer with 20 neurons and logistic sigmoid as its activation function. The prediction horizon (PH) used is thirty minutes long; six steps, where each step is five minutes. Table 6 summarizes the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of the different hypoglycemic prediction models for the different patients. The prediction window (PW) used in this study is twice PH.

Table 6. The performance of the prediction model (NARX) for the different patients

It is important to note here that Table 6 shows that the average RMSE performance of predicting future glucose values on a 30 minutes prediction horizon using NARX is 13.29; which is accurate when compared with the result reported in (Georga, Fotiadis, & Protopappas, 2011; Pérez-Gandía, et al., 2010) with RMSE of 16.02 and 17.45, respectively. Figure 6 shows the predicted waveform of the subcutaneous glucose along with the actual one for patient 9 on a prediction horizon of 30 minutes. The two waveforms are pretty close. It is interesting here to note that using NARX for predicting the glucose for the other patients have produced similar good results as the ones presented in Figure 6.

As mentioned above, the TS-ANN based prediction process generates two arrays for each patient, namely, Predicted\_Hypo and Actual\_Hypo. A simple MATLAB script was written to calculate Accuracy, Specificity, and Sensitivity for the Predicted\_Hypo vs Actual\_Hypo using Equations 1 through 3. The resulting performance is shown in Table 7.

The performance of the neural network based subcutaneous glucose prediction for 30 minutes of a prediction horizon is accurate as seen in Figure 6, however the predictors are not accurate in forecasting hypoglycemia as it is observable from the low Sensitivity values of Table 7. It is important to note here that the focus of this paper is not on developing models that are accurate predictors in the euglycemic/normal range; instead we need to develop predictors that are precise in forecasting the extreme low blood glucose values/hypoglycemia. For that purpose, we used a cost function to penalize out-of-range glucose deviations. By default and in all predictors, the cost of all errors is equal to 1. In the case of cost sensitive classifier, different cost is used for different errors. Thus for a predictor that is striving for lower error rate, avoiding the higher cost error will be prioritized.

6\. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

Medical machine learning has gained huge interest lately. Diabetes is considered the world's fastest-growing chronic disease. It needs continuous self-management and control to maintain blood glucose level within the normal range. Such a management is needed to prevent complications, and hypoglycemia events. Hypoglycemia is a condition that occurs when blood glucose drops too low. The occurrence of hypoglycemia may result in seizures, unconsciousness, and possibly permanent brain damage or death.

The study presented in this paper, aims at predicting hypoglycemia within short intervals. Specifically, several time sensitive artificial neural networks are investigated and evaluated for predicting hypoglycemia occurrences in type I diabetes mellitus using the recent history of CGM subcutaneous glucose measurements. The data utilized in this study belong to a population of 10 diabetic patients. An individual model was designed for each patient using NARX (Nonlinear Autoregressive Network with Exogenous Inputs). The inputs to NARX are the recent history of subcutaneous glucose measurements, plasma insulin after subcutaneous injection of insulin and plasma glucose rate of appearance after carbohydrate absorption. The output of NARX is the subcutaneous glucose measurements in a prediction horizon of 30 minutes. The final step of this approach is to use the predicted subcutaneous glucose measurements in determining the occurrence of hypoglycemic events. The model is able to predict hypoglycemia events within a prediction horizon of thirty minutes with an average specificity of 98.2%, an average accuracy of 97.56% and an average sensitivity of 80.19% with a maximum value of 93%.

For future work, more input features to NARX should be investigated, e.g. exercise, heart rate and metabolism rate. Different types of predictors, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), should be evaluates and compared with NARX performance. In addition to the drawn blood samples, plasma insulin needed to be drawn and compared with the simulated values. As far as the meal modeling is concerned, we suggest to use patient's diary and nutrition tables rather than relying on the patient's estimation of carbohydrate quantity in a meal. Moreover, we recommend that the proposed models be tested on a larger number of patients.

ABSTRACT

The change of lighting conditions and facial pose often affects the driver's face's video registration greatly, which affects the recognition accuracy of the driver's fatigue state. In this paper, the authors first analyze the reasons for the failure of the driver's face registration in the light conditions and the changes of facial gestures, and propose an adaptive AAM (Active Appearance Model) algorithm of adaptive illumination and attitude change. Then, the SURF (speeded up robust feature) feature extraction is performed on the registered driver's face video images, and finally the authors input the extracted SURF feature into the designed artificial neural network to realize the recognition of driver's fatigue state. The experimental results show that the improved AAM method can better adapt to the driver's face under the illumination and attitude changes, and the driver's facial image's SURF feature is more obvious. The average correct recognition rate of the driver's fatigue states is 92.43%.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Fatigue driving has become one of the important causes of traffic accidents. According to the World Health Organization, 35%-45% of traffic accidents are caused by fatigue driving (Khushaba, Kodagoda, Lal & Westenberg, 2011). Fatigue driving usually refers to the emergence of psychological and physiological dysfunction of the driver after a long drive in a row, which in turn leads to the decline of the driver's driving ability. Driving fatigue, as a physiological response, almost occurs on every driver under certain conditions; therefore, the study of the driver fatigue level identification technology on real vehicle operating conditions has a positive effect on reducing traffic accidents due to fatigue driving (Qu, Cheng & Lin, 2013).

According to the data sources of driver's fatigue monitoring systems, driver fatigue monitoring systems are divided into two categories: intrusive and non-intrusive. Intrusive fatigue monitoring system mainly relies on the acquisition of the driver's physiological data, to analyze how the physiological characteristics of the driver change, so as to monitor his fatigue state. The data used in such systems include ECG signals, EEG signals and eye signals, etc. (Picot, Charbonnier & Caplier, 2012; Zhang, Wang & Fu, 2014; Correa, Orosco & Laciar, 2014). Non-intrusive fatigue monitoring system will not interfere with the normal driving of the driver in the monitoring process, the data acquisition and fatigue monitoring can objectively reflect the driver's actual operating behaviour or state. At present, the non-intrusive method has become a hot spot in the field of driver fatigue monitoring.

Fatigue monitoring system based on driver's face video is a kind of non-intrusive method, and the driver's facial video data acquisition is easier. Therefore, the research of fatigue monitoring based on facial state has become a research hotspot (Jung, Shin & Chung, 2014; Cheng, Zhang & Feng, 2007; Ma & Cheng, 2010). Driver's facial feature point location and extraction has been an important research content in face image processing (Wang, Qu & Bi, 2013); however, due to frequent light changes on the driver's face during the process of driving, the facial features extraction, positioning and registration are often inefficient or even fail.

In order to achieve accurate registration of driver's face images in real vehicle condition, this paper analyzes the existing classic AAM algorithm and proposes an improved method, and designs a driver fatigue state identification method using neural network classifier.

This remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 shows the details of the proposed algorithm. Section 3 presents experimental results and section 4 concludes the paper.

2\. METHOD

2.1. Overview

This method describes the whole process of driver facial fatigue recognition based on video images. In the real vehicle driving condition, the intensity of the driver's facial image is greatly affected by the change of lighting and its position, which makes the face registration of the driver's video image poorly robust. The Active Aesthetic Model (AAM) is one of the classical algorithms for the feature extraction of facial features (Iain & Simon, 2004; Suo, Zhang & Sun, 2013). In this paper, the popular method of facial feature localization, AAM, is applied to the facial registration of drivers and the reasons for the influence of illumination variation on AAM algorithm are analyzed, and an improved AAM algorithm is proposed. Then, the SIFT feature extraction is performed on the registered face video images. As when the driver is in the fatigue state, the driver's eyes are often closed, based on this fatigue characteristic, the driver's fatigue state identification is realized with the designed artificial neural network. The whole process of the method is as shown in Figure 1.

2.2. The Active Appearance Model

The Active Appearance Model (AAM) is, based on the Active Shape Model (ASM), obtained by statistically modeling textures (shape-independent images obtained by deforming the face images to the average shape) and integrating the shape and texture statistic models into the appearance model.

The shape of a human face can be represented by a vector of N feature points, x\= (x[1],y[1], x[2],y[2],…, x[68],y[68]), in which the coordinate of the i\-th point is represented as (x[i],y[i]). For a training set with K samples, the mean value is:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m01](i/ch070.m01.svg) (1)

The covariance matrix of the sample can be expressed as:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m02](i/ch070.m02.svg) (2)

The eigenvalues and eigenvectors of W are:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m03](i/ch070.m03.svg) (3)

where λ[k] is the k\-th eigenvalue of W and p[k] is the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue. The bigger λ[k] is, the more important the change model represented by its corresponding p[k] is. The eigenvalues are sorted from large to small, and the eigenvectors corresponding to the first M eigenvalues are combined to form a new principal axis P:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m04](i/ch070.m04.svg) (4)

Then any face shape in the face shape subspace can be approximated by the mean shape plus the weighted sum of the new spindle system and a set of control parameters, as shown in Equation (5):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m05](i/ch070.m05.svg) (5)

where ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m06](i/ch070.m06.svg) is the average apparent vector, p is the transformation matrix of the apparent principal component eigenvector, b is the statistical apparent parameter controlling the apparent change, i.e. b\= (b[1]b[2]…b[M])^T.

After completion of training and learning, the average apparent ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m07](i/ch070.m07.svg) and principal component matrices p are deterministic, so the apparent vector x of the image is determined only by the model parameter b. Change parameter b can generate a series of different shape of the face model, as shown in Figure 2.

| Figure 2. AAM apparent model based on feature points |

| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.f02](i/ch070.f02.png) |

Based on the AAM model, a basic idea of feature registration of AAM is to input a new face image, which is the optimization process of an apparent parameter b, so as to achieve the best match between model texture and input texture. In this paper, a heuristic parameter search strategy based on the change of texture prediction parameters is proposed by COOTS et al. This strategy utilizes the linear relationship between the input and model texture variation δ[g], model parameter variation δ[c] and similar transformation parameter variation ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m08](i/ch070.m08.svg). The parameters can be predicted by linear regression. The optimization search process is shown in Box 1.

The AAM algorithm can locate the facial feature points and segment the facial region more accurately when the driver's face attitude angle is not too large and the illumination condition is relatively uniform. However, when the facial attitude angle is large or the illumination is not uniform, the AAM algorithm will fail.

The facial texture changes caused by lighting are local. The local texture model of the AAM algorithm cannot describe the non-linear change of the illumination condition effectively. Therefore, to solve the problem of light should start from the local texture modelling. In order to improve the robustness of AAM algorithm to illumination change, the local texture model based on self-quotient map is proposed in this paper, improving its illumination adaptively. The self-adaptive self-quotient can be calculated by Equation (6) (Saint, Chen & Medioni, 1991; Jiang & Huang, 2010):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m15](i/ch070.m15.svg) (6)

where R is the self-quotient graph, I is the original image, and F is the adaptive smoothing filter. Adaptive smoothing is similar to that of anisotropic diffusion filtering, making great smoothing to low-contrast area and maintaining the discontinuous area. The main idea of adaptive smoothing is that it is convoluted by a 3 × 3 filter kernel, which reflects the local non-continuity of the current pixel, so the smoothing can achieve the effect of self-adaptation.

The AAM algorithm is sensitive to attitude variation. The main reason is that the global apparent model of AAM algorithm is obtained by statistic learning of a large number of samples. The new spindle system P\= \[P[1],P[2],…,P[M]\] obtained by PCA is composed of the most important M patterns. In order to ensure the registration precision of the 68-point AAM global apparent model based on PCA, the shape of the training sample should be statistically averaged, that is, to ensure the algorithm is sufficient for the new face sample. The main change pattern obtained by PCA should reflect the difference between different face configurations as much as possible while suppressing the influence of attitude change on the shape model. Therefore, the angle range of training samples cannot be too large. On the other hand, if the angle of the training sample varies widely, it is difficult to search for the optimal registration pattern in a relatively relaxed face shape subspace. Registration accuracy and the angle range that AAM algorithm can be applied to is a pair of irreconcilable contradictions. Considering that the differences between different people are mainly reflected in the shape of face, the difference between the local region samples made up of the eyes and the nose is very small, which has stronger clustering compared to the whole face, so new AAM shape models can be established in the local region. Good clustering characteristics can extend the applicability of the model to a larger angle. In this paper, we selected 10 subset points on the contours of the eyes and noses in 68 feature points of the global apparent model, and established the second layer AAM local shape model, as shown in Figure 3. Further search is performed on the basis of the general position of the eyes of the global shape model output to increase the adaptability of the AAM algorithm to the gesture.

2.3. The Surf Features Extraction

David G. Lowe, Professor of British Columbia University, Canada, summarized the existing detection methods based on invariant techniques to find the invariant features of the image in terms of position, rotation and scaling and proposed a new image matching method - SiFT (David and Lowe,2002; Brown & Lowe, 2002). The main idea of scale-invariant feature extraction is that each detected feature point is accompanied by a corresponding size factor. When we want to match different images, we often encounter different image scales, which make the distance of the feature points in different images become different and the objects become different sizes. If we correct the size of the feature point, it will cause mismatch of the intensity. In order to solve this problem, H. Bay et al. proposed a scale-invariant SURF feature detection, adding the scale factor to the calculation of feature points. SURF is similar to SIFT algorithm. The latter is more stable, more feature points detected, but the complexity is higher, while SURF boasts simple operation, high efficiency, and short operation time. SURF feature has been widely used in image engineering (Bay, Tuytelaars & VanGool, 2006; Li, Chen, Ren & Tirumala, 2014a, 2014b; Li, Pen, Chen, Gui & Song, 2014; Li, Chen & Gui, 2015; Li, Peng, Chen & Zhou, 2015).

For a given image, SURT (Speeded Up Robust Features) non-variant feature extraction will be conducted as follows (Luo & Gwun, 2009):

*   Step 1: construct Gaussian smoothing filter as shown in Figure 4. Smoothing of direction x is to rotate direction y to 90° and the filter will renew the pixel value according to the weight coefficient of the template. For the pixel of a certain position (x,y), filtering with the template in Figure 4 produces the result:
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m16](i/ch070.m16.svg)

If det(H) is less than zero, the pixel is an extreme point; otherwise it is marked as empty. ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m17](i/ch070.m17.svg) and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m18](i/ch070.m18.svg) represent the two-order derivative of the directions x and y respectively, and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m19](i/ch070.m19.svg) represents the mixed partial derivative of directions x and y of the pixel:
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m20](i/ch070.m20.svg) (7)
    
*   Step 3: mark the extreme point in Step 2 as SURT feature point.

For any point with concentrate non-variant features, calculate the Euclidean distance between this point and other feature points, with the equation as follows:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch070.m21](i/ch070.m21.svg) (8)

where x[i],y[i] is the coordinate of the feature point. Choose the adjacent area with less than 30 feature points as the effective block. Taking the biggest and the second biggest blocks as the center, clip a rectangle area of 35\*100 as the human eye area.

2.4. The Driver Fatigue Recognition Based on BP Neural Networks

Artificial neural networks (ANNs) have been widely used in the field of intelligent information processing because of the simulation of biological processes to reflect the characteristics of the human brain, based on modern neurobiology (Wang, 2008a, 2008b, 2009a, 2009b, 2009c, 2009d, 2009e, 2010b, 2011a, 2011b, Wang, Baciu, Yao, Kinsner & Zhang, 2010; Wang & Chiew, 2010). Neural network classification is a classical statistical machine learning method. It does not require the statistical properties and prior knowledge of the sample-related domain. Artificial neural network has high recognition accuracy and fast recognition speed (Subasia & Ercelebi, 2005). This is why this paper uses the neural network classifier to identify the driver's fatigue status.

Artificial neural network is a mathematical theory model mimicking human brain or behavior. It is a non-algorithmic, nonlinear, and adaptive system, which is composed of a large number of appropriate interconnected computing processing units. One unit is a neuron and can be expressed as (Dreiseitl & Lucila, 2002):

A=f(WP+B) (9)

where W is the weight vector of the artificial neural network, B is the threshold vector of the network, P is the input vector, and f is the transfer function.

Most neural networks require certain training rules, that is, constantly adjusting the network link weight, so that the error between the ideal output and the actual output is minimum. Training is actually a process of establishing a non-linear mapping between the performance parameter value and the corresponding operating condition value. The neural network training process needs to adjust the weight W and the threshold B by learning the samples. Neural network learning is done through specific training algorithms, whose development is based on learning some rules which is the learning mechanism imitating the biological system. At present, different structures and types of neural networks have been reported (Basheer & Hajmeer, 2000; Chaudhuri & Bhattacharya, 2000). This paper uses multi-layer perceptual neural network (MLPNN) to realize driver's fatigue classification. The backpropagation training algorithm is used to train the neural network classifier.

The MLPNN structure includes an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. When the driver's face fatigue characteristics occur, the neural network input will be different. Therefore, this paper uses a four-layer network to identify the driver's fatigue status. The four layers include: an input layer, two hidden layer, an output layer. The surf feature of the facial video image is the input to the neural network. The fatigue levels (normal state and mild fatigue) of drivers are the network output. Different from the input and output layers, the number of nodes in the hidden layer theoretically cannot be determined yet with any scientific or universal method. The network will have no ability to reflect the difference between the different patterns with too few hidden layer nodes, so that the network fitting results approximate a linear relationship. Excessive number of nodes in the hidden layer will cause the network to over-fit, resulting in the low generalization ability of the network to data not trained. In addition, with the increase in the number of nodes, network computing time will become huge, and its engineering applications will face difficulties. Typically, the number of the most popular hidden layer nodes is obtained experimentally. In this paper, the number of nodes in the hidden layer is S1 = 6 and S2 = 6. Figure 5 shows the design of the ANN structure. Meanwhile, the other parameters of the network are: adaptive learning coefficient: 0.085; momentum coefficient: 0.97; MSE: 0.0001; activation function: tangent sigmoid.

3\. EXPERIMENTS AND DISCUSSION

3.1. Driver Face Registration Based on Improved AAM

In order to verify the accuracy of the AAM algorithm for registration of the driver's face in the actual driving environment, some key frames were selected from the video sequences collected from the actual road experiment. The key frames covered images of faces with uniform illumination in frontal attitude, in small attitude angle and in large attitude angle respectively and those with uneven illumination. The AAM algorithm is used to register these images. The experimental results are shown in Figure 6. It can be seen from the results that AAM algorithm can more accurately locate facial feature points and segment facial regions when the driver's facial attitude angle is not too large and the lighting conditions are relatively uniform. However, when the facial attitude angle is large or illumination is uneven, AAM algorithm will fail. The (b) and (c) in the second row in Figure 6 are cases where the registration fails due to uneven illumination. The (d) and (e) in this row are cases where the registration fails due to large attitude angles. In the third row in Figure 6, (b) and (c) show the adaptively to illumination by the improved AAM algorithm, and (d) and (e) show the registration results of the improved AAM algorithm, which is insensitive to the change of attitude angle. It can be seen that the driver's facial illumination and posture changes all affect human face registration in real vehicle condition, and the improved method proposed in this paper is adaptive to illumination and attitude transformation, and can correctly realize driver 's face registration.

3.2. The Surf Feature Extraction

In order to verify the effectiveness of the improved AAM algorithm for driver fatigue identification, based on the experiment in Figure 7, we have extracted the SURF eye-area features of the human face. The experimental results are shown in Figure 7: the first horizontal line is the key image frames under the real vehicle working condition, and the second horizontal line is the automatic extraction of the SURF features of the human eye after the AAM algorithm registration. The third row is the automatic extraction of the SURF features of the human eye after registration of the improved AAM algorithm. Lines (b) and (c) are the SURF features extracted under the illumination change in the real vehicle condition, from which it can be clearly seen that the improved AAM algorithm has more complete features extracted from the human eye; Lines (D) and (e) in Figure 7 are the SURF characteristics extracted under the driver's attitude change in real vehicle condition, which shows that when the attitude is deflected, the improved AAM algorithm registration extract more SURF features from both eyes, while SURF features extracted with the original AAM algorithm are concentrated in one eye position. Therefore, from the distribution of the extracted SURF features, the improved AAM algorithm is more effective for the human eye feature extraction under actual vehicle conditions.

3.3. The Fatigue State Recognition Using BP Network Classifier

In order to validate the effectiveness of the designed artificial neural network for the classification of drivers' facial features, it is necessary to determine the test evaluation criteria of driver fatigue. Carroll et al. (Carroll, Blisewise & Dement, 1989) used facial fatigue assessment methods based on facial image videos in medical research, and the results show that the fatigue evaluation method based on facial image videos is an effective method. Wierwille et al. (Wierwille & Ellsworth, 1994) first applied this method to driver fatigue assessment. In order to demonstrate the accuracy, consistency and reliability of driver fatigue assessment methods based on facial video, Wierwille et al. first organized six expert scoring teams, who were trained by observing a large number of fatigue driving behaviors, such as rubbing eyes, rubbing face, winking, posture adjustment, yawning and other acts of resisting fatigue, as well as eyes closing, nodding, body sideway leaning and other deep fatigue behaviors, so as to obtain perceptual knowledge of driving fatigue characteristics. Then, the six specialists rated the driver's fatigue status according to the DGS (Descriptive Graphics Scale), and tested the individual differences between the team members based on the evaluation results. Finally, Wierwille used EEG signals to verify the accuracy of the driver fatigue assessment method based on facial image videos. The results of Wierwille's research show that the expert-based scoring method based on facial video is an accurate, reliable and consistent method for assessing driver's fatigue status.

As the expert video scoring method based on facial image videos is completed after the end of the experiment off-line, it will not interfere with the driver, nor block face image with electrodes like in EEG measurement. And the consistency and universality is good, so this method is used as the benchmark of fatigue evaluation in this paper, as shown in Table 1 (Chen & Ma, 2010), the evaluation scale.

Table 1. Driver fatigue status rating scale

| Fatigue Status || Level || Characteristics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Normal state || 0 || Eyes are open normally, blink quickly, with active eyeball, well concentrated, keep attention to the outside world, upright head position, rich facial expressions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mild fatigue || 1 || Eyes tend to close, time of tendency to close eyes within 1 minute cumulate to 1-2 seconds, degree of openness become smaller, blink slower but more frequently, decreased eye activity, dull eyesight; yawning, deep breathing, sighing, swallowing, winking, shaking head, scratching the face and other actions to resist fatigue, less attention to the environment. |

Fatigue samples in this paper were collected from 10 testers, and the test time amounted to 40 hours. According to the evaluation criteria in Table 1, the valid samples were selected as 6000 images. Among them, the number of conscious samples was 3200, and fatigue samples 2800. During the experiment, 50% of the total training samples were tested by cross validation. The remaining samples were used for fatigue testing. The extracted SURF features (20-dimensional vector) are fed into the designed artificial neural network, and the experimental results are shown in Table 2 and Table 3. Table 2 shows the results of the BP neural network on the SURF features, which is from the improved AAM algorithm. Table 3 shows the results of the BP neural network on the SURF features, which is from the original AAM algorithm. From the results of Table 2 and Table 3, it can be seen that the improved AAM algorithm has a higher correct recognition rate for driver fatigue identification.

4\. CONCLUSION

Based on the improved AAM algorithm, this paper designs a method to identify the fatigue state of the driver under real vehicle operating conditions. Based on the analysis of the AAM algorithm, this paper discusses the reason of driver's face registration failure, and puts forward a method to improve the AAM algorithm from two dimensions: light and attitude. Although the contribution of texture features to human face registration is taken into account in the primitive AAM algorithm, the calculated results are more sensitive to the non-linearity of the illumination variation, which reduces the matching between the active apparent features and the actual facial features of human facial feature points, and thus affecting the face positioning and registration. In this paper, by introducing self-quotient graph, we construct the active face feature representation based on self-quotient graph, and realize the accurate registration of driver under different lighting conditions. At the same time, the AAM algorithm uses the PCA method to have a global learning of the driver’s face, so that the global accuracy of registration and the angle range that AAM algorithm can be applied to is a pair of irreconcilable contradictions. Based on this, this paper constructs the second layer local shape model based on the typical features to reduce the sensitivity of the face pose to the AAM algorithm and enhance the adaptive ability of the AAM algorithm to the pose. The experimental results show that the improved algorithm can greatly improve the accuracy in extracting and positioning the SURF feature points of the driver's eyes. The training and test results of BP neural network further verify that the method has a higher performance on the driver fatigue state identification. Therefore, the method proposed in this paper has important engineering significance for driver fatigue monitoring.
