# Chapter 71

An Empirical Study

*   Sanjeev Prashar  
    Indian Institute of Management Raipur, India
*   S.K. Mitra  
    Indian Institute of Management Raipur, India

ABSTRACT

With Internet invading geographic boundaries and diverse demographic strata, online shopping is growing at exponential rate. Expected to grow by 45 per cent to $7.69 billion by the end of 2015, India’s ecommerce market has emerged as one of the most anticipated destinations for both multinational and domestic retailers. Since their success will depend on their ability to attract shoppers to buy online, it becomes relevant for them to decipher Indian consumers’ attitude and behaviour towards online shopping and to predict online buying potential in India. The effectiveness of marketing and promotional strategies and action plans also will have to be pivoted around the potential available in the market. This empirical study explores the accuracy, precision and recall of four different classifying techniques used in predicting online buying. The forecasting ability of logistic regression (LR), artificial neural network (ANN), support vector machines (SVM) and random forest (RF) in the context of willingness of shoppers’ to buy online has been compared. Analysis of the data supported most of the predictions albeit with varying level of accuracy. The outcome of the study reflects the superiority of artificial neural network over the other three models in terms of the predicting power. This paper adds to the knowledge body for online retailers in reducing their vulnerability with respect to market demand and improves their preparedness to handle the market response. Managerial implications of the findings and scope for future research have been deliberated.

INTRODUCTION

Radically changing the business models, E-commerce has significantly changed marketing communications and distribution systems, besides altering systems and processes in consumer services. Moving away from a mass marketing approach to a one to one relational paradigm, e-marketing has ushered interactions with consumers in real essence where their inputs are valued. Firms, now offer goods and services not only through traditional channels like company owned and/ or independent retail outlets, but also through online virtual stores. Besides adding a new channel of distribution, businesses are increasingly seeking to engage with their consumers through personalised interactions facilitated by this medium. Companies are assisting potential customers in identifying appropriate products or alternatively customising products to meet their requirements. In either case, faster firms are able to fulfil the requirements of their potential customers, more likely shall purchase happen. Hence, practically every major company with a retail operation has its own web site and online sales facilities, where web personalisation has become an essential element. The universal endeavour is to improve the customers’ experience and encourage their loyalty.

On business side, global e-commerce sales touched $1.316 trillion in 2014 up 22.2% from $1.077 trillion in 2013 (eMarketer, 2014). It is further forecasted that this would rise to $1.592 trillion in 2015 representing 6.7% of sales. The same would increase to $2.489 trillion or 8.8% of sales by 2018. In the Indian context, this category of retail sale is expected to grow by 45 per cent to $7.69 billion by the end of 2015 (eMarketer, 2014).

However, being active in an e-business environment does not necessarily imply business results. Clients or visitors of e-commerce websites are rarely loyal to a specific website while searching for a particular product or category (Johnson et al., 2000). Also, the conversion rate, defined as the percentage of website visits that lead to a purchase, is very low (Bucklin et al., 2002). One of the reasons attributed here is cost involved in browsing. The cost of visiting e-commerce sites is very miniscule in comparison with that in an offline world. This usually results in a delay of purchases (Moe & Fader, 2002). The availability of information on a web augurs clients’ ability to compare the offers of several competitors. Besides this, even buying online hasn’t yet evolved as a well-accepted behaviour in many markets and varies widely with product/service category (Van den Poel & Leunis, 1999). Sismeiro and Bucklin (2004) indicated that almost three-fourth of internet users browsed or searched for a specific product, but nearly two-third of the visitors never used it to actually buy something. Most of the time it is used as information source (Van den Poel & Leunis, 1999). The intent of the visitors (browse, search or purchase) is not noticeable.

Internet choice behaviour is more dynamic that provides more and varied types of consumer choices. Marketers have the opportunity to personalise the choice environment and respond in numerous ways at any moment in time. Since, this choice behaviour, in many respects, is substantially different from the behaviour that is already thoroughly explored in a traditional store-retail setting (Bucklin et al., 2002), a lot of research is still needed to be undertaken concerning Internet usage. Consequently, other models are needed to understand Internet behaviour and make predictions about it.

Predictive modelling has gained an important role in marketing, as it helps managers to analyse customers’ response and drive the decision process. The array of models being used for predictive analysis includes both statistical models and artificial intelligence based models such as neural networks. The objective of predictive models is typically to forecast a response measure for each customer, as a function of a host of independent variables (predictors). Most of the studies conducted in the context of online consumer behaviour have focussed on using structural equation modelling (SEM) for predicting online behaviour of an individual. Few studies like Chang et al. (2011), Eroglu et al. (2001), Mazaheri et al. (2011), and Wu et al. (2013) have also used the stimulus organism response (SOR) model. Nevertheless, these studies were limited in scope as they fell short in utilizing analytical modelling techniques for predicting online purchasing behaviour.

To address this gap, the present study examines the accuracy and quality of predictability of online consumer buying behaviour with the help of select four techniques – logistic regression, artificial neural network, support vector machines and random forest. The relationship between various determinants of online behaviour (independent variables) and online buying (dependent variable) has been modelled. The models were confirmed on the test set obtained from respondents and compared against each other for accuracy. Further, receiver operating characteristic curves and cumulative lift charts were used to examine the performance of the four binary classifiers.

This paper is organised as follows: a brief overview of the relevant literature has been provided in the forthcoming section and related is to the conceptualisation of our research. The description of the methodology used is detailed in the following section. The empirical results are discussed in the next part followed by the conclusions of research.

LITERATURE REVIEW

Over the last decade and half, many researchers in the field of online consumer behaviour have endeavoured to recognize key antecedent factors that have significant and important influence in shaping consumer behaviour research in the online setting. Literature is full of studies that project various determinants of online consumer behaviour. These antecedents/determinants, not expansively recorded, comprise of social, demographic aspects and characteristic of shoppers, the type of products or services being purchased, the quality of online services provided by e-retailers, the retail store’s website quality and complexity, ease of use and helpfulness of retail site, the impact of brand – both retail site brand and the brand of goods and services available on the site, the number of years of experience on the internet, previous online shopping experience (pleasant or unpleasant), acceptance of web-buying in the society value attained through online shopping, shopping orientation and motivation, trust and perceived risk, etc. (Chiu et al., 2014; Hernandez et al., 2011; Liao & Cheung, 2001; Rajamma & Neeley, 2005; Shergill & Chen, 2004; Wolfinbarger & Gilly, 2003).

One of the earliest studies, Donthu and Garcia (1999) reported that shoppers prefer online shopping over offline stores owing to their own convenience orientation. Accordingly, online shopping provides multiple benefits to consumers, both functional and practical, including easy access to a wide range of products, services and information. Substantiating this, Szymanski and Hise (2000) opined that convenience amounting to time saving and easier browsing is an important enabler of e-satisfaction. Bellman et al. (1999) included elements such as online shoppers’ demographics, their attitude towards e-shopping and the amount of money they spend annually on online shopping. The study revealed that shoppers who spend more money on web-shopping generally have a more digitalised lifestyle - these shoppers stay on the internet for a longer time and receive more electronic mails. The more the time a consumer spends online, more is the likelihood of him/her making an online purchase. The span of time spent online and the number of months a consumer is online were identified as predictors of online buying behaviour (Lohse et al., 2000). It is also established that an archetypal online shopper had a “wired” way of life.

In view of burgeoning concerns about security and privacy issues, studies have been carried out to identify factors which lead to e-satisfaction. Earlier study by Bellman et al. (1999) reported that though many shoppers have worries about e-shopping, factors like privacy, safety and security related issues were reported to be less significant predictors of online shopping behaviour. However, Szymanski and Hise (2000) posited that transaction security is one of the enabling factors of consumer e-satisfaction along with other factors like online convenience, site design and merchandising. This study noted that a decent website design, having quick, organized, and easy-to-navigate sites, has an important role in providing satisfaction to shoppers.

In their study on consumers’ online buying decisions, Lowengart and Tractinsky (2001) focussed on “which internet stores shoppers buy from” rather than “whether they bought online or not.” According to this study, the type of products being purchased online had a major impact on shoppers’ decision making. While shopping for high value products, more dimensions of the e-store are considered as against the dimensions considered while purchasing low value products. High value products tend to make consumers look for more information about the product and evaluate their perceptions regarding the financial risks associated. On the other hand, while shopping for low value products, shoppers don’t consider the dimensions of risk and product information. Perceived risks related to transactions’ security, shoppers’ education level and computer compatible skills, representative retail price in the e-market, perceived quality/ image of online retailers, Internet usage level and network speed were found to be positively and significantly associated with consumers’ willingness to shop online. However, shopper’s perceptions about relative life content of products on the internet had negative effect on willingness to shop (Liao & Cheung, 2001).

Liang and Lai (2002) noted that the basic required factors are essential for shoppers to choose whether to shop online or not, whereas factors that motivate consumers help them to choose on which online retail they should shop. Dennis et al. (2002) opined that offline retail stores might struggle to compete on an assortment of merchandises, prices and convenience, although consumers have many questions regarding the convenience of e-shopping. These offline stores could entice shoppers by giving them better overall experience – thrilling, stimulating, exciting, pleasant and amusing and one that gives them a change from the monotonous routine of life. Many online buyers still worry about the security of transaction related features of online retail stores. This can provide the offline retail stores a competitive edge over electronic commerce sites by providing better customer service, inducing trust, generating positive image and providing wholesome experiential shopping trip. It was also found that even the younger consumers had a higher inclination towards shopping in offline stores than on electronic stores, as it was more gratifying and cordial (Dennis et al., 2002).

In an experimental survey using the constructs of Technology Adoption Model - perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, Childers et al. (2001) attempted to understand consumers’ attitude towards shopping online. The authors posited that in the hedonic situation of internet shopping, perceived usefulness is a better predictor of attitude in comparison to ease of use while in utilitarian settings, they were similarly predictive. Purchasing intention was found to be directly and indirectly connected with attitude towards online shopping and prior experience of e-purchasing (Shim et al., 2001). Chiu et al. (2014) found that functional and hedonic values have positive significant impact on repeat purchase intention. It was also found that utilitarian values had stronger impact on intent to repurchase than hedonic values. Risk was found to have significant negative impact on online repurchase intention.

Belanger et al. (2002) study reports that consumers gave more importance to security features as compared to security seals, privacy statements and privacy seals while purchasing goods or services on the internet. However, vis-à-vis ‘pleasure’ features (convenience, ease of use, web aesthetics), consumers perceived privacy and security features as less important influencers. Internet shopping invokes multiple value dimensions amongst the shoppers and that these value dimensions additively contribute to preference towards the Internet retailer and future intentions (Overby & Lee, 2006). The study found that consumers indeed perceive utilitarian value and hedonic value to be important in their preference for online retailers and future intentions, though utilitarian value was a stronger predictor than hedonic value. It is noted that online shoppers turn to the Internet primarily for utilitarian reasons, such as price savings and convenience. The findings also indicate that, though utilitarian value is relevant for both frequent and infrequent online shoppers, hedonic value appears to play a significant role for infrequent shoppers but not for frequent shoppers. Discussing dissimilarity between utilitarian and hedonic motivational values, Kim and Eastin (2011) stated that hedonic is more emotional whereas utilitarian is more intellectual. Accordingly, the enjoyment in online shopping is a hedonic inspiration and the usefulness of online shopping is a utilitarian inspiration. The results of this study showed that shopper’s impulse buying is positively and significantly related to hedonic motivations.

As against most of the studies in the area that were conducted using surveyed data, Chu et al. (2008) using scanner panel data, found that consumers have lower price sensitivities while shopping online as compared to when they shop offline. This price sensitivity was related to the demographics of the shoppers and was inversely associated with the distance to the nearest offline store. Besides website design, on-time and proper delivery of goods have a positive significant impact on customer satisfaction (Liu et al., 2008). Proper transaction ability and payment were also found to significantly impact customer choice of an online web portal. However, the authors did not find any impact of rapid response time on customers’ satisfaction.

Scrutinizing the effect of many precursors of online trust and distrust on a consumer and website characteristics, Chang and Fang (2013) demonstrated that a tendency to trust significantly impacts trust in online medium and tendency to distrust affects online distrust. Online expertise has significant and positive influence on trust in online medium. Web aesthetics and navigation ease didn’t have any significant impact on either trust or distrust in online source.

Atmospherics, as a subject of interest among marketers, is not very old. In traditional retailing, Kotler (1973) defined it as the “conscious designing of the space to create specific effects on buyers.” It is noted that the retail store settings and atmospherics are more prominent than other marketing inputs that are not present at the point of purchase (Baker et al., 1994). In online settings, marketing researches have amassed a multitude of facts showing that website’s atmospheric features exert substantial influences on online consumer behaviour (Hausman & Siekpe, 2009; Koo & Ju, 2010; Manganari et al., 2011; Ranganathan, 2012). The focus of these studies has been on the impact of atmospherics on the nature and outcomes of shopping in online retailing (Kim & Lennon, 2010; Loureiro et al., 2013). Mummalaneni (2005) found that pleasure and arousal completely mediated the association between website signals and satisfaction. Ha et al. (2007) developed an exhaustive catalogue of online atmospheric stimuli that include music, sale promotion material, colour pattern and presentation, product displays, and mix and match. Since information and entertainment are two essential elements of websites, Eighmey (1997) defined the internet as an “infotainment” medium. Here, informativeness is the ability of a website to make information available (Hoffman & Novak, 1996) and entertaining website is considered to be fun, cool, exciting, and imaginative (Chen & Well, 1999).

In one study, Koo and Ju (2010) verified the impact of website atmospherics of e-stores on the emotional states of online shoppers, which tends to have a subsequent influence on behavioural intention. It is observed that atmospheric cues - graphics, colours, and web-links positively affect emotions of pleasure and arousal. Liu et al. (2013) indicated that the website cue (visual appeal) positively affects consumers’ internal reaction (normative evaluation and instant gratification). Identifying factors that impact website re-visitation, Craig-Lees et al. (2013) reported site commitment, satisfaction, social influences and medium involvement to be important ones.

The comprehensive review of online consumer behaviour literature provides a number of predictor variables that have influence on consumers’ shopping behaviour in the online medium and can be used to predict online shoppers buying behaviour.

SELECT TECHNIQUES USED

Technique 1: Logistic Regression (LR)

Also referred to as logit regression or logit model, this direct probability modelling technique is used to determine the relationship between dependent variable and one or more independent variables (Freedman, 2009). As per Walker and Duncan (1967), it is popularly used in situations where dependent variable has only two available categories. This technique is used to predict a binary response on the basis of one or more predictor variables. The likely outcomes of a single trial are modelled using a logistic function, as a function of explanatory (predictor) variables (Conklin, 2002; Hosmer & Lemeshow, 2004).

Technique 2: Artificial Neural Network (ANN)

This technique was developed as ageneralized outcomes of mathematical models of human cognition through biological neurons. It is considered as an information processing system that has certain performance characteristics in common with human neural biology. Neural networks are a family of methods that use a number of simple processors which are linked together to 'learn' the relationships between sets of variables. Widely used modelling technique for analysing the nonlinear relationship amongst the elements, neural network has been vastly used in managerial decision making including in the area of marketing like forecasting demand, segmenting markets, estimating a shopper’s choice (Paliwal & Kumar, 2009). Many studies have posited that neural networks technique is better predictor in terms of the predicting power as compared to other techniques, including econometric modelling such as linear regression (Ainscough & Aronson, 1999; Hruschka, 1993).

Technique 3: Support Vector Machines (SVM)

A supervised learning model, support vector machines is a non-probabilistic binary linear classifier that is used for classification and regression analysis (Hearst et al., 1998). Here, a learning algorithm analyses data and recognizes patterns therein. According to Platt (1999), an SVM training algorithm constructs a model for a given training set by marking each element for belonging to one of two categories. Then it assigns new examples into one category or the other. Examples in the SVM model are depicted as points in space in a manner, where examples of the different categories are distinguished by clear gaps (Shmilovici, 2005). Thereupon, the new sets are mapped in accordance with the categories they fall into.

Technique 4: Random Forest (RF)

Random forest is basically a group of simple decision tree predictors, each capable of generating an outcome when presented with a set of predictor values. It can also be thought of as a meta-estimator that puts together large number of decision tree classifiers on numerous sub-samples of the dataset and average out each outcome in order to improve predictive accuracy and control over-fitting. This technique removes the drawback of overfitting of training dataset associated with decision trees.

METHODOLOGY USED

This cross-sectional study has been undertaken using the following steps:

*   a. Existing literature was exhaustively scanned to identify various dimensions related to online buying among shoppers. This included variables influencing online buying decisions and e-satisfaction. The tentative list of thirty-two variables was prepared and shared with a small panel of five experts that included three academicians and two professionals from e-retailing firms. After discussions, two variables were merged into others and the final list was prepared with thirty variables (refer Table 1). These variables were framed into statements using seven-points Likert’s scale where ‘1’ and ‘7’ represented least and highest agreement respectively. Besides questions seeking respondents’ demographic information, the questionnaire had one question to measure the output variable – “Have you purchased any product online in last six months?” The alternatives offered were ‘Yes’ and ‘No.’
*   b. After piloting the survey instrument with select respondents in the Indian metro-towns of Delhi and Kolkata for five days, the same was finalized for comprehensive data collection. The instrument was administered to the part of a population referred as a sample. The population of this study includes the Internet using young Indians between the age group of 18 years and 28 years, living in metropolitan cities. Using non-probability convenience sampling, the respondents were contacted in five major Indian cities – Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bengaluru. Majorly, the respondents were contacted at fast-food outlets, business process outsourcing companies, shops of mobiles, apparel and accessories, movie theatres, educational institutions, and Internet cafes. After receiving their confirmation to participate in the survey, respondents were briefed about the purpose of the study and then asked to fill out the questionnaire. This data collection process from 265 respondents took twenty-eight days. Due care was taken to rotate days and locations of data collection.
*   c. After rejecting the incomplete questionnaires, data from 228 respondents was put to analysis. The data set was randomly divided into two parts – training set consisted of 159 (70%) and test set had 69 responses (30%). The confusion matrices using select four techniques and ROC curves were drawn.

To assume models to be generalizable, their suitability was checked using split-sample validation. The derived models were assessed using test/ validation set. For this, values - actual and predicted, of each observation were classified as either 0 or 1. If the estimated probability is below 0.5, then predicted value of observation is rounded to 0, while in case it is more than 0.5, the value is rounded off to 1.

A specific layout, known as contingency or classification matrix is used to present the performance of the algorithm undertaken. Here, columns present instances in a predicted class and rows represent the actual class. The combinations are available in Table 2.

Table 2. Classification Matrix Combinations

| Observed  || Predicted |
| --- | --- |
| Will Not Purchase Online || Will Purchase Online |
| Did Not Purchase Online || True Negative (TN) || False Positive (FP) |
| Purchased Online || False Negative (FN) || True Positive (TP) |

Using the values, the core measure – predictability (accuracy of predictions) of four models was calculated. It represents the fraction of observations with correctly predicted classifications. This is calculated by dividing (TP+TN) by (TP+FP+FN+TN).

Besides this, the other predictive indicators – Precision and Recall were also calculated with the help of the confusion matrix. Also called as ‘confidence’ in Data Mining, Precision denotes the fraction of the predicted positive cases that are correct. This is calculated by dividing TP by a sum of TP and FP. Precision effectively estimates an overall posterior probability and is therefore a meaningful performance measure when detecting rare events. Precision combines results from both positive and negative samples and so is a class prior dependent. On the other hand, a fraction of relevant instances that are retrieved is termed as Recall. The primary objective of calculating Recall (or Sensitivity) is to determine the goodness of a model at identifying the positives. These two measures highlight different aspects of a model’s classification performance and so selecting the most appropriate performance measure is clearly application dependent.

RESULTS AND ANALYSIS

Table 3 presents the outcomes obtained from four different classifying methods.

Table 3. Confusion matrices

| Technique  || Observed || Predicted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No || Yes |
| LR || No || 41(TN) || 8 (FP) |
| Yes || 7 (FN) || 13 (TP) |
| ANN || No || 42 (TN) || 5 (FP) |
| Yes || 6 (FN) || 16 (TP) |
| SVM || No || 46(TN) || 10 (FP) |
| Yes || 2 (FN) || 11 (TP) |
| RF || No || 39(TN) || 9 (FP) |
| Yes || 9 (FN) || 12 (TP) |

The three desired indicators were calculated for four techniques. Table 4 provides the summary of these classification measures.

Table 4. Accuracy, recall and precision

| Method || Accuracy || Precision || Recall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LR || 78.26% || 61.90% || 65.00% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ANN || 84.05% || 76.20% || 72.73% |
| SVM || 82.61% || 52.40% || 84.62% |
| RF || 73.91% || 57.14% || 57.14% |

The accuracy values in Table 4 represent the correctness of our classification. It is the fraction of correctly classified online buyers with regard to all shoppers in the sample. Using the ANN modelling technique in the present study, we got the accuracy of 0.84. This implies that nearly 84% of the shoppers were correctly classified as either online shopper or not. Similarly, SVM, LR and RF models gave the accuracy of 82.61%, 78.26% and 73.91% respectively. Thus, we note that artificial neural network, with the highest forecasting accuracy in predicting the online buying behaviour, is superior to other individual classification methods.

Precision signifies the proportion of predicted positive cases that are correct. Here again, artificial neural network gave the highest precision value (0.727), indicating that when this model predicts the sample to be an online shopper (‘yes’), 72.73% of the time it is correct. Further, we note that logistic regression, support vector machines and random forest had precision of 61.9%, 52.4% and 57.14% respectively.

The last indicator ‘recall’ (or sensitivity) reflects the capability of models to correctly recognize the online shoppers that have been properly predicted. This is one of the most important characteristics of any restricted model. From the study, we note that SVM has the highest value of sensitivity (84.62%), implying that a model has very good ability for identifying online shoppers. This was followed by ANN, LR and RF techniques. Positive predictive value and sensitivity focus only on the true positive cases and predictions.

A predictive model, which provides high values for both precision and recall, would be considered as a better model. From Table 4, it can be seen that ANN model has high values for accuracy and precision, whereas SVM has a highest recall value. With respect to errors, ANN has the least value for Type I error, also called as False Alarm, whereas SVM has least for Type II error.

RECEIVER OPERATING CHARACTERISTIC OR ROC CURVE

The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve is a graphical representation of performance of a binary classifier with varied discrimination threshold. The true positive rate (sensitivity) is plotted in y-axis against the false positive rate (1-Specificity) in x-axis for various decision cut-off points. Area under the curve (AUC) of a ROC curve describes the effectiveness of a prediction model/system by defining the model’s capability to correctly anticipate the happening or non- happening of pre-defined events (Brenning, 2005). It is known that the closer AUC is to 1, the better is the prediction accuracy. It shows perfect predictive accuracy, when it equals 1 (Lee & Dan, 2005). ROC analysis facilitates in selecting possibly optimal models and rejecting suboptimal ones (Refer Figure 1)

| Figure 1. ROC curve |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch071.f01](i/ch071.f01.png) |
| --- |

For the study, ROC curves were drawn for the four modelling techniques. Here, we note that all the four ROC curves were closer to the upper left corner. On a closer look, it is visible that artificial neural network (ANN) curve is most close to the upper corner, with logistic regression and support vector machines curves closely following it. The area under the curve (AUC) is a statistical summary of ROC curve and is a combined measure of sensitivity and specificity on the relative position of it. It is used as a validity measure of the model. The AUC score of a good predictive model lies close to 1, while a classifier without any (or poor) predictive ability would lay close to the diagonal with an AUC measure of equal to or under 0.5. The AUC of the binary classifiers used in the study is present in Table 5.

Table 5. Area under the curve

| Method || Area under the Curve (%) |
| --- | --- |
| LR || 79.56 |
| --- | --- |
| ANN || 86.01 |
| SVM || 78.77 |
| RF || 69.19 |

Table 5 indicates the superiority of artificial neural network as a classifier. With an area under the curve value at 0.86, being closer to 1, it implies that if we randomly select an online buyer and a non-online buyer, there is 86% probability that the model-predicted pseudo-probability of an online purchaser will be higher for the online buyer than for the non-online buyer.

CUMULATIVE GAIN AND LIFT CHARTS

To substantiate the significance of a predictive model, lift curve may be used. As a measure of the effectiveness of a classifier model, lift is the ratio between the results obtained with and without the predictive model. It manifests advantages of using a classification/predictive model as compared to not using the model for a given data set. In the present study, cumulative gain and lift charts have been used as visual aids for measuring and comparing the performance of the models. Figure 2 represents the cumulative lift curves for all the four models used in this study.

| Figure 2. Cumulative lift charts of the four models |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch071.f02](i/ch071.f02.png) |
| --- |

From Figure 2, we note that the chart for ANN is close to the left boundary till about 30% samples are considered. This implies that by contacting only 30% of online shoppers based on the model, more than 40% of online shoppers can be reached. SVM model also performs well till about the initial 30% samples (with slightly less resultant population) and thereafter the curve shifts away from left margin. Although the initial performance of LR model for small sample percentages is not as good as compared to ANN and SVM models, the model improves performance at about 50% sample level, at which about 70% online customers can be reached. This conveys a positive edge of ANN classier over the other three.

DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION

In this study, we have developed confusion matrices on the output of four modelling techniques to determine the accuracy, precision and recall of predictive models. As per Allenby et al. (2002), the quality of any model depends on the accuracy of its prediction, where it reflects that fraction of the total number of predictions, made by the model, that are correct. A good predictive model plays a significant role in analysing the consumer buying behaviour and determining (forecasting) sales. From Table 4, it is observed that artificial neural network technique is significantly superior to the other three techniques in terms of accuracy and precision. This result is further supported by ROC curve (Table 5), which shows that area under the curve of ANN model (86.01%) is significantly higher than others. However, support vector machines emerged as an exception by giving better recall value.

Considering the exponential growth of e-commerce in India, this research contributes to the literature in diverse ways. To the best of our knowledge, vide this study, artificial neural network and other predictive techniques have been pioneered in the domain of online consumer buying behaviour in India. An examination of each of the predictor variable will show its relevance in contributing to online buying and this would help online marketers in understanding consumers’ decision whether to buy online or not. The findings of this study would help online managers and retailers to determine the forecasts for the specific set of target segments in a specific period under a standard set of market conditions. For this, managers shall have artificial neural network as a handy tool under the condition when they endeavour to reduce Type I error. On the other hand, for reducing Type II error, managers may strive for using support vector machines as a prediction tool.

As discussed in the study, precision and recall are two parameters that can be used by the online retail managers to strategize their decisions. Manifests about the percentage of positive predictions being correct, precision is calculated by dividing total true positive cases by the sum of true positive and false positive cases. False positive cases are the samples that were predicted by the system to be ‘buyers’ but were observed to be ‘Non-online buyers.’ For online retailers, it would mean that they would stock the goods for these certain number of consumers (as predicted by the model), but in reality, a less number of customers would turn up at the site. This would result in excessive inventory with the retailer, thereby increasing his inventory carrying cost. This severely costs the retailers of perishable goods. Also, in case of products where there is an imminence of fall in price, the retailers may end up accumulating losses. Therefore, a good predictive model would help the retailer by giving higher precision value and reduced left-over inventory to be held and the cost incurred subsequently.

On the other hand, recall refers to the capability of predictive models in correctly recognizing the true positive cases that have been predicted as ‘buyer.’ This is calculated by dividing the true positives by the sum of true positives and false negatives. From retail managers’ perspective, false negative represents those cases that have been predicted by the model as ‘Non-online buyers,’ but were actually observed to be ‘buyers.’ This implies that based on the models’ predictive results, the retailer would stock a certain amount of products, but it turns out that shoppers more than predicted had arrived. This stock-out situation would result in losing customers to competitors as the retailer was not able to serve them. This has severely bad implications for the retailers with imminent competition and where the market has less brand loyalty. The cost of losing customers would be manifested in terms of providing an opportunity to shoppers to try competitive products.

This trade-off between precision and recall can be stated in marketing as the trade-off between keeping excess inventory versus losing out customers. Hence, it becomes pertinent for marketing managers to use predictive modelling techniques, more specifically those models that give higher values for both precision and recall. In this study, artificial neural network was found to give higher values for both precision and recall and hence could be considered as a better predictive model in comparison of other three models.

Thus, pioneering the use of predictive techniques like logistic regression, artificial neural network, support vector machine and random forest, the study has compared and suggested the superiority of ANN in the area of online purchasing. This study is a precursor to the understanding that managers need to avoid unnecessary marketing action plans and focus only on the most contributing variables (as specified in the study for predicting online shoppers’ behaviour). The results of this study would help online retail managers to select the appropriate model for predicting their future sales.

Besides a scope of conventional limitations of any survey research, for this study, being limited to Indian market, generalization of the conclusions is difficult. For future studies, it would be worth to test the predictability of such model using cross-country comparison. The cross-sectional research design in this study might have incapacitated the dynamic aspects in forecasting online buying. Hence, for more accurate results, the same may be tested with longitudinal analysis. Future studies may examine the influence of demographic variables on predictability of this model.

# Chapter 72

*   Eliano Pessa  
    University of Pavia, Italy

ABSTRACT

The nature itself of organizational psychology makes the study and modeling of emergence processes the key topic of this science. In this regard we can distinguish between two kinds of emergence: the one related to individual constructs and the other to collective constructs. In the former case the presence of suitable individual and contextual features gives rise to the emergence of suitable individual attitudes of holistic nature. In the latter case the features of single individuals belonging to a group, and reciprocally interacting, give rise to the occurrence of collective features and phenomena. In the last years both kinds of emergence have been studied through computational models. In this chapter we focus on the contribution of Artificial Neural Network (ANN) models to this modeling activity. As regards the emergence of individual constructs there is a consistent number of ANN-based models, most of which formulated in terms of recurrent networks. A review of their successes and failures constitutes a first part of the chapter. Instead, the emergence of collective constructs has been so far modelled by resorting to agent-based models. However, in recent times the ANN models have begun to be used with increasing frequency in this field. Namely, each agent can be modelled in an easier way by representing its structure through a suitable neural network. The final part of the chapter is, therefore, devoted to the problems underlying the use of ANNs as constituents of agent models.

INTRODUCTION

Within a previous chapter of this book we discussed the usefulness of ANN models in order to describe the processes of emergence which characterize most aspects of Organization Science. The conclusions reached in this chapter can be thus summarized:

*   1\. The emergence processes are of the foremost importance in all domains of Economics and Organization Science, so as to make their study and modeling an unavoidable necessity;
*   2\. In principle some kinds of ANN models can be used to describe and model emergence processes; however, the most suitable models appear to be the ones based on recurrent networks;
*   3\. A correct and efficient use of recurrent networks in modeling emergence processes requires a specific and high mathematical as well statistical expertise, a circumstance which, up to recent times, hindered their application to the above quoted domains.

In the present chapter we will shortly review some concrete examples of applications of ANN models to Organizational Psychology. Our aim will be, firstly, to assess the successes and failures of these models, and, in the second place, to understand how they could be related to other models, like agent models, best known within Social Sciences and, in particular, Organization Psychology. This understanding could open the way to an easier and friendly use of recurrent ANN models. Our arguments will be based on a distinction between two kinds of emergence processes: the ones related to the emergence of individual constructs and the others to the emergence of collective constructs. In the former case the presence of suitable individual and contextual features gives rise to the emergence of suitable individual attitudes of wholistic nature. In the latter case the features of single individuals belonging to a group, and reciprocally interacting, give rise to the occurrence of collective features and phenomena. It is to be underlined that both kinds of emergence are of equal importance (and often concomitant) within Organizational Psychology.

In recent times there has been within Organizational Psychology an increase of the interest in the use of computational models (see, for instance, Weinhardt and Vancouver, 2012). This interest concerned also ANN models (even if agent-based models still seem to be more popular among organizational psychologists). However, despite this circumstance, so far we didn’t observe an explosive increase of the number of papers dealing with applications of ANNs to Organizational Psychology. A possible explanation of this lack of papers could be based on the fact that the use of ANN models requires a lot of mathematical and software expertise, often scarce among organizational psychologists. While this chapter does not pretend to help in filling this cultural gap, notwithstanding we will preliminarily introduce some rudimentary notions about the ANN models so far used in Organizational Psychology. Therefore the aim of the following section is to allow the readers to understand at least the general concepts underlying these models.

THE ANN MODELS USED IN ORGANIZATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY

The world of ANN models is very wide and many textbooks have been written to describe at least its fundamental aspects (here we are forced to limit our quotations to few titles such as Bishop, 1996; Graupe, 2013; Haykin, 2009; Rojas, 1996; Rumelhart and McClelland, 1986). Within the present context we will be content with saying that, generally speaking, an ANN model is nothing but a network including two main components: the nodes, or units (often called neurons), and the links between units, often called connections (some people use the expression synapses, or synaptic connections). It is important to remark that each connection is associated with a numerical value, called synaptic weight, or, more simply, weight. The name ‘neurons’, given to the units, is related to the fact that, in order to have an admissible ANN, the units must have a time behaviour of a neuron-like kind. This requirement can be fulfilled in many ways, the most simple consisting in associating with each unit a numerical quantity, known as activation, which can vary with time according to evolutionary laws mimicking the ones observed in biological neurons. In the simplest cases this is equivalent to consider the activation x(t) as a single time-dependent variable, whose dynamical evolution is ruled by a law having a general form like:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch072.m01](i/ch072.m01.svg) (1)

where α is a parameter, I(t) the value of the input coming to the neuron at time t, and s another parameter, commonly called threshold. The symbol F denotes a threshold-like function, i.e. a function whose output is very close to a saturation value as soon as its argument is positive (the case in which the input overcomes the threshold value). Instead, when the argument is negative, the output is very low (or even negative).

The generic law (1) characterizes the so-called McCulloch-Pitts units (or neurons). The latter allow a large number of different concrete implementations, dependent on the choice of time nature (continuous vs discrete), and of the specific form of threshold-like function. Within the traditional ANN literature the networks made of McCulloch-Pitts neurons are very popular and easier to use, chiefly when the input to the i\-th neuron is given by the simple law:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch072.m02](i/ch072.m02.svg) (2)

Here the symbol w[ik] denotes the weight associated to the connection linking the output of the k\-th neuron to the input of the i\-th one. This law allows a simple transfer of activation from a neuron to another. It is to be remarked that the laws (1) and (2) are far from being biologically plausible, so that in more recent times the McCulloch-Pitts neurons have been often substituted by the so-called spiking neurons. These latter are ruled by rules far more complex than (1) and (2) and enter into play every time we need to deal with networks having a closer resemblance with the ones present within biological brain (a list of references on this subject includes Gerstner and Kistler, 2002: 2014; Dayan and Abbott, 2005; Izhikevich, 2007; Trappenberg, 2010; Sterratt et al., 2011).

Besides the kind of units, other two aspects characterize the AAN models most often used in Organizational Science: the kind of learning procedure able to change the connection weight values, and the kind of architecture of connections themselves. As regards the learning procedures it is usual to distinguish between four different categories: the supervised learning, the unsupervised learning, the direct learning, and the recurrence learning. Without entering into technical details, we limit ourselves to describe in a very general way these categories as follows. A supervised learning procedure is based on the difference between the effective output of the network taken into consideration and the wanted (or correct) output, known in advance and supplied by a teacher. In this case the learning algorithms are designed in such a way as to change the network parameter (generally the connection weights) values in order to reduce the amount of this difference. On the contrary, the unsupervised learning does not require a teacher nor a wanted output. The change of network parameter values at a given time step is based only on a comparison between the actual values and the ones of the momentary input pattern. The expression ‘direct learning’ is used to denote all situations in which the change of connection weight values is a local process, regarding only the two units linked by the connection under consideration, and depending on the correlation between the momentary activities of these units. Finally, the recurrence learning occurs whenever the behaviour of the network consists in a time sequence of outputs, at the end of which the behaviour itself is assessed on the basis of suitable criteria. At the end or even in the intermediate steps the network receives a feedback under the form of a rewarding signal. The learning algorithm is designed is designed in such a way as to maximize the value of this signal as the behaviour proceeds. Each one of the previous categories include many different kinds of algorithmic implementations, whose detailed study is performed by a discipline known as machine learning (more detailed information can be found in the textbooks on ANNs quoted above and in Anthony and Bartlett, 1999; Alpaydin, 2014).

Turning now our attention to the other important feature of ANN models, that is the architecture, we remark that its categorization is based on a subdivision of a given network into layers of units. Each layer includes all units which, on the basis of some criterion, can be considered as belonging to the same category. It is very popular the subdivision based on input layer (including all units having an input line coming from the external environment), output layer (including all units having an output line sending the activation to the environment), hidden layer (including all units lacking both input and output lines connected with the environment). This kind of subdivision, however, is not mandatory: for instance in some monolayered networks each unit can have both input and output connections with the environment. In any case, the presence of more than one layer helps to classify the connections as a function of the direction of the information flow they can support. Thus, all connections involved in the information propagation along the direction going from the input to the output layer are categorized as feedforward. Analogously, the connections involved in carrying the information in the opposite direction, i.e. going from the output layer towards the input layer, are categorized as feedback. The attribute lateral is used to denote the connections linking the units becoming to the same layer.

This elementary taxonomy allows to characterize in a simple way the architecture of most ANNs. Among the most popular examples we can quote the multilayer Perceptron, an architecture consisting in three layer of units (input, hidden, output) connected only by feedforward links. Feedback and lateral connections are absent, so that the only possible information flow is the one which starts from the input layer (owing to the external input), goes to the hidden layer, and then reaches the output layer, where the information is sent to the environment. Thus, this architecture represents the simple model of an input-output system. When it is enriched by adding feedback connections, we obtain a more complicated kind of architecture, categorized as recurrent network. A network of this kind, however, can be implemented even by resorting only to a single layer. It is to be recalled that, if we increase the number of unit layers, this implies also a more consistent increase of the possible combinations of the different kinds of connections. In turn, this gives rise to a remarkable growth of the mathematical difficulties involved in the implementation of learning procedures on these networks. This circumstance allows to understand why, despite the unlimited number of possible applications of ANN models, the ones concretely used are, most often, enough simple. In the next section we will discuss how these architectures have been really used to describe the emergence of individual constructs in Organizational Psychology.

THE EMERGENCE OF INDIVIDUAL CONSTRUCTS

The models described in this section have not been introduced by people working within Organizational Psychology. Rather they come from the efforts made by a number of cognitive scientists in order to build efficient connectionist models of some psychological processes and constructs which for long time have been considered as impossible to describe in terms of traditional modeling tools. Notwithstanding they are of high interest for organizational psychologists and for this reason have been included within this review.

The individual constructs described in these models can be thus classified: 1) personality, 2) attitude formation, 3) person perception, 4) stereotype formation, 5) group biases, 6) strategy choices, 7) decision making. We remark that, while the topics of the categories 6) and 7) have already been taken into consideration by a number of connectionist models (even if not related with Organization Science), the topics of the other categories 1)-5) have been considered for long time as a challenge by a number of connectionists, more interested in traditional cognitive processes such as memory, learning and perception.

Starting with the personality models, we first take into consideration the simplest one, introduced by Quek and Moskowitz (2007). The used neural network consists in a traditional multilayer Perceptron involving 3 layers: input, hidden and output. This network learns through a supervised procedure to reproduce in a correct way the input-output relations experimentally observed in a series of individual data. The latter have been obtained from a number of participants through an event-contingent recording procedure (for a detailed description of the latter see Moskowitz, 1994).

The authors applied the model to two different effects: the influence of the social status on the behaviour, and the influence of gender differences to communal behaviours. In the first case the input layer contained 3 nodes, representing, respectively, a higher social status (boss), an equal social status (coworker), and lower social status (supervisee). The output layer contained only 2 nodes, coding the behaviours of dominance and submissiveness. In the second case the numbers of input and output nodes were unchanged. The interpretations, of course, were different: the input nodes coded the gender of the subject, the presence of a same-sex friend, and the presence of a romantic partner, while the output nodes coded the occurrence of two behaviours, i.e. agreeable and quarrelsome. Despite the simplicity of the used model, in both situations a supervised learning based on the 80% of the cases experimentally observed allowed a correct prediction of the behaviours observed in the remaining 20% of cases. We must, however, underline that this result does not entail that the model is a good model of personality. Rather, it can be used to support the claim that, perhaps, ANN models can be useful when studying personality effects.

A far more complex connectionist model of personality has been introduced by Read et al. (2010). This model is an extension of a previous neural network model of personality introduced by Read and Miller (2002). Both models belong to the category of dynamical models of personality (see, e.g., Mischel and Shoda, 1998), which view personality as a dynamical construct, influenced by the actual goals and environmental feedbacks, rather than as a fixed structure, defined by a set of measurable features. In the model of Read et al. the personality dynamics is ruled by two main motivational systems, called approach and avoidance systems. The latter are complemented by two other systems, the disinhibition and the constraint system. Finally, the concrete working of the model is made possible by the introduction of two further systems, one devoted to code the situational features related to the actual environment, and the other coding the actual resources (material or psychological) owned by the subject. The neural network implementation of this model is based on a complex multilayered architecture, including a layer coding the motivational approach system, a layer coding the motivational avoidance system, a layer coding the situational features system, a layer coding the actual resources system, and a layer coding the output behaviours. This architecture does not include layers devoted to dishinibition and constraint systems, whose working modalities are included within the form of the rules used to compute the activation state of the network units. It includes, instead, a hidden layer intermediate between resources, as well as situational layers, and motivational layers. And another hidden layer is inserted before the behaviour layer. The high complexity of the model architecture is due essentially to the fact that it coincides with the one of a general psychological theory of personality.

Another source of technical complexity comes from the fact that the many inter-layer connections are both of feed-forward and feedback kind. This induced the authors to describe the activation dynamics by resorting to a special neural algorithm, known as Leabra (O’Reilly and Munakata, 2000). Even if the latter is easily available, its operation, based on mimicking some specificities of biological neuronal activities, is rather complex (a summary can be found in the appendix of O’Reilly and Frank, 2006).Without entering into more details, we will limit ourselves to highlight the following features of the algorithm:

*   1\. Each unit is treated as if it would be a biological neuron and is therefore described by the momentary value of a membrane potential V[m]; at any time step the latter changes a function of three different input influences; excitatory, inhibitory and leak (this one producing a spontaneous activity decay);
*   2\. While the excitatory influence is computed, as usual in all neural network models, through a weighted sum of all synaptic activations coming from other neurons, the inhibitory influence must, instead, follow a rule called k-winners-take-all (kWTA), requiring that only the inhibitory neurons having the strongest k activations can send their output activation to other neurons;
*   3.
    
    Once known the value of the membrane potential, the neuron output y is computed through the formula:
    
    ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch072.m03](i/ch072.m03.svg) (3)
    

where θ denotes a suitable threshold, γ is a gain parameter, and the + subscript indicates that the content of the expression in the brackets is set to 0 if its value is less than 0;

*   4\. There are two forms of learning affecting the connection weight values: associative and error-correcting; the former is a sort of direct learning sensitive to the correlational structure of the inputs, while the latter is a supervised learning related to specific task structures.

The model has been trained on a set of artificially prepared connections between inputs and outputs. The obtained model behaviours fit in a reasonable with some qualitative features characterizing the relationships between personality types and behaviours reported in clinical literature. Besides, the model makes some predictions which still wait for an empirical validation. These circumstances allow to consider this model of personality as promising. However, the complex algorithm ruling its dynamics prevents so far from using it within the context of a large number of interacting individuals, where simpler models, such as the one of Poznanski and Thagard (2005), appear less plagued by computational problems.

The last model of personality which we introduce is based on a cognitive architecture, named CLARION, and built some time ago to model a number of different cognitive processes occurring in human beings (see Sun, 2002; 2003). This model is described in a detailed way in (Sun and Wilson, 2014). The used architecture consists of a number of subsystems: the action-centered subsystem, the non-action-centered subsystem, the motivational subsystem, and the metacognitive subsystem. The role of action-centered subsystem is to control actions (physical or mental), using and maintaining procedural knowledge. Instead, the role of non-action-centered subsystem is the one of using and maintaining declarative knowledge. The motivational subsystem provides the motivations underlying perception, action and cognition. Finally, the metacognitive subsystem monitors, directs, and modifies in a dynamical way the operations of the other subsystems. Each subsystem includes two representational levels: the explicit (or top), and the implicit (or bottom) one. These two levels interact and cooperate to their operation. This circumstance requires the introduction of two kinds of description: the symbolic, localist one, and the connectionist, distributed one. Thus, within this architecture both symbolic computations and neural network activities cam coexist and cooperate. Needless to say, this fact increases the complexity of the whole architecture, which becomes even greater than the one of the Read et al. model. Another characteristic of this architecture is that within all subsystems most choices are made in a stochastic way, in turn based on a suitable probability distribution.

Leaving aside all questions connected to the algorithmic implementation of CLARION, it seems evident that the complexity and generality of this architecture allow to reproduce in a correct way, after a suitable choice of parameter values, practically almost all results of simulations performed to validate other personality models, as well as other cognitive processing models. However, this raises the question: in what contexts is this model more useful? The same arguments used for the Read et al. model suggests that the context of large groups of subjects is poorly suited. The context of design of a single humanoid robot seems more suited, but how much is the realization of a project of this kind useful to understand human personality? A strong principle allowing the operation of this model is that all choices are ruled by stochastic processes fulfilling the classical probability theory and a sort of Bayesian optimization. But the validity of this principle for human beings is still the object of an intense debate (see, e.g., Oaksford and Chater, 2009; Wang et al., 2014; Aerts et al., 2014).

As regards the second category of ANN models of individual constructs, dealing with attitude formation, the proposed models are much more simpler than the ones describing personality. We will shortly discuss two models, both based on recurrent networks. In principle, these networks should be the best candidates for exhibiting emergence phenomena and, at a first sight, one should expect that only in these cases we could rightly speak of ‘emergent’ individual constructs. Unfortunately this does not seem the case, at least in the first of the two models, proposed by Van Overwalle and Siebler (2005), which use a linear autoassociative network, where ‘emergence’, at least at the higher level, is not possible. Their model contains 3 kinds of units: the ones representing the attitude objects, the ones representing the possible attributes (cognitive nodes), and the ones representing the possible valences. All these units are interconnected through recurrent links. Moreover, each unit can receive input from the environment (external activation) as well as from other nodes (internal activation). The distribution of external activation depends on the choices of the experimenter and on the goal of the simulation under consideration. The operation of the model requires that an external input produces an activation of some units, and that this activation, owing to the connections between units, can be spread to the other network units. After a small number of time steps, the reached distribution of unit activations is considered as equivalent to an equilibrium distribution. At this point a learning rule produces a change in the connection weights. Typically the learning phase is very short and the number of its iterations (if any) is very small. The model output is given by the final unit activation values (mainly the object attitudes and valence ones) and the final connection weight values. The update rule for the unit activations is:

∆a[i] = net[i] – D \* a[i] (4)

where a[i] denotes the activation of the i\-th unit at time t, ∆a[i] is the change of activation value at this time, D is a spontaneous decay coefficient, and the total input net[i] is given by:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch072.m04](i/ch072.m04.svg)

the symbol w[ij] denoting the input connection weights associated with the i\-th unit, E and I representing suitable coefficients, and the symbol ext[i] denoting the momentary external input to the unit under consideration.

Instead, the weight updating rule (also called delta rule) is:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch072.m05](i/ch072.m05.svg) (5)

where the symbol ε denotes a further parameter.

This model, after a preliminary learning phase, needed to fix the initial connection weight values, is able to exhibit in the simulations the qualitative trend of some effects experimentally observed, concerning the attitude formation. However, the absence of criteria granting for the effective reaching of activation equilibrium values, after a spreading activation phase, casts some doubts on the reliability of model predictions.

A partly similar, but a little bit more complex model of attitude formation is the one introduced by Monroe and Read (2008). The main conceptual difference with the previous model is that this time the attitude is viewed as the result of a process of constraint satisfaction in which the evaluation of the attitude object is nothing but an equilibrium value reached after an interaction between the concrete knowledge related to the object and the information on the object given by a suitable persuasive communication. The typical connectionist model of attitude evaluation therefore contains two main units, one coding the object to be evaluated (two possible states of activation: 0 = object not taken into consideration, 1 = object taken into consideration), and the other the evaluation value (possible activation within the interval from 1 to -1), linked through recurrent connections with layers of units, one coding the concrete knowledge about the object (the authors call it Cognitorium), and the other coding the information coming from the persuasive communication.

The operation of this model starts, after a suitable initialization phase devoted to fix the initial values of connection weights, by activating the object unit and letting the activation spread in the network. The activations of all other units are updated according to a non-linear threshold-like function, similar to the one used for McCulloch-Pitts neurons quoted in the second section. The spreading process continues until the changes of activations fall, for all units, under a given threshold. At this point all the weights of the model are updated according to a law of the form:

∆w[ij] = ε\*(x[i]\*x[j] – x[i]\*w[ij]) (6)

where ε is a suitable parameter.

This updating law characterizes a direct learning and allows a self-organization of the network satisfying all constraints imposed by the initial activation values, due to an external input given by the experimenter to specific units. Then the activation value of the evaluation unit gives a measure of the attitude towards the object taken into consideration. This simple model has been, in some cases, generalized in different ways so as to grant for the reaching of a better form of self-organization. In any case, the simulations performed on artificially built situations reproduced the results obtained by the simulations of other models as well as some qualitative features, known from literature, of the process of attitude formation and change. It is also to be highlighted that this model is one of the very few which explicitly tries to deal with the problem of self-organization and emergence. Its relative simplicity allows to consider it as a convenient prototype for studying this topic within the context of ANN models.

Here, without entering into further details, we will limit ourselves to mention other models, which applied the previous kinds of ANN models to person perception (Van Overwalle and Labiouse, 2004), decision making and strategy choices (Lord et al., 2003; Glöckner and Betsch, 2008), study of group biases (Van Rooy et al., 2003) and, more in general, social cognition (Van Overwalle, 2007; 2011). This literature collectively suggests that the recourse to ANN models could be a promising way to deal with the emergence of individual constructs. At the same time it is easy to understand that so far we are only at the beginning of this road and that many technical problems still wait for a solution. Such a circumstance accounts for the still frequent resort, within Organization Science, to old (and linear) statistical models. As we will see in the next section the situation is worse when we deal with the problem of describing the emergence of collective constructs.

THE EMERGENCE OF COLLECTIVE CONSTRUCTS

Within Organization Science the computational modeling of behaviour of a large number of interacting individuals is traditionally performed by resorting to computer simulations of the so-called Agent-based models (see for reviews Macal and North, 2010; Fioretti, 2013). The latter require the introduction of a suitable virtual environment, of the actions which can be performed within it, and of a number of entities, called (artificial) agents, each one of which is able to monitor some aspects of the environment and to decide the specific action to be performed. There are, of course, many possible kinds of agent models, but all share a general feature: each agent can be always considered, in a way or in another, as endowed with a sort of inner cognitive system (eventually elementary). This circumstance suggests that ANN models could be useful to Agent-base simulations, just because many ANNs can be considered as compact representations of artificial cognitive systems, or of set of such systems.

Notwithstanding the presence of this possibility, the resort to ANNs in Agent-based simulations has not been so popular, mainly owing to the fact that even the simplest models of this kind are characterized by a not trivial complexity level, including a number of parameters, whose specification is needed even for allowing the operation of a single neuron. This entails that the description of a consistent population of artificial agents, each one represented by a single ANN, could be faced up to a combinatorial explosion of the parameter number. In a number of cases this problem is dealt with by introducing a small number of agents. An example is given by the agent-based simulation of social evolution performed by Sun and Naveh (2007). Within it the agents live in a100x100 2-dimensional world and their only goal is to survive picking up the food eventually present in the environment. Unfortunately (or happily) each agent is modelled through a specific version of the CLARION architecture, quoted in the previous section. Despite the simplicity of the task performed by each agent, the complexity of CLARION forced the authors to take into consideration a population of not more than 30 agents. And this number, as it is well known, puts severe limits to the statistical reliability of the obtained simulation results.

A more tricky choice has been made by authors working on the agent-based models of financial markets (see Zimmermann et al., 2001; Grothmann, 2002). The simplicity of the environment and tasks performed by the single agents allowed to represent each agent through a single non-linear neuron or, in more complex cases, by a small recurrent network. This allowed to simulate the dynamical evolution of a financial market including even up to 200 agents. In any case, despite some success, the problem of the simulation of dynamics of a large number of interacting complex neurons is far from being solved. This problem has some aspects in common with the ones of the so-called molecular dynamics simulations, largely used in physics, chemistry and engineering. Without mentioning this topic, we limit ourselves to remark that in the recent years a number of methods have been introduced, in order to deal with these problems by minimizing the computational costs (see, for an example, De Wolf et al., 2006). It is hoped that in the next future these methods will allow to perform more extensive simulations of agent-based models, in order to better understand the processes of emergence of collective constructs.

CONCLUSION

The review of the previously quoted models suggests an unpleasant conclusion: the observed complexity of the human behaviours within the organizations is too great to be captured by simple psychological models, based or not on ANNs. This difficulty is particularly strong in the case of collective effects occurring in large communities. What are the causes of this situation? The answer is obvious: without incommoding the complexity theorists, it is well known that one of the most characteristic features of a complex system is that, being complex, it is impossible to find a unique model fully describing in a correct way all its possible behaviours. We must resign ourselves to the fact that the ‘correct model’ can exist only within the world of simplest systems, such as the ones studied by Newtonian mechanics. In the world of complex systems the existence of a plurality of different models, all describing different aspects of the same system, is the rule rather than an exception.

However, once recognized this state of affairs, the next step is the one of choosing the aspects of the system under study which we feel to be most important for our investigation. This choice, of course, automatically implies that other aspects will be neglected. This process of choice, though necessary, has often occurred without awareness and without the use of technical instruments, like the ones offered by mathematics and statistics. And this lack of systematicness is one of the causes of the actual confusion in the application of neural network models to Organization Science. On the other hand, the importance of the practical consequences of these models often induced to neglect more theoretical (or ‘philosophical’) discussions about the deep meaning of the adopted hypotheses. The vague resemblance of ANN behaviours with the ones sometimes observed in biological brain neurons does not authorize to think that these two systems are equivalent in some sense. And it is probable that this improper equivalence will continue to be accepted until the connectionist approach will find a sound philosophical and mathematical foundation. The actual development in this field allow to hope that this foundation will be reached in the next future.

# Chapter 73

*   Mohammadreza Hajiarbabi  
    University of Kansas, USA
*   Arvin Agah  
    University of Kansas, USA

ABSTRACT

Human skin detection is an important and challenging problem in computer vision. Skin detection can be used as the first phase in face detection when using color images. The differences in illumination and ranges of skin colors have made skin detection a challenging task. Gaussian model, rule based methods, and artificial neural networks are methods that have been used for human skin color detection. Deep learning methods are new techniques in learning that have shown improved classification power compared to neural networks. In this paper the authors use deep learning methods in order to enhance the capabilities of skin detection algorithms. Several experiments have been performed using auto encoders and different color spaces. The proposed technique is evaluated compare with other available methods in this domain using two color image databases. The results show that skin detection utilizing deep learning has better results compared to other methods such as rule-based, Gaussian model and feed forward neural network.

1\. INTRODUCTION

Human skin detection is an active area of research in computer vision. Skin color is an indication of race, health, age, etc. (Fink et al., 2006). In video images, skin color shows the existence of humans in media; therefore, in recent years significant research efforts have been focused on skin detection in images (Elgammal et al., 2009). Skin detection has numerous applications, such as identifying and filtering nude pictures on the internet (Felck et al., 1996), detecting anchors in TV news videos (Abdel-Mottaleb et al., 1999), face detection (Das et al., 2015; Gondaliya et al., 2015; Hajiarbabi, 2014), etc. There are several factors that make the skin detection problem a challenging one. These include issues such as the similarity between human skin color and other entities like color of sand, walls, etc. (Alshehri, 2012), differences of illumination between images, images being taken by different cameras with different lenses, the ranges of human skin colors due to ethnicity, and others.

The first step in human skin detection is choosing a color space. The most common color spaces that can be used are RGB, YCbCr, and HSV (Singh et al., 2003). The color spaces can be used individually or the information of the color spaces can be combined (Hajiarbabi, 2014).

Deep learning methods are a type of neural network. In Neural Networks when the number of hidden layers increases, the back propagation algorithm often does not train the network well. Deep learning methods introduced advanced methods for training a neural network with multiple hidden layers. Neural networks have several parameters such the number of nodes in the hidden layer, the random initial weights, etc... that make neural network to be very flexible unlike other methods used for skin detection. The results show that deep learning outperform other methods that have been used in skin detection in case of precision and accuracy and have comparable results in terms of recall and specificity relative to other methods.

This paper is organized into 5 sections. In Section 2 Gaussian method and rule based methods are discussed, which are two popular methods in skin detection. In Section 3 deep learning is described and in Section 4 skin detection using deep learning is presented. The experimental results are included in Section 5.

2\. METHODS FOR SKIN COLOR DETECTION

Different methods have been used for detecting human skin in images. Among them Gaussian, rule-based, and neural networks are some of the more popular approaches.

The Gaussian model (Wu et al., 2008) uses the YCbCr color space. The density function for Gaussian variable is used to make a decision of whether or not a pixel belongs to human skin. The parameters of the density function are calculated using training images. If the probability is more than a given threshold then that pixel is considered as human skin. Chen et al. (2008) used conditional probability density function and Bayesian classification in order to define some rules for detecting human skin. RGB was used as color space. The rules are:

Kovac et al. (2003) introduced two sets of rules one for indoor images and one for images taken in daylight illumination. Kovac also used RGB as color space. The rules are:

*   For indoor images:
    
    R\>95, G\>40, B\>20, max{R,G,B} – min{R,G,B}>15, |R‑G|>15, R\>G, R\>B
