Kong et al. (2007) introduced rules which utilized two different color spaces of HSV and normalized RGB. RGB color space contains the information of illumination. HSV and normalized RGB both reduce the effects of illumination. The rules are:

0.4≤r≤0.6, 0.22≤g≤0.33, ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m07](i/ch073.m07.svg), 0≤H≤0.2, 0.3≤S≤0.7, 0.22≤V≤0.8

Neural network has been used in skin color detection in a number of research projects. Doukim et al. (2010) used YCbCr as the color space with a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) neural network. Two types of combining strategies were used, and several combining rules were applied. A coarse to fine search method was used to find the number of neurons in the hidden layer. The combination of Cb/Cr and Cr features produced the best result.

Seow et al. (2003) used a three-layered neural network and the RGB as the color space. Then the skin regions were extracted from the planes and were interpolated in order to get an optimum decision boundary and the positive skin samples for the skin classifier. Yang et al. (2010) used YCbCr color space with a back propagation neural network. The luminance Y was sorted in ascending order, and the Y values were divided into some intervals. The covariance and the mean of Cb and Cr of each interval were calculated and used to train the back propagation neural network. In Hajiarbabi (2014) back propagation neural network was used with RGB, YCbCr and HSV color spaces. The information of the color spaces was applied to neural network, and different networks were combined together in order to increase the detection rate. Al-Mohair et al. (2012) introduced another method using neural network.

3\. DEEP LEARNING

In neural networks, using more than one hidden layer usually not only decreases the performance rate but also increases the training and testing time (Tesauro, 1992). The reason is that by increasing the number of layers, it becomes too difficult to infer the conditional distribution of the hidden activities (Hinton et al., 2006). A greedy layer wise unsupervised learning algorithm was designed for Deep Belief Networks (DBN) by Hinton et al. (2006). The idea is that to learn a complicated model, it is efficient to learn and combine a set of simpler models. In the greedy algorithm each model receives a different representation of the data (Hinton et al., 2006). A non-linear transformation is applied to the input vectors which produces output vectors for the next model. The upper layers of the DBN contain abstract concepts of the inputs and the lower layer shows the low level features of the input. The classifier will first learn the low level features and by combining this information it learns the abstract concepts (Hinton et al., 2006).

In a multi-layer generative model, there are directed connections, except for the top two layers which interact using undirected connections. Considering W[0] as the weight between the first and second layer in the model, the goal is to learn W[0], and once W[0] has been learned, higher-level data at the first hidden layer can be generated using ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m08](i/ch073.m08.svg) (Hinton et al., 2006). The generative model can be trained using the following algorithm (Hinton et al., 2006):

*   1\. By using the assumption that all the weight matrices are tight, learn W[0].
*   2\. After W[0] is learned, freeze W[0], and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m09](i/ch073.m09.svg) is used in the first hidden layer in order to infer factorial approximate posterior distributions over the states of the variables.
*   3\. In the final stage, all the higher weight matrices are tied to each other, except W[0], which is untied from other weight matrices. A Restricted Boltzmann Machine (RBM) model of the higher-level data is learned. These data were produced by using ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m10](i/ch073.m10.svg) to transform the original data.

A DBN can consist of several RBM networks. A RBM is a special kind of Boltzmann Machine with the difference that the nodes in each layer are not connected to each other (Hinton et al., 2006). For generating data, Gibbs sampling can be applied between layers. By knowing the states of the units in one layer, the units in other layers are updated in parallel until the system reaches its equilibrium distribution (Hinton et al., 2006). There are several methods for generating data, among them contrastive divergence is a fast way for generating data using Gibbs sampling (Maryaz et al., 2001). In contrastive divergence learning the difference between the two kullback-Leiber divergences is minimized.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m11](i/ch073.m11.svg)

P⁰ is the distribution of the data and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m12](i/ch073.m12.svg) is the equilibrium distribution (Hinton et al., 2006). It has been stated in (Maryaz et al., 2001) that contrastive divergence in restricted Boltzmann machine is efficient and practical. One problem in the learning process is that learning the weights one layer at each time is not optimal. When the weights in the higher layers are learned, the weights in the lower layers are not optimal anymore (Hinton et al., 2006). In order to correct the weights an up down fine tuning is also needed (Hinton et al., 2006). In the down-pass only the bottom-up recognition weights are changed. Hinton et al. and Bengio et al. have done experiments on MNIST database using deep learning methods (2007; 2006). MNIST is a handwritten digits database which contains 60,000 samples for training and 10,000 samples for testing. Researches have published results on MNIST database using different techniques. Hinton et al. and Bengio et al. experiments show that deep learning has much better performance compared to other techniques (2007; 2006).

4\. SKIN DETECTION USING DEEP LEARNING

The first step in skin detection was to gather training samples. In this case around 100,000 pixels for skin and 200,000 for non-skin pixels were collected from more than 1000 images chosen from the Web. The skin and non-skin pixels were chosen manually from the images. For human skins the pixels were chosen from different ethnicities. The non-skin pixel has an enormous category, so a variety of different pixels were chosen, especially from the objects whose colors are very similar to that of the human skin.

The next step was to choose the color space. Experiments have shown that using the information from more than one color space produces better results (Hajiarbabi, 2014); therefore, RGB, YCbCr, and HSV were used as color spaces. Also because Y and H contain the illumination information which gives no information about the human skin color, these two were excluded from the training process, resulting in the input to the network being a vector consisting of eight values.

Auto encoder was used as the deep learning structure (Hinton et al., 2006). Around 75% of samples were used for training and the rest for validation. Different numbers of neurons were examined in the hidden layers. Three hidden layer were used in the structure. The results were tested on the UCD (UCD database) and VT-AAST (Abdallah et al., 2007) databases. The UCD database contains 94 and VT-AAST database contains 286 images. Both databases include images from different races and the images vary from one person in the image to multiple people. Both databases also contain the images after cropping the face skin.

The experimental results are reported as precision, recall, specificity and accuracy:

Precision or positive predictive value (PPV):

Sensitivity or true positive rate (TPR) equivalent with hit rate, recall:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m14](i/ch073.m14.svg)

Specificity (SPC) or true negative rate:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m15](i/ch073.m15.svg)

Accuracy (ACC):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch073.m16](i/ch073.m16.svg)

In the skin detection experiments, P is the number of the skin pixels. N is the number of the non-skin pixels. TP is the number of the skin pixels correctly classified as skin pixels. TN is the number of the non-skin pixels correctly classified as non-skin pixels. FP is the number of the non-skin pixels incorrectly classified as skin pixels. FN is the number of the skin pixels incorrectly classified as non-skin pixels.

5\. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

Different Auto encoders with different number of nodes in the hidden layers were considered in this experiment. The number of nodes in the hidden layers ranged from 250 to 500 with a 50 interval between each experiment. Figures 1 and 2 show the accuracy, recall, precision and specificity compared to the number of nodes used in the hidden layer on UCD and VT-AAST database.

As can be seen in Figure 1 and Figure 2, the best results occur when the number of nodes in the hidden layer is 450. The other observation is the tradeoff between recall with precision, accuracy and specificity. The reason is that for having higher recall which is detecting more skin pixels correctly, then the probability that to detect more non-skin pixels as human skin is higher which will reduce the precision and vice versa.

When detecting faces there may be some parts of the skin inside the skin components that have not been detected as human skin; and also some small pixels from the back ground that have been considered as human skin. In order to increase the skin detection rate, some morphological operations were applied to the images. The first operation that was applied to the image was filling the holes. This operation considers the pixels which are inside a skin component as skin. The other operation that is used is the opening method, which removes the small pixels from the image (Hajiarbabi, 2014).

6\. CONCLUSION

In this paper deep learning was used in order to detect human skin in color images. The results show that deep learning has better performance in terms of recall and accuracy compared to other methods including rule based methods, Gaussian method and neural network. Although, deep learning’s computational complexitymay be not better than other methods, but it’s much better performance makes it a more suitable method for detecting human skin pixels. For future work other deep learning methods such as deep belief net can be used for skin detection.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Computer Vision and Image Processing (IJCVIP), 5(2); edited by Jose Garcia-Rodriguez, pages 1-13, copyright year 2015 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).

# Chapter 74

Is There a Relationship between Deep Learning and Online Education as an Informal Learning Process?

*   Theresa Neimann  
    Oregon State University, USA
*   Victor C. X. Wang  
    Florida Atlantic University, USA

ABSTRACT

Informal learning is a universal current phenomenon of learning via participation, experience, or learning via student-centered knowledge creation. It stands in stark contrast with the traditional view of didactic teacher-centered learning. Online education can be regarded as a positive and self-directed form of informal learning. Whether or not deep learning takes place for the online learner is a controversial topic for many educators. This chapter will discuss the benefits and challenges of the relationship between informal online learning leading to deeper learning. But, what isn’t controversial is that in this century more education has been delivered in digital platforms than in any other time in history. For most providers of education to remain highly competitive, they must engage in electronic education of some form by moving beyond the brick and mortar of the traditional classroom. Informal learning has become the impetus resulting in the extensive and intensive application of electronic education.

INTRODUCTION

John Dewey (1933, 1938), a proponent of informal learning realized its value in motivating students. But what he couldn’t foresee was how the Internet and online learning would verify his hypothesis.

Today the global education community has become the buzz term in the realm of education and training. Learners in every location around the globe must acquire new skills, be literate, and understand constantly changing dynamics in globalization (Schrum, 2000, p. 91). College courses taught in the United States of America can be taken by students in Asia. Likewise, courses taught in Europe can be taken by learners in North America. More and more nontraditional learners are taking online courses either to supplement other courses or to complete a degree completely online. Today’s average worker tends to be more mobile than in the past. Whether studying from abroad or studying in one’s home country, online education offers the flexibility to attend classes from anywhere there is Internet access.

American educator from the 19^(th) and early 20^(th) century, John Dewey (1933, 1938) argued that informal education was the foundation for all formal education. A proponent of informal education he argued for the challenge of maintaining a balance between the two forms of learning—informal and formal (Dewey, 2010). Dewey seemed to be discussing about successfully combining these two forms of learning as if two sides of the same coin, one of the weightiest problems with which the philosophy of education has to cope is the method of keeping a proper balance between the informal and the formal, the incidental and the intentional, modes of education (Dewey 2010b).

Dewey’s main proposition is that learning and education are social and interactive processes, and thus the school itself is a social institution through which social reform can and should take place. He was a strong proponent of democratic principles embedded in education (Dewey, 2010). That is Dewey did not agree with one-way transfer style of authoritarian schooling, because it did not fit the model found within democratic societies. In its place, learners needed educational experiences which enabled them to interact in a social educational context, as that is how they learn to become valued, equal, and responsible members of society. He believed that students thrive in an environment where they are allowed to experience and interact with the curriculum, and all students should have the opportunity to take part in their own learning (Dewey, 2010b).

Through the various online learning platforms Dewey’s kind of interactive informal learning can take place naturally. As digital natives, today’s students not only interact in a digital world, but they thrive on this form of knowledge discovery. Informal learning is often a spontaneous response to their digitally wired social environments, as learners navigate the personal, social and work journeys of their daily lives. Because technology is embedded in our daily lives informal learning is naturally a byproduct. The online instructor becomes the facilitator, partner in the learning process and a guide that allows students to impose their own ideas and therefore take ownership in their learning and discovery processes.

Coomb and Ahmed (1974) define informal learning as:

The lifelong process by which every individual acquires and accumulates knowledge, skills, attitudes and insights from daily experiences and exposure to the environment – at home, at work, at play: from the example and attitude of families and friends; from travel, reading newspapers and books; or by listening to the radio or viewing films or television. Generally informal education is unorganized, unsystematic and even unintentional at times, yet accounts for the great bulk of any person’s total lifetime learning—including that of a highly ‘schooled’ person. It is any organized, systematic educational activity, carried on outside the framework of the formal system, to provide selected types of learning to particular subgroups in the population, adults as well as children. (p. 8)

Online learning needs to be viewed as is a form of active informal learning, because education is on an adventure that spotlights active online learning (Coomb & Ahmed, 1985). Interactive sharing of creative and innovative ideas in an informal learning experience has become a daily human exercise in both Western and Eastern learning cultures. Today, more than at any other time in history, thanks to Web-based learning platforms, such as social media tools, TED Talks, YouTube, open courseware, blogs, and various phone Apps that interact with the Internet, it is possible for anyone to become knowledgeable and expert in a broad range of content topics. Traditional learning assumed that learning experiences must be filtered through formal teacher-centric methods. Yet, the plethora of online learning portals such as social media access of today, proves this to be untrue. There are several prevalent examples of informal learning experience that should be considered as forms of online informal learning: Online blogs that present technical data, Wikipedia, an online encyclopedia, daily Facebook posting, and YouTube instructional videos.

Furthermore, digital literacy includes informal learning (Coomb & Ahmed, 1974, 1985). Digital Literacy is very important as is media literacy. Teachers and students can learn from each other as they exploit and access the many ways online learning can promote deep learning and informal. There are many online digital podiums for informal learning that promotes deep online learning.

THE MODERN PHENOMENON OF ONLINE LEARNING

Distance education has been viewed as a way in which to offer informal learning to those who are geographically separated from traditional institutions, have obligations that limit their ability to attend regular courses or have other exceptional challenges (Coomb & Ahmed 1985; Schrum, 2000). In the new century, E-learning or electronic education has almost replaced distance education with the advent of web 2.0 technologies. Like traditional age learners, many nontraditional age learners have become what we call “netizens”, roaming the web to take classes to get certificates or degrees for professional development or to reenter employment. Distance education has evolved from passive media (paper, audio and video broadcast) to an engaged informal learning process through the internet network and communication technologies. And it has the capability to deliver courses to large numbers of learners anywhere anytime (King, 2006).

Access to knowledge or degree programs can be just a few mouse clicks away and learners can comfortably learn in a conducive/physically comfortable environment such as a home or an office. Distance education technologies have broken down the four walls of a traditional classroom.

Theoretical Framework

Educators in Western cultures, especially North America, emphasize higher-order thinking skills, namely analysis, synthesis, and evaluation in Bloom’s (1956) taxonomy. Critical thinking theory was advanced two thousand years ago in Europe and it is still being addressed and expanded by contemporary theorists. Critical theory informs adult and higher education (Brookfield, 2005). Critical thinking and problem solving have become the buzz terms in teaching and learning in Western cultures. While Dewey (1933, 1938) popularized “learn by doing,” Knowles popularized andragogy. One of the most debated principles of andragogy is that adults prefer self-directed learning. There is then, a divide between teacher-centered learning and self-directed online learning that can also include critical thinking, problem solving, and critical theory. In part this divide is demonstrated in formal and informal learning styles, but a closer examination of the issue reveals that informal learning is known for its creativity and innovation, and conversely, teacher-centered learning is often driven to achieve increased test scores on standardized assessments.

Incorporating Andragogy and Cultural Competence in Online Learning

Although distance learning technologies have the capability to reach beyond the traditional classroom learners, this is not to say that instructors can just go ahead and dump their courses onto the computer screens. To implement successful teaching and learning in a classroom without borders, instructors need to take into consideration first of all andragogical and cultural issues. Shrum (2000) reminds instructors to ask these questions, “What are the instructional and personal goals of this course for all students?” “What is the purpose of this course?” Like traditional courses, course objectives for online teaching and learning must be created. These course objectives may be similar to traditional course objectives. To add to Shrum’s questions, questions that should be asked can be “Where do my students come from?” “Do they prefer Western instructional methods or Eastern instructional methods?” “What kind of prior experience do they bring to this classroom without borders?” “What are my instructional strategies to accommodate their learning needs?” “If my instructional methods do not work with this group of learners from a particular region in the world, do I have alternative instructional methods that I can fall back on?” “What are the political issues that I should always avoid when teaching a particular group of learners?”

In case instructors prefer to teach online by using pre-recorded videos, videos should reflect the characteristics of learners to incorporate andragogical principles to make online teaching and learning more effective. Adult pedagogy is synonymous with andragogy, which means the art and science of helping adults learn if a particular teaching situation requires them to do so (Knowles, 1979, 1980, 1984). Although a helping relationship with learners in an online classroom fits learners from Western countries, a directing relationship may best fit learners from authoritarian countries. Ko and Rossen (2004) discuss the following barriers to observe and to overcome when there are students from different parts of the world participating in an online course: Selecting a common language, conflicting schedules, and cultural patterns of learning. Once the language has been determined in which to communicate, the instructor needs to decide whether any assistance regarding language interpretation will be given to students who need it. Ko and Rossen (2004) suggest having a bilingual instructor or assistant who can help with translation. The assistance may be in the form of interpreting reading text, communications and assignments. Conflicting schedules may be a barrier to students from other countries. Semesters may begin at different dates, depending on the country. In addition, students from different countries may observe different religious holidays from the United States. As mentioned above, if students are from a culture based on an instructor-centered teaching environment, they may be uncertain when to speak up in the online classroom. Instead they may wait to be guided by the instructor. To overcome this obstacle, instructors may provide detailed instructions within the syllabus to outline how to ask questions or participate in discussion forums.

Writing in 1996-1997, Duchastel suggested that an instructor rethink the traditional classroom model to one more fitting the electronic processes and global resources:

*   • Static content to specifying goals to pursue,
*   • One answer to accepting a diversity of outcomes,
*   • Representing knowledge to requesting production of knowledge,
*   • Evaluating at the product level to looking to the task level,
*   • Individual efforts to building learning teams (p. 224).

It is important to mention that instructors have the necessary skills to teach online and to not simply dump the materials used previously in a traditional face-to-face class into the classroom without borders. Organizations may have to provide both financial and supportive resources to build instructors’ skills in order for them to instruct successfully online. A study of two hundred and thirty-nine (239) participants found that online facilitating was the most important skill that online instructors should possess. Participants also said lecturing, evaluating and mentoring online were important (Kyong-Jee, Bonk, & Zeng, 2005). According to Davidson-Shivers and Rasmussen (2006), instructors may find teaching online more time consuming than in a traditional classroom setting. Kubin (2002) found that when instructors teach online, they have to devote up to two (2) or three (3) times the amount of time they would normally spend teaching in a four-walled classroom.

Further, adult learning theory such as authentic learning, relevant materials, and negotiating assignments are required to ensure participation and involvement necessary to meet course objectives. However, with this in mind: these instructional strategies may not work in authoritarian cultures where a teacher-dominated mode of instruction is highly valued (Wang & Bott, 2003-2004). Thinking only in the universal terms of adult learning theory makes it difficult for instructors to adapt to local social contexts in which particular situations contradict our beautifully reasoned analysis of adult learning theory (Brookfield, 1986, 1995). “When in Rome, do as the Romans do” is not a bad strategy when teaching in an online classroom. “One size fits all theory” may not work with learners with different social and cultural backgrounds. It is also a truism that learners from different countries may have different learning styles. For example, learners from authoritarian cultures may prefer rote learning and memorization skills. Learners from democratic countries may prefer problem-solving and critical thinking skills. Whereas learners in Western countries enjoy learner-centered learning, learners in authoritarian countries require their teachers to be knowledge dictators.

Once andragogical questions are answered, the instructors can turn to the organizational questions. It is a common rule that courses should be arranged from simple to complex. Assignments must be aligned with interaction. Synchronous activities must be arranged in advance. Group size may influence the communications patterns. The challenge to most instructors is to create interaction within the course. It is easy to consider how learners can interact with course content. However, it is hard to determine if deep learning as found in Bloom’s higher cognitive skills are taking place online. The instructors might want to require discussion on topics of the course, or have students post comments upon various readings for others and provide immediate feedback about global resources that have been investigated. Laurillard (1993) describes four ways of supporting interaction with learners in the classroom without borders:

*   1\. A need for discursive language in order to understand each other’s conceptions.
*   2\. Adopting an adaptive perspective, so that the focus shifts as each student’s needs shifts.
*   3\. Authentic activities for students to demonstrate their understandings.
*   4\. Reflection on the student’s work.

These are foremost issues that instructors must consider in order to be successful in an online classroom. Of course, there may be other outstanding issues to consider in addition to the foremost issues.

Informal Learning as Self-Directed Learning

Knowles’ work on self-directed learning continues to shape the culture of adult education over the decades. It also reflects the culture of online learning, one that values autonomy and independence and centers on the self. Other learning formats may emphasize the importance of lecturing and teacher-centered learning. Knowles (1975) popularized the notion of self-directed learning nearly three decades ago, but even earlier, Tough (1967, 1971), a Canadian researcher and writer, built on the work of Houle (1961) to provide us with the first comprehensive description of self-directed learning. The early work on self-directed learning emphasized self-planning. Learners were seen to be responsible for setting their own goals, finding resources, and carrying out learning projects. According to Dewey (2010), this is also the hallmark of informal learning. Yet, at the same time, North American culture values achievement on standardized tests which do not usually support autonomy and independence. A landmark book by Candy (1991) made sense out of the different facets or strands of the concept of self-directed learning in the literature up until that date. He distinguishes between self-direction as a goal and a process—something that educators should aspire to and a way of organizing instruction. He goes on to distinguish between self-direction as a method of teaching and self-direction as a characteristic of learners. Knowles’ understanding of self-direction, for example, was as a way to organize instruction, but at the same time, he believed that adult learners would prefer self-directed learning if given a choice.

According Wang and Cranton (2014), the notion that self-direction is a characteristic of learners is best illustrated through Gugliemino’s (1977) Self-Directed Learning Readiness Scale (SDLRS) and the many studies that employed that scale in conducting empirical research over the decades. Candy further analyzes the notion of self-directed learning as a “method.” He argues that it is not a single approach, and it is not a dualism; that is, self-directed versus other-directed. In Wang and Cranton’s (2014) work in Cultures and Self Directed Learning, Candy proposes that there is a continuum of self-directed to teacher-directed, a suggestion which was taken up by several researchers and theorists after the publication of his book. Candy proposes that there are four dimensions of self-directed learning. Personal autonomy is a characteristic of learners. It includes a “broad disposition toward thinking and acting autonomously in all situations...” (p. 101). Self-management involves learners making decisions about their educational programs— selecting programs and courses, for example. Learner control, on the other hand, refers to learners having control over the decisions within a course or program—having input into the objectives of the course, selecting methods by which they learn, and participating in the evaluation of their learning.

Autodidaxy refers to independent and individual learning projects that individuals engage in outside of formal educational settings (the kinds of activities that Tough investigated in his early research). Later writing recognizes the complexity of self-directed learning, including its link to autonomy and empowerment, its interactive nature, and its political dimensions (Brookfield, 2000; Mezirow, 2000). Merriam, Caffarella, and Baumgartner (2007) describe three adult education goals: to enhance the ability of adult learners to be self-directed, to foster transformative learning as central to self-direction, and to promote emancipatory learning and social action. What does all of this mean for us as we consider how to encourage students to take their knowledge into their practice? When students are passive recipients of information, they do not learn how to learn beyond that. When we set up our teaching and learning community so as to enhance self-direction, empowerment, and autonomy, we are helping students to develop personally, take responsibility for their own learning, learn to think critically, and learn to learn (Wang & Cranton, 2014). If this is achieved deep learning is taking place. If we expect students to transfer knowledge from one context to another, they need to be able to do these things. As teachers, we are models. Those of us who teach in professional programs are models of the profession we represent. We are adult educators who teach other adult educators. Naturally, our students look to us as a model of how an adult educator practices. If we were to give lectures on how to use group work, we would not be providing a very good model. By teaching in ways that are congruent with the philosophy and values of our profession, we are being authentic, and our students can look to us for an example of how to become a professional (Wang & Cranton, 2014). There is a paradox here, however, and we should be conscious of it. On the one hand, we want to socialize our learners into a profession—to help them acquire the values of the profession. On the other hand, we want our students to be critical thinkers, to question and reflect, indeed, to critically question the values of the profession.

Online Learning Cultures Shape Good Learning

Different learning cultures exist in different learning platforms and they shape learning. We agree that educational conditions in different learning cultures affect learning. In the past, Christian monks enjoyed learning in well secluded places where learning could not be bothered by outside noise. Dewey emphasized “playful” experience of children through which children learn by interacting with the environment, and which excites and ignites the learning desires of learners. It is interesting that Thomas Jefferson posited that governments that govern best govern least (Gutek, 2011). Educational theorists translated Jefferson’s principle into an andragogical principle that “teachers that teach best teach least.” Carl Rogers (1951, 1961, 1969, 1980), an educational psychologist who promoted client-centered theory, proposed that one person cannot teach another individual directly, but rather can facilitate learning. Knowles, who was a student of Carl Rogers, later emphasized the “helping” role of adult educators, indicating that instructors should enjoy this helping profession in adult education by providing minimal guidance if learners are self-directed learners. Based on these prevalent learning theories, Western educators have indeed prescribed online learning cultures and these online learning platforms affect learning in online learning cultures in a variety of ways. Although they are not necessarily applied in practice, there is some agreement about what educational conditions in the online learning culture encourages learning. Effective learning is likely to take place in teaching environments with the following characteristics (Biggs, 1996):

1\. Online teaching methods are varied, emphasizing a variety of student activity, self-regulation and student centeredness, with much cooperative and opportunities for other group work. 2. Content is presented in a meaningful context. 3. Classes are small. 4. The online classroom climate is welcoming and supportive. 5. High cognitive level outcomes are expected and addressed in assessment. 6. Assessment is online-based and conducted in a non-threatening atmosphere

How MOOCs and Open Course Ware Are Changing the Way We Educate

Challenges facing higher education that have added to the popularity of Massive Online Open Courses (MOOCs) are that higher education has increasingly been saddled with regulations and bureaucracy in every department from student services to risk management to instruction and finances (The Chronicle of Higher Education, 2011). Departments increasingly find it difficult to stay abreast of new laws affecting tertiary education. Students increasingly find it difficult to pay for their education while attending classes on campus. College campuses lock in many students who need to work but cannot do so while attending traditional classes. These facts have created the need for more online courses which may affect the survival of many brick and mortar institutions (Mooc News and Reviews, 2015).

For example, the challenges as a result of change are felt in the financial realm of education. Financial pressures and the burdens of the complexities of compliance issues on universities and community colleges are unprecedented, especially government compliance pressures and low enrollment pressures. Sooner or later, the heaviness of regulation and bureaucracy are going to be too great to bear and will force institution closures. Sweet Briar and 17 other colleges are expected to close by 2017.

Change is the driving factor behind the rising popularity of open online learning. Change is reshaping the way we learn and change is in every disciplinary field and economic endeavor; it is inescapable because the world around us is changing with remarkable speed. Change often ushers in new directions and new paradigms, as it forces the retooling of preexisting models (Taylor, 2010).

How Massive Online and Open Course Ware Are Changing the Way We Educate

Challenges fronting higher education that have furthered the popularity of Massive online open courses (MOOCs) are that institutions of higher learning have increasingly been burdened with regulations and bureaucracy in every department from student services to risk management to instruction and finances (The Chronicle of Higher Education, 2011). Departments gradually find it demanding to stay up-to-date of new laws affecting tertiary education. Learners increasingly find it problematic to pay for their education while attending classes on campus. College campuses deadlock in numerous learners who must work for a living but cannot do so while attending traditional classes. These facts have created the need for more online courses which may affect the survival of many brick and mortar institutions (Mooc News and Reviews, 2015).

Among the challenges as a result of change, are felt in the financial realm of education. Financial burdens and the problems of the complexities of compliance issues on universities and community colleges are unprecedented, particularly government compliance stresses and low enrollment pressures. Sooner or later, the weightiness of regulation and bureaucracy are going to be too great to bear and will force institution closures. Sweet Briar and 17 other colleges are expected to close by 2017.

Change is the driving influence behind the rising popularity of open online learning. Change is reshaping the way we learn and change is in every disciplinary field and economic endeavor; it is inescapable because the world around us is changing with remarkable speed. Used as a guide, change often brings new directions and new paradigms, as it forces the retooling of preexisting models (Taylor, 2010).

It is no surprise that many universities and colleges cannot change fast enough to meet the demands placed upon them; for example, the time it takes to retool the college and university to fit the needs of a new, varied emerging work force is often too late for the retooling process to be complete (UDEMY, 2014). In other words, the changing marketplace requires new structures to be adopted and adapted within the infrastructure of institutions and by the time these systems are in place, the needs of the workforce and marketplace have changed again requiring new updates.

Open online courses provide a solution to this dilemma. The flexibility, low cost, and almost compliance free environment of the Internet allows courses to be developed quickly, offering the student instant access (Technology Outlook, 2014). In 2012, the online enterprises many of us are cognizant of, erupted on our cyber radar. Educators, universities, social entrepreneurs, community colleges, charitable foundations, and venture capitalists began creating initiatives to join the finest online tools with the best, and most well-regarded teaching available. This was how many open courses were established, such as for-profit Udacity and Coursera and nonprofit Harvard’s edX and MIT’s Opencourseware edx. The reaction they received was massive, with millions of students signing up for each class (moocnewsandreviews, 2014). When University of Michigan conducted its first online course, more than 800 students signed up for a free online health policy course. The course was part of the University’s medical and dental school curriculum, and undergraduate, graduate, and professional students were enrolled.

The chief advantage behind the phenomenon of MOOCs is the un-commodification of education; however, most databases and online material are in the English language. Approximately 80% of the knowledge found on the Internet is in English (Walshok, 1995). Everyone in the global community can get a free or very cheap education and can access knowledge anywhere they have access to the Internet and if they can speak the languages offered online. This philosophy fits in with the growing U.S. knowledge-based economy (EMSI, 2014).

The distinct role of the massive online knowledge modalities is that they are cores and hubs of new and evolving knowledge development (The Chronicle of Education, 2011b). This fact uniquely equips open online learning to consolidate and facilitate interaction among various knowledge resources in methods that more efficiently maintain economic progress, enhance human resources across the life span, and sustain vital civic culture. Online knowledge-based educational platforms and formats are diverse.

Open Course Ware enterprises range in scope from paralleling traditional classroom-sized accomplishments to the emerging MOOCs model, which enables large-scale participation by anyone in the world with Internet access. Space, place, and time take on new meaning as the traditional classroom is contained on the laptop or smartphone (SPARC, 2014).

Educators recognize the value of education is mostly independent of the platform of delivery. What makes open online courses so attractive are that classes can be accessed practically anywhere there is Internet access and service. Mobile devices such as smartphones or tablets have a growing role in learning within these new networks.

Another predecessor to the MOOC is iTunes U, launched by Apple in 2007, to offer educational materials for download. In no time, numerous colleges and universities joined the site, creating courses especially designed for the format, or simply posting podcasts, video lectures, or textbooks for free, downloadable by anyone in the world (moocnewsandreviews, 2014). These are good reasons open online learning are increasingly becoming more popular. All these various learning platforms can handle the challenge of exponential knowledge advancment. The phenomenon of knowledge growth is that new knowledge is growing at exponential rates particularly in the arenas of engineering, law, and medicine. Traditional classrooms alone with the teacher-centered approach such as one professor lecturing are not adequate anymore to keep pace with new breakthroughs in knowledge. However, to convert a traditional classroom to a classroom without walls, there are important issues for educators and practitioners to consider. The next section delves into these prominent issues associated with the classroom without borders.

EXPANDING HORIZONS IN ELECTRONIC EDUCATION

Positive aspects of electronic education are many. Around the globe distance learning has been the answer for many people that are land-locked. For example, faced with travel barriers, students in the Arctic who are looking for educational opportunities can take classes. The Arctic dwellers live within unique national boundaries, have different language and east-west cultures, but they are coalesced due to the environment (Thorvaldsen & Richards, 2011). “The University of the Arctic (UArctic) started in 2001 as a virtual university with the mission to ‘Empower the residents of the Circumpolar North, by building human capital through higher education’” (Thorvaldsen & Richards, 2011, p. i). UArctic networks educational institutions and research efforts from Russia, Norway, and Canada to offer coursework and field opportunities online for the North (Thorvaldsen & Richards, 2011).

Scotland, through their “Open University” (Thorvaldsen & Richards, 2011) is another remote area of the globe that also employs this kind of distance learning and can offer coursework to diverse learners. Over ninety percent of the land in Scotland is considered rural. By studying online, provides the remote students in Scotland access to education; removing the physical barrier created by the huge land mass of rural Scotland (Macintyre & Macdonald, 2011). In the northern reaches of Alberta, Canada and Iceland educate adult learners, as well as at Aarhus University in Denmark, where there is a coalition between six countries who study autism, distance learning is filling a gap for those who live in remote environments (Thorvaldsen & Richards, 2011).

Another popular example of global education innovation is Coursera, the Brazilian for-profit open online courseware provider, which has partnered with the University of Sao Paulo and the State University of Campinas in Brazil to create new courses that began in 2015 (Education DIVE, 2014b). The online courseware provider’s volunteer translator community is working with the Lemann Foundation, a non-profit education group in Brazil, to make 28 existing courses available in Portuguese by the end of 2015. Veduca, an online course provider that translates MOOCs into Portuguese has also been working since June 2013 with the two universities, Edukwest reports (Winkler, 2015). Coursera’s first Brazil-created MOOC was on finance and entrepreneurship courses. The MOOC provider has also taken on R7, one of Brazil’s leading Web portals, as a partner in its extension into the country. Coursera is considering the opportunity of not only a Brazilian educational market, but for reaching 215 million Portuguese speakers worldwide. While Veduca is much smaller than Coursera, it has a head start in the market with the two Brazilian universities offering a combined 31 Veduca MOOCs so far, including a master’s business degree in engineering and innovation (EducationDIVE, 2014b).

In China, where there are more rural or vast areas and the citizenry is more diverse, e-learning has also been successfully initiated (Chen, Chen, & Wang, 2009). And, although China is in different stages of rolling out e-learning between eastern and the western regions of China, China is building its distance learning infrastructure in order to continue the growth of the country (Wang, Zhu, Chen, & Yan, 2009). The growth in Chinese e-learning has not only focused on secondary education, but adult and lifelong learning, all of which wrap around three types: “e-delivery, e-teaching; and e-education” (Chen, Chen, & Wang, 2009, p. 82). E-delivery is run by the Chinese government and uses satellites, Internet and other methods to cost-effectively education rural K-12 students as well as enhances the training of teachers (Chen, Chen & Wang, 2009). E-teaching assists student learning in K-12 and higher education and E-education focuses on higher education and lifelong learning, the latter including “…radio and TV universities, networked and online higher colleges” (Chen, Chen, & Wang, 2009, p. 83). “Modern distance education has become an important part of the Chinese lifelong educational systems” (Chen, Chen, & Wang, 2009, p. 87).

Besides the benefits in public higher education learners that e-learning holds, adult learning is being augmented in corporations. Ettinger, Holton and Blass, 2006 (as cited in Chen (2008, p. 45) state the following reasons corporations use e-learning

*   • Creating competitive advantage, by aligning workforce with company strategy,
*   • Globalization, ability to reach anywhere in the world,
*   • Information age, using highly developed tools to communicate,
*   • Demand for post-secondary and life-long learning,
*   • Budget constraints for both internal and external education.

Types of e-learning that are being used in corporations include: exclusive Internet coursework, face-to-face teaching with technology (hybrid), synchronous, and asynchronous delivery (Chen, 2008). E-learning is being used for workplace learning. Workplace learning is described as learning or training activities in the workplace (Rosenberg, 2006). Businesses recognize that in order to call themselves a learning organization, they need to encourage learning and provide an easy and flexible access for its members. According to Bates (2005), businesses understand it is more cost effective to offer e-learning and keep employees onsite rather than pay to have employees go offsite to an independent learning site. Businesses see the value in continually improving the employees’ skills. By providing employees with an increasing repertoire of knowledge management, businesses can give themselves the title of learning organizations as Senge (1990) brought this concept to popularity. In Senge’s words

…organizations where people continually expand their capacity to create the results they truly desire, where new and expansive patterns of thinking are nurtured, where collective aspiration is set free, and where people are continually learning to see the whole together. (p. 3)

In Europe there are increasing incentives to introduce or to continue with online learning. Due to new technology the government recognizes that different skills are needed in the workplace, this creates a need for lifelong learning. To promote learning in industry in the United Kingdom, the government created the University for Industry (UFI). This was then renamed ‘learndirect’. In order to attract existing employees and potential employees, computer-based learning materials are placed in various public places called learn direct centers. Examples of the learn direct centers are libraries, hospitals and colleges (Brown, Murphy, & Wade, 2006). According to Blocker (2005), the following are advantages for workplace e-learning: Reducing costs, increased access to information, placing accountability on the employees for learning, and improving employee competence.

In a survey of over one thousand (1000) executives from North America, Asia, and Europe, the following areas within the organization could be linked positively to e-learning: Retention: Employees were more likely to remain with the organization when they had access to and participated in training

*   • Employee Attitudes and Culture: When employees had access to training and had participated in training, their attitude toward the organization was positive.
*   • Improved Work Performance: Employees believed training helped to build their skills and some thought the improved skills led to increased work performance.
*   • Customer Satisfaction: In some organizations, there was a positive correlation between customer satisfaction scores and training and development. (Cheese 2003)

In their study of sixteen (16) professionals responsible for training in eleven (11) organizations, Brown, Murphy and Wade (2006) found that more than ninety (90) percent of participants confirmed that additional funding would be invested toward e-learning. Participants indicated that flexibility was a benefit because e-learning provided 24/7 access to information. They also thought that the up to date information was delivered consistently to all learners. However, twenty eight (28) percent of participants thought that because the learners accessed the materials at their desk, they experienced more interruptions than if they had gone to a learning center that was located away from their desk. It can be clearly seen that e-learning within organizations is increasing.

A last consideration of adult learning that harnesses distance or e-learning is the cost. An article by Kruse (2006) looks at a cost-benefit analysis and financial breakdown of the costs for online and face-to-face learning. There are indirect and direct costs, fixed and variable costs, and one time and continuous costs that an educational organization must investigate in deciding whether to continue a face-to-face venue or an online approach. Kruse (2006) identifies specific steps to assess these two models, making cost comparisons fairly easy and objective. The first step is a data gathering phase as well as the assessment of baseline data, which are considered to be assumptions. The first assumption analyzes course requirements like length of the course, student numbers, learning time, seat time reduction, and student and teacher compensation values (Kruse, 2006). Within step two, the design of the curriculum and development costs are also compared between these two models, and then step three determines delivery costs, which are the cost of giving the instruction (Kruse, 2006). Step four compares administrative and maintenance costs, while step five summarizes each of the total costs (Kruse, 2006). It seems that this is a logical approach to a cost-benefit analysis and that the delivery cost of a face-to-face teacher is almost eight times more than a technology-based delivery (Kruse, 2006). When machines, whether it is IT or another mechanized version of human labor is assessed, machines may be less costly over the long run than are the human counterparts they mimic. It is also worth mentioning that labor costs often times are the largest cost for an organization. It will be interesting to see however, if andragogical methods are still needed in curriculum development, or if the teacher will be antiquated as technology advances. However, The introduction of Web-based education and open universities has seen an increase in access to professional development within the health professional education marketplace. Economic efficiencies of Web-based education and traditional face-to-face educational approaches have not been compared under randomized controlled trial conditions (Maloney et al., 2012, p. 1).

Limitations to Online Learning

There are e-learning limitations and these include budgetary concerns, reactions by staff, reactions by students, and lack of infrastructure. Kyong-Jee, Bonk, and Zeng, (2005) reflected that there are challenges involved with e-learning for both training professionals and learners. They went on to describe the challenges as a perfect e-storm (Bonk, 2004). The new technologies being introduced, the need for new assessment tools, the ever increasing needs for training and the forever shrinking financial resources that training professionals have to use.

Other problems that e-learning presents is the portability of content may be difficult between systems and organizations, hardware and software changes and interfaces, employee motivation and resistance to new learning methods (Chen, 2008). Some students reacted to e-learning by saying that is has been difficult to obtain information from the instructor and it hindered the students’ time management regarding their learning (Lynch, 2004). When students meet in a traditional classroom, a normal expectation is that the instructor is present to facilitate learning and to answer any questions students may have. To help students manage their time, Lynch recommends the students create a timetable that includes deadlines and study times. Furthermore the question needs to be posed about whether students themselves feel remote from not being physically present in a learning community. Macintyre and Macdonald, (2011) reported after having conducted a study, that while some students living in the rural areas of Scotland and participating in the Open University in Scotland did consider themselves as remote when considering the availability of access to education some students did not. Macintyre and Macdonald, (2011) identified one student as not agreeing with the feeling of being remote

… depends what you are remote from…I don’t see myself as remote at all…I have telephone broadband all the services…what you are looking at is simply distance from your tutor or other learners…in terms of access to usual communication channels, you are not. (p. 8)

Students accessed their coursework online, on the telephone and communicated with their instructor either on the Internet or the telephone. Students mentioned that they kept in touch with their instructor also through online forums. Students often talk about the feeling of community when they go to college or how they enjoy the college experience. These students in the study said the ties and connections they had with the instructors helped them to feel the college experience.

It is also necessary to discuss the ease of e-learning in terms of the digital divide and censorship that many nations practice. A digital divide is thought of in many aspects, and the general idea of this is those that do not have access to technology are technologically disenfranchised. If we examine this concept globally, there are countries that do not have the technological infrastructure. There are indicators that express why there is technical disenfranchisement, and these include but are not limited to: access, use, literacy in developing countries (Ruth, 2012), although the countries that have made great advances between “…2008 to 2010 are developing ones: Armenia, Saudi Arabia, Kenya, Vietnam, Belarus, Azerbaijan, Oman, Morocco, Moldova, and Qatar (ITU, 2011).

As we continue to network in more of a global sense, there are countries that control the message or monitor communications, which can ultimately decrease the use of technology and learning. There are self-regulating efforts that users may make if in fact the information that is shared is either filtered, cleaned, or censored (Guins, 2009). There are censors that are placed on hardware and infrastructure to track communication and this may include V-chip television, blocking mechanisms, cleaned up versions of media, and Internet filtering (Guins, 2009). With more and more of the world’s population having access to the Internet, activism is more easily constructed in a synchronous or asynchronous venue with citizen expression for dissenting views regarding governments. It is these emancipating technological ideas that can cause governments to control the content and transmission of information.

Different governments may have different reasons why censorship that can prohibit e-learning may exist. For example there may be censorship due to political repression, sacrilegious behavior, and moral behavior, and filters, are designed, although not always functional in excising information. Reporters Without Borders, an international agency, ranks countries regarding the level of the censorship (Warf, 2011). Countries that seem to be more open and have less Internet censorship are the United States, Northern Europe, Canada, New Zealand, and Japan (Warf, 2011). Countries that are more prohibitive of Internet communication include China, Burma/Myanmar, Iran, North Korea, and Vietnam (Warf, 2011). Countries also judge how many people have access to the Internet, called penetration rates. If certain countries have lower penetration rates, this may indicate that less people have access, although cybercafés offer access, which are more than likely being carefully scrutinized (Warf, 2011). Wealthier countries tend to have higher penetration rates and show a greater degree of freedom (Warf, 2011). However, even with a “sanitized Internet” like Cuba and China embraces, there are those who are arrested for inappropriate or anti-hegemonic behavior (Warf, 2011).

Although we have discussed China in terms of a positive adult e-learning, China may not be able to promote online international e-education if in fact it continues the censoring of the Internet. According to (Warf, 2011)

The Communist Party of China has long exerted strict, centralized control over flows of information within and across the nation’s borders, largely through the Ministry of Information Industry (MII), although Internet policing is conducted primarily through the Ministry of State Security. (p. 8)

Through the use of the “Great Firewall,” and national choke points to monitor and restrict popular search engines, although these search engines, which are ironically American companies are servicing the Chinese by self-censoring (Warf, 2011, p. 8).

Technological applications are numerous and not just educational, but social media networking is building relationships in a global manner. Though chat rooms, blogs, instant messaging, cell phones, texts offer social activism platforms they are generally monitored, and “Microsoft’s MSN Spaces blog-hosting site agreed to conform to government ‘guidelines’ in return for freedom from censorship at the ISP level” (Warf, 2011, p. 9). These types of monitoring may not only deter foreign investors in China, but may prohibit freedom of speech or expression when it comes to online learning. Engagements in education outside of China’s borders may be problematic in terms of discussion of politics, government, civil rights, and other content that may enter an educational course.

Vietnam is also a country that scrutinizes Internet communication and has only one ISP license to control connections outside the country (Warf, 2011). Warf (2011) shares

The state uses a complex system of firewalls, access controls, and strenuously encouraged self-censorship. Email is regularly monitored by searches for key words. Vietnam has imprisoned those who dare to use the Internet to speak out again government…(p. 10)

Iran also has a centralized monitoring system through the Ministry of Information and Communication Technology (Warf, 2011). Websites and blogs are heavily restricted and licensed, and email is blocked, although the Iranian government has eased cyberspace restrictions as of late due to the lack of being able to effectively manage censorship efforts (Warf, 2011).

Although Russia is no longer the Soviet Union, there are similarities in cyberspace policies to that of China (Warf, 2011). In addition,

The archipelago of countries consisting of Russia and neighboring states – a region long known for many governments that resist transparency, abuse human rights, and rely on state-controlled media – exhibits numerous attempts to restrict access to the Internet as a well as govern its contents. (p. 11)

To go further, there are trends to Internet use and restrictions that could directly impact the use of e-learning, and according to Karlekar and Cook (2009) some of the issues are:

*   • Expanding censorship,
*   • Privatization of censorship,
*   • Lack of transparency and accountability,
*   • Legal issues,
*   • Cyber attacks,
*   • Access to technology,
*   • Content restriction,
*   • Content validity,
*   • Curtailment of user rights.

A western nation that is using a degree of censorship and which may come as a surprise is Australia. The Australian government is not disclosing what sites are blocked, and this is an issue of transparency (Baubauer, 2009). When the Labor Party was voted in conservative groups put pressure on the new government for increased filtering and compulsory censorship.

Other e-learning barriers are reported by Vrazalic, MacGregor, Behl, and Fitzgerald (2009) and include not being able to have direct contact with an instructor, the language of instruction, stress, complexity, and difficulty of the technology use, the interest level of e-learning, e-learning quality, e-learning and learning style, time to become e-learning literate, and lack of motivation. Dennett and Vasquez-Colina (2012), address the issue of not being able to have direct contact with an instructor and recommend incorporating a variety of methods to encourage interaction between students, peers and the instructor. If these options are not made available, students run the risk of losing the connection between themselves and the instructor. This may result in students dropping out of the course. Digital tools to encourage interaction include wikis, podcasts, blogs and avatars. By using podcasts to deliver a welcome message or an announcement regarding an assignment, instructors can create a sense of actually being present in the classroom without borders. In addition, students hear the warmth in the instructor’s voice; something that cannot be heard when reading text (Lucking, Robert, Christmann, & Wighting, 2011). In a classroom with walls, instructors are able to provide immediate feedback to students. In a classroom without walls, instructors need to ensure prompt feedback is given so that students do not feel isolated and detached (White & Weight, 2000). Instructors need to understand how they can improve and be provided with recommendations to do better or even receive feedback to let students know to continue the good work they are already doing. Immediate feedback is crucial to avoid student frustration.

In summation, there are limitations that are both external to the learning environment and internal to the learning environment. And, there exists a digital divides or disparities on an individual level to the state level in terms of access, use, and infrastructure. As technology becomes the vehicle for communication and learning, and the infrastructure and technology becomes cheaper, the digital divide should theoretically become more narrow allowing fewer citizens around the globe to be disenfranchised.

CONCLUSION

To create a classroom without walls depends on not only distance learning technologies, but also the global education community and institutional and individual stakeholders. First and foremost, the technicians, instructional designers/faculty and administrators must have a solid foundation regarding how students learn. In other words, without any knowledge of andragogy, nobody is in a position to design effective learning packages delivered online for pre-adults or adults. This raises an important issue for accreditation bodies throughout the world. In North America, some accreditation agencies are not equipped with reviewers who are well versed in either web 2.0 technologies or instructional strategies. However, they are the ones who offer directives or accreditation to institutions of higher learning and other organizations. The best way to describe this is that this is a misguided process, leading to more ineffectiveness of electronic education of any kind.

The growth in the practice of online learning requires institutions of higher learning and some non-educational providers to develop classrooms without walls. Though online education can be regarded as a positive and self-directed form of informal learning, salient issues such as how andragogical issues are applied can determine, whether or not deep learning can take place.

As Shrum (2000, p. 103) suggested, “as a community of scholars and educators, we must create more avenues for sharing of experiences and research among all the international players, be willing to describe difficulties, and take feedback from learners. The challenges are substantial, but the potential rewards are worth the efforts

# Chapter 75

*   Murad Khan  
    Sarhad University of Science and Information Technology, Pakistan
*   Bhagya Nathali Silva  
    Kyungpook National University, South Korea
*   Kijun Han  
    Kyungpook National University, South Korea

ABSTRACT

Big Data and deep computation are among the buzzwords in the present sophisticated digital world. Big Data has emerged with the expeditious growth of digital data. This chapter addresses the problem of employing deep learning algorithms in Big Data analytics. Unlike the traditional algorithms, this chapter comes up with various solutions to employ advanced deep learning mechanisms with less complexity and finally present a generic solution. The deep learning algorithms require less time to process the big amount of data based on different contexts. However, collecting the accurate feature and classifying the context into patterns using neural networks algorithms require high time and complexity. Therefore, using deep learning algorithms in integration with neural networks can bring optimize solutions. Consequently, the aim of this chapter is to provide an overview of how the advance deep learning algorithms can be used to solve various existing challenges in Big Data analytics.

INTRODUCTION

Big Data and deep computing have gained a smashing popularity over the past few decades. The emergence of Big Data was accompanied by the exponential growth of digital data. Big Data has been defined in multiple aspects and perspectives. In general, Big Data is a prodigious amount of digital data, which is strenuous to manage and analyze using generic software tools and techniques. According to the National Security Agency, 1826 petabytes are processing by the internet on a daily basis (“National Security Agencey: Missions Authorities, Oversight and Partnerships”, 2013). Surprisingly, in 2011 it was found that the world’s data volume has grown in nine times within five years. This extraordinary growth rate is estimated to reach 35 trillion gigabytes in 2020 (Gantz & Reinsel, 2011). Due to this exponential digital data generation, Big Data continues to receive an extreme attention from the industrial experts as well as from the interested researchers. In fact, Big Data requires expeditious processing over voluminous data sets with high variety and high veracity (Zhang, Yang and Chen, 2016). Therefore, it creates a compelling demand to discover and to adopt technologies capable of speedy processing on heterogeneous data. Numerous embedded devices connected to the network generates heterogeneous data. Figure 1 illustrates a classical architecture of heterogeneous devices connected over different communication technologies. Generic characteristics of Big Data is known as three V’s of Big Data i.e. variety, velocity, and volume. A variety of data is referred to multiple formats of data being stored. For example, a collection of text, image, audio, video, numeric, etc. data types in structured, semi-structured, and unstructured forms are considered as data sets with variety. The size aspect of the data is the volume of data. In a modern technological era, data volume is rapidly growing with the invention of social media and popularity of embedded devices. In fact, the data generation speed is known as the velocity of Big Data. The technological advancements have influenced the dramatic increase in the velocity. Moreover, Big Data includes incomplete, redundant data as well as inaccurate and obsolete data. Thus, it is denoted that Big Data consists of high veracity data. Consequent to the rapid growth in digital data, myriads of opportunities in numerous fields i.e. educational services, enterprises, manufacturing services, social networking and much more are emerging. Consequently, these opportunities of Big Data have geared the research community towards data-driven discovery. Indeed, Big Data phenomenon has influenced all aspects of the social lifestyles in the modern world. Even though, Big Data occupies a colossal amount of data, discovering precise knowledge from the gathered data is not an easy task. Henceforth, the spotlight is focused towards the standard representation, storage, analysis, and mining of Big Data. The extreme heterogeneous nature of Big Data hinders the capability of feature learning by conventional data mining methods and algorithms. In fact, not only the advancements of the existing technologies, it is required collaboration among associative teams as well in order to extract valuable knowledge from Big Data. The advancements of the computation capabilities and enhanced machine learning mechanisms have broadened boundaries of data analytics and knowledge discovery procedures. However, the extraction of knowledge from Big Data using conventional learning algorithms is an extremely laborious task. It might be impossible in certain scenarios. The large volumes of data demand the scalability of the algorithm in order to process Big Data. Moreover, the great variety of data requires the algorithm to identify hidden relationships among heterogeneous data. The interest groups have yearned to discover novel mechanisms to accomplish the tedious task, which cannot be fulfilled by the conventional learning algorithms. Efforts in the recent past have identified that the integration of deep learning with high-performance computation offers favorable outcomes in knowledge extraction from Big Data.

The conventional learning algorithms occupy shallow learning architectures. In contrast, the deep learning algorithms incorporate deep architectures (Bengio and Bengio, 2000). The deep learning mechanisms utilize machine-learning techniques such as supervised learning and unsupervised learning to learn hierarchical relationships among heterogeneous data. Accordingly, it classifies the data autonomously (Ranzato, Boureau and Yann, 2007). Deep learning algorithms have gained a wider acceptance from the research community due to its remarkable performance in various domains i.e. speech recognition, computer vision, fraud detection, and advanced search. The deep learning algorithms classify and process natural signals based on the data processing mechanisms of the human brain. In the past few decades, leading global organizations with a massive amount of data collections i.e. Apple, Google, and Facebook has decided to take a step forward towards the deep learning to receive tremendous benefits from Big Data. Deep belief networks (DBN) and convolutional neural networks (CNN) are well established deep architectures. The conventional learning mechanisms tend to trap in local optima, which leads to performance deterioration. Even though the collection of unlabeled data is a cheap task, these data are neglected in conventional algorithms. Thus, DBN architecture is introduced to learn features from both labeled and unlabeled data, while overcoming the above-stated drawbacks. The DBN includes two folds 1) unsupervised pre-training and 2) supervised fine-tuning. DBN utilizes stack/s of restricted Boltzmann machines (RBM) to perform pre-training. This helps the DBN to avoid local optima. Concisely, DBN uses a greedy approach to learn unlabeled data and uses back propagation to fine-tune the learned variables. CNN is another deep learning architecture consists of multiple layers. In CNN, there are separate layers for feature representation and classification. The process initiates with the two altering layers. One performs the convolutional operations and the other one reduces the size of the next layers. The CNN follows a bio-inspired process to learn hierarchical features. Further, it automatically learns feature hierarchies and provides translational invariances to a certain extent. The performance of CNN is preserved due to the learning strategies it follows i.e. local receptive field, shared weights, and sub-sampling.
