ABSTRACT

Accidental fall detection for the elderly who live alone can minimize the risk of death and injuries. In this article, we present a new fall detection method based on "deep learning and image, where a human body recognition model-DeeperCut is used. First, a camera is used to get the detection source data, and then the video is split into images which can be input into DeeperCut model. The human key point data in the output map and the label of the pictures are used as training data to input into the fall detection neural network. The output model then judges the fall of the subsequent pictures. In addition, the fall detection system is designed and implemented with using Raspberry Pi hardware in a local network environment. The presented method obtains a 100% fall detection rate in the experimental environment. The false positive rate on the test set is around 1.95% which is very low and can be ignored because this will be checked by using SMS, WeChat and other SNS tools to confirm falls. Experimental results show that the proposed fall behavior recognition is effective and feasible to be deployed in home environment.

1\. INTRODUCTION

The world is facing an alarming rate of aging. Europe first entered an aging society, of which Germany was called the “European Nursing Home” (Regnier, 1994; Lukas et al., 2013). In China, it is estimated that the number of elderly people over the age of 60 will increase to around 2.55 billion by 2020, accounting for 17.8% of the total population; the number of elderly will increase to 29 million, and the number of elderly who is living alone will increase to 1.18 billion; at the same time, the elderly dependency ratio which is defined as the number of elderly people born per 100 working-age population will increase to about 28%. Figure 1 shows the statistical data of elderly in China. Fall detection of the elderly is a major public health problem (Noury et al., 2007). If the fall occurs without timely rescue will result in rising medical costs and increasing demands for healthcare services. Research by Iio et al. (2016) shows that timely rescue of the elderly after a fall can effectively reduce the risk of death by 80% and the risk of long-term hospitalization by 26%. With the development of Internet of Things (IoT) technology (Gubbi et al., 2013), many sensors-based methods are proposed for the elderly healthcare and security (Suryadevara & Mukhopadhyay, 2012; Ferreira et al., 2018; Hernández-Penaloza et al., 2018). Elderly populations are more prone to benefits from using wearable devices (Kekade et al., 2018), but those devices are attached to the users, and result in uneasiness or discomfort while wearing them in public areas (Fang et al., 2016). Comfortable wearing feel and wearing mobility are the important issues for wearable devices to be used in helping the elderly (Morizono, Oda, Motomura, Sakamoto, Takeshita & Matsubara, 2016; Wang, Yang & Dong, 2017).

| Figure 1. Statistical data of elderly in China |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch078.f01](i/ch078.f01.png) |
| --- |

Ambient intelligence (AmI) is also important and helpful for improving quality of life (Obukata, Cuka, Elmazi, Oda, Ikeda & Barolli, 2017) and improving health for elderly (Campos et al., 2016). Lotfi et al. (2017) proposed an ambient assisted living platform to help the carers and the elderly person. De Paola et al. (2017) proposed a context-aware system for ambient assisted living which exploits Dynamic Bayesian Networks to process sensors’ data and infer user's behavior and health conditions. In addition, position-based information technology is vital for implementing IoT application (Xu, Wu, Li, Zhu & Wang, 2018; Xu, Ding, Li, Wang & Li, 2017), monitoring of elderly and impaired people (Antoniazzi, Paolini, Roffia, Masotti, Costanzo & Cinotti, 2017), and other related system (Ishida, Ando, Uchida & Shibata, 2016).

With the development of pattern recognition and artificial intelligence, computer vision, IoT, AmI and multi-sensor technology, the detection of elderly fall presents automated, intelligent and remote. Usually, the detection system uses image sensor, sound sensor, accelerometer sensor, etc. to collect various information about the fall process, and then uses the pattern recognition method to judge if the fall occurs. If a fall event occurs, the alarm device or remote call is triggered immediately (Zigel et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2014). Aiming at the deficiencies of the fall detection system based on wearable sensors and environmental sensors, a low-cost video surveillance solution based on depth data analysis and image processing for elderly fall detection is proposed in this paper.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In section two, an review of the sensors and other IoT technologies used in fall detection is provided. In section three, we present a fall behavior recognition model based on deep learning and image processing. The implementation and experimental results are given in section four. At the end, conclusions and future work are given in section five.

2\. RELATED WORK

Different fall detection systems can be constructed for different applications using different types of sensing devices and different fall detection algorithms. According to the different sensing devices and detection methods, the mainstream methods of fall detection can be divided into the following three categories: wearable sensor-based methods, environmental sensor-based methods, and computer vision-based methods.

A wearable sensor-based fall detection system determines their motion status or position information by sensors worn on the elderly person's body. Pierleoni et al. (2015) proposed a fall detection system that uses a high reliability wearable device for elderly fall detection. Kang (2018) presented an IoT-based fall prevention technology to prevent, predict and detect falls in advance, which is divided into two methods: the image data analysis method and sensor data analysis method. Chen et al. (2016) presented a human action recognition system that can real-time consider a comprehensive set of human actions which uses a depth camera and an inertial sensor. Kinect sensor is widely used for elderly care (Gasparrini et al., 2014; Bevilacqua et al., 2014). Most wearable sensors (such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, etc.) are cheaper, more accurate and easier to operate than environmental sensors, but they are highly invasive, which is their biggest drawback.

The environmental sensor-based method places the sensor around the environment (Igual et al., 2013; Demiris & Hensel, 2008), which is typically in indoors. The signals used for detection include pressure, vibration, audio, infrared arrays, and so on. Most environmental sensor-based methods use pressure sensors to detect and track objects. Because it senses all pressure changes around the object, this is prone to false alarms and reduce the accuracy of the fall detection.

With the development of computer vision and image processing technology, computer vision-based fall detection has become an important method. The computer vision-based detection method can be divided into single camera and multi-camera detection according to the number of cameras (Rougier et al., 2013; Cucchiara et al., 2007). Compared with the above two methods, the computer vision-based method is less invasive to the elderly and has higher precision and robustness.

There are still some other work done which is relevant to image processing which is a must for vision-based fall detection. Iio (2018) proposed an image processing application framework that consists of mobile device and web application for attendance management, however, the students need to upload the selfie photographs and signatures by themselves which is very inconvenience in the real implementation system. An improved image classification algorithm is proposed for building an image classification system, which is based on weighted visual dictionary of K-means cluster (Liu, Cai & Zhang, 2018). Experimental result shows that the algorithm is feasible to descript image information which can provide image classification and can be used in unmanned-navigation and machine-vision areas. In order to solve the deficiencies of the classical image restoration algorithms, a new structure tensor-based image inpainting algorithm (STIA) is presented (Liu, Liu & Zou, 2016).

Together with the IoT, Cloud computing technology is also used to perform fall detection. Melillo et al., (2015) propose a Cloud-based smart m-health platform which can be developed to collect and automatically analyze biomedical signals for risk assessment of falls in hypertensive patients. Lai et al., (2014) presented a collaborative computing framework of Cloud and wireless body sensor network applied to fall detection and 3-D motion reconstruction. Shen et al., (2018) implemented a Fall detection system based on Cloud.

However, earlier depth sensors have not been widely used because of high price and poor accuracy. Microsoft's Kinect sensor has the advantages of accuracy, stability, and real-time access to deep images. It has a good application prospect in the fields of motion target detection, obstacle recognition, path planning, and fall detection. However, the price of Kinect device is also higher than ordinary camera. In this paper, deep learning is introduced to process image, and fall behavior detection model is built with using an ordinary camera to get the video source to perform fall detection. The experimental results show that the presented method is feasible and low cost, which can be deployed in the smart home environment.

3\. FALL RECOGNITION MODEL

This paper proposes a fall detection method based on deep learning and image processing without relying on wearable devices and sensors. In this study, a new data source which is produced by our designed image collection system is used as the basis for the fall judgment, so some of the existing open data sets for fall detection cannot be used. In order to reduce the workload of sample labeling, this paper divides human activity events into two categories, namely, FALL and NoFALL. All pictures are labeled FALL or NoFALL. Therefore, the detection of fall events is abstracted as the classification of FALL and NoFALL. In this paper DeeperCut model (Insafutdinov et al., 2016; Pishchulin et al., 2016) is used to extract person skeleton from the detection environment. Inspired by Du et al., (2015), the human skeleton is decomposed into five parts, e.g., two arms, two legs and one trunk. In this paper, the human skeleton is decomposed into five parts: two arms, two legs and one head, that is shown in Figure 2. 14 key points of human skeleton are used to detect human body and perform fall detection. In order to protect the privacy about the detected person (Edgcomb et al., 2012), the 14 points data are finally processed and stored in real "application, where the photograph or the video is not stored.

| Figure 2. The 14 key points of human skeleton |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch078.f02](i/ch078.f02.png) |
| --- |

The training data preparation process of the fall detection model is shown in Figure 3. Firstly, the camera collects human activities behavior and stored them as video which is stored .mp4 files. Secondly, those .mp4 files are cut into high-frequency pictures and labeled. Thirdly, the pictures are put into the DeepCut model, which outputs the coordinates and confidence data of the 14 key points of the human body. Lastly, these image output data and label are iput into the fall detection depth neural network, and the fall detection model is output. The used deep neural network model is shown in Figure 4. In the fully connected layers, the implemented operation is the output which is equal to activation(dot(input, kernel)+bias). The activation() is the activation function of element-by-element calculation, the kernel is the weight matrix of this layer, the bias is the partial vector. The activation function used in the first five layers is tanh, shown as formula (1), and the last layer is classified using the softmax function (Ahmed et al., 2015). Here we use the two-category form of the Softmax function. Equation (2) represents the probability that the softmax regression predicts one of the categories, where θ is the input vector. At the end, the built fall detection model is used to judge the video which is real-time from an ordinary camera.

4\. IMPLEMENTATION AND EVALUATION

Raspberry Pi is widely used in IoT environment (Obukata, Cuka, Elmazi, Oda, Ikeda & Barolli, 2017). In this paper, a camera is connected to Raspberry Pi platform. A HP PC equipped with an Intel Core i5-6300HQ CPU (2.30 GHz, 4 cores), 8 GB RAM, 4GB GTX965M GPU, Ubuntu 16.04 OS is used to process video and image which can be obtained from the camera based on Raspberry Pi.

The test room is 5m×5m and covered with a camera. Two people simulated falls and no falls in random human activities. Figure 5 shows the home environment of our experiment, where the HP computer is used as server. 44 videos were collected in the experimental home environment, of which 42 videos were used as training data and 2 videos were used as test data. There are many fall postures and dozens of non-falling postures, including squats, bends, sitting and other suspected falls. The video is cut into approximately 10,000 pictures by frame, of which about 2,500 pictures are fall behaviors. These pictures are labeled with FALL or NoFALL and then put into the DeepCut model. The data of the 14 key points of the human body are output, and then put these data into the fall detection depth neural network to output the model for training. After about 200 times of training, the accuracy of detection fall is stable at around 98%, Finally, a model with 150 iterations was adopted. Then the built fall model is used to do the test in the test data set. Figure 6 to Figure 12 show some test examples for detecting person’s behavior about FALL and NoFALL, where NoFALL includes the following behaviors: erect walk, sit down, bend over, squatting down. In addition, NoFALL also test some abnormal conditions, which are listed in the following and shown in Figure 10 and Figure 11: part of the body’s behavior is blocked and obscured, part of the body is on the edge of detection camera. Fall behavior detections examples are shown in Figure 12.

A test including 1229 events are performed in our experiments. The performance of the fall detection was evaluated using the test arrangement with the same as the literature (Rimminen et al., 2010). The performance is tested using sensitivity and specificity, where sensitivity shows the ability to detect fall events, and specificity shows the ability to classify not fall events.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch078.m03](i/ch078.m03.svg) (3)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch078.m04](i/ch078.m04.svg) (4)

where TP (True Positive) is the fall events to be successfully classified, FP (False Positive) is the fall events to be incorrect classified, TN (True Negative) is the NoFALL events to be successfully classified, and FN (False Negative) is the activities to be incorrect classified.

Table 1 shows the number of events in test results. From Table 1 we can see that the presented method obtains 100% fall detection rate at the experimental environment, where the sensitivity of our method is 93.1%, and the specificity is 97.3%. The false positive rate on the test set is around 1.95%. In fact, this kind of false positive is unlikely to happen continuously. For example, if an old man bends over and is detected as falling, he or she will recover in a short time to the state of upright walk, so we have set a certain mechanism in the system to deal with this situation, and the impact of the 1.95% false positive rate can be greatly reduced or even ignored. We all know that in terms of computer vision image processing, the processing speed of images is very important, and the requirements for hardware performance are also very high. After testing, under the premise of ensuring accuracy, the processing time of 100 images is approximately 19.2 seconds. The average time for one picture is less than 0.2 seconds, so the proposed method deployed on the cloud platform takes up very little resources and can perform high concurrency.

In our implemented system, when the fall is real-time detected, the server will recall WeChat and SMS interface to send the fall message or picture to the event subscriber. 5\. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

Considering that the presented method avoids the wearable sensors’ disadvantages, the results are very helpful to detect falls among the elderly. This system is mainly designed for elderly people living alone, but it has good scalability and is suitable for anyone who has hidden dangers and is difficult to take care of themselves, such as elderly people in nursing homes, patients in hospital inpatient departments, mentally deficient people, and infants whose brains are not yet fully developed, and so on. The fall detection system acquires images through the installed webcam and uploads them to the cloud for processing. If the cloud server detects the fall, it will notify the outside world through SMS and WeChat, the pixel requirements of the camera are not high, and the whole system is low-cost and easy to deploy. Currently, our system does not consider the messages encryption between web camera and cloud server, and we consider that an attribute-based encryption which is cloud-aided online/offline ciphertext-policy in the standard model (Wang, Zheng & Wang, 2017) will be used for improving our system’s security and privacy protection in future work.

ABSTRACT

According to the recent surveys, breast cancer has become one of the major causes of mortality rate among women. Breast cancer can be defined as a group of rapidly growing cells that lead to the formation of a lump or an extra mass in the breast tissue which consequently leads to the formation of tumor. Tumors can be classified as malignant (cancerous) or benign (non-cancerous). Feature selection is an important parameter in determining the classification systems. Machine learning methods are the most commonly used methods among researchers for breast cancer diagnosis. This paper proposes to investigate the WBCD (Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset) which comprises of 683 patients and implements the chosen features to train the back propagation neural network. The performance is then analyzed on the basis of classification accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictor values, receiver operating characteristic curves and confusion matrix. A total of 9 features has been used to classify breast cancer with an accuracy of 99.27%. According to the recent surveys, breast cancer has become one of the major causes of mortality rate among women. Breast cancer can be defined as a group of rapidly growing cells that lead to the formation of a lump or an extra mass in the breast tissue which consequently leads to the formation of tumor. Tumors can be classified as malignant (cancerous) or benign (non-cancerous). Feature selection is an important parameter in determining the classification systems. Machine learning methods are the most commonly used methods among researchers for breast cancer diagnosis. This paper proposes to investigate the WBCD (Wisconsin Breast Cancer Dataset) which comprises of 683 patients and implements the chosen features to train the back propagation neural network. The performance is then analyzed on the basis of classification accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictor values, receiver operating characteristic curves and confusion matrix. A total of 9 features has been used to classify breast cancer with an accuracy of 99.27%.

INTRODUCTION

Breast cancer is the malignant tumor, which starts in the cells of the breast and can attack surrounding tissues or extend to remote areas of the body. Typically, breast cancer either starts in the cells of lobules that are the milk-producing glands, or the ducts which over time can occupy the nearby healthy breast tissue and create their way into the underarm lymph nodules or the small organs which filter out the foreign substances in the body. If the cancer cells get into the lymph nodules, then they have an alley way into the other parts of the body. There were more than 2.8 million women with the history of breast cancer in the U.S that comprises women presently being treated and the women who have completed the treatment in 2014. A woman’s possibility of breast cancer more or less doubles if she has a first-degree relative like mother, sister, and daughter who has been analyzed with breast cancer. About 15% of women who get the breast cancer have a family member identified with it. About 5-10% of breast cancers can be connected to gene mutations hereditary from one’s mother or father. Mutations of the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes are the most ordinary. Women with the BRCA1 mutation have a 55-65% risk of increasing the breast cancer before age 70, and frequently at a younger age that it classically develops. For women with the BRCA2 mutation, this risk is about 45% (Acharya et al., 2008; Sengupta et al., 2014).

Although breast cancer is considered to be one of the most fatal diseases, it is also one of the most curable diseases if it can be diagnosed at an early stage. Early diagnosis needs a precise and reliable diagnosis procedure that allows physicians to distinguish between benign breast tumors and malignant ones (Abbadi et al., 2014). Since, the radiologists find difficulty in mammographic examination the scope of human error in precise diagnosis of the disease increases, thus resulting in the need for the development Computer Assisted Detection (CAD) (Wani et al., 2014). The concept of CAD involves taking into account the roles of both the computer and the physicians on equal grounds. The results of the computer need not be better than the result developed by the physicians; rather they need to be complementary. When lateral chest images are diagnosed with the help of CAD, the general presentation in the recognition of lung swellings is enhanced when integrated with another CAD scheme for testing PA chest images. CAD also finds its way in reliable and precise detection of vertebral fractures, thus making the early detection of osteoporosis possible (Doi, 2007).

The evolution of automated diagnosis was spurred by the need to assist physician in decision making. Machine learning methods have become indispensable in the field of medical science and hence are currently being employed in various classification methods due to their meticulous prediction performance. Machine learning involves learning a specific set of rules whereby the first step is the collection of dataset. If this dataset has been obtained by any random method then it cannot be subjected to survey since it might contain noisy, irrelevant or redundant data. Here data preprocessing and feature subset selection comes in as the second step which is responsible for removing all irrelevant and redundant data, thus making the data more concise so that the algorithms can perform with more efficiency. Thus, choosing a suitable classification technique is imperative for the correct diagnosis of a disease and gets the desired results. Various classifier techniques have been used such as Support Vector Machines combined with feature selection in (Subashini et al., 2009), analysis of SEER Dataset for Breast Cancer Diagnosis using C4.5 Classification Algorithm in (Rajesh et al., 2012), Naive Bayes Classifiers: A Probabilistic Detection Model for Breast Cancer (Kharya et al., 2014).

This paper proposes to use Levenberg-Marquardt back propagation algorithm to train the system. This algorithm was chosen due to a high rate of successful classification. Neural networks are those information processing systems, which are formulated and enacted to model the human brain. An artificial neural network is a competent information processing system which replicates the characteristics of a biological neural network. ANNs possess a large number of highly interconnected processing elements called nodes or units or neurons, which usually operates in parallel. There is a connection link connecting every neuron and each connection link is associated with weights which contain information about the input signal. The information is used by the neuron net to elucidate a particular problem. Ann’s collective behavior is designated by their ability to learn recall and generalize training patterns or data similar to that of a human brain. They have the skill to model networks of original neurons found in the brain. In this study, 90% of the overall dataset is used for training, 5% for validation and rest 5% for testing.

BACKGROUND

Extensive research has been carried out for efficient breast cancer treatment and a number of research reports have been submitted with different accuracy levels for different diagnosis methods. In 2009 M. F. Akay et al. proposed on SVM-based method integrated with feature selection which has ensued in the highest classification rate of 99.51%. In 2011 S. Aruna et al. proposed to detect breast cancer with a feature selection algorithm CSSFFS (Constrained Search Sequential Floating Forward Search) based on SVM which aspired to achieve a feature subset with Balanced Error Rate (BER). Post feature selection method, a total of 15 features has analyzed the accuracy and BER for WBDC dataset as 98.2425 and 0.0226; respectively. In 2012, Rajesh et al. proposed C4.5 classification algorithm on SEER dataset to distinguish patients into “Carcinoma in situ” (beginning or pre-cancer stage) or “Malignant potential” group with an accuracy of 86.7%. Priyanga and Prakasam (2013). proposed a system for cancer prediction system based on data mining. It estimated the risk of the skin, breast, and lung cancers. It provided the earlier warning to the users. In 2013, Azizi et al. developed an indigenous computer assisted diagnosis method for the treatment of breast cancer which is based on the amalgamation of three support vector machine classifiers. In 2014 S. Chaurasia et al. discussed the approach of using Support Vector Machine using variable features selection method for breast cancer prognosis and the accuracy was evaluated to be 96.4%.

In the year 2014, Sumbaly et al. proposed to use a Decision tree algorithm-CART as a classification method to calculate the accuracy, time required to build a model and size of the tree based on the various Breast Cancer datasets both including and excluding the feature selection method.

METHODOLOGY

Back Propagation Neural Network (BPN) Algorithm

Initially all the inputs are applied and corresponding outputs are calculated. Here the initial outputs could be anything as initial weights are arbitrary values. The error of neuron B is found. Error is (Desired result – observed result), in other words:

ErrorB = OutputB (1-OutputA) (TargetA– OutputA) (1)

Next, the weight is changed. Let W[1] be the new (trained) weight given by:

W[1]\= W[1] + (ErrorB x OutputA) (2)

The differences for the hidden layer neurons are assessed. But, these errors can’t be calculated directly; and hence it is required to back propagate them from the output layer. So we need to take these errors from the output neuron and run them backward through its weights to obtain the underlying layer errors. After obtaining the errors for the hidden layer neuron, go to step 3 to change hidden layer weights. By repeating this method a network can be trained with any number of layers.

Breast Cancer Detection in Classification Paradigm

Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) is the technology used for discriminating and imitation of cancer. Even though CAD is not edged to a single type of cancer, the large number of CAD schemes to date have been intended and applied for the diagnosis of the breast cancer. Computer-Aided Diagnosis (CAD) requests more and more awareness for the brain tumor diagnosis. Computer-Aided Diagnosis system (CAD) can be awfully valuable in detecting and diagnosing the breast abnormalities former and sooner than distinctive viewing programs. This paper presents the recovery and ANN (Artificial neural network) based categorization system for the computer aided diagnosis of the breast cancer using texture features. There are various training mechanisms used in ANN classification such as trainlm, trainrp, trainscg, etc. Among all these training mechanisms, trainlm has been opted for breast cancer diagnosis due to its capability to produce results of high accuracy as compared to trainscg and trainrp, which has an accuracy of 97.66% and 98.24%; respectively.

In order to distinguish between a normal and abnormal breast image using CAD software, a training based system was used. Specifically, artificial neural network (ANN) methodology was employed as shown below in the Figure 1. Levenberg-Marquardt back propagation algorithm was used for training the system. This algorithm was chosen due to a high rate of successful classification. ANN’s can be thought of as weighted directed graph where artificial neurons are thought of as nodes and the directed edges in between the nodes denote the connection between neuron output and input. Depending upon the connection pattern, ANN can be grouped under two broad categories i.e., feed forward network and feedback network. Utilizing ANN, it can automatically learn itself from previous experiences. Learning is a basic form of intelligence. This algorithm provides a numerical solution for minimizing a non-linear function and with a fast and stable convergence. This algorithm is mostly used for training small and medium sized problems in ANN. This technique can be used to overcome the slow convergence of traditional back propagation algorithm and the instability problem of the steepest descent optimization method. In this study, data of 683 different patients were collected which included either benign or malignant patients. Normal patients were not taken into consideration. The various features which include clump thickness, bland chromatin, and uniformity of cell shape, single epithelial cell size, bare nuclei, normal nucleoli, marginal adhesion, and mitosis were able to distinguish between a benign breast and a malignant one based on the trained set. The features have been discussed below:\-

*   1\. Clump Thickness: Benign cells lean to be clustered in mono layers, whereas cancerous cells are frequently assembled in multi layers.
*   2\. Uniformity of Cell Shape: Cancer cells are liable to diverge in size and shape. That’s why these constraints are important in seminal whether the cells are cancerous or not.
*   3\. Marginal Bond: Normal cells apt to attach mutually but cancer cells tend to misplace this capability. So loss of union is a symbol of malignancy.
*   4\. Single Epithelial Cell Size: It is related to regularity which already mentioned above. Epithelial cells that are considerably inflamed may be a malignant cell.
*   5\. Bare Nuclei: This is a tenure used for the nuclei which is not enclosed by the cytoplasm. Those are usually seen in benign tumors.
*   6\. Bland Chromatin: Describes an identical “texture” of the nucleus seen in benign cells. In the cancer cells the chromatin leans to be coarser.
*   7\. Normal Nucleoli: Nucleoli are the small formations seen in nucleus. In usual cells the nucleolus is typically very small if noticeable at all. In the cancer cells the nucleoli turn into more famous, and occasionally there are more of them.
*   8\. Mitosis: The most familiar form of cell division is called the mitosis. It is used for expansion and renovate. During the mitosis, a cell makes a strict copy of it and cracks into two new cells. Each cell surrounds an accurate copy of the original cell's chromosomes in their 23 pairs. This is the basis why all the cells in an organism are genetically equal.

The efficiency of the classifier was determined by the ratio of the number of correctly classified high risk CAD to the actual high risk CAD patients. For the optimal feature selection varying combinations of training, validation and test ratio were implemented.

In Figures (2-6) given below, the confusion matrix, ROC curve, performance validation, error histogram and regression curve respectively are seen for the 683 breast cancer patients. A confusion matrix as shown in Figure 4 contains information regarding actual and predicted classifications which are performed by a classification system. The performance of such systems was measured using the data in the matrix. The entries present in the confusion matrix represent the following meaning:

*   • a is the number of correct predictions that an instance is negative,
*   • b is the number of incorrect predictions that an instance is positive,
*   • c is the number of incorrect of predictions that an instance negative, and
*   • d is the number of correct predictions that an instance is positive.

Accuracy (AC) is defined as the proportion of the total number of predictions that are correct. It is calculated using the following equation:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch079.m01](i/ch079.m01.svg) (3)

In this study, high risk CAD denotes an abnormal breast and low risk CAD denotes a normal breast. While, defining the standard performance metrics for sensitivity analysis were adapted by defining true negative (TN), true positive (TP), false negative (FN) and false positive (FP). This implies that TN is the total number of low-risk CAD cases that are classified as low risk CAD. TP is the total number of high-risk CAD cases that are classified as high risk CAD. FN is the total number of high risk CAD cases that are classified as low risk CAD. FP is total number of high risk CAD cases that are classified as low risk CAD.

Sensitivity is known as the probability that a classifier will give a high risk CAD label for a breast dataset, and is computed as TP/ (TP+FN). Specificity is a measure of the probability that the classifier will result in a low risk CAD label when used on low risk CAD patients and is calculated as: TN/(TN+FP). Positive predictive value (PPV), which is defined as the probability of patient’s label as high risk CAD correctly diagnosed, is denoted as TP/(TP+FP). Negative predictive value (NPV), which is given as the probability of patient’s label as high risk CAD incorrectly diagnosed and is calculated as TN/ (TN+FN). Accuracy is defined as the ratio of the number of correctly classified high risk CAD to the high risk CAD patients, and is calculated as (TP+TN)/ (TP+FP+TN+FN).

*   In our study TP= 442, FP=3, FN= 2 and TN=236.

We have obtained 99.27% successful classification accuracy in our study.

It performs accurate classification for all the positive cases and negative cases correctly. The (0, 1) point denotes that the true positive rate is 1 (all) and false positive rate is 0 (none). The (0, 0) point denotes a classifier that predicts all the cases to be negative, whereas the point (1, 1) corresponds to a classifier which predicts every case to be positive. The point (1, 0) is the classifier which represents that it is incorrect for all the classifications.

CONCLUSION

In this current study, back propagation neural network is used to classify benign and malignant images. Here, different features are extracted from the whole image without any manual selection of region of interest (ROI). Selection of features from ROI is always a lengthy task which is biased by the person’s experience and degree of precision. Our proposed system shows 99.27% accuracy, while sensitivity and specificity is 99.55% and 98.74% respectively. A high accuracy along with sensitivity and specificity shows the effectiveness of our proposed system.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Breast Cancer: Breast cancer is the expansion of cancer from breast tissue. Symptoms of breast cancer may comprise a lump in breast, an alter in breast shape, liquid coming from the nipple, a red peeling scrap of skin or dimpling of the skin,. In those with outlying increase of the disease, there may be swollen lymph nodes, bone pain, yellow skin or shortness of breath.

Machine Learning: Machine learning is the scientific discipline that compacts with the structure and study of the algorithms which can be learnt from data. Such algorithms function by the building a model based on the inputs and using that to create forecasts or conclusions, relatively than subsequent only unambiguously programmed instructions.

Malignant: Malignancy is the trend of a medical condition to become progressively inferior. It is the most familiar as a categorization of cancer. A malignant tumor distinguishes with a non-cancerous benign tumor in which a malignancy is not the self-limited in its growth. It is competent of invading into contiguous tissues, and may be proficient of spreading to distant tissues. A benign tumor has not any of those properties.

ABSTRACT

Cervical Cancer is one of the most common cancers among women worldwide. Few concerns have arisen such as the shortage of skilled pathologists leading to increase in burden on them. This requires a need for efficient and accurate method that diagnoses cervical cancer without human intervention. In this paper, an automated system is developed for diagnosis of cervical cancer using image processing techniques and neural networks. The system is developed using Cytology images taken from Bangalore based cancer pathologist. MATLAB image processing toolbox is used to extract features from cytology images that are used for discriminating various stages of cervical cancer. The dominant features used for diagnosis are Nucleus to cytoplasm ratio, shape, and color intensity along with nucleus area, perimeter and eccentricity. These features are used to train the neural network using Back-propagation algorithm of supervised training method. The cytology cells were then successfully classified as non-cancerous, low- grade and high-grade cancer cells.

INTRODUCTION

Cervical cancer in women is one of the most common cancers worldwide, next only to breast cancer. Middle- aged women between the ages of 40-55 years are mostly affected by this cancer. Every year cervical is diagnosed in about 500,000 women globally and is responsible for more than 280,000 deaths annually (Medindia, n.d.). Nowadays there is a wide variation in the number of cervical cancer cases across the globe. Risk factors include smoking, unprotected sex or having HIV infection, prolonged use of birth control pills. In the western side, prevalence of this disease is gradually decreasing because of the early detection through regular screening. 80% of the new cervical cancer cases occur in developing countries, like India, which reports approximately 1/4^(th) of the world’s cases of cervical cancer each year (Medindia, n.d.).

The National Cancer Control Program (NCCP) formulated and funded by the Ministry of Health, Government of India has stressed upon the implementation of community based cervical screening program at least in select districts of each state. The NCCP has made provision for fund to be given to all the states to implement the cancer control program that includes cervical cancer screening activities (Satija, n.d.; Basi, Chowdhury, n.d.).

Cervical cancer occurs when abnormal cells in the cervix multiply at a faster rate and grow out-of-control. The abnormal changes that the cervical cells develop transform them to a pre-cancerous state which is referred to as ‘Cervical Intraepithelial Neoplasia’ (CIN). Based on its degree or intensity, these changes are classified as low grade CIN and high grade CIN. This cancer is caused by a virus called Human Papilloma Virus (HPV).

Two popular screening tests which help in the early detection of cervical cancer or prevent cervical cancer are: (i) Pap test (or Pap smear)-looks for pre-cancer cell changes on the cervix. (ii) HPV test- looks for the HPV virus that causes the cell change. Another popular screening method is the Liquid Based Cytology (LBC). LBC is a way of preparing cervical samples for examination and diagnosis in the laboratory. Detection rate is higher using LBC than Pap test. All these processes are proved to be time consuming and might yield erroneous results. This paper presents an efficient and proficient method for the diagnosis of cervical cancer using Artificial Neural Networks from cytology images.

In the machine learning and cognitive science, ANN is a family of statistical learning model inspired by biological neurons. ANNs learn from standard data and capture the knowledge contained in the data. Trained ANNs approach the functionality of small biological neural cluster in a very fundamental manner. They are the digitized model of biological brain and can detect complex nonlinear relationships between dependent as well as independent variables in a data. Nowadays, ANNs are widely used for medical applications in various disciplines of medicine (Al-Zaytoonah, 2011).

The neural network is trained using the back-propagation algorithm of the supervised training method.

Lassouaoui, Hamami, and Nouali (2007) discuss morphological description of Cervical Cell Images for the pathological recognition. This may be used to develop a computer system which can help doctors in tracking the cervical cancer. It includes various algorithms for detection of the cellular components and the stage of discriminating the abnormal signs of cells. The descriptions are ratio core cytoplasm, the nuclear deformity, the cytoplasm deformity, the heterogeneous texture of each cell component and anisocariose. The obtained characteristic vectors of each cell are the input of the recognition stage of computer system of tracking the cervical cancer.

Supriyanto et al. (n.d.) developed a detection system that is able to differentiate between normal and cancerous cells by using colour intensity classification. Another method is proposed by Karthigai et al that separate both the nucleus and cytoplasm from the Pap smear cervical cytology images using linear contrast stretching. Further fuzzy thresholding and active contours were used by Karthigai and Krishnaveni (2013).

A novel method for automated detection of breast cancer using Artificial Neural networks has been proposed for the detection of Breast cancer in early stages (Singh, Harini, & Surabhi, 2014; Singh, Sushmitha, Harini, & Surabhi, 2014). Various techniques were designed for the classification of WDBC dataset only. The three features used for classification were area, perimeter and eccentricity. Singh et al. (2014) used only 20 images provided by WDBC dataset. The real clinical based slides were not verified by the methods used by Singh et al. (2014) and Singh et al. (2014). Also many important morphological features (Lassouaoui et al., 2007) were not explored in that paper.

The work is an extension to the work of Singh et al. (2014) and Singh et al. (2014). This paper focuses on maximum dominant features as compared to all the cited references. With the inputs from Cancer pathologist, the prominent morphological features like shape, nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio and colour intensity were added to the work done in Singh et al. (2014). Moreover, the work is developed and validated with real clinical slides rather than from available database. In addition to the three added features, area, perimeter and eccentricity of ref Singh et al. (2014) is also used to develop more robust diagnosis system. A Graphical User Interface was developed to give the final diagnosis result for the specific case to be non-cancerous, low-grade or high-grade cancer from REAL biopsy slides directly.

The major contribution of this paper is an integration of all the works mentioned above along with inputs from cervical cancer pathologist is considered. Important feature of nucleus to cytoplasm ratio is added for efficient classification of cancer. Over hundreds of real cervical cell images from Bangalore based pathology clinic is used for development and validation of the proposed method. Also, ANN is used to design an automated system to classify biopsy cell images into cancerous and non-cancerous. Cancerous cells are further classified as Low-grade and High-grade cells. This is implemented on GUI for an Automated System.

MORPHOLOGICAL FEATURES

Biological features in the biopsy slide images presented in Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3 that distinguish between non-cancerous, low-grade cancer and high-grade cancer cells is studied in order to extract these features. Morphologically cancer cells are characterized by larger nuclei having an irregular size and shape. In these malignant cells, nuclei in the cells are prominent; cytoplasm is scarce and intensely coloured.

As per the inputs given by a pathologist, the three main distinguishing features between cancerous and non-cancerous cells are:

*   1. Nucleus-to-Cytoplasm Ratio: It is seen that this ratio is high for cancerous cells and less for non-cancerous cells, because of the larger nuclei (Karthigai & Krishnaveni, 2013; Mahanta & Bora, 2012); 
    *   2\. Shape: Depending on the intensity of the cancer, the cancer cells are of two types, Low-grade and High-grade. Low-grade cells are mostly circular in shape whereas high grade cells are tapered and possess spindle like structure;
    *   3\. Colour Intensity: Colour intensity is one the important cell morphological features that distinguishes between Cancerous and non-cancerous cells. Colour intensity is referred to colour pixel distribution in a cell. The larger nuclei area indicates the bigger proportion of darker pixels in the cell. Cancerous and non-cancerous cells have distinctively different colour intensity distribution (Lassouaoui et al., 2007; Supriyanto et al., n.d.).

In addition to these prominent features, nucleus area, nucleus perimeter and eccentricity (Singh et al., 2014) of the cell are also considered.

PRE-PROCESSING TECHNIQUES

This section includes information about the pre-processing techniques followed:

*   • RGB-to-Gray Scale Conversion: The real-time images collected were of high-resolution and in JPEG format. The function ‘rgb2gray’ converts the colour image (Figure 4) into a gray-scale image (Figure 5).
*   • Intensity Adjustment: The contrast of the gray scale image is enhanced by transforming the values using Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE). The ‘imadjust’ function operates on small regions in the image, called tiles, rather than the entire image. Presented in Figure 6.
*   • Gray-Scale to Binary Conversion: The gray-scale image is converted to binary image. The ‘im2gray’ function replaces all pixels in the input image with luminance greater than level with the value 1 (white) and replaces all other pixels with the value 0 (black). Presented in Figure 7.
*   • Complementing and Filling Holes in the Image: ‘imcomp’ computes the complement of the image where black and white are reversed. The function ‘imfill’ fills the holes in the binary image. In this function, a hole is a set of background pixels that cannot be reached by filling in the holes the background from the edge of the image. Presented in Figure 8.
*   • Morphological Opening of the Image: The morphological function of erosion followed by dilation, using the same structuring element for both the operations. Function ‘imopen’ is used.
*   • Edge Detection: Out of 5 methods of edge detection - Sobel, Prewitt, Log, Robert and Canny, Canny edge detection technique gave the best results. Edge detection results may be improved further, though the present result is sufficient to diagnose the cancer using neural network. Canny method finds edges by looking for local maxima of the gradient of the image. Presented in Figure 9.
*   • Watershed Segmentation: Identifies the watershed regions of the input matrix which have any dimension. Presented in Figure 10.
*   • Perimeter: This process returns a binary image containing only the perimeter pixels of objects in the input image. The MATLAB function implemented here is the ‘bwperim’. Presented in Figure 11.
*   • Labelling: Every object in the cell image and the nuclei image is labelled for the correct mapping of cell to its nuclei. Presented in Figure 12.

FEATURE EXTRACTION

The pre-processing is followed by the feature extractions which are used to distinguish between the cell images:

*   • Nucleus-to-Cytoplasm ratio: Separation of the nuclei from the cell involved the following steps: converting the RGB image to gray- scale, applying a ‘Gaussian’ filter and setting a threshold to separate nuclei. The threshold value is set by observing the intensity values of the nuclei using ‘impixel’ function in MATLAB. Area of nuclei and cell is calculated using ‘regionprops’. Ratio of these areas is calculated. A threshold value for the ratio is set to distinguish cancerous and non-cancerous cells. Presented in Figure 13 and Figure 14.
*   • Shape: To determine the shape of the cell, major-axis length and minor-axis length of the cell is considered. The ratio of these lengths is calculated. Presented in Figure 15.
*   • Colour Intensity: Intensity of each cell in the image is calculated. Non-cancerous cells have a higher intensity value and Cancerous cells have a lower intensity.

PROCEDURE

Real time biopsy images are acquired in JPEG format and converted to gray scale for processing. Out of 38 images, 12 are high grade cancerous cell images, 10 are low grade cancerous cell images and 16 non-cancerous cell images. Each cell image has approximately 4-7 detectable cells totalling to 228 cells approximately.

Once pre-processing is done on the image, features from the cell are extracted.

After extraction of features from all the images, ANN is used to train the network to classify cells as non-cancerous, low-grade and high grade. Supervised training algorithm (Back Propagation) is used to train the network (Lassouaoui et al., 2007; Supriyanto et al., n.d.).

Network consists of 6 input neurons, 2 output neurons and 20 hidden layers. 6 input neurons represent the 6 features- Nucleus area, Nucleus perimeter, Colour intensity, Nucleus-to-Cytoplasm Ratio, Major axis-to-Minor axis Ratio and Eccentricity. The 2 binary output neurons represent: (0,0) – non-cancerous, (0,1) – Low Grade and (1,1) – High Grade. After experimenting with different number of neurons in the hidden layer, neural network with 20 hidden layer neurons gave the best result.

Back propagation is a form of supervised training. When using a supervised training method, the network must be provided with both sample inputs and anticipated outputs. The anticipated outputs are compared against the actual outputs for given input. Using the anticipated outputs, the back propagation training algorithm then takes a calculated error and adjusts the weights of the various layers backwards from the output layer to the input layer.

Graphical User Interface (GUI) is incorporated to ease the user experience. The user does not have to type or give any commands; instead there are specific commands that enable user to perform tasks. The GUI consisted of 6 push buttons and 3 axes as presented in Figure 16. The 6 push buttons and their functions:

*   • Load Image: To select the biopsy slide image and display on axis1.
*   • Detect Edge: To display edge detected cell of the selected image on axis2.
*   • Detect Nuclei: To display edge detected nuclei of the selected image on axis3.
*   • Load Input: Extracted features from the biopsy slide in the vector form to be fed to the neural network.
*   • Analyse: Neural network processes the input feature vector to classify cell into low-grade, high grade or non-cancerous. Presented in Figure 17, Figure 18, and Figure 19.
*   • Exit: Exit from GUI.

DISCUSSION OF RESULTS

Features from around 38 images were extracted. This formed the input database for the neural network. The input parameters included nucleus area, nucleus perimeter, cell eccentricity, nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, major axis-to-minor axis ratio and colour intensity of the cell. After the training of the Neural Network, the biopsy slide images were successfully classified as non-cancerous, low-grade and high grade cells. Neural network was interfaced on GUI to increase the convenience of usage.

The work is developed and validated with REAL clinical slides rather than from available database as in Singh et al. (2014) and Singh et al. (2014). A Graphical User Interface was developed to give the final diagnosis result for the specific case to be non-cancerous, low-grade or high-grade cancer from REAL biopsy slides directly which is not seen in any of the literatures mentioned.

The accuracy obtained is 79%, with sensitivity and specificity of 94% and 68.2% respectively. Accuracy, sensitivity and specificity obtained in Singh et al. (2014) is 97.51%, 96% and 99.12% respectively. However, Singh et al. (2014) used WDBC database for slide images. The method presented in this paper is robust enough to handle the biopsy slides directly from a cancer diagnostic centre. However, further work may be carried over to improve the accuracy of the method. Supriyanto et al. (n.d.) used only one feature (Colour intensity) whereas Karthigai and Krishnaveni (2013) and Mahanta and Bora (2012) also used only one feature (Nucleus to Cytoplasm ratio) for diagnosis of cancer. They did not indicate the accuracy of their results. Moreover, classification of stages of cancer is not explored in the seen literature. This work could achieve specificity of 68.2% (classification between high grade and low grade cancer) which may be improved in further work.

CONCLUSION

Current prevalent method used by pathologists for the diagnosis of cervical cancer is to manually observe the morphological changes in the cells by physical examinations; however, manual observation is very subjective and poses several problems. The proposed method of automated diagnosis of cervical cancer can reduce such discrepancies and workload of pathologists.

Objective of neural network based cancer detection was successfully achieved by classifying the images into cancerous and non-cancerous cells. Cancerous cells were further classified into high grade and low grade cancer. However the classification accuracy between high grade and low grade needs further work. Neural network based method is classifying the cancer slides based on six important features, i.e. nucleus area, nucleus perimeter, cell eccentricity, nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio, major axis-to-minor axis ratio and colour intensity of the cell. Image processing toolbox of MATLAB is used to extract these features from REAL slides obtained from Bangalore based cancer diagnostic centre.

Accuracy obtained with proposed method is 79%. Further work may be carried out to improve accuracy of this method. Also the complete automated system (image processing steps and neural network system) may be implemented on DSP hardware.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Biomedical and Clinical Engineering (IJBCE), 4(2); edited by Natarajan Sriraam, pages 26-39, copyright year 2015 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).
