# Chapter 87

A Critical Review of the Use and Implications for Learner-Centered Pedagogies

*   Anne W. Kanga  
    Catholic University of Eastern Africa, Kenya

ABSTRACT

This chapter is a critical review of conventional and not so conventional Student-Centered Learning (SCL) pedagogies. Additionally, in the African context, educational institutions have been caught up in a theoretical approach to teaching and learning, characterized by a desire to pass examinations. Consequently, this approach leads to surface learning as opposed to deep learning. Hence, teaching and learning outcomes lack quality and definitely fails to meet and promote skills required by the fast changing modern and postmodern global world. To address this need, this chapter examines the following: Overview of SCL pedagogies; Conventional and not so Conventional SCL pedagogies; Implications for SCL pedagogies to learners, instructors, curriculum, and assessment. Finally, this chapter examines the misconceptions and advantages of adopting SCL in the light of learners and instructors.

INTRODUCTION

Informed by Confucius classical adages, “I hear and I forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand” (Confucius, 551-479 BC/2013), to learn without thinking \[and doing\] is labour in vain. As pointed out by O’Neill and McMahon (2005), to think without learning is desolation to the 21^(st) century rationale for Student Centered Learning (SCL). Hence, it is critically important to challenge, inform, and acquaint the 21^(st) century Teacher Education Programs (TEPs), instructors and learners to appreciate and adopt SCL pedagogies for effective teaching and learning, and most importantly, to nurture lifelong learners who are reflective, independent, active, creative and emotionally engaged in the teaching/learning process and later in the work place.

Many terms and phrases have been used to explain SCL also sometimes referred to as child-centered learning (CCL). However, for the purposes of this paper, and key audience – learners, teacher, and teacher education programs, the term SCL will be used. Additionally, since the focus of the handbook is teacher education and professional development, the concepts instructor and teacher are used in this paper to denote educators trained in pedagogy required to teach at the level of Teacher Education programs and educators trained to teach at the basic education level respectively. Abdullah, Osman, Shamsuddin, Yusoff and Ismail (2012) define student-centered learning pedagogy “as putting students first and focusing on the students’ needs, abilities, interests and learning styles, with the teacher \[instructor\] as a facilitator of learning” (p. 24). Student-Centered Learning has also been referred to as flexible learning, experiential learning and self-directed learning (Burnard, 1999; Taylor, 2000 as cited in O’Neill & McMahon, 2005.). There is no single widely agreed definition of SCL.

However, scholars and proponents of SCL approaches to teaching/learning concur that SCL is based on the philosophy that the student is at the heart of the learning process, that is, the student is the focal point of the process (Di Napoli, 2010; Education International, 2010; Harris, Spina, Ehrich & Smeed, 2013; Student Centered Learning, SCL, 2010). As the authors further contend, the role of the instructor remains indispensible especially at the level of addressing individual learner’s needs.

In this paper, I adopt Collins and O’Brien’s (2003) understanding of SCL as I perceive it as more operational. In their text, Dictionary of Education, Collins and O’Brien operationalized SCL as:

An instructional approach in which students influence the content, activities, materials, and pace of learning. This learning model places the student \[learner\] in the centre of the learning process. The instructor provides students with \[varied\] opportunities to learn independently and from one another and coaches them in the skills they need to do so effectively. The SCL approach includes such techniques as substituting active learning experiences for lectures, assigning open ended problems, and problems requiring critical or creative thinking that cannot be solved by following text examples, involving students in simulations and role plays, and using self paced and/or cooperative (team-based) learning. Properly implemented SCL can lead to increased motivation to learn, greater retention of knowledge, deeper understanding, and more positive attitudes towards the subject being taught (p. 343).

Student Centered learning can also be understood from its attributes which according to Iowa Core (n.d) are: “Construction of learning, collaborative learning, metacognition, educator/student partnerships, and authentic assessment” (p.2). In the light of SCL, by reflecting on their experiences, learners are better able to construct their own understanding of their world. This leads to deep learning as opposed to surface learning (O’Neill & McMahon, 2005).

Collaborative learning as a philosophy of interaction and personal lifestyle where individuals are responsible for their actions, including learning, respecting abilities and contributions of their peers has been found to make learning exciting and consequently improve learning outcomes. This was observed by Vygostky (1978) who asserted that learning is a social activity and therefore influences brain development. Vygostky further stressed that what learners can do with the assistance of others influences their brain development positively. As I have argued in this paper, SCL is highly collaborative in nature and practice.

Meta-cognition is the ability to reflect on ones current level of understanding, be able to decide whether it is adequate, and seek out and develop new approaches to understanding (National Research Council, 2000 as cited by Iowa Core, n.d). Hence, learners working together are better able to not only learn from others, be more self reflective, but the presence of peers is more likely to help them develop resilience and be able re-engage in a problem as opposed to giving up.

Student Centered learning encourages instructors and learners to work together more closely. With the instructor as a guide, a mentor and monitor, this relationship has the potential to blossom as he/she becomes an active participant of the team, who guides, manages activities and directs the teaching/learning process (Iowa Core, n.d).

Finally, authentic assessment and mainly formative assessment as an attribute of SCL helps to identify the differentiation of individual learning as a central component of student learning. A SCL approach helps the instructor to identify individual learner’s progress and identify gaps that need remedial. In its focus and practice, SCL approach and process informs progressive assessments (Iowa Core, n.d).

In light of the aforementioned understandings and attributes of SCL, this paper advances and foregrounds how teacher education and professional development can successfully engage a typical 21^(st) century classroom of learners that is characterized by diversity, disruptive and emerging technologies such as computer technology and related devices. Whereas there is no silver bullet to this achievement, SCL pedagogies have proven to be effective in empowering learners as teaching/learning process shifts from a teaching approach to a learning approach (Harris, Spina, Ehrich & Smeed, 2013; Keengwe, Onchwari & Onchwari, 2009; O’Neill & McMahon, 2005).

Specifically, this paper will critically analyze the concept - SCL pedagogy and bring out an understanding of conventional SCL pedagogies such small group teaching, case study method, seminar, tutorial, project method, improved lecture etc. Not so conventional SCL pedagogies especially in the African context to be discussed in this paper are but not limited to: problem based learning, peer observation, web supported inquiry based learning, competence based learning, debates, portfolio writing, and field trips among others. Advantages and challenges embedded in the use of SCL pedagogies are also addressed. Finally, a section on what adoption of SCL pedagogies means to learners, instructors and the work place is hoped to both challenge and appraise instructors and learners alike to embrace and appreciate SCL pedagogies.

In their book “preparing teachers for a changing world: What teachers should learn and be able to do”, Darling-Hammond and Bransford (2005), noted: “In the recent past, many teacher programs have been criticised for being overly theoretical, having little connection to practice, offering fragmented and incoherent courses, and lacking in clear, shared conceptions of teaching among faculty” (p. 391). They further noted that beginning in the late 1980s, teacher education reforms began to produce program designs representing more integrated, and coherent programs that emphasize a consistent vision of good teaching and learning.

According to Darling-Hammond and Bransford (2005), “What teachers \[learners\] learn matter as much as how they learn” (p. 395). More importantly, is the fact that learners learn different things not only from diverse programs, but they vary in their sense of self efficacy and effectiveness as a consequence of their learning experiences. Several studies have shown a positive relationship between teacher effectiveness and the quantity of training teachers have received in subject matter and content specific teaching methods (Begle, 1979; Druva & Anderson, 1983; Ferguson & Womack, 1993; Goldhaber & Brewer, 2000; Monk, 1994; Monk & King, 1994).

Dynamics cut across everything we are and do. Societies and respective institutions are dynamic. Specifically, from the mid 20^(th) Century, through the 21^(st) Century, a typical classroom has undergone radical changes in terms of demographics; nationalities; racial; ethnicities; lifestyles; age; different abilities; cultural responsiveness; SES among other categories of social difference. All these issues of diversity notwithstanding, for the last two decades, educators and researchers have expressed concern over the declining quality of teaching/learning and consequent educational outcomes. As this paper underscores, a paradigm shift in teaching and learning where focus shifts from the teacher and the teaching process, to the learner and the learning process has become inevitable (ONeill & McMahon, 2005). This has come as a re-awakening in the teaching process as evidenced by literature dating back to classical philosophers such as Socrates and later on by 20^(th) Century critical educational theorists such as Freire (1970). In his book “Pedagogy of the Oppressed”, Freire argued that as a higher education faculty member, he saw his role as a facilitator of learning, guiding his students to be active and critical participants and agents of their own learning.

Whereas, much has been achieved in this paradigm shift especially in the developed nations such as Canada, USA, UK, Australia, and other European Union nations (Sablonniere, Taylor & Sadykova, 2009), much needs to be done in terms of theorizing, research and practice in developing countries. Although Sablonniere et als study focused on Central Asia, their views mirror other third world contexts as they emphasized:

In Western societies, teachers and students have been exposed to both the teacher/expert and student centered approaches from public debates and also real life experiences in classrooms…In the United States, Canada and the European Union, teachers \[instructors\] spend significant resources to promote a student centred approach at all levels of education…such as cooperative learning, student centered instruction and hands-on learning. In Contrast to Western countries, the controversy surrounding teacher expert versus student- centered in Central Asia is radically different (Sablonniere et al, p. 1).

In the following section, an overview of SCL, historical, philosophical, theoretical, and tenets underpinning it are discussed.

SCL PEDAGOGIES: HISTORICAL, PHILOSOPHICAL, AND THEORETICAL PERSPECTIVES

In this chapter, I envision SCL as an approach, an idea, a process and a product informed by history, philosophies and theories. As a teaching/learning approach, SCL calls for teaching/learning strategies that focus on the needs, preferences, and interests of the learner. (Keengwe, Onchwari & Onchwari, 2009). It is also an idea that represents both a mind set and a culture often characterized by innovative methods of teaching and learning that emphasise students as the key players in learning by promoting their active participation at all stages of the teaching and learning process (Abdulla, Osman, Shamsuddin, Yusoff, & Ismail, 2012).

As a process, SCL aims at allocating students more time to construct their own knowledge, to explore, to research, to solve problems, and to engage in self reflection, while instructors act as facilitators (Abdualla, et al). It is also important to note that, as a process, SCL is dynamic, with new and better teaching and learning practices developing. Hence, its meaning and practice adopts a contextual understanding that is also influenced by time, emerging technologies and innovations. As a product, SCL is characterised by some of the following outcomes: more learner/instructor collaboration; development and acquisition of generic competencies and soft skills; education becomes a democratic practice where all are involved; students exhibit higher order thinking skills; lifelong learners; engenders cognitive maturation and meta-cognitive abilities (Ahn & Class, 2011; ESU, 2010).

The history of SCL can be credited to classical philosophers like Confucious, Socrates among others who argued for a hand on approach to teaching and learning. Later 20^(th) century theorists like John Dewey, Jean Piaget, Lev Vygotsky, Carl Rogers and Maria Montessori among others advanced the SCL theory and debate focusing on how students learn. Specifically, they focused on experiential education, with the learner as the centre of the teaching/learning process. Carl Rogers emphasized that “the only learning which significantly influences behaviour is self discovered” (Nooney, 2013).

Philosophies that inform SCL are progressivism, social re-constructionism and exisitentialism (Abdualla, et al). Progressivists see learners as individuals who have the right to progress at their own pace and they demand that teachers allow that to happen. John Dewey a major proponent of this theory, argued that SCL is a democratic practice in education, whereby individual learners bring their experiences into the classroom together with their needs and concerns. Hence, central to SCL, is the fact that teachers \[instructors\] need to respect diversity among learners and differences in them (Abdualla, et al).

Inherent in SCL is the social constructivist view. Proponents of this view argue that “education plays a crucial role in helping to solve society’s problems…This approach emphasises that education should address such problems” ((Abdualla, et al, p. 8). This view resonates with the view that education should be a panacea to society’s problems.

From an existentialist’s point of view, SCL aims at having the learner’s choice and free will to decide and be responsible for their own learning. SCL approaches such as competence based learning (Buswell & Becket, 2009) resonate with this philosophical view.

TENETS/PRINCIPLES OF SCL PEDAGOGIES

Education International \[EI\] and European Students’ Union \[ESU\] (2010) suggest some principles upon which SCL is anchored, which are:

*   Principle I: SCL requires an Ongoing Reflective Process. Teachers, students and institutions need to constantly reflect on their teaching, learning and infrastructural systems in order to continuously improve the learning experience of students. Ongoing reflective process also ensures that the intended learning outcomes of a given course or programme component are achieved in a way that stimulates learners’ critical thinking and transferable skills:
*   Principle II: SCL does not have a “One-Size-Fits-All” Solution. This is based on the idea that all higher education institutions, teachers and students are all different. As such, SCL is a learning approach that requires learning support structures which are appropriate to each given context and teaching and learning styles appropriate to those undertaking them.
*   Principle III: Students have Different Learning Styles. SCL recognises that students differ in their pedagogical needs. Some learn better through trial and error, others learn through practical experience. For some learners much is learned by reading literature, while others need to debate and discuss theory in order to understand it.
*   Principle IV: Students have Different Needs and Interests. All students have needs that extend beyond the classroom. Some are interested in cultural activities, others in sports or in representative organisations. Students may have families or may be faced with psychological conditions, illness or disability.
*   Principle V: Choice is Central to Effective Learning in SCL. Students like to learn a variety of things and hence, any offer should involve a reasonable amount of choice. Learning can be organised in liberal formats, such as at colleges of liberal arts or choice can be offered in a more traditional, disciplinary style.
*   Principle VI: Students have Different Experiences and Background Knowledge. \[Hence\], learning needs should be adapted to the life and professional experience of the individual concerned. For instance, if students already have considerable experience in using Information and Communication Technology (ICT), there is no point in trying to teach them the same thing again. If they already have considerable research skills, perhaps it would be better to help them apply these skills in practical research projects. Personal experiences can also be used to motivate students (e.g. by allowing them to share a personal story to illustrate a point and to reflect on their overall experiences).
*   Principle VII: Students should have Control Over their Learning. Students should be given the opportunity to be involved in the design of courses, curricula and their evaluation. They should be seen as active partners who have a stake in the way that higher education functions. The best way to ensure that learning focuses more on students is by engaging s them in how their learning should be shaped.
*   Principle VIII: SCL is about ›Enabling‹ not ›Telling‹. In simply imparting facts and knowledge to students (telling) the initiative, preparation and content comes mainly from the teacher\[instructor\]. The SCL approach aims to give the student greater responsibility enabling the student to think, process, analyse, synthesize, criticise, apply, solve problems, etc.
*   Principle IX: Learning needs Cooperation between Students and Staff. It is important that students and staff cooperate to develop a shared understanding both of the problems experienced in learning, as well as their problems as stakeholders within their given institution, jointly proposing solutions that might work for both groups. In the classroom, such cooperation will have a positive effect as the two groups increasingly come to consider each other as partners. Such a partnership is central to the philosophy of SCL which sees learning as taking place in a constructive interaction between the two groups.

CONVENTIONAL AND NOT SO CONVENTIONAL SCL PEDAGOGIES

In the foregoing discussion, critical to SCL is that learners are instructed less, lectured and talked at less. Instead, more time is used in learner engagement that requires them be proactive, active as opposed to being passive. These teaching /learning pedagogies that call for more learner engagement are discussed under two themes –Conventional and not so conventional SCL pedagogies. Simply, my definition of conventional in this paper is derived from the Dictionary meaning as what is generally done, and or SCL pedagogies that have been used in teacher education and especially, the pre-computer age. These have been, but not limited to: Improved lecture, questioning method, small group teaching (SGT), case study, seminar, tutorials, project method, Laboratory method, field trips, and portfolio writing (Brown & Atkins, 2002). Some of these pedagogies will be discussed briefly later.

The “not so conventional” SCL pedagogies are those for the purposes of this paper that call for more instructor reflection, innovation, ingenuity, and of course pedagogies that are ICT based. The latter, are SCL pedagogies that are “post computer age”. Selected “not so conventional SCL pedagogies in this paper are: problem based \[teaching\] and learning (PBL), Inquiry based learning (IBL), challenge based learning (CBL), peer observation/peer supported review of teaching (PSRT), Web supported Inquiry based learning (WSBL), and competence based learning (CBL).

Selected Conventional SCL Pedagogies

Small Group Teaching

Teachers/instructors who implement SCL move from whole-class instruction to small group and individual teaching (TEAL Centre, 2012). SGT teaching aims at getting students to talk, think and do. It also aims at developing communication skills such as listening, explaining, questioning and responding). In addition, SGT develops intellectual and professional competencies as well as promoting personal growth of students (Brown & Atkins, 1998). This method requires a controlled number of participants so that all group members can actively participate in the discussion (Ogula & Osongo, 2009). The variation of small group teaching encompasses buzz groups, brainstorming and snowballing (Brown & Atkins, 1998).

Although there is no consensus as to the number of members of small groups, Cuseo (n.d.) argues that when discussions occur in small groups ranging from two to four students, students become involved. Conversely, Ogula and Osongo suggest five to eight students as an optimal group size. In the light of SCL, instructors focus on topics of interest to small groups and create inquiry into those areas (TEAL, 2012). Active participation, face-to-face contact and purposeful activity are indispensible to ensure the learning process. As a result of this, there will be free exchange of ideas, students develop intimacy among themselves, students can detect their limitations on an issue and this propels them to search for more information in the areas of concern. Above all, SGT helps to develop leadership qualities (Ogula & Osongo, 2009).

Case Study Method

A case study is a strategy of inquiry in which an individual explores in depth a programme, event, activity, process, or one or more individual (Creswell, 2009). In similar way, case study has been defined as an in depth examination of a situation or a problem so as to understand the underlying causes or principles (Mugenda & Mugenda, 2003; Ogula & Osongo, 2009).

Within SCL context, different types of case studies may be used. For instance, Ogula and Osongo (2009) identified the following types of case studies: critical incident case study, next stage case study, live case study, major issues case study and role play case study. Critical incident case study – This involves the learners to follow a series of events leading to a problem occurrence with the hope of establishing the cause of the problem. In this type of case study, students are requested to find out the additional information needed to get a comprehensive scenario of the circumstances that led to the problem. Rawsthorme (n.d.), however, defines critical incident as an examination of a situation of unique interest.

Next stage case study entails a sequential description of a case and students are asked to mention what is likely to happen next. In live case study, students are presented with a situation and are expected to find out what is to be done about the situation. This is intended to test students’ factual knowledge of the situation, background as well as their ability to think quickly and carefully in analyzing issues in a short time.

Another type of case study is the major issues case study. Ogula and Osongo (2009) indicate that in this case, students are presented with an issue with a mass of information much of which is irrelevant to the issue. Thereafter, students have to indicate the issue or situation, identify what is relevant to it and suggest adequate solutions for the situation.

Role play case study is an additional type of case study envisaged in SCL. Under this variant, students are asked to act out the roles of main characters involved in an incident. They are then required to draw a conclusions on the incident.

Case study increases students’ active participation in the teaching and learning processes, validate experiential learning and offer relevant and realistic discussion of concrete issues and problems (Brown & Atkins, 2002). It also enhances students’ ability to find out the principles and causes behind certain phenomena. Additionally, case study empowers students to acquire knowledge, skills and attitudes that enable them to solve problems on related cases (Ogula & Osongo, 2009).

Tutorial Method

Charles (1977) defined tutorials as small, interactive classes that allow teaching staff to amplify and explain material delivered through lectures, and to monitor students’ progress and to facilitate discussion. Mills and Alexander (2013) defined tutorial as an approach to small group teaching in which students are required to write tutorial essays that involve researching, writing and critical thinking that brings about learning. According to the Griffith Institute for Higher Education (2015), tutorial is not a repeated lecture but it provides opportunities for participation by individual students who may respond to questions or pose questions of their own.

In tutorial approach, writing is crucial to student developing critical and informed perspectives of the topics to be explored. Following this approach, topics are presented for discussed between the tutor and tutees. The instructor acts as a constructive critic who helps the students explore possible avenues, rejecting one approach in favour of another. As Plalfreyman (2002) pointed out, the whole tutorial process turns around how one sees things, how one evaluates and, how one tends to connect one fact with another. Tutors also have the function of setting the student the task of expressing her/his thoughts articulately and then to assist her/him in subjecting her/his creation to critical examination. Apart from this, tutorials promote creative, transformative and even subversive nature of learning.

As a variant of SGT, tutorials enable the tutors to provide individual attention to students along with promoting a spirit of teamwork among students and the tutors (Ogula & Osongo, 2009). Tutorials also enable tutors and students to engage in a dialogue that demands more sophisticated levels of understanding and suggests new conceptions of learning (Plalfreyman, 2002). Taken as a complement to lectures, tutorials enable tutors to correct any misunderstanding and/or misconception that arose during a lecture (Griffith Institute for Higher Education, 2015; Ogula & Osongo, 2009).

Other forms of tutorial method of teaching as advanced by Curzon (2003) are: skills teaching tutorial, remedial tutorial, supervision tutorial and small group post lecture tutorial.

Not so Conventional SCL Pedagogies

Problem-Based Learning

Among the teaching methods that instructors may use to execute and implement the theoretical and practical teaching and learning approaches related to SCL include: PBL, IBL, Challenge based learning, PSRT/PR, WSIBL and CBL (Iowa CORE, n.d.). Within SCL context, problem-based learning enables students to learn more effectively as this method is based on the premise that by applying the knowledge students’ gain early on during the course of their learning, they are exposed to situations they would normally face outside the classroom and can thus become more adaptable (EI & ESU, 2010). Problem-solving learning also entails shifting instructors’ role from dispensing information to guiding the construction of knowledge by their students around ill-defined problems. Students are vested with the responsibility to refine the problem, develop research questions, investigate the topic using a variety of primary source material and work out a number of possible solutions before identifying the most reasonable ones (Johnson, 2009 as cited by Iowa CORE, n.d.).

As Ali et al. (2010) put it, in PBL, learners turn from passive listeners and receivers of information to active, free self-learners and problem solvers. In addition, the students learn new knowledge by facing the problem to be solved instead of feeling bored. On the other hand, the teachers/instructors act as facilitators, rather than primary sources information or dispensers of knowledge. This propels teachers/instructors to engage learners in marshalling information and using their knowledge in applied real settings.

Inquiry-Based Learning

Inquiry-based learning has as its main objective to provide learners with the opportunity to synthesize knowledge from various areas of learning and critically and creatively apply it to real life situations ((Iowa CORE, n.d.). IBL lays much emphasis on posing questions, gathering and analyzing data, and constructing evidence-supported arguments (Hmelo-Silver et al., 2007 as cited by Iowa CORE, n.d.). In the SCL approach, instructors act as supervisors of the teaching/learning process particularly in the institutions of higher learning where learners undertake research in their final year.

Challenge-Based Learning

According to (Johnson et al., 2009 as cited by Iowa CORE, n.d), CBL is a collaborative learning experience in which instructors and students work together to learn about compelling issues, propose solutions to real problems and take action. This strategy demands that students reflect on their learning and the impact of their actions as well as publish their solutions to a worldwide audience. CBL resonates with action research approached as collaboration between instructors and learners.

Peer Observation/Peer Supported Review of Teaching/\[Learning\] (PSRT)

Peer observation is a collaborative, developmental activity oriented approach in which professionals\[peers\] offer mutual support by observing each other teach, explaining ideas taught and observed, sharing ideas about teaching and students’ feedback and trying out new ideas (Bell, 2005). It is a collaborative non-judgmental \[teaching\] /learning process that involves two or more peers. It is intended to be a mutual process where all participants benefit from the ensuing dialogue. Its overall objective is to raise the status and role of teaching/\[learning\] to improve quality of the (\[teaching\]/learning experience (Gosling & Mason O’Connor, 2009). As D’Andrea (2012) pointed out, it is a forum for sharing teaching practices as opposed to making teaching a private activity

Web Supported Inquiry Based Learning (WSIBL)-E-learning

The WSIBL sometimes referred to as e-learning, online learning with its classroom as the cyber classroom has become a popular SCL strategy for several reasons such as medium for string information, presenting, gathering, sharing, processing and using information at will (Dong, 2009; Yao, & Yao, 2003; Zhang & Nunamaker, 2003). In a fast changing and dynamic world, WSIBL benefits learners and instructors by providing content in distributed infrastructure outlets, allowing collaboration and interaction, content delivery in various forms (i.e print, graphics, videos, animation etc), providing a friendly interface, not limited to time and space, and retrieval of information in a timely manner. However, success of WSIBL is highly dependent on reliable electricity, internet supplies and competent IT technocrats. Other than the various social media platforms used to facilitate Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs) like Coursera.org, several other software that run MOOCs are Moodle, WebCT, Blackboard among others. These softwares serve as excellent cyber classrooms for both instructors and learners.

Competence Based Learning

Competency based learning (CBL) and assessment is a process where an assessor works with a trainee to collect evidence of competence, using the benchmarks provided by the unit standards that comprise the national qualifications (Buswell, & Becket, 2009). In the course of a semester a learner may be required to undertake a series of tasks for assessment purposes such as assignments, projects, tests, exams or labs. It is the sum of all these assessments that deem a trainee to be competent (or not), based on set unit standards. The overall objective in CBL is mastery of knowledge and skills in the selected skill(s). To gauge whether competence is achieved or not, assessment process should be considered to be part of the learning process so that gaps can be identified as learning opportunities to help develop skills, not failures. It is a collaborative process to be negotiated with the learner.

IMPLICATIONS OF SCL TO SELECTED STAKEHOLDERS, LEARNING ENVIRONMENT, ASSESSMENT, AND LEARNING OUTCOMES

In order to have a comprehensive picture of SCL, it is worth considering what this paradigm shift in teaching and learning means to students, teachers/instructors, teaching methods, learning environment, assessment and learning outcomes. The following sections provide discussions on each of these aspects.

The Student

As an approach to learning, SCL requires that students choose not only what to study but also how to study (Di Nipali, 2010; O’Neill & McMahon, 2005; Teaching Excellence in Adult Literacy, TEAL Centre, 2012). In addition to this, SCL is committed to teaching students how to think (Tsui, 2002), how to learn and develop lifelong learning skills such as critical thinking, problem solving and communication skills (Cuseo, n.d.). Therefore, within SCL, learners are empowered to become active participants in their own learning (Harris et al. 2013). In so doing, students spend less time being lectured at or talked at and more time involved in the learning activities that demand them to do something (O’Neill & McMahon, 2005). This learner involvement helps them to construct their own knowledge, explore, solve problems leading to self-direction (Abdullah, Osman, Shamsuddin, Yusof & Ismail, 2012). As such, this approach incorporates teaching strategies that focus on the needs, preferences, and interests of learners (Keengwe, Onchwari & Onchwari, 2009).

More so, SCL takes into account students’ emotional states of mind, learning rates, talents, feeling of efficacy, backgrounds, interests, abilities and experiences (McCombs & Whilsler, 1988). Additionally, SCL approach considers students’ language differences, diverse learning styles, sexual orientation, learning disabilities, different developmental levels, socio-economic status, learning experience, religion, social class, race, ethnicity, physical and emotional abilities (Keengwe et al, 2010), and so, each student needs to be taken as distinct and unique (TEAL Centre, 2012).

In SCL, students are active participants in their own learning process, they take responsibility for their learning, and they are co-creators in the learning process. Additionally, students construct their own meaning by talking, listening, writing, reading and reflecting on content, ideas, issues and concerns (Di Napoli, 2004). In this regard, SCL is considered informed by the constructivist perspective of learning. This perspective posits that students must construct and reconstruct knowledge, in order to learn more effectively (Education International, 2010). This implies that students are active participants in creating their own knowledge by connecting between new information and their existing knowledge, experience and ideas (Harris et al. (2013). Reconstruction of knowledge requires students to work in collaboration with other students (TEAL Centre, 2012). Similarly, students are required to work with instructors to select learning goals and objectives based on authentic problems and students’ prior knowledge, interests and experience (Di Napoli, 2004).

Implication for Instructors

Within SCL framework, instructor assumes the role of a guide who helps students in the difficult process of constructing their knowledge (De la Sablonnniere, Talyor & Sadykova, 2009). Instructors also play the role of facilitators or mediators of the learning process (Ali, Hukamdad, Akhter and Khan (2010) as “students cannot be taught – they can only be helped to learn” (Jones, 2007, p. 25). Jones also asserts that as facilitators, instructors assist and encourage students to develop their skills while retaining the role of source of information, advice and knowledge. As such, teachers/instructors and students are a team working together and the former ensure that everyone student benefits from the lesson, supporting one another.

Other key tasks of facilitators include being but not limited to: (a) an educational designer who designs and creates learning tasks and classroom conditions that are conducive to active student involvement; (b) educational coach whose role consists of facilitating the learning rather than presenting it (O’Neill & McMahon, 2005), coordinating and orchestrating learning while students play the role of active participants in the learning process; (c) educational assessor who evaluates the effectiveness of learning by collecting data on learning outcomes and using this data as feedback to improve the learning process (Cuseo, n.d).

According to TEAL Centre (2012), instructors view of SCL learning acknowledge and accommodate different learning modalities and provide structure without being overly directive. They also listen to and respect each learner’s point of view, encourage and facilitate learner’s shared decision-making while helping them work through difficulties by asking them open ended questions to assist them arrive at conclusions or satisfactory solutions. As Di Napoli (2004) argues, instructors in the context of SCL, need to embrace three philosophies namely, progressivism, social reconstructionism and existentialism. In the progressivism view, teachers/instructors should see students as individuals who have the right to progress at their own pace and they should allow that to happen. Teachers/instructors also allow students to progress at different rates considering their individual characteristics (Abdullah et al. (2012). Since students \[learners\] bring to classroom their experiences, needs, interests and concerns, teachers/instructors need to respect the diversity among students and differences between individual students (Abdullah et al., 2012, Di Napoli, 2010).

SCL approach also envisages social constructionist instructors who can create lessons that both intellectually and emotionally stir students about the inequalities that surround them. Social constructivists view the role of education as helping to solve society’s problems and education should address such problems. So, the reconstruction of society has to take place through education (Abdullah et al., 2012). Another SCL philosophy that teachers/instructors need to adhere to is existentialism. Teachers/instructors abiding with this perspective must readily accept their students as they are, as they exist and not decide what and how the students should learn. Existentialists attach the great importance of human existence and free will to decide and be responsible for oneself (Abdullah, et al., 2012). In line with this, students are given options in shaping their courses and in choosing the area of learning (units) within their study programmes (El & ESU, 2010; O’Neill & McMahon, 2005; TEAL Centre, 2012).

Implications for the Learning Environment

The environment in which learning takes place is paramount to SCL approach. Abdullah et al. (2012) pointed out that a student-centred environment (SCE) tailors all aspects of service delivery and support to the needs of students. In addition, SCE focuses on students needs, not on their wants. And so, the goal of SCE is to create a SCL community that is committed to excellence in experimental learning \[experiential\], and one that assists the maturation of students as whole individuals with different backgrounds. Abdullah et al suggest that an educational institution “needs to create an environment where learning takes place anywhere, at any time, in many forms and by diverse means” (p. 36).

Three indispensible characteristics of the SCE have been advanced by Abdullah et al. These include physical environment, social environment and authentic environment. In their view, physical environment helps students enjoy a more positive learning environment, which likely will help them develop greater passion for learning and lead to more success in their learning endeavours. Availability of instructional materials and equipment (Ogula & Osongo, 2009), laboratory equipment, for example, encourage learning progress (Abdullah, et al. 2012).

The enhancement of the quality of SCL requires an authentic environment. Consistent with this characteristic, the learning environment should be aligned with the way learning occurs in a real-life setting. This can be achieved by letting students learn by solving problem in real-problem contexts. The problem gives the purpose and motivation for learning. Abdullah et al. consider social environment in reference to the following aspects of learning: what a student is curious about learning; teaching strategies to accommodate: (a) individual needs intellectually and emotionally and (b) student’s needs such as collaboration, communication and peer approval. As TEAL Center (2012) noted, the learning environment supports positive interactions among learners and provides a supportive space in which students feel appreciated, acknowleged, respected, and validated. In the light of SCL environment, a social environment has to be dynamic, trusting, and respectful and promote students’ objective and objective learning styles (Abdullah et al). Harris et al. (2013) stated that positive, trusting relationships between instructors and students hold the potential to improve students’ learning as well as it improving and even protecting the psychological and emotional well-being of the students.

Following SCL perspective, the learning environment has to be organized around four pillars: Knowledge-centered learning; student-centered assessment and community-centered (Froyd & Simpson, n.d.). Knowledge-centered learning emphasizes students developing their knowledge to facilitate transfer of their learning to new contexts and application of their learning to open-ended challenges that include problem-solving, critical thinking and design. While student-centered envisage students as co-creators in the learning process, as agents with ideas and issues that deserve attention and consideration, the SCL environment acknowledges that previous knowledge strongly influences future learning and thus attempts to build on prior knowledge. Regarding assessment-centered learning environment, it has the role to provide opportunities for feedback and improvement (formative) throughout the learning process leading to evaluation (summative) at the end of the learning process (Di Napoli, 2004). In this regard, students work jointly with instructors to define performance criteria and develop self-and peer assessment skills.

Implications for Student Assessment

In the context of SCL, assessment for learning is one process that identifies the differentiation of individual learning as a central element of students’ learning. Education International \[EI\] and European Students’ Union \[ESU\] (2010) argue that student assessment should be tailored to reflect the philosophy and goals of SCL and that the best forms of assessment need to be aligned with the learning goals.

As Heritage (2008 as cited in Iowa CORE, n.d.) argues, the process of student assessment requires that teachers/tutors establish learning progressions, identify the gap between students’ current knowledge and the learning progression and use various assessments to provide individualized feedback. Among the techniques for assessing learning outcomes include class assignments, group projects, observation of students’ participation in various learning activities, checklists, performance tasks and end of semester examinations (Ogula and Osongo, 2009). In addition to formative assessment, EI and ESU (2010) have provided other assessment methods that are compatible with SCL approach. These comprise criterion-referenced assessment and norm-based assessment, peer-and self assessment, take-home essay or assignment, assignment proposed by students and oral communication.

Di Napoli (2004) argues that in SCL assessment is predominantly formative in character. Formative assessment can take on a variety of forms: diaries, logs and journals, portifolios, peer-and self assessment, learning contracts and negotiated assessments, projects, group work, profiling and identification of own skills and competencies (EI &ESU, 2010). In order to ensure effective formative assessment, Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) identified seven principles underlying formative assessment as good feedback practice to both teachers/instructors and students.

In the view of Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006), as an effective feedback practice, formative assessment:

*   1\. Help clarify what good performance is (goals, criteria, expected standards);
*   2\. Facilitates the development of self-assessment (reflection) in learning;
*   3\. Delivers high quality information to students about their learning;
*   4\. Encourage teachers/tutors and peers dialogue around learning;
*   5\. Encourages positive motivational beliefs and self-esteem;
*   6\. Provides opportunities to close the gap between current and desired performance and
*   7\. Provides information to teachers/tutors that can be used to help shape the teaching.

According to TEAL Centre (2012), in SCL framework, assessment relies on portfolios that include both instructors-developed and self-assessments. Apart from this, evaluation considers various intelligences, uses authentic assessments and fosters self-reflection. Nicholson (2011) emphasizes on the nature of assessments in student-centered learning. For him, assessments are meaningful and authentic, for they allow students to apply the skills and knowledge they have gained to solve real problems.

Implications for the Learning Outcomes

Currently, there is no agreed upon definition of the term “learning outcomes” (Adam, 2004). However, learning outcomes can be defined as the knowledge, skills and understanding a student would be expected to acquire as a result of the learning experience (European Communities, 2009 as cited by EI & ESU, 2010). It has also been defined as a written statement of what a successful student is expected to be able to do at the end of the module/course unit or qualification (Adam, 2004; Nicholson, 2011). Thus, learning outcomes are concerned with learning achievement of the students rather than the intentions of the teachers/instructors as expressed in the aims and objectives of a course (Adam, 2004).

In SCL approach, the focus is on the intended learning outcomes, or what the students will be able to do at the end of a lesson or course (EI & ESU, 2010). Student-centered outcomes are usually expressed in behavioural terms that use active verbs to express what behaviours the student will show to demonstrate they have achieved the objectives (Houlden & Collier, 1999). As Nicholson (2011) asserts, within SCL context, both students and teachers/instructors work together to construct knowledge, making students active participants in the learning process.

MISCONCEPTIONS AND ADVANTAGES ASSOCIATED WITH SCL IN THE LIGHT OF LEARNERS AND INSTRUCTORS

Reacting to challenges of applying student centred approach to teaching and learning, Sablonniere, Taylor and Sadykova (2009) reiterated, “the question of what should be taught and how it should be taught becomes a matter for the very future survival of the society”, p. 1). This resonates with classical calls for best educational practices that have been the center of intellectual inquiry debates since the time of classical scholars to the present 21^(st) century educationalists and researchers. In the course of writing and reflection on the content in this paper, I was persuaded that imagined challenges of SCL are not only a contradiction in terms, but are for the most part informed by misconceptions associated with SCL.

As pointed out by Abdulla et al, SCL is misconceived in the following aspects: requiring more and greater resources; inappropriate for teaching large and diverse groups; that it undermines the teaching profession; students have more work; instructors have more work; PBL equated to SCL; SCL not suitable to all disciplines; and learners learning less of the subject matter. Looking at the principles of SCL (Educational International & European Students’ Union, 2010) and, the philosophies informing SCL (Abdulahi et al), all discussed earlier, one is brought to the attention and rationale for SCL which are: making learners active; proactive; and responsible participants in the teaching/learning process; making learners more engaged; effective and enjoy learning etc. On the part of the instructor, SCL makes them more reflective in their theory and practice; reject negativity that comes from complaining of large class sizes; insufficient resources; demotivated learners; and poor remuneration among others (Buswell & Becket, 2009).

CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Consistent with SCL is that instructors work with learners to determine the learning strategies which are self-paced and consistent with the needs of individual learners. The Learners are exposed to direct access to various sources of information ranging from books to online databases and surrounding communities. In the process, they are assisted to solve problems/tasks by making principled and informed use of these resources (Di Napoli, 2004).

As I have argued in this paper, whereas SCL pedagogies should be informed by learners’ needs, there is a tendency to avoid the “not so conventional” SCL pedagogies, which tend to call for more instructor reflection, innovation, ingenuity, and integration of computer technology to the teaching/learning process.

In terms of implications and what SCL pedagogies mean to the stakeholders, curriculum, environment and learning outcomes, it is critically important to make the entire process democratic by incorporating all stakeholders in the design, implementation and assessment processes of SCL. This way, misconceptions associated with SCL will be demystified.

In the light of the aforementioned conclusions, and in the light of Teacher Education and Professional development, I make the following recommendations:

*   • Make SCL theory, and practice central in teacher education programs
*   • Induction of novice instructors to SCL pedagogies by senior faculty members
*   • Motivate and reward instructors who excel in SCL pedagogies
*   • Recommend clear teaching philosophies in teacher recruitment (Kanga, 2016).

This research was previously published in the Handbook of Research on Learner-Centered Pedagogy in Teacher Education and Professional Development edited by Jared Keengwe and Grace Onchwari, pages 373-390, copyright year 2017 by Information Science Reference (an imprint of IGI Global).

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Conventional SCL Pedagogies: These are the SCL pedagogies generally used, and or SCL pedagogies that have been used in teacher education and especially, the pre-computer age. These have been, but not limited to: Improved lecture, questioning method small group teaching, case study, seminar, tutorials, project method, Laboratory method, field trips, and portfolio writing.

Disruptive and Emerging Technologies: These are technologies that displace established procedures. They are also technologies that shake up the industry usually creating a completely new industry and how processes are carried out. Examples are computers that displaced the typewriter, email that transformed communication, cell phones, laptop and mobile computing, cloud computing, social networking among others.

Educator: Term is broadly used to mean a professional in the field of education such as a teacher, principal, administrator, lecturer, professor involved in the theory and practice of teaching and learning.

Lifelong Learning and Learners: This is learning inculcated through SCL pedagogies, usually resulting to lifelong learners, who are intrinsically motivated.

Instructor: In this paper, the concept is used to denote educators trained in pedagogy required to teach at the level of Teacher Education programs. Depending on different contexts, these are educators with masters and PhD degrees or their equivalent in education.

Not so Conventional SCL Pedagogies: These are the SCL pedagogies in the author’s view that call for more instructor reflection, innovation, ingenuity, and of course many pedagogies that are computer based. Most of these pedagogies are “post computer age”. Selected “not so conventional SCL pedagogies in this paper are: problem based \[teaching\] and learning, Inquiry based learning, challenge based learning, peer observation/peer supported review of teaching (PSRT), Web supported Inquiry based learning (WSBL), and competence based learning.

Pedagogy: In the art/or science of teaching and learning

Student Centered Learning: instructional approach in which students influence the content, activities, materials, and pace of learning. This learning model places the student (learner) in the centre of the learning process.

Teaching Philosophy: This refers to the critical reflection that informs an instructor’s approach to scholarship, teaching and learning.

# Chapter 88

*   Mohammed Akour  
    Yarmouk University, Jordan
*   Wasen Yahya Melhem  
    Yarmouk university, Jordan

ABSTRACT

This article describes how classification methods on software defect prediction is widely researched due to the need to increase the software quality and decrease testing efforts. However, findings of past researches done on this issue has not shown any classifier which proves to be superior to the other. Additionally, there is a lack of research that studies the effects and accuracy of genetic programming on software defect prediction. To find solutions for this problem, a comparative software defect prediction experiment between genetic programming and neural networks are performed on four datasets from the NASA Metrics Data repository. Generally, an interesting degree of accuracy is detected, which shows how the metric-based classification is useful. Nevertheless, this article specifies that the application and usage of genetic programming is highly recommended due to the detailed analysis it provides, as well as an important feature in this classification method which allows the viewing of each attributes impact in the dataset.

INTRODUCTION

Software systems are becoming more complicated day after day, consequently the likelihood of defects affecting the system components is expanding. On the other hand, software testing takes up effort, time and budget. The application of data mining such as machine learning approaches to the Software Defect Prediction (SDP) process is a major beneficial and resourceful development. Software experts view SDP as a critical stage where the quality of the software is being tested as it plays a big role in minimizing the claims in software engineering about not being able to find solutions within budget and the time agreed upon. In addition, it provides the customers response concerning the quality of the software which has revealed to be much more satisfactory than before. Countless data mining experts have substituted manual defect prediction methods with a classification model where the software is being classified to being faulty or non-faulty. SDP is considered to be a major part of the testing phase of the SDLC in which testing resources are being efficiently applied with no violations due to the rigorous testing performed (Arora, Ishani, Tetarwal, & Saha, 2015).

Genetic Programming (GP) is one of the evolutionary computation methods that is used for classification and has proven its productivity particularly for dynamic and non-linear classification. In this research paper, four datasets will be studied and classified using GP and Neural Network (NN) to study and experiment the effects of GP and its performance in the classifying procedure and perform a comparison between the NN classification and GP classification. four datasets are collected from Promise Software Engineering Repository, NASA Metric Data Program which are CM1, KC1, KC2, JM1 datasets (Menzies, Tim & Stefano, 2004).

NN is an information-processing model that is stirred by how a human’s nervous system performs, where a great number of neurons exist in the brain, this is the fundamental part of the NN model. Neurons are vastly interconnected and perform together to resolve intricate problems. Inputs, weights and bias form the model of a neuron, and there are two types of models: Feed forward and Feed backward NN. The downside of NN is that they are rather problematic to implement due to their complexity (Gayathri, & Sudha, 2014). In order to achieve higher reliability in software and enhance the quality of the software, NN is widely researched and compared with other models and popular in the area of software defect prediction.

The SDP is a vital topic in the field of software engineering with many researches on the issue. Nevertheless, most of the studies have been achieved through design and requirement metrics. The exact and correct estimation of software susceptible to defects can help developers minimize time of testing, costs and enhance the whole procedure of testing by concentrating on classes and functions that are compromised. Software defected datasets have a lot of noise with little faulty classes in comparison with classes that don’t contain any bugs. Hence, the classification performance is also minimized due to the imbalanced attributes in the dataset. It is important to note the difference between GA and GP as GP concentrates on the aspect of Classification whereas GA is an optimization method. Correct classifications of faulty software classes can direct test efforts, decrease budgets, progress testing method by concentrating on defective classes and refactoring solutions that are classified as erroneous by building a fault classification model which has shown progression with a mean probability detection of 71% (Menzies et al., 2010).

The OO method unlike old-style programming is built on objects, where information and control are placed separately. OO has become the center of software engineering. This model delivers a novel and enhanced technique to analyze a problem, plan a solution and implement it. It offers better reliability, maintainability and reusability, due to Encapsulation in OOP reusability is accomplished.

Evolutionary algorithms have effectively proven useful in testing software. The use of Object oriented (OO) metrics in predicting defect prone classes were demonstrated by many researchers. Measuring the quality of OO software is not straightforward. Applying genetic algorithm to object-oriented software to uncover defects could be an efficient method.

White, Fan and Oppacher Introduced a model called Basic Object-Oriented GP (OOGP), where object-oriented ideas were added to GP for the purpose of progressing the capacity of GP to handle bigger problems. Outcomes specify that OOGP can resolve specific problems with reduced populations and fewer generations (White, Fan, & Oppacher, 2011).

BACKGROUND

This section presents the related works and studies to the GP and SDP fields and the application of data mining techniques. This chapter is partitioned to three main sections; to begin with the Genetic Algorithm and Programming in testing, software defects and classification approaches is introduced, the second is Neural Network Classification approaches, third is comparisons of machine learning approaches in software testing.

Classification is a common method for software defect prediction in which modules are classified, by a combination of software metrics, into non-faulty or faulty, by a classification model derived from data of earlier developments. Many types of classifiers have been used in this field, such as NN, ensembles, tree-based methods, statistical approaches, nearest-neighbor approaches and support vector machines.

Various OO metrics have been designed to support finding faults in software, OO software quality is supported by using metric measurements, which assists in correct, rapid analysis of software quality. Many have researched defect prediction methods but there is little contribution to effects of genetic programming in this field.

On the issue of OO use with GP Wappler and Wegener designed a method to automatically create test cases used for structure-oriented unit testing of OO software. The method proved successful. strongly-typed genetic programming was used for method call sequences. The function set was resultant from the signatures of the functions of the test cluster classes; the type set was resultant from the inheritance relations of the test cluster classes and set-based typing to realize polymorphism (Wappler & Wegener, 2006).

Malhotra and Singh also demonstrate how OO metrics performed on faulty software through a model using Response for a class (RFC) and Cyclometric Complexity (CC) delivers higher accuracy. The model predicted higher accuracy with AUC 0.829 (Malhotra, & Singh, 2012). Another study by Malhotra and Garg show how using genetic algorithm results in 30.76%-88.33% reduction in number of test cases and 20% - 60% savings in time to build test cases in comparison to path testing method (Malhotra, & Garg, 2011).

Genetic Algorithm and Programming in Testing, Software Defects, and Classification

The aim of GA in software is usually for optimization purposes. However, there have been some studies on the effect of GA in software defect prediction. Evett et al. applied GP to software quality modeling in order to produce software quality models with software metrics as inputs and predictions as outcomes of the sum of bugs that will be found. An ordinal estimation criterion, instead of the number of bugs for the models formed by applying GP. This technique is successful for increasing reliability to the most fault-prone segments of the software. GP is also used to show the performance in industrial dataset through ordinal evaluation procedures (Evett, 1998).

Researchers have studied the effect of GA in bug fixing such as Arcuri who proposed a GA to automate the task of bug fixing, results in reducing efforts and costs is a problem. the main idea is optimizing the programs by using a fitness function which relies on the amount of component tests that have been passed. More improved fitness functions were developed when proper description of an oracle of the buggy software was provided. Hence, providing improved outcomes, the fitness function was built upon the amount of unit tests passed. GA reducing efforts and costs is a problem of importance and research in open source software. Many methods have been initiated in order to aid the decision makers of software projects. Everyday matters that distress scheduling and triaging isn’t highly researched. Park et al., addressed these issues as well in generating practical human resource allocations. In the literature GA has been studied to find solutions for testing and triaging problems (Arcuri, 2008; Park et al.,2014).

GA was used by Puri and Singh to uncover faulty classes and have deemed using GA in OO software a success. As GA shows high rate of Probability of Detection and low Probability of False Alarms. to discover critical classes and metrics in jEdit project that are inclined to defects. probability of detection was found with 0.875 and Probability of false alarms was of 0.44. also shows accuracy of 0.705 (Puri & Singh, 2014).

Although there is little research in this field, researchers have found applying GP in classification have deemed high accuracy, Bhowan et al used unstable data and developed a multi-objective GP. This research used six binary data sets to demonstrate that the multi-objective GP methods, it produced an accurate set of genetic program classifiers along the minority and majority classes, mainly found when a mixture of supremacy rank and supremacy count is involved in the fitness (Bhowan et al., 2013).

Wahono, Satria, & Herman developed a technique that uses genetic programming and the ensemble bagging procedure for SDP which attained high accuracy where GA handles noisy attributes and the bagging method is used to improve the class imbalance problem. They conducted a comparative study of ten classifiers used on NASA MDP data and the results demonstration that the proposed method attained better accuracy than other known classifiers. Another approach with positive results using GA classification is by Wahono, Satria, Suryana, & Ahmad where GA and Swarm Optimization have the ability to handle noise in attributes and the bagging methods to lessen the class imbalance issue. Applies these methods in order to compare ten classifiers on NASA MDP datasets for SDP for solving SDP and shows high accuracy and performance in classification (Wahono, Satria, & Herman, 2014; Wahono, Satria, Suryana, & Ahmad, 2014).

Kaminsky & Boetticher Also predicted defects by using GP on KC2 dataset and applied 21 function metrics. The impact of data equalization was researched and T-test was applied for performance assessment. data starved domains were partitioned to two clusters: Explicit: Project cost approximation traces and Implicit: where bug prediction traces. There are suitable data ideas but datasets aren’t scaled or well-adjusted. This study demonstrates that data equalization is beneficial when applied with GP. Nevertheless, training takes more time due to the increasing of data volume. Whereas the fitness was 12 for a standard dataset, it was 81.4 for the equalized set and T-test demonstrates that this was a weighty variance (Kaminsky & Boetticher, 2014).

Panichella et al, uses Genetic Algorithm to accumulate and organize an ideal IR procedure to be used in software engineering, this technique is proposed due to its task independence through its ability to detect duplicated bug reports, the combinations of IR and GA reflects all probable groupings of conducts for the numerous stages of the IR procedure (Panichella et al., 2016).

Neural Network Classification Approaches

Neural Networks have been studied widely in the literature for classification purposes. Many studies researched the issue of software defect prediction using NN as well as a combination of other machine learning methods. Multi-layer neural networks and support vector machine (SVM) was developed by Askari, Mahdi, & Bardsiri. and used on 3 NASA datasets. The goal was to generate a fast and exact non-linear classification method for the prediction of software defects. This model provides good results and efficient on small and big data sets which is the biggest benefit of combining NN and SVM but still hasn’t totally included evolutionary algorithms which didn’t help the accuracy as much as it could have (Askari, Mahdi, & Bardsiri, 2014). So, the reason behind using NN is that it enhances and shows a growth in the generalization ability of the learning algorithm in predicting software defects and the use of SVM prevents from overfitting matters and decreases the classification margin. Another study on defect prediction with NASA datasets was introduced by Catal and demonstrates a comparison of the most effective classification techniques. SVM and low-density separation proved to having higher and more enhanced performance than expectation-maximization algorithm. As well as that low-density separation can better handle larger data sets than SVM (Catal, 2014).

Defect prediction models are built to classify the software to either having defects or not, this process has an effect on software development process. The cost of wrongly classifying a defected software or class is higher than wrongly classifying a non-defected class, Zheng has generated a prediction model by the use of NN and three cost-sensitive boosting algorithms. Results show advantages to the use of threshold-moving in decreasing costs of misclassification (Zheng, 2010).

Arar & Ayan also took under consideration cost of misclassifying and developed a hybrid classifier model was built for the aim of the defect prediction issue by including a parametric cost-sensitivity attribute to NN through using an innovative error function where the value and the effect of the costs of misclassifying negative and positive classes are established with related coefficients, this approach has an effect on the recall, probability of false alarm and the accuracy. five NASA datasets were used to apply this method and compare amongst them. Outcomes demonstrate its performance is better than the others but not significant. More concentration should be on preprocessing of the data, feature selection and many data mining concepts instead of finding another classifier (Arar & Ayan, 2015). Park, Byoung-Jun, Oh, & Pedrycz, applied polynomial function-based neural networks in predicting bugs, rules are built by fuzzy clustering. In the experimented synthetic data was used and particular software engineering datasets. The effect coming due to the sum of rules as well as the values of the Area Under Curve trained on the weighted cost function. And outcomes have shown high True Positives of detecting bugs and lower False Positives (Park, Oh, & Pedrycz, 2013).

Henceforth, the wide study of NN on classification issues shows the need for NN to be enhanced and applied in a way to maximize its potential and using it alone will cause some generalization issues. Alexandru et al. addressed the problem of improving GAs for adjusting NN to increase the accuracy of the prediction process and developed a method based on GA to solve the restrictions of outdated techniques by modifying the training algorithm in order to include defects/changes in the artifacts which have higher significances within the organized list of artifacts. They predicted the number of faults in 10 data sets from PROMISE repository using GP and evaluated the outcomes using recall, error rates and completeness measures. This study shows high accuracy in prediction of defects. Nevertheless, shows that GP doesn’t performed well on small data sets (Alexandru et al., 2015) Kumar and Yadav have presented a software defects valuation model using Bayesian belief networks (BBN) and metrics of early phases of the SDLC. BBN is very beneficial wherever appropriate unbiased data are not present. As the primary phases of the SDLC, metrics are rather problematic to measure because of the unclearness of their interconnectedness (Kumar, & Yadav, 2017).

Comparisons of Machine Learning Approaches in Software Testing

Song, Jia, Shepperd, Ying, & Liu developed a framework using a benchmark procedure of evaluating and assessing many learning methods and choosing the top technique and then predicting defects. Morera & Jenkins compared the genetic method to the Song method. This study shows better performance of the genetic method. Representing eight of ten data sets, the data set where the Genetic approach had less performance was PC2 while the data set with more performance was MC1. The size of MC1 represented the best Area Under Cover 0.858 due to it being the larger data set as well as KC1 with Area under cover of 0.82. But, the Song method demonstrates MC1 to have 0.82 and KC1 to have a 0.69 Area Under Cover (Morera & Jenkins., 2015; Song et al., 2011). Used the same data set in order to perform a comparative study between the base learners and ensemble methods. They believe in that the prediction of faulty modules of systems under test at early stages contributes to the overall quality of software products. In their experiments they evaluate the performance of 11 base learner against the ensemble methods in term of the prediction accuracy and ROC (Akour, Alsmadi, & Alazzam, 2017).

Finding the source of failures is very important and not only if software is defected or not. Lessmann, Baesens, Mues, & Pietsch study the process of choosing a classification model which should not be based only on prediction accuracy. There should be conditions such as computational productivity, usability and they focus on comprehensibility, as it uncovers the nature of detected associations and enhances the process of improving our general understanding of software faults as well as what causes these faults (Lessmann, Baesens, Mues, & Pietsch, 2008). Challagulla, Bastani, Yen, & Paul focus on finding how GP can enhance the process of defect prediction through finding the association between features. They performed a comparison between diverse machine learning models and shows that there is no specific learning method that gives the best results for all the data sets. Yet, Inquiry based learning method and 1R show rather improved evenness in prediction accuracy compared with SVLR, NND, LoR, NB, JDT. Simple FSS approaches achieve better results than PCA. So PCA isn’t suitable for software bugs, neither are the size or complexity metrics. Challagulla, Bastani, Yen, & Paul Also shows that Bayesian belief networks (BBN) are the best model to show the association between features using probabilistic models (Challagulla, Bastani, Yen, & Paul, 2005). Making connections between faults and uncovering their correlations aims to support executives as well as development teams. Felix, Amarachukwu, & Lee have found an association of the number of faults with every predictor attribute. Displaying a strong positive association with the average defect rate and a weak positive association with the average fault density (Felix, Amarachukwu,& Lee, 2017).

Rahman compares the Greedy-X approach to the manual approaches of bug assignment and triaging, this study shows improved triaging as it performed on nine open source Eclipse projects, this study also shows that there are better methods such as Genetic algorithm. The issue with this method is that triaging process gets more complicated when letting a team member shift from fixing one bug to fix a minor bug. Enhancement is needed on the profile data in the Greedy-X method. The use of IR methods as solutions for software programming needs a cautious building of a procedure containing numerous stages, such as stemming, weight of words, as well as using many IR algorithms and the performance of IR methods and techniques depends on the specific use and application (Rahman, Mainur, Ruhe, & Zimmermann 2009; Valls, Ballestín, & Quintanilla, 2002).

Anvik, Hiew & Murphy introduced an approach that applies a machine learning algorithm to the open bug repository to learn the kinds of reports each developer resolves. So, this method works as follows: as a report is submitted in the source of bugs, a classifier formed by a machine learning method proposes a trivial sum of team members appropriate to find solutions. This technique is found to have produced precision of 57% and 64% on the Eclipse and Firefox and applied the same technique on the GCC open source software with not as much of positive results as Eclipse and Firefox. Contains four stages: first, describing the properties of bug reports, second, for each report a label is provided, third, selecting reports as training for the supervised learning machine and finally using the algorithm to generate the classification model for recommending assignments (Anvik, Hiew, & Murphy, 2006).

METHODOLOGY

In this study, we try to investigate the effect of GP on SDP to answer the following questions:

*   • How GP is used for classification?
*   • Can we discover the association amongst the accuracy, prediction scheme, and the dataset features?
*   • What is the accuracy of using GP on software defect prediction?
*   • How does GP differ from Neural Network Classification in terms of performance and accuracy?

In order to study the performance of GP, the main steps are summarized as follows:

*   Step 1: Looking for the dataset, our dataset contains SDP data.
*   Step 2: Processing the dataset to prepare it to apply to the GP.
*   Step 3: Applying GP on the dataset using Heuristic Lab tool.
*   Step 4: Applying NN classification on the dataset using Heuristic Lab tool.
*   Step 5: Classifying the dataset to defective and non-defective class.
*   Step 6: Evaluating the accuracy of the GP classification.
*   Step 7: Evaluating the accuracy of the NN classification.
*   Step 8: Comparing both GP and NN classification methods.

This research has undergone through a series of operations to classify the effect of using GP on SDP which can be summarized using Figure 1.

Data Collection and Preprocessing

The datasets used are from the PROMISE Software Engineering Repository. Four datasets were collected CM1, KC1, JM1, KC2 by Tim Menzies (Menzies, Tim & Stefano, 2004), The creators are NASA Metrics Data Program.

Preprocessing the data and cleaning it from irrelevant data is an essential step for any dataset. However, these datasets didn’t need any cleaning, only transformation was applied on the class label to convert it from string type (true/false) to binary (0/1). The second step will be to split the data into training and testing data to apply the data to the heuristic lab program.
