# Chapter 91

*   Veronica Chan  
    University of Regina, Canada
*   Christine Chan  
    University of Regina, Canada

ABSTRACT

This paper discusses development and application of a decomposition neural network rule extraction algorithm for nonlinear regression problems. The algorithm is called the piece-wise linear artificial neural network or PWL-ANN algorithm. The objective of the algorithm is to “open up” the black box of a neural network model so that rules in the form of linear equations are generated by approximating the sigmoid activation functions of the hidden neurons in an artificial neural network (ANN). The preliminary results showed that the algorithm gives high fidelity and satisfactory results on sixteen of the nineteen tested datasets. By analyzing the values of R2 given by the PWL approximation on the hidden neurons and the overall output, it is evident that in addition to accurate approximation of each individual node of a given ANN model, there are more factors affecting the fidelity of the PWL-ANN algorithm Nevertheless, the algorithm shows promising potential for domains when better understanding about the problem is needed.

INTRODUCTION

Artificial neural network (ANN) is a popular data mining approach, in a wide range of area of study (Xu & Zang, 2008; Yaremchuk & Dawson, 2008), because of its high classification or predictive accuracy, and resistance to noise. However, in addition to high prediction accuracy, researchers often need to gain better understanding of the problems at hand (Chan, 2007), and ANNs are black boxes that cannot be interpreted. To overcome this deficiency, the rule extraction approach can be adopted so as to generate explicit information from the analysis results of the trained ANNs. The objective of this study is to develop a decompositional neural network rule extraction algorithm for non-linear regression problems. The approach adopted is to model a given dataset using the ANN approach and the originally trained neural network is assumed to be a three-layer feed-forward backpropagation neural network with a sigmoid activation function. Since these are the most common types of neural network models, this will be the target models on which rule extraction will be performed. Also, based on experience, one hidden layer in an ANN is typically sufficient to solve most non-linear problems without overfitting. Although the pedagogical type of rule extraction algorithms is better in terms of computational complexity and generality than decompositional algorithms, the decompositional approach is the focus because the objective is to explore the trained neural network and “open the black box”. The algorithm approximates the activation functions of a given ANN model with piece-wise linear (PWL) equations and generates explicit information in the form of numerical formulae. The targeted problems are regression problems related to engineering domains. In terms of expressive power, we would like to generate “rules” expressed as linear numeric functions in the form of

Y = a[1]x[1] + a[2]x[2]+… + b

Since the research objective is to understand the working mechanism of the trained neural network model, fidelity to the trained ANN will be the primary evaluation criterion of the developed algorithm. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 discusses the motivation of the work based on observations derived from some previous works, and some background literature related to research work on ANN rule extraction algorithms. Section 3 describes the proposed methodology and Section 4 presents analysis of some preliminary results. Section 5 gives some directions for future work and Section 6 is the conclusions.

BACKGROUND LITERATURE AND MOTIVATION

There are three approaches to ANN rule extraction: (1) decompositional, which extracts rules by examining the activation and weights of the hidden layer neurons; (2) pedagogical, which extracts rules by mapping the relationships between the inputs and outputs as closely as possible to those given by the trained ANN model without opening up the “black-box” of the ANN models; and (3) eclectic, which is a hybrid of the two previous approaches. Most studies on ANN rule extraction focus on classification problems (Augasta & Kathirvalavakumar, 2012), when in reality many problems encountered in the real-world contexts are regression problems. In classification problems, the output variables are class labels, whereas in regression problems, the output variables are continuous values.

Rule extraction algorithms for ANN can be classified into three approaches based on the criterion of translucency of the algorithm: decompositional, pedagogical and eclectic (Andrews et al., 1995) The approach of decompositional algorithms aims to extract rules by examining activation functions and weights of the hidden layer neurons, and this type of algorithms are considered to be completely translucent. On the other end of the translucency spectrum is the pedagogical approach, which extracts rules by mapping the relationship between the inputs and outputs as closely as possible to that given by the trained ANN model without exploring the ANN models. The underlying ANN models are still viewed as a “black-box” and “translucency” is not a priority. The eclectic approach is a hybrid of the other two approaches and lies in the middle on the translucency spectrum.

Since decompositional algorithms involve examining the underlying ANN model, they generally involve more complex computation than pedagogical algorithms. Some of the proposed decompositional algorithms generate rules by clustering the weighted links between the input and hidden neurons with similar values (Towell & Shavlik, 1993; Setiono & Liu, 1995, 1997; Odajimi et al., 2008). Others involve finding the combination of input value weights to the neuron (Krishnan et al, 1999). In Kim & Lee (2000), rules were generated by replacing the neurons in the first hidden layer with logic gates. The pedagogical approach maps the relationships between the inputs and outputs as closely as possible to those given by the ANN model without analysing the underlying ANN model. In Thrun (1993), Thrun mapped the input/output relationships using Validity Interval Analysis, which is similar to sensitivity analysis. In Craven & Shavlik (1996) and deFortuny & Martens (2012), the trained ANN was used as an oracle to construct a decision tree, and/or other “white-box” algorithms. Saad and Wunsch (2007) extracted rules by finding the hyperplanes that represent the NN decision boundary using NN inversion techniques. A reversed engineering approach was also used (Augasta & Kathirvalayakumar, 2012). An eclectic approach is generally any approach that lies in the middle on the translucency spectrum between the decomposition and pedagogical approaches. Some sample work of the eclectic approach include Hruschka & Ebecken (2006), which proposed clustering the activation values using a genetic algorithm (GA), Mohamed (2011) which employed GA for solving the optimization problem of the output function, and Al Iqban (2011), which extracted rules by replacing each of the hidden neurons with a decision tree.

Most of the proposed ANN rule extraction algorithms target classification problems, which are problems that involve categorical variables as outputs. However, in many engineering problems, the output variables involve numeric or continuous values. Some studies that aim to extract rules by approximating the hidden sigmoid activation functions into some piece-wise linear functions include Setiono et al. (2002), Setiono & Thong (2004) and Wang et al. (2011), and the approximation is illustrated in Figure 1. The differences among the algorithms proposed in Setiono et al. (2002), Setiono & Thong (2004) and Wang et al. (2011) lie in the method each used to solve the PWL approximation. In order to generate sets of rules with high fidelity to the underlying neural network, the accuracy of the PWL approximation is crucial. While Setiono et al. (2002) solved the PWL approximation by “minimizing the area bounded by the hyperbolic tangent function and the linear approximating function”, Setiono & Thong (2004) generated the PWL equations by minimizing the sum of squared errors between the activation function and the PWL functions. By contrast, Wang et al. (2011) suggested that neither of the previous methods gave desirable approximation accuracies, and proposed solving the approximation problem with the least squares approach. The approach was applied on one UCI (University of California Irvine (Lichman, 2013)) dataset and the results gave lower values of the mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean absolute error (RMAE) compared to the two algorithms suggested in Setiono et al. (2002) and Setiono & Thong (2004).

| Figure 1. Approximating the activation function (sigmoid function) with a three-piece linear approximation function |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.f01](i/ch091.f01.png) |
| --- |

Most decompositional algorithms suggest grouping the hidden activation values into classes. By contrast, the PWL approximation approach groups the activation values into linear functions. This makes the algorithm useful for regression problems and is an interesting approach. However, a weakness with the approach in Wang et al. (2011) is that the authors only demonstrated their algorithm on one simple UCI dataset. In this study, an improved version of the algorithm based on the one proposed in Wang et al. (2011) has been developed for modeling more complicated regression problems. The improved version of the algorithm, which is called the piece-wise linear neural network (PWL-ANN) algorithm is presented in Section 3.

METHODOLOGY

The PWL-ANN algorithm is built on two concepts. First, the piece-wise linear (PWL) algorithm is responsible for approximating the hidden activation functions of a trained neural network. Secondly, the neural network with the hidden layer replaced by the generated PWL equations is called the piece-wise linear neural network (PWL-ANN). Rapidminer (trademark of Rapidminer) has been used to train the neural network, and the rule extraction algorithm is written in R. The main steps of the PWL-ANN algorithm are as follows:

Training the Neural Network for a Given Dataset

The data is first normalized to the range of \[-1, 1\] before training and Rapidminer’s neural network model (trademark of Rapidminer) was used to model the dataset. The model uses a sigmoid function and a linear function as the activation functions for the hidden layer and the output layer, respectively. The training cycles were set to 500 with a learning rate of 0.3 and a momentum of 0.2, both are default settings. Only a single hidden layer is considered, and the number of nodes in the hidden layer by default in Rapidminer is given by: (number of input attributes + number of output attributes)/2 +1. The model is trained with a 20-fold cross-validation, and Rapidminer provides information on the trained ANN model and its performance in terms of the root mean squared error. The weights of the nodes of the trained model given by Rapidminer are used in the PWL approximation algorithm.

Approximating the Activation Functions of the Hidden Neurons of the Trained ANN Model Using the Three-Piece Linear (3PL) Functions

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.m01](i/ch091.m01.svg)

where ξ is the sum of the weighted input:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.m02](i/ch091.m02.svg)

where w[i] are the weights and θ is the bias.

The sigmoid function can be approximated using a three-piece linear function, L(ξ); such that:![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.m03](i/ch091.m03.svg)

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.m04](i/ch091.m04.svg)

As shown in Figure 1, ξ[0] and -ξ[0] are called the breakpoints (BPs) of the piece-wise linear equations. The challenge of finding an accurate 3PL equation lies in locating the breakpoints, which can be found by performing a brute-force search on the dataset. The steps involved in approximating the activation functions are as follows:

Let M be the total number of data points in a given dataset,

*   1\. Sort the data points in ascending order.
*   2\. Divide the dataset into M/d number of subsets, where d is the number of data points per subset and this value determines how frequently the data points within the dataset are tested. Each tested point becomes a potential breakpoint, in other words, the break points are the points at which the function changes. For example, d=1 means each point will be tested and d=10 means every 10 points of the dataset will be tested.
*   3\. For each subset, consider the last data entry of the subset, ξi, as the breakpoint. Solve the linear equations for the data entries in the subintervals of \[0, ξi\] and \[ξi, ξmax\] using the least squares approach. Record the mean squared error (MSE) given by the two lines.
*   4\. Repeat step (iii) with all the subsets.
*   5\. The set of equations with the lowest value of MSE is considered the best solution.

Due to the symmetry of the sigmoid function, it is only necessary to locate one breakpoint, ξ0, and the other breakpoint will be -ξ0. Based on this constraint, two possible approaches can be adopted to solve the 3PL equations:

*   • Either the dataset that lies on the left, i.e. negative ξ values, or right, i.e. positive ξ values, hand side of the y-axis is used, the choice favors the side that has the larger set of data.
*   • The absolute values of ξ are used to solve the linear equations and it is necessary to locate only one breakpoint, ξ0. The L(ξ) values of negative ξ can be obtained by 1 – L(ξ).

Extracting Rules from the Approximated Linear Functions

After the activation functions of the hidden neurons are approximated using 3PL equations, the sigmoid functions are replaced with the 3PL functions and the PWL-ANN model is derived. Then rules in the form of linear functions can be extracted from the PWL-ANN model.

To illustrate the result of the algorithm, consider a neural network with three inputs and three hidden neurons as shown in Figure 2.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.m05](i/ch091.m05.svg)

which can be simplified as

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.m06](i/ch091.m06.svg)

where

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.m07](i/ch091.m07.svg)

and are all constants. For each of the given input, we can now find the corresponding multiple linear equation that calculates the output. These linear equations become the output “class” of the dataset and if-then rules can be generated based on these classes.

PRELIMINARY RESULTS AND ANALYSIS

To assess performance of the PWL-ANN algorithm, it was tested on 19 datasets, among which 15 datasets were obtained from the UCI repository (Lichman, 2006) and the Weka project (Hall et al. 2009), and 4 datasets (number 16 – 19) were obtained from the post-combustion carbon dioxide capture process system implemented at the Clean Energy Technology Research Institute (CETRI) located at the University of Regina, in Regina, Saskatchewan, Canada. These datasets were chosen because they all have continuous output values. The characteristics of the datasets are summarized in Table 1. For the discrete attributes, dummy variables were used to represent the different classes of that attribute. For example, for an input attribute that has the classes of sunny, cloudy, and windy, with the dummy coding, the classes are labeled as 1, 2 and 3.

Based on the same PWL-ANN algorithm, three approaches in solving the PWL approximation process were adopted:

*   1\. Approach 1: Using the larger half of the dataset with d = 10;
*   2\. Approach 2: Using the larger half of the dataset with d = 3;
*   3\. Approach 3: Using the absolute values of the dataset with d = 3.

As mentioned in Section 1, the primary evaluation criterion is fidelity of the generated rule sets to the originally trained ANN. While accuracy of the PWL-ANN algorithm is also considered, the predictive accuracy of the PWL-ANN model is constrained by the predictive accuracy of the trained ANN model. In other words, if the trained ANN model has low accuracy, then the PWL-ANN model of this trained ANN model would also have low accuracy. To evaluate fidelity, the values of R2 and mean square error (MSE) given by the ANN and the PWL-ANN models are compared. MSE measures the deviation of the predicted value to the actual value; and R2 shows how close the actual values are to the fitted line. The values of R2 and MSE can be calculated as follows:

![Mathtype978-1-7998-0414-7.ch091.m11](i/ch091.m11.svg)

Since an important research objective is to generate explicit information from the ANN models, the evaluation criterion adopted is that the PWL-ANN algorithm would produce similar values of R² and MSE as those produced by the ANN model on all the datasets. In order to more easily compare the results from the applications of the algorithm to the datasets, the percentage difference between the MSE given by the proposed PWL-ANN algorithm is compared to the MSE given by the trained ANN. When the percentage difference between the MSE’s is high, it means the PWL-ANN model demonstrates poor fidelity to the original ANN model. The analysis of the percentage difference between the MSE’s and R2’s has two objectives. First, the analysis aims to determine which of the three approaches listed earlier gives the best general performance. Secondly, it aims to investigate the causes for the poor performance of the algorithm on a particular dataset; the approach adopted is to analyze the performance of the three approaches on each individual dataset. The datasets identified with high percentage differences between the MSE’s and R2 will be the focus of the analysis, and the analysis is presented as follows.

Overall Performance of the Three Approaches

In both approaches 2 and 3, a small value of d is used, which means more data points are tested as the potential break points. Using these approaches ensure a more fine-grained approximation of the curve is implemented. Hence, the performances of Approach 2 and 3 can be expected to be better than Approach 1. This hypothesis is valid and it can be seen in Table 5 that approach 1 gives the best fidelity for only 3 datasets, while approaches 2 and 3 give the best performance for 6 and 9 datasets, respectively. The difference between approach 2 and 3 is that approach 2 uses half of the values on the sigmoid curve, whereas approach 3 uses the absolute values and all the data points on the sigmoid curve. Since approach 3 outperforms approach 2, we can conclude that among the three approaches, the best performance is given when the full range of values is included and when a finer grained approximation is used. Thus, in future work, the absolute values and a small value of d will be used for the PWL approximation.

Performance of the Three Approaches on Each Individual Dataset

An analysis of the R2 values in Table 3 reveals that the PWL-ANN models give close performances to the ANN models on all datasets, even for the dataset on which the ANN model did not give good predictive performance. Based on the premise that a R2 value that is close to 1 indicates higher predictive accuracy of the model, it can be seen from Table 3 that the R2 given by dataset #12 is only 0.0949, which reflects low accuracy, and the values given by the PWL-ANN models are 0.0981, 0.0838 and 0.0875, which show similar performance to the ANN model.

Table 4 and Figure 3 show that aside from dataset #1 (approach 1 and 2), #6, #7, #13 and #15, most of the datasets demonstrate reasonable fidelity to the original ANN with a percentage difference in MSE of below 20%. The analysis aims to identify the causes for the poor performances of the PWL-ANN algorithms. The datasets with a MSE percentage difference greater than 150% include (aside from dataset #1) datasets #6 and #15, as shown in italics in Table 4 and indicated by the tall columns in Figure 3. These datasets deserve careful examination because of their high MSE percentage differences. Dataset #1 will not be examined because its performance was improved from 373.75% in approach 1 to 15.52% in approach 3. Similarly, datasets #6 and #7 will not be examined because their MSE percentage differences are just over 20%, which can be considered acceptable. Thus, the datasets to be examined include only datasets #6 and #15.

In some of the cases, the PWL-ANN models even outperformed the ANN models in terms of accuracies: in dataset #14, the PWL-ANN models give higher R2’s than the ANN model. As pointed out by Zhou (2004), the criteria of accuracy and fidelity can be contradictory. If the assumption is that the underlying ANN model gives good accuracies, then if the proposed rule extraction algorithm has a high fidelity to the ANN model, the rule extraction algorithm will also demonstrate good accuracy. This will fulfill both of the objectives on fidelity and accuracy. However, if there is a dataset for which the underlying ANN model does not predict well, then the rule extraction algorithm can only accomplish one of the two objectives: either it models the ANN model very well, such that the algorithm also gives poor prediction, or it generates a set of rules that gives good accuracy; and the result of data #14 demonstrates this contradiction. Since our primary evaluation criterion is fidelity, it is not expected that the PWL-ANN model should outperform the ANN model. Therefore, the PWL-ANN modeling result of dataset #14 is considered not satisfactory.

Two Hypotheses to Explain Poor Performance of the PWL-ANN Algorithm

*   Hypothesis 1: If the PWL Approximation of All Nodes are Highly Accurate (with R² > 0.99), then the Fidelity of the PWL-ANN Model Should be High.

This hypothesis suggests a causal relationship between the accuracy of the PWL approximation as indicated by the R2 and MSE values and the fidelity of the PWL-ANN mode to the original ANN model. Tables 6 and Table 7 illustrate this relationship for datasets #6 and #15. The two tables show the values of MSE and R2 of each node given by the PWL equations in the three approaches for datasets #6 and #15, respectively. It is assumed that if the PWL approximation is highly accurate as indicated by a R2 value of greater than 0.99, then the PWL-ANN model generated by the algorithm will demonstrate high fidelity to the original ANN, and this will be indicated by a low percentage difference value. This hypothesis was supported by dataset #6 but not by dataset #15. By analyzing the R2 values in Table 6, it can be seen that some of the nodes in dataset #6 have an R2 of less than 0.99 (the values are indicated in italics). In this case, the PWL-ANN models demonstrate poor fidelity to the original ANN models. By contrast, in Table 7, approaches 2 and 3 both gave R2 values that are greater than 0.99 for all the nodes in dataset #15, and yet the MSE percentage differences are still above 150%. This shows that high fidelity of the PWL-ANN model to the original ANN model cannot be guaranteed even when each individual node has been accurately approximated.

*   Hypothesis 2: Insufficiency of the Three-Piece Linear Equation Approximation.

Since it has been established from the analysis for hypothesis 1 that accurate approximation of each individual node of the original ANN model cannot guarantee good fidelity of the PWL-ANN model to the original ANN model, the analysis now turns to investigate more specific values within the nodes. The second hypothesis assumes that the poor performance of the PWL-ANN algorithm is due to insufficiency of the three-piece linear equation in approximating the curve in the sigmoid functions. In other words, while some of the data values that fall on the curve of the sigmoid functions in some of the hidden nodes have significant influences on the overall performance of the PWL-ANN, these points on the curve are not adequately modelled. As a consequence, the PWL-ANN model shows poor fidelity to the original ANN model. It is important to note that this hypothesis does not assume that omission of all the points that lie in the curves of all the hidden nodes cause the poor fidelity to the original ANN model. Rather, the omission of some combination of points in some nodes is the culprit. If this hypothesis is true, a more fine-grained PWL approximation, such as a five-piece linear approximation, on the appropriate hidden nodes would improve performance of the algorithm.

To test the hypothesis on the insufficiency of the three-piece linear equations, the data points that lie in the curve of the hidden nodes are removed one at a time and these subsets of data are used to generate new sets of 3-piece linear equations for the PWL-ANN models. The data points are eliminated one hidden node at a time so as to reveal which sets of data points have positive effects on the MSE of the PWL-ANN model. Since application of the PWL-ANN algorithm to dataset #6 demonstrated poor performance, this elimination process was applied to dataset #6. The results are shown in Table 8, whose left column indicates the modelled dataset, and the right column indicates the MSE values given by the subsets. The first row of Table 8 shows the MSE values derived from applying the PWL-ANN algorithm to the original dataset using Approach 3. Subset 1 refers to the dataset that has the data points lying on the curve of the first hidden node removed and Subset 2 refers to the data points lying on the curve of the second node removed and so on.

The result from this analysis suggests hypothesis 2 is valid. It shows that the accuracy and fidelity of the PWL-ANN model can be improved by better approximating the sigmoid function. Hence, future work involves increasing the “pieces” in the piece-wise linear equation from 3-piece to 5-piece, so as to improve the approximation of the curves in the hidden nodes.

DISCUSSION

The analysis results suggested that the accuracy of the PWL-ANN model can be improved by increasing the number of pieces, or breakpoints (BPs) in the piece-wise linear equations. In fact, Setiono et al. (2002) suggested a 5-piece approximation algorithm in their work and their results showed that the 5-piece approximation outperformed the 3-piece approximation. Some weaknesses in their work include: their application dataset has less than 700 data points and the complexity of the 5-piece linear application algorithm was not considered. In fact, a 5-piece linear approximation requires significantly more computation time, and this is especially true for industrial datasets, e.g. the CO2 capture plant datasets in our study have over 10,000 data points. A promising step forward in this research is to extend the brute-force search algorithm explained in Section 3 to locate more break points. Instead of locating only one breakpoint for a 3-piece approximation because of symmetry of the sigmoid function, a 5-piece linear approximation will require locating more than one breakpoint. It will also be necessary to examine and consider the computing time required to process a 3-piece (1 breakpoint) and a 5-piece (2 breakpoints) approximation on different sizes of datasets.

While increasing the number of breakpoints can improve accuracy of the PWL-ANN model, this approach has the possible trade off of increasing complexity of the overall system. By increasing the number of pieces or linear equations at each node, the possible combinations of equations also increase significantly. With a 3-piece approximation of each hidden node, the number of possible combinations of equations is 3j, with j being the number of hidden nodes. If all hidden nodes are approximated with 5-pieces, the number of possible combinations of equations will become 5j. This trade-off between the number of pieces and complexity of the system needs to be considered. Therefore, the number of pieces within the piecewise equation per node should be determined based on consideration of both system complexity and desired accuracy of the PWL-ANN model.

CONCLUSION

In this study, we presented an artificial neural network rule extraction algorithm based on a 3-piece linear approximation of the hidden neuron activation function, which is assumed to be a sigmoid function. By replacing the activation functions with the PWL equations, rules in the form of linear equations that relate the inputs and outputs of a given dataset can be generated. Three approaches for solving the PWL approximations have been presented and all three approaches were tested on 19 datasets. The results show that the best performance is given when the full range of data values is included and when a finer grained approximation is used. The algorithm gives satisfactory fidelity on sixteen out of the nineteen tested datasets. An analysis of the values of R2 given by the PWL approximation on the hidden neurons and the overall output shows that in addition to the precision of the approximation of each individual node, other factors also play a role in determining fidelity of the PWL-ANN algorithm. Further investigation is required to determine what those factors may be.

Some directions for future work include the following:

*   1\. An analysis of the number of breakpoints for the piece-wise linear equations so that the number of breakpoints required for a given node can be adjusted to achieve the desired accuracy; and
*   2\. A sensitivity analysis on the weights of each hidden node so as to investigate whether there is any correlation between the hidden weights and the overall performance of the PWL algorithm.

This research was previously published in the International Journal of Cognitive Informatics and Natural Intelligence (IJCINI), 11(2); edited by Kangshun Li, pages 57-73, copyright year 2017 by IGI Publishing (an imprint of IGI Global).

# Chapter 92

Role-Playing Together in a Participatory Simulation

*   Sharona T. Levy  
    University of Haifa, Israel

ABSTRACT

The topic of learning through collaborative role-playing in computer-based participatory simulations of complex systems in STEM is presented. Participatory simulations are networked classroom activities aimed at learning about complex systems. In the process of learning, students query its underlying structure and explore its spatial, temporal and mathematical patterns in various conditions. The importance of understanding complex systems is highlighted, driving the main question in this chapter: How can we design learning experiences that support students’ deep learning of emergent systems? The motivations behind using participatory simulations and their various designs are described as well as some of the more central learning research, cumulating with five studies into designs for such activities in science. Based on this research, eight design principles are introduced and future research directions are proposed.

INTRODUCTION

Participatory simulations (hence, partSims) are networked classroom activities that immerse students in collaborative role-playing in a social experiment into complex systems. As a design for learning, students experience the system as its entities, orchestrators and explorers. They are each an individual agentic entity acting and interacting locally. The class itself is the investigated system made up of many such entities, where students orchestrate experiments. Through these experiments, they explore emergent processes. The unique aspects of learning with such a design lies in traversing between these three perspectives, which provides for a more robust conceptual understanding of the system. Several simulations of this type have been developed over the years, targeting the learning of systems in STEM and social systems, approaching a wide range of topics: epidemics, evolution, bee-hives, global warming, structure of matter, traffic, topics in probability and statistics, functions, geometry, sharing resources, economic markets and more. One of the goals of this chapter is to pull out a set of design principles for such simulations, both out of previous research and out of a series of studies conducted by the author and her students. Such an abstraction of a variety of designs could light the way to further design, use in schools, pedagogical supports and research into this unique learning environment.

Complex systems are prevalent in our world, spanning several orders of magnitude. Students learn about systems in science whose micro-level entities range from sub-atomic particles, electrons, molecules, cells, individual organisms in an ecosystem, all the way up to the stars and planets that comprise our universe. Reasoning about such systems has become an essential part of STEM education (Chen & Stroup, 1993) and recently, of computational literacy (Weintrop et al., 2016). Providing students with access to learning about systems has become of vital concern.

This chapter presents participatory simulations, a design for learning about complex systems that has students role-play individual elements within a system, becoming an integral part of it. In the process, they strategize and conduct experiments, analyze and reflect upon their results. The teacher’s role is central in designing the activity, connecting it with other learning taking place, eliciting students’ descriptions of experiences and their ideas, supporting conversations that involve local and global perspectives of the simulation that took place, and helping students concretize experiments they would like to conduct. This design can be viewed as an extension of computer models that represent dynamic multiple entities (ABMs, or agent-based models), where some of the “computation” is shifted from the computer to people. For example, in the Dancing with Molecules partSim people role-play gas molecules (Levy et al., 2015). They determine which way and when to move. However, their speed is determined by the computer simulation based upon energy considerations. In the TrafficJams partSim (Figure 1), students drive cars (right hand interface) and decide whether to shift lanes or slow down (Levy, Rotem & Linyevsky, 2015). However, the computer simulation sets up the roads which constrain the motion and provides collective information, such as the average speed (left hand interface). For example, in the average speed plot, one can see the speed first oscillate and then take a downward dip as a traffic jam forms. On the students’ computer, they can see the cars around them but not beyond. They can speed up or down and shift lanes, limited by the cars up ahead and the road itself. As a group, they can observe the teacher’s computer that provides the full view of the road from a birds’-eye view, and notice how the traffic jams – high density of cars – gradually spread through the system. They can design experiments aimed at smoothing the traffic flow or speeding it up, using a variety of strategies, such as limiting the speed or the distance between cars. This distribution of computation between a group of people and the simulation provides for enough constraints from the computer so that the conceptual structure of relationships is retained and can be explored and discovered through people’s actions and collaborations.

Complex systems are made up of many entities that interact among themselves. The individual actions and local interactions among these entities emerge into global behaviors (Bar-Yam, 2003; Vicsek, 2002). Global patterns are described in ways that are distinct from those used to describe the individuals. Understanding systems presents a challenge for learners as it requires a host of coordinations: between local and global perspectives, among individual elements, between static and dynamic qualities of the system. In fact, one of the more demanding coordinations involves noticing, integrating and patterning parallel processes related to several entities as they act and interact in a shared landscape. Assisting people in learning to think in parallel ways about a collection of interacting objects clearly needs a distinct set of supports.

Simulations of epidemics have been the drosophila fly¹ of research into partSims conducted with several platforms, as will be described in the next section (Colella, 2000; Klopfer, Yoon & Perry, 2005; Stroup & Wilensky, 2014; Neulight, Kafai, Kao, Foley, & Galas, 2007). When modeling the spread of disease in a population, people are represented as micro-level individual entities. These people move about, some cross longer distances, some stay closer to home; a few move more rapidly, most are more sedate; some are friendlier than others and tend to congregate. If an individual contracts a contagious disease, their subsequent meetings with people might infect them in turn. This micro-level account of the system includes descriptors such as location, speed, meetings and the local interaction of passing on a disease. Descriptions of the whole population over time and space might include the number of sick people and the rates at which the disease spreads or how it moves between specific locations. Containing the disease may be the goal of the group investigation. Investigating how individual behaviors impact whether or not the disease is contained, helps relate the micro- and macro-levels, is one of the main goals in learning about complex systems. Noticing such relations provides clues and cues into capturing the emergent processes mobilizing and stabilizing the system.

In this chapter, research and several studies and designs of partSims are described. The motivating question in the chapter is: “How can we design learning experiences that support students’ deep learning of emergent systems?”

BACKGROUND

Emergence is one of the fascinating and challenging ideas in reasoning about systems: how do many distributed simple interactions produce persistent and stable global patterns? Several designs for learning address this issue: constructing, exploring and participating in models. In constructing computer models people represent a system’s entities and their properties. They construct the model with code or code-blocks, using simple actions (such as move, turn) and interactions (such as change direction upon collision) at the micro-level (e.g. Papert, 1983; Wilkerson-Jerde, Gravel & Macrander, 2015; Guo et al., 2016) to describe these entities’ behaviors. Upon running the model, they view the emergent behaviors in a display that includes other representations, such as graphs and monitors. They can then change the model and explore it, informally or formally constructing a space of behaviors, the system’s landscape. A second design involves exploring a given model (e.g. Pallant & Tinker, 2004; de Jong & van Joolingen, 1998; Stieff, 2011). This form is most popular in schools, as there are no coding requirements. Most models display a visualization of the computer simulation and opportunities to manipulate global variables. Students change the variables, run the model, observe it and any other associated representations, such as monitors and graphs. PartSims offer a third way of accessing the relationship between local and global patterns by participating in a social simulation. In partSims, people are role-play entities in a system on a social platform. The interactions between participants’ actions and other objects in the simulation within the constraints built into the simulation result in the system’s overall behavior. These experiences – as individuals, and as a collective - become an object of question, manipulation and discussion, transforming the classroom itself into the explored system. In this chapter, partSims are described and several studies into their instantiation are presented.

PartSims have been implemented with a variety of platforms, different from each other in whether they are portable, have a public display of the overall system, whether there is a central computational simulation, and whether or not running the simulation is part of additional activities. Three kinds of platforms are described: portable clients, computer-based clients and simulations set within a MUVE (multi user virtual environment).

Portable Clients. One early platform involved electronic badges (Borovoy, McDonald, Marin & Resnick, 1996). People wore the badges on their clothes while walking around a room in a conference. When two people met, their badges communicated the number of questions out of five they both answered the same. People looked at each other’s badges and could use this information to start conversations. While it is certainly a game and fun ice-breaker, this is also a simulation of how using simple information about the relationship between people could create stronger and weaker alliances, clusters, groups and networks. The first version held information only locally between individuals. Understanding the process for the whole group over time involved conversations and analytical activities of representing information to portray the group’s evolution. In a later version, Borovoy et al. (1998) extended the use of these electronic badges by including global information. Displays of “Community Mirrors” provided visualizations of the community dynamics. In one version, they simulated the passing of memes via such tags. People could copy memes they liked from other people’s badges or recommend a particular meme to someone they met. As a group, this simulated the replication and obliteration of ideas in a society, so that some ideas become anchored and clustered, while others become extinct. These badges were later used to simulate epidemics and other complex phenomena and were named Thinking Tags, small wearable microprocessor-driven tags (Colella, 2000). Klopfer, Yoon and Perry (2005) further extended this work using handheld computers instead of badges, so that more intricate information could be used and displayed on the individual hardware. In their use of the handheld computers, the display turned inwards to the students, different from the badges that showed information about the person outwardly, to other people. They developed a broad range of simulations – predator-prey systems, games of economics, genetics, viruses and more.

Computer-based clients were developed by Wilensky and Stroup (1999) in their creation of HubNet, a component of NetLogo (Wilensky, 1999) which supports the creation of partSims. Considering the question of portability, they formed two versions of HubNet. One involved using graphical calculators, a portable client. The second version used computers as the clients in the system. This system has been used to create a broad range of simulations such as controlling traffic lights in a grid of driving cars and gas particles (Wilensky & Stroup, 2002; Stroup & Wilensky, 2014). It is also used in the studies described hence.

Simulations set within a MUVE. Neulight, Kafai, Kao, Foley & Galas (2006) present a third way of conducting partSims. Their investigation of the spread of disease took place in WhyVille, which is a MUVE (multi user virtual environment) that engages many students with various kinds of activities. The disease simulation is just a part of a range of events and topics participants could engage with. The larger scale of the simulation and its more dispersed focus present a form of learning through partSims that is more akin to everyday life.

Classroom research into learning with partSims is quite sparse. Colella (2000) explored how high-school biology students used Thinking Tags to learn about the spread of disease. During three weeks, the students conducted several investigations. These investigations began with the challenge of meeting as many people as possible without getting sick. There were no public displays in this study, and students accessed global data only at critical points to confirm their hypotheses. Several aspects of the simulation were explored: students’ engagement as seen in their excitement and sense of truly experiencing the simulation; the process that took place as the students stepped back to figure out confusing situations; the students’ design of several experiments varying their behaviors to find out about the dynamics of the system; the inclusive nature of these activities as the students were all interdependent in conducting their experiments; and how experimental design of investigations into the structure of the system happened only in the later simulations. Ares, Stroup & Schademan (2009) analyzed high-school students’ discussions and learning of mathematics by having them each control an elevator among a series of elevators in a HubNet simulation. During the lesson, students were highly active both in participating in the activity and in contributions to the class conversation. These discussions primarily involved observing and describing the simulation, but also predicting, asking for clarification and explaining. The teacher’s role was creating very open invitations: invitations to predict, but also to elaborate and explain. Klopfer, Yoon & Perry (2005) explored teachers’ perceptions of partSims and found that they saw affordances regarding motivation, engagement and self-directed learning. Stroup & Wilensky (2014) describe sixth-grade and high-school students’ reasoning about epidemics and traffic flow in the context of partSims. They find complementarity between two forms of reasoning: the agent-based account of the system, that begins with individuals and builds up; and the aggregate collective account that is framed in terms of populations, rates and flows.

These studies also present a set of design principles for partSims. Some of the design principles suggested by Colella (2000) include a high level of flexibility and iterativity to accommodate many kinds of experiments that include varying the participants’ behavior patterns, and including a clear goal for the first activity. In using Thinking Tags, students wore the badges on their clothes so that the technology was kept unobtrusive to support communication among the students, a design principle implemented in some of the platforms but not others, simple displays for the individual student client, coherent regularities in the simulation that can be gradually uncovered through their investigation, make the focus phenomenon happen in the inter-personal space, facilitate similar but non-identical experiences for participants so that comparing them helps capture distributions of behaviors and associations between conditions and related results, and enabling students’ invention of exploration strategies. In describing the design of the Elevators activity, Ares et al. (2009) stress the importance of having multiple solutions to problems posed to the students; and the combination of private spaces on the students’ displays and public displays for group deliberations. Articulating these design principles is important to further develop, test and question this learning design. The next section offers additional principles to help build up an understanding of the kinds of learning that can take place.

RESEARCH INTO LEARNING WITH PARTICPATORY SIMULATIONS

This chapter presents several studies into social partSims: a collaboration among a group of people and a computer simulation in enacting the behaviors of a system. In our lab, we have developed several partSims, geared at learning systemic phenomena. These are presented as five short studies. These studies are described as designs and principles of the learning environment and as experimental results regarding learning and processes. Threaded throughout the studies is an accumulating set of design principles guiding the creation of each environments as well as the designs themselves. Design principles that have been described in previous research are not included. Each study also describes the process of learning and its outcomes. The topics learned include chemistry (global warming, phases of matter), traffic flow and epidemics. The audiences are diverse, ranging from elementary, middle-school to high-school among regular and special education students. In fact, one intention of this presentation is to show the diversity of users and uses for this learning design.

Dancing With Molecules to Learning About Global Warming

Design principles:

*   1\. Everyday experiences as a resource for students’ actions.
*   2\. Riding then Driving inanimate objects.
*   3\. Scaffolding models for simple component processes.

The simulation “Dancing with Particles” was developed in response to a middle-school science teacher’s enduring difficulties in teaching about global warming (Levy et al., 2011; 2015). Upon surveying existing teaching materials, several drawbacks were detected. Some materials were verbal and visual-spatial but not dynamic, so that the many different processes taking place at the same time are difficult to relate (Groves & Pugh, 1999). In some model-based learning materials, the basic entities in the system are moving packets of energy, which are a less familiar and non-intuitive, preventing learning of the system through the micro-level entities’ behaviors (NetLogo Climate Change model, Tinker & Wilensky, 2007; Varma & Linn, 2012).

We wanted to approach the topic by using everyday experiences as a resource for students’ actions, the first design principle. We selected the experience of moving through world at different speeds, as speed is the individual molecule’s “contribution” to the gas temperature. This led us to re-frame global warming in terms of air molecules’ speed. Since speed and energy are interchangeable for heat conduction, the main mechanism by which atmospheric air is heated, this seemed a fair exchange².

However, even after this transformation, we could not avoid the many parallel processes taking place in global warming, one of the main challenges in forming a coherent explanation of the phenomenon. Our solution was to design a partSim that would have students be a molecule in the system. For a single molecule, there is only one process happening at a given time. The molecule moves in a straight line unless other forces act on it, it can change direction and speed upon collision and gravity pulls the molecule towards earth. If it is an emission gas molecule, such as carbon dioxide, then upon absorbing infrared radiation it can transform the absorbed radiation into another molecule’s speed by colliding with it.

Our initial conjecture was that starting with a single entity and experiencing its history through the different transformations would be easier to follow and provide for deeper learning of how global warming transpires. Participants would be able to note changes and what led to these changes. Relating these causes and effects would support a more mechanistic understanding. By placing several students-as-molecules together, they could then broaden their scope to the space of the class and the simulation. By comparing their experiences within the shared space, they could see the similarities in the underlying rules and notice the distribution of properties such as speed. This could enable students to gradually understand and integrate both the sequence for a single molecule with the parallel processes taking place for many molecules.

| Figure 2. Dancing with molecules simulation |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch092.f02](i/ch092.f02.png) |
| --- |

The Dancing with Molecules simulation was designed so that participants can control their molecule’s direction of motion, but not their speed (Figure 2). They decide which way to turn and when to move forward. However, their speed is determined by the simulation code based on energy and momentum conversation. Gravity is automatically added as a bit of extra downwards motion at each time segment. Molecules that reach the top of the screen disappear. Molecules that hit the ground bounce like a basketball.

What is important is that the main outcome of global warming – increasing temperatures – is also the main change experienced by the students at the micro-level. They experience speed as their own increased or decreased motion across the screen: for each forward mouse tap, they advance further (fast) or closer (slow). This form of representing speed is quite common in gaming environments. As a group, some are faster and some are slower at a given time; however, on average, they all become faster when the temperatures rise. After the initial experiences of moving as molecules in the system, they could also follow the collective changes on the temperature plot. Finally, they also experienced how emission gases (such as carbon dioxide) transform radiation into increased molecular speed. This would be a crucial step in understanding the paradox of how such a small proportion of emission gases could impact the whole atmosphere, making all of earth’s gaseous molecules faster.

Two rounds of classroom studies were enacted. The first round (Almog, 2011) was with 18 middle-school students. The second round (Zoubi, 2015) took place with 14 high-school students, majoring in science. In both cases, the learning sequence was accompanied by paper or web-based worksheets and involved both class-wide and individual learning. The unit began with a motivating scenario describing the impact of global warming on polar bears, followed by a general presentation of global warming. When shifting to the simulation, one of the central concerns was that the students would develop a perception of molecules as living decision-making entities. Here, the second design principle – Ride then Drive inanimate objects – comes into play. Build-up introductory activities had students “ride” the molecules before they could actually “drive” them, to ensure they begin with a scientific understanding of molecular motion. The unit ended with a teacher-led integration and consolidation of the topic.

In the earlier round of research, middle-school students were challenged with saving all living creatures in the world (Almog, 2011). They played nitrogen molecules in the atmosphere, first riding then driving their molecule. A turtle representing all living things could be either healthy, sick or dead depending on the temperature. The temperature was displayed in a plot. They could do this by coordinating their own motion and behavior as nitrogen molecules, such as running away from carbon-dioxide molecules. They could also adjust general features in the model, such as radiation flux, the amounts of different substances in the air, adding and removing factories.

In practice the activity was quite confusing. The first activities involved getting used to being a nitrogen molecule and finding themselves in their personal and class view. Only later did they control their motion and follow the temperature plot. In the class discussion, they suggested a few strategies that could control the temperature. These ideas included figuring out the impact of emission gases by adding a factory and adding water to the simulated world. The designs were written up on the class display, discussed and voted upon. After clarifying what it meant to run a particular strategy as an individual, they tried some of these out. However, the goal of the activity was not clear. Some of the processes taking place were not even noticed. At the end, we found that they had secretly used a background chat tool, mainly in banter and jest. However, interspersed among these jokes, they also asked each other advice as to what they should be doing in the simulation and what some of the representations meant.

Questionnaires used to assess their understanding of global warming showed no significant differences with a pair t-test as the class means regressed (!) from pretest to posttest: 25 (10) to 19 (11). A typical answer in the posttest shows a superficial understanding that did not include any mechanistic information: Global warming is a process by which all of the world warms up by a few degrees. Because of the increasing amounts of emission gases. Less sun rays can leave the atmosphere. The interviews and enactment were analyzed in depth to find the disconnections in reasoning about the system, which processes were not mentioned or were not tied into the whole explanation. Based on these results, the simulation was re-designed.

Several modifications were made. One involves the third design principle: including scaffolding models for simple component processes. Activities were designed to clarify some of the component processes and relationships, such as the impact of gravity on molecules’ motion, and the transfer of energy upon collision. Some of these activities took place outside of the partSim, using simple models. Planting trees was added to the simulation to broaden the scope of solution strategies for counteracting the effect of emission gases. The questionnaires were also re-designed to test for each of the component processes and concepts, to clarify which concepts were learned and which weren’t and how they were integrated into an explanation of global warming.

Research with high-school students in the second round (Zoubi, 2015) showed a rise in questionnaire scores from 46 (20) to 86 (17), with a paired t of 6.477 (p<0.01). They demonstrated a deeper understanding in the interviews and questionnaires regarding the components of gravity, solar radiation, absorption of radiation by earth, molecule speed and collisions, temperature. They could also combine these components into a mechanistic explanation of global warming, e.g. The small amount of CO2 influences global warming by absorbing heat radiation and transferring this energy to other molecules through collisions, which raises the molecules’ speed, which is expressed as a rise in temperature. Several runs of the simulation were conducted, experimenting with the simulation, such as changing gravity. During the simulation students called out to each other, e.g. Come on… Hurry up! Class discussions of the simulation were marked by gestures and body motion, that seemed to emulate either the molecules, such as moving their arms to mimic the shape of the carbon-dioxide molecule before and after absorbing radiation; or, a view of an individual molecule, for example tracing the parabolic path of the molecules.

The following discussion of whether the molecules’ speed changes shows the generative role of the social arena as the students’ parallel experiences are compared:

*   S1: Changes, changes… \[S1’s molecule’s speed\]
*   S2: For me, it’s constant!
*   S3: For me, it changed twice!
*   S4: Also for me, it’s constant.
*   S2: You’re right! It does change.
*   S5: It doesn’t collide (laughter).
*   S6: That means that each molecule has its own motion!
*   S7: Here! Look, this time it collided.

In comparing experiences of their molecule’s speed, some students claim it doesn’t change, while others declare it changes. Notice how several students participate in the discussion, a noted feature of partSims. They share their varied personal experiences of speed. This helps S2 shift in her perception of her own experience: she now notices her own speed change. Immediately following this shift, an explanatory idea about collisions is introduced. S6 then comes up with a global concept of diversity or distribution of the molecules’ histories “each molecule has its own motion”. This helps S7 shift the talk about speed from a general perspective to a moment-by-moment perspective, noticing a collision, an event crucial to speed change. To summarize, in this short exchange we can see how having students be air molecules together in the Dancing with Molecules simulation results in animated discussion ranging from micro-level molecular descriptions to macro-level distributions and back to a more mechanistic micro-level description.

Students gradually coordinated their personal experiences as a molecule to an integrated view of the system. In order to follow this process of coordination, the students’ utterances during several simulation runs were coded as (a) being about their personal molecule alone, e.g. My molecule is moving slowly or Here, I’m starting to move; as (b) focusing on their own molecule but also noticing its local surroundings, e.g. I’m moving faster than you! or Don’t collide into me”; or as (c) taking a global view of the system Because there are more collisions between the molecules, they change their speed accordingly, which influences the average temperature. Figure 3 shows how these perspectives evolved during nine runs of the simulation. Earlier, an individual personal view of the system was dominant. Gradually a local-interactive view became more apparent (runs 2-5). Once perception of the local surroundings of the molecule was reached (run 5), it was then integrated with a global view as well so that in the next (run 6) and final (run 9) run we see all three perspectives used in the class conversations. The gradual shift from an individual to a local view, and only later to include a global view has been previously demonstrated by Stroup and Wilensky (2002).

| Figure 3. Students’ views of the system along successive simulation runs |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch092.f03](i/ch092.f03.png) |
| --- |

One aspect of running such simulations in a classroom involves noise. These activities captivate most students and involve intrigues and excited exchanges. While the classroom will not be silent, it will be engaged. In measuring the level of noise in the class during the nine runs, we could see an increase between the first half and the second half of the activities. Rather than petering out, the activity continues to engage them throughout, as seen previously by Colella (2000), Ares et al. (2009) and Klopfer et al. (2005). The conclusion of analyzing the videos for on-task versus off-task noise-generating activities for each student (Figure 4) we can see a strong reduction in off-task activities and the activities progress.

| Figure 4. Level of noise in class during activities with the participatory simulation, on-task and off-task activities |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch092.f04](i/ch092.f04.png) |
| --- |

To conclude this section, we have seen students’ engagement sustain during the activity, as their local and global perspectives developed, changed and coordinated. We have also seen the modifications needed to make the simulation accessible to learning that included, broadening the range of activities, creating clear goals and supporting learning of the separate processes when the studied phenomenon involves several combined processes.

MeParticle WeMatter: Learning About the Structure of Matter and Phase Change

Design principles:

*   1\. Seemingly off-task talk during the simulation reflects processing and learning in a convivial way.
*   2\. Design for local micro-level understanding in the initial partSim runs.

After successfully simulating a gas in Dancing with Molecules, the next step was simulating a liquid and its transitions to the gaseous phase. Including inter-particulate forces was the ensuing challenge. As others before us, we were inspired by the Nobel-prize physicist Richard Feynman’s summary of the most basic principles of scientific knowledge: If, in some cataclysm, all scientific knowledge were to be destroyed, and only one sentence passed on to the next generation of creatures, what statement would contain the most information in the fewest words? I believe it is the atomic hypothesis (or atomic fact, or whatever you wish to call it) that all things are made of atoms — little particles that move around in perpetual motion, attracting each other when they are a little distance apart, but repelling upon being squeezed into one another. In that one sentence you will see an enormous amount of information about the world, if just a little imagination and thinking are applied. (Feynman, 1964). We wanted to transform this minimal set of assumptions –particles’ perpetual motion and inter-particulate repulsions and attractions - into students’ experiences, forming a basis for understanding a variety of chemical and physical phenomena (Langebeheim & Levy, 2015; 2016).

Let’s imagine water in a glass as many particles moving about and then focus on two neighboring particles. When these two particles come close together, pulls attract them together and pushes keep them apart. When the pushes and pulls are balanced, we have reached equilibrium. However, this equilibrium is dynamic. When the water is hotter, this means the particles can move faster and “jiggle” about more frequently. We could have the students move closer and farther away from each other, once again constrained by energy conservation. However, here’s the big leap - let us apply this to many particles at once. Each particle can “feel” a number of neighbors, attract and repel with each – the sum of these forces operating right back at the particle. The MeParticle WeMatter partSim (Levy, Langbeheim et al., 2014) that was designed for learning about phases of matter, using a complex systems approach. As in the Dancing with Molecules partSim, the students first ride the molecules and then drive them. They determine their direction of motion and when it takes place. Lennard-Jones forces between the closer particles in the fluid are computed and these in turn, determine the particle’s speed (Verlet 1967).

Imagine you were the brown particle (Figure 5) and decided to approach a gang of green particles. You might tread carefully. As you come closer, you are “captured” by sticky forces pulling you towards two particles. Because one particle is closer than the other, its force is also stronger. You can see this as thicker or thinner bubble gum connecting the particles. If you try to detach yourself, this may not be so easy; although with the right angle, you might pull apart one of the bubble gum threads, probably the one with the weaker force.

You then dive into the gang of moving green particles. You are gradually surrounded by more and more neighbors and the web of forces gets stickier to maneuver. When you move around, you can see that some particles detach from your back, those in the middle keep you stable and you attach to new particles further up. You are always keeping some of your webby forces, detaching from some in the back, attaching to some in the front.

These experiences provide students with a particle’s perspective on what it means to be a liquid or a gas, or what it means to turn from a gas particle to a liquid particle. Positioning students as one-particle-among-many focuses them on the interactions the particle undergoes. Moreover, as action-based perception helps them attend to the local environment, they may notice the formation and dissipation of flexible “clumps” of particles. From a global perspective, the social aspect of the activity of conducting an experiment together may encourage students to notice larger emergent patterns in the system, such as clustering, temporary ordering within a cluster or evaporation mechanisms.

| Figure 5. MeParticle WeMatter participatory simulation |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-0414-7.ch092.f05](i/ch092.f05.png) |
| --- |

Research into learning vaporization was conducted with two classes of ninth-grade students where one class participated in the MeParticle WeMatter simulation while the second class only observed the simulation as it was projected on a screen (Langhebeheim & Levy, 2015). Both classes completed pre- and post-test questionnaires. Comparison of their questionnaire results shows that the participatory group explained heat conduction significantly (p<0.05) better than the observing group in the post-test. For example, in the post-test responses to the question: “Explain how the hot plate causes the fluid’s temperature to increase”, the participatory group introduced more ideas related to heat conduction as due to energetic interactions between particles and intensified motion of the particles in the liquid when the temperature goes up. At the same time, in the observers group we found a greater increase in students’ correct drawings of the global configuration of particles during phase transition from liquid to gas. Figure 6 shows two responses when students are asked to draw the state of the system during phase change. The frequency of correct responses to both heat conduction mechanism and phase transition global configuration questions is shown in Figure 7. We can see that in the question requiring a micro-level understanding of how heat is conducted, observers did not change their responses from pre- to posttest, while the participatory group increased by about 30%. For the question requiring a global view of system, both groups increased in their perception of phase change; however, the observers’ increase was much greater (43% versus 25%).

Among the students participating in the simulation, we see a focus on individual particles. During the simulation run, personal identities and interactions are in the limelight:

*   Student 1: … I am “Safed cheese” \[they could label their particles\]
*   Other Students: Booom! We got one out. Yeah!

This exchange demonstrates the fourth design principle: Seemingly off-task talk during the simulation reflects processing and learning in a convivial way. Similarly, for the students who observed the simulation the focus is on the complete aggregation of particles, as they argue what its shape is like:

*   Student 1: It looks like a boat, a man lying in a boat …
*   Student 2: No, it is a dead bird! …. Ahh…it IS a boat... but really small.
*   Student 3: But you aren’t paying attention to the motion of the particles!
*   Student 2: No, it is actually a plate
*   Student 1: It’s a boat, like in Venice

In this brief case study, we can see that one of the main advantages to using partSims is in noticing interactions and building up a mechanistic explanation of change in the system and does not necessarily support a perception of global patterns. However, this probably results from the brevity of the study. In lengthier interventions (Colella, 2000; Stroup & Wilensky, 2014) and in the study into students’ learning about global warming, it was found that students gradually decentered from the individual view to include and coordinate it with the global view. This demonstrates the fifth design principle: Design for local micro-level understanding in the initial partSim runs.

Keep Me Healthy!

Design principles:

*   1\. Adaptation with respect to population and current goals.
*   2\. Reruns for reflection.

The study engages students with moderate cognitive-impairment in learning about the spread of contagious diseases and applying this learning to improving their own health. Among cognitively impaired individuals, there is a much higher rate of contagion, resulting mainly from behaviors such as using someone else’s cutlery (Krahn, Hammond & Turner, 2006). We have replicated the study in three schools in the north of Israel and found a three-fold increase in morbidity with respect to other students in the same school (Okal, 2015). Normally, these students are taught about health-preserving behaviors via instructions with no explanations.

The goal of the design was to support the students in creating a rich explanatory model of disease transmission they could adapt to with health-preserving behaviors. The overall design of the learning unit is based upon a well-established constructivist framework for special education students, The Circle of Internalization Method (Reiter, 2003)³ that includes students’ successive problem-solving and discussions to establish explanatory knowledge. We adapted the Disease epidemic partSim (Wilensky & Stroup, 1999), demonstrating the seventh principle: Adaptation with respect to population and current goals. Students move their avatars in a common space. An individual is infected and can further infect nearby individuals upon contact. Adaptations included (Figure 8): having movies created of each run, so they could be viewed repeatedly and discussed in detail; creating spaces where the sick individuals could go rest or receive care so they could simulate health-seeking in real-life situations; replacing text by icons; personalization of the avatars by using human figures colored with an individually-meaningful color; increasing the size of the widgets and reducing their number (Levy & Okal, 2015). The partSim was used several times along a sequence of nine activities and was a central focus of the unit. The activities were grounded in students’ story-telling stories of their own experiences being ill and included alternating individual work and group problem-solving and reflective activities. Reflective discussions related to the simulation runs, using their movies to re-enact the experience, demonstrated the eighth principle: Reruns for reflection. Each lesson included at least three such group activities, discussing the experiences.

Four 9-11 years-old students (two males, two females) with moderate cognitive-impairment and no other impairments participated in the study (Okal, 2015). Two additional students participated in the learning activities, but were not part of the data collection. A pre- and posttest questionnaire regarding perceived health locus of control (Wallston, 2007) was adapted and reviewed by experts to ensure suitability. Another pre- and posttest engaged the students as a group in a physical simulation of contagion. Activities with the simulation were videotaped at each computer. Analysis of students’ actions in the simulations and their comparison provided a measure of health-seeking behaviors and their progression.

The pre- and posttest questionnaire did not provide us with results, as the students did not understand the questions, even with additional supports advised by an expert researcher in the field. The pre- and posttest physical simulation showed an increase in the mean number of health preserving behaviors from M1=20 (SD=2) to M2=34 (SD=4), a 66% increase. When analyzed in greater detail, the increase was due mainly (two-thirds) to self-preserving behaviors (e.g. not using another child’s towel) rather than others-preserving (e.g. staying at home when you’re sick so that you won’t pass the disease to other children).

During the activities and discussion, students grew to articulate an understanding of why specific behaviors were important to preserving their health. In comparing four consecutive runs of the simulation (Figure 9), the number of steps the students made until they got sick, until they reached the doctor and until they went home was recorded. Across time, we can see an increased “survival” rate in the simulation as seen in the rising number of steps taken before succumbing to disease, and a greater swiftness in adopting self-preserving behaviors (getting home or to a doctor).
